_about: Hebrew & Greek mode marks, by chapter, from the Translation Differences tool (jayms-tool-data). Built by scripts/build-hebrew-greek.py.

John|1.title: John 1:1
John|1.summary: The Word was God, or the Word was a god. The difference is one missing article.
John|1.plain: Say it three ways. **Sam is the doctor.** That picks out one doctor, the one we were talking about. **Sam is a doctor.** That makes Sam one of many. **Sam is doctor.** That is not English, and your ear rejects it. But it is perfectly good Greek, and it means neither of the first two. It means Sam has the nature of a doctor. English gives you the and a and nothing else. Greek has a third option, and it is the one John used.
John|1.whyThis: Because the clause is where the New Testament comes closest to a bare statement of the deity of Christ, and the entire weight of it sits on a word that is not printed. Logos gets the attention and is not in dispute. The article is in dispute, and it is the one an informed Jehovah's Witness at your door will be working from.
John|1.kjv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John|1.others: Every mainstream English version reads the Word was God. The New World Translation reads a god, and the entire argument turns on the article.
John|1.seeing: Greek has a definite article and no indefinite one. In the last clause the first God has the article, ton theon, and the second does not, theos. Word order also matters: theos stands before the verb. A Greek noun in that position without an article is normally qualitative. It is telling you what the Word is, not which individual the Word is.
John|1.why: English has to insert something. You must write the God, a god, or God, and each of those says more than the Greek did. The Greek had a way to say what something is by nature without identifying it as a particular individual, and English does not.
John|1.rule: When your versions split between God and a god, or between the truth and truth, look for whether the Greek noun has the article. Absence of the article in Greek is not the same as a in English. It usually means the writer is talking about character rather than identity.
John|1.choosing: Rendering it a god takes the missing article as indefinite. Rendering it God takes it as qualitative. The qualitative reading is the standard grammatical one and it also makes sense of the middle clause: the Word was with God, so the Word is not simply identical to the one he was with, and yet is what that one is.

John|1.title: John 1:1a, 3
John|1.summary: Was, and came to be. Two verbs one verse apart, and the whole prologue turns on the difference.
John|1.plain: **The house was there. The shed came to be there.** Both sentences put something in a yard. The first one does not tell you the house ever started. The second one tells you the shed had a beginning. English can say this if it works at it. Greek says it with two different verbs and never has to explain.
John|1.whyThis: Because the difference between existing and beginning to exist is the entire argument of the prologue, and John makes it with two ordinary verbs rather than with an adjective. It is also the pattern that makes verse 14 land, where the Word finally takes the becoming verb.
John|1.kjv: In the beginning was the Word... All things were made by him.
John|1.others: English uses was for the first and were made for the second, which hides that both are ordinary verbs of being and becoming.
John|1.seeing: Verse 1 uses en, the imperfect of eimi, to be. Verse 3 uses egeneto, the aorist of ginomai, to become or come into existence. John keeps them apart with complete discipline through the whole prologue: everything created gets ginomai, and the Word gets eimi. Verse 14 is the hinge, where the Word finally takes egeneto, became flesh.
John|1.why: English was covers both existing and starting to exist. Greek has separate verbs, so the distinction is built into the vocabulary rather than argued in a footnote.
John|1.rule: Watch which verb a writer uses for existence. If a Greek text alternates between eimi and ginomai in the same passage, the alternation is almost never accidental.
John|1.choosing: No translator disputes the parsing. The difficulty is that no English rendering can keep the two verbs visibly distinct without paraphrasing, so every version loses the pattern and study Bibles have to point at it in a note.

John|1.title: John 1:1b
John|1.summary: The Word was with God. The preposition is not the one you would expect for with.
John|1.plain: **I sat with my wife.** **I turned to my wife.** Both put two people together. Only the second one tells you which way anyone was facing. English with is a flat word. Greek had a choice here and picked the turned-toward one.
John|1.whyThis: Because most readers move straight past the preposition to the nouns on either side of it, and the preposition is where the relationship is. It is a small word doing structural work, which is the general lesson: in Greek, prepositions and articles carry weight English gives to word order.
John|1.kjv: and the Word was with God.
John|1.others: Every English version reads with. Some commentaries offer toward, or face to face with, and none of that reaches the text.
John|1.seeing: The preposition is pros with the accusative. Its ordinary sense is motion toward or orientation facing. Greek had meta and syn available for plain accompaniment, and John used neither. Pros with a person in the accusative carries a sense of being turned toward, in relationship with.
John|1.why: English with is flat. It covers standing next to someone and being in a relationship with them, and no English preposition carries orientation the way pros does.
John|1.rule: When a writer picks an unusual preposition where a plain one was available, the preposition is part of the argument. Check which one was the obvious choice and ask why it was passed over.
John|1.choosing: With is not wrong and there is no better English. The question is only how much weight the preposition will carry, and commentators divide on whether pros here is genuinely relational or simply Koine usage drifting toward the accusative.

John|1.title: John 1:1c
John|1.summary: Why call a person a Word? The Greek noun covers far more than a unit of speech, and two different backgrounds are competing for it.
John|1.plain: **You have my word.** **Word got around.** **He is a man of his word.** Not one of those is about a unit of speech. English already stretches this noun a long way past its dictionary entry, and you have never once been confused by it. Greek stretched it further, in directions English never went.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is the word everybody notices and nobody explains. The article entry on this same verse deliberately set logos aside, since the article is where the argument is. But a reader who has just been told the Word was God is entitled to ask why John called him a word in the first place, and the answer is not in any English dictionary.
John|1.kjv: In the beginning was the Word, and the Word was with God, and the Word was God.
John|1.kjvWhy: the capital W is a translator's decision, not a feature of the Greek
John|1.others: Every English version reads Word, capitalised. A handful of older attempts tried Reason or Discourse and none of them stuck.
John|1.seeing: Logos covers a spoken word, a statement, an account in the bookkeeping sense, a reasoned argument, and the rational principle ordering the universe. Greek philosophy, especially Stoic, had been using the last of those for centuries. Jewish writers in Greek had their own use: Philo of Alexandria made logos a mediating figure between God and the world, and the Aramaic targums habitually replace the name of God with memra, the word, in exactly the places where God acts.
John|1.why: English word means a unit of speech and very little else. There is no English noun that simultaneously means an utterance, a rational order, and a mediating agent, so a translator prints Word and adds a capital letter to warn you that more is going on.
John|1.rule: When a translation capitalises a common noun, that is a translator making an interpretive decision in punctuation. Greek manuscripts were written without any case distinction at all. Ask what the capital is doing before you accept it.
John|1.choosing: The Greek-philosophy background makes John's opening a bid for a pagan audience, using their word for the ordering principle of reality and then telling them it became a man. The Jewish background makes it a comment on Genesis 1, where God speaks and things exist, and on the targums where the Word of the LORD does what the LORD does. The two are not exclusive and most commentators now take both, with the Genesis echo carrying more weight because John's first three words are the opening of Genesis.

John|1.title: John 1:5
John|1.summary: The darkness did not comprehend it, or did not overcome it. The verb means both and John probably wanted both.
John|1.plain: **I could not grasp the rope.** **I could not grasp the idea.** One English verb, two completely different failures, and only the rest of the sentence tells you which. Now imagine a sentence where the rest does not tell you. That is this verse.
John|1.whyThis: Because the verse is the prologue's first statement about the conflict, and whether darkness failed to understand or failed to overpower sets the tone for the whole Gospel. It is also your first encounter with John's habit of meaning two things at once, which you will meet again at 3:3 and 19:30.
John|1.kjv: And the light shineth in darkness; and the darkness comprehended it not.
John|1.kjvWhy: comprehended is one of the two live readings, not a quaint rendering
John|1.others: Modern versions split. Some read overcome, some read understand, and most footnote the other.
John|1.seeing: Katalambano means to seize, to take hold of. Applied to the mind it becomes grasp, understand. Applied to a hand or an army it becomes seize, overpower. Both are ordinary uses of the same verb.
John|1.why: No single English verb means both grasp-with-the-mind and grab-by-force. Comprehend and overcome are two different English words, and a translator has to pick one.
John|1.rule: Some Greek verbs cover a physical action and a mental one with the same word, because the mental sense is a metaphor the language never stopped noticing. When your versions split between a physical and a mental rendering, this is usually why.
John|1.choosing: Comprehended, the older reading, fits the theme of recognition that runs through the prologue and into verses 10 and 11. Overcome fits the light-darkness conflict and reads more naturally in a sentence about darkness. John writes with deliberate double meanings elsewhere in this Gospel, at 3:3 and 3:8 and 19:30, which is the argument for not choosing.

John|1.title: John 1:9
John|1.summary: Coming into the world. Nothing in the Greek tells you whether that describes the light or the man.
John|1.plain: **I saw the man with the telescope.** Who had the telescope, you or the man? Nothing in those seven words decides it. English does this constantly and you usually work it out from context. When the context does not settle it, a translator has to.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is the clearest place in the chapter where translations differ without a single word changing. Learning to spot attachment ambiguity means you stop reading a rearranged sentence as a neutral update and start reading it as a decision.
John|1.kjv: That was the true Light, which lighteth every man that cometh into the world.
John|1.kjvWhy: the King James attaches the phrase to the man; the modern versions attach it to the light
John|1.others: Modern versions almost all attach it to the light: the true light, which gives light to everyone, was coming into the world.
John|1.seeing: The participle erchomenon can attach to the light or to every man. Greek word order is flexible enough that position does not settle it, and the participle's form fits either. This is attachment ambiguity, the same phenomenon as an English sentence where you cannot tell which noun a trailing phrase modifies.
John|1.why: English forces the phrase to sit next to one noun or the other. Word order in English is what carries grammatical relationship, so the moment you write the sentence in English you have decided.
John|1.rule: When a modern version rearranges a King James sentence rather than changing its words, look for a participle or a modifying phrase that could attach in more than one place. The rearrangement is the decision.
John|1.choosing: Attaching it to the man produces the King James reading, every man that comes into the world, which is a Jewish idiom for everyone born. Attaching it to the light produces a statement about the incarnation and fits the next verse, he was in the world. The second has the better contextual case and the first has the older tradition.

John|1.title: John 1:12
John|1.summary: Power to become the sons of God. The word is closer to right or authority than to power.
John|1.plain: **I gave him the power to sign the cheque.** In 1611 that meant permission. Today most people hear ability. The sentence never changed. The word slid underneath it.
John|1.whyThis: Because this is the verse people quote about becoming children of God, and the noun that governs the whole promise now means the wrong thing in English. It is also the model case for the entire semantic-shift category, which is the largest single class of King James misunderstanding.
John|1.kjv: But as many as received him, to them gave he power to become the sons of God.
John|1.kjvWhy: power was accurate in 1611 and now points at the wrong idea
John|1.others: Modern versions read right, or authority. Power has dropped out because English power now means capacity, and the Greek is about entitlement.
John|1.seeing: Exousia is delegated authority, the right to do something because someone with standing has granted it. Greek has a separate word for raw capability, dunamis. John chose the authority word.
John|1.why: English power slid toward capacity and strength. In 1611 it still covered granted authority, which is why the King James reading was accurate then and misleads now.
John|1.rule: When the King James and a modern version differ by one abstract noun, check whether the English word moved. Power, conversation, prevent, suffer, let and comfort have all shifted since 1611, and the Greek behind them has not.
John|1.choosing: There is no Greek dispute. This is an English shift, and the modern renderings are correcting for it rather than correcting the King James translators.

John|1.title: John 1:13
John|1.summary: Not of blood. The Greek says bloods, plural, and the plural is a Hebrew way of speaking.
John|1.plain: **He comes from money.** English lets you say that about a family line. It does not let you say **he comes from bloods**, even though several other languages do exactly that. When a language makes a word plural where yours never would, the writer is probably thinking in another language.
John|1.whyThis: Because an English reader cannot see it at all, and it is one of the small pieces of evidence that the writer thought in a Semitic language. The theology of the verse survives the flattening. The window into the author does not.
John|1.kjv: Which were born, not of blood, nor of the will of the flesh, nor of the will of man, but of God.
John|1.others: No English version renders the plural, because bloods is not English.
John|1.seeing: The Greek is ex haimaton, a plural of haima. Greek does not ordinarily pluralize blood. Hebrew and Aramaic do, most clearly for bloodshed and blood-guilt; some interpreters extend the same idiom to descent and bloodline as the sense at work here, though that extension leans more on how this verse itself is read than on independent Hebrew examples of damim meaning lineage. Either way, this is Semitic idiom coming through a Greek sentence.
John|1.why: English blood has no meaningful plural. Bloods reads as an error, so every translator silently singularizes it, and the trace of the underlying idiom disappears.
John|1.rule: When a Greek noun is plural where English would never pluralize it, suspect a Hebrew or Aramaic idiom underneath. The New Testament is Greek written largely by people who thought in a Semitic language.
John|1.choosing: The core observation is not in question: Greek does not ordinarily pluralize blood, and this plural is a trace of Semitic idiom. How far that idiom extends to a sense of lineage is a separate, more interpretive question. Either way, the loss is unavoidable and worth knowing about, because it is one of the small pieces of evidence that the writer's first language is showing.

John|1.title: John 1:14a
John|1.summary: Dwelt among us. The verb is built on the word for tent, and the whole Old Testament is inside it.
John|1.plain: **He stayed with us** against **he pitched his tent with us.** The second one is a picture, not just a fact. If your family has camped in the same spot for forty years, the second sentence means something to you that the first does not. That is the difference here.
John|1.whyThis: Because the verb is the hinge between the prologue and the whole Old Testament. Was made flesh gets the attention and is uncontested. Dwelt is the word that ties the incarnation to the tabernacle, and in English it is the blandest word in the sentence.
John|1.kjv: And the Word was made flesh, and dwelt among us.
John|1.others: Modern versions read dwelt, or lived, or made his dwelling. Some add a footnote reading tabernacled.
John|1.seeing: Eskenosen is from skene, tent. The related noun is what the Septuagint uses for the tabernacle, the tent where God's presence settled among Israel. The verse is not saying the Word moved into the neighbourhood. It is saying the tabernacle happened again, in a body.
John|1.why: English dwelt is a plain word with no architecture in it. There is no English verb meaning to pitch a tent and take up residence as the presence of God, so the allusion has to be carried by a footnote or lost.
John|1.rule: Greek words built on concrete nouns often carry the noun with them. When a verb looks abstract in English, check what object it was built from, because the Septuagint may have been using that object for four hundred years already.
John|1.choosing: No dispute about meaning. The dispute is whether to write tabernacled, which is precise and archaic, or dwelt, which is readable and flat. Every major version has chosen readable.

John|1.title: John 1:14b
John|1.summary: Full of grace and truth. That is a Hebrew pair, and it comes from Exodus 34.
John|1.plain: **Come good and early.** That is not two instructions. Good and early is one idea said with two words, and nobody hears it as a list. English does this and then forgets it does. Hebrew does it constantly.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is a quotation and it does not look like one. Learning to recognise a Hebrew word-pair is what lets you hear the Old Testament under a Greek sentence, and this pair comes from the single most important self-description God gives in the Torah.
John|1.others: All English versions read grace and truth. None can show that the phrase is a quotation of a formula.
John|1.seeing: Charis kai aletheia is widely taken as the Greek rendering of hesed we-emet, steadfast love and faithfulness, the pair God speaks over himself in Exodus 34:6 when Moses asks to see his glory. John has just said we beheld his glory. The allusion is to a specific scene.
John|1.why: English grace and truth reads as two abstract nouns joined by and. In Hebrew the pair is a fixed formula with a single referent, covenant loyalty, and the second word steadies the first.
John|1.rule: When two abstract nouns are joined in the New Testament and both are common Septuagint words, check whether they are a Hebrew word-pair rather than two separate ideas. Hebrew often says one thing with two words.
John|1.choosing: Nothing in the translation is contested. What is contested is how firmly to press the Exodus 34 allusion, and the glory language in the same verse is the strongest argument for pressing it.

John|1.title: John 1:16
John|1.summary: Grace for grace. The preposition normally means instead of, which makes the phrase hard rather than warm.
John|1.plain: **I traded one car for another** against **I stacked one book on another.** For and on point in opposite directions. One replaces, one piles up. The Greek word here is normally the trading one, and almost every English Bible prints the stacking one.
John|1.whyThis: Because the phrase is usually preached as abundance and the preposition normally means replacement, and verse 17 goes on to describe exactly a replacement. It is the best example in the chapter of a comfortable rendering quietly deciding an argument.
John|1.kjv: And of his fulness have all we received, and grace for grace.
John|1.kjvWhy: grace for grace preserves the preposition modern versions smooth over
John|1.others: Versions read grace upon grace, or one blessing after another, or grace in place of grace. The spread is unusually wide.
John|1.seeing: Anti ordinarily means instead of or in place of, as in a substitution. It is the preposition behind antichrist and anti-type. Reading charin anti charitos as grace piled on grace requires anti to mean something closer to upon or succeeding, which is a much rarer use.
John|1.why: English has no preposition that means one thing replacing another of the same kind in a continuous series. In place of sounds like a swap and upon sounds like a stack, and the Greek sits between them.
John|1.rule: When a preposition is doing unexpected work, look up what it ordinarily means before accepting a rendering that feels comfortable. Comfortable renderings of prepositions are where a lot of quiet interpretation hides.
John|1.choosing: Grace upon grace reads as abundance and is the majority modern choice. Grace in place of grace reads as the new covenant replacing the old, which is exactly what verse 17 goes on to describe with Moses and Christ. The context supports the harder reading more than the translations do.

John|1.title: John 1:18
John|1.summary: The only begotten Son, or the only begotten God. The manuscripts do not agree and the difference is enormous.
John|1.plain: Two different problems wearing the same coat. First: two old copies of a letter say different words, so which did your grandmother write? That is a manuscript question. Second: what did she mean by the word she used? That is a dictionary question. Usually you only have one of these at a time. Here you have both, in the same clause.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is the only place in John 1 where the manuscripts themselves disagree about something this weighty, and it stacks a textual question on top of a lexical one. If you want to understand why your footnotes exist, this is the verse to learn them on.
John|1.kjv: No man hath seen God at any time; the only begotten Son, which is in the bosom of the Father, he hath declared him.
John|1.kjvWhy: only begotten Son is one side of a manuscript split, printed as if settled
John|1.others: Modern versions read the only God, or God the one and only, or the one and only Son who is himself God. Each is a different decision about the same clause.
John|1.seeing: Two things are happening at once. First a textual split: the earliest papyri and the great uncials read monogenes theos, while the majority of later manuscripts read monogenes huios. Second a lexical question: monogenes is traditionally rendered only begotten, from a supposed link to gennao, to beget, but the second half of the compound is more likely genos, kind or class, giving one of a kind.
John|1.why: English has to resolve both questions before it can print the sentence. There is no way to write a clause that is undecided between Son and God, or between begotten and unique.
John|1.rule: When versions differ on a noun this weighty, check whether the split is textual or lexical before assuming an agenda. Here it is both at once, which is rare, and each question has a separate body of evidence.
John|1.choosing: Son has the weight of tradition, the majority of manuscripts, and the fact that John calls Jesus the Son constantly. God has the earliest manuscripts and is the harder reading, which usually counts in its favour, and it closes the prologue where it opened, with the Word being God. Only begotten is the older lexical reading and one of a kind has the better etymology.

John|1.title: John 1:41-42
John|1.summary: John stops the narrative twice to translate a word for you, which tells you who he thought was reading.
John|1.plain: **He grabbed the bonnet, which is what the British call the hood.** You just learned two things. What a bonnet is, and that the writer assumes you are American. Writers who stop to translate are telling you who they expect to be reading.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is the author telling you, inside his own narrative, who he expects to be reading. Very little else in the New Testament gives you that directly, and it costs you nothing in translation, which is why nobody notices it.
John|1.kjv: We have found the Messias, which is, being interpreted, the Christ. ... Thou shalt be called Cephas, which is by interpretation, A stone.
John|1.others: Versions keep the glosses because they are in the text. Some smooth them into parentheses.
John|1.seeing: Messias and Kephas are Aramaic words carried into a Greek sentence, and John immediately supplies the Greek equivalent. He does the same thing at 1:38 with Rabbi, at 9:7 with Siloam, and at 20:16 with Rabboni.
John|1.why: There's no translation loss here. The point is what the habit reveals: the writer is working from an Aramaic-speaking setting and writing for readers who are not in it.
John|1.rule: When a biblical writer translates a word inside his own sentence, he is telling you about his audience. Those glosses are some of the most direct evidence in the New Testament about who a book was written for.
John|1.choosing: There is nothing to choose. The entry is here because it is the clearest example in John of the seam between the language of the events and the language of the book.

John|1.title: John 1:51
John|1.summary: Verily I say unto you. The you is plural, and Jesus has been talking to one man.
John|1.plain: **Are you coming?** One person, or everybody in the room? English cannot tell you. Southerners fixed it with y'all because the language lost something it used to have. It used to be you for a crowd and thou for one person, and the King James still has both.
John|1.whyThis: Because it is the first of the great promises in John and it is addressed to a group, not to Nathanael alone. The lesson generalises: a very large share of the promises and commands people apply to themselves privately are plural in the Greek.
John|1.kjv: Verily, verily, I say unto you, Hereafter ye shall see heaven open.
John|1.kjvWhy: ye marks a plural that modern English has no way to show
John|1.others: No modern version can show it. English lost the distinction when ye and thou dropped out, which the King James still had and no longer communicates.
John|1.seeing: Nathanael is the one being addressed, and the pronoun turns plural at this verse. The promise widens from one man to everyone standing there and, arguably, to the reader. The King James actually marks it with ye, which modern English cannot.
John|1.why: English merged the plural you and the singular thou into one word. Every other major European language kept the distinction and English gave it up, which means every New Testament you is ambiguous in English and unambiguous in Greek.
John|1.rule: Whenever a New Testament promise or command feels personal, check whether the you is plural. A very large share of them are, and they are addressed to a congregation rather than to an individual.
John|1.choosing: No dispute exists. English simply cannot do it without writing you all, which no version will print.

John|2.title: John 2:4a
John|2.summary: What have I to do with thee. A Hebrew idiom carried word for word into Greek.
John|2.plain: **What's that got to do with me?** English has almost the same idiom and it can be sharp or merely distancing depending entirely on who says it and how.
John|2.whyThis: Because the English reads as a rebuke to his mother and the phrase is a fixed Semitic expression about shared business, which is a different kind of sentence.
John|2.kjv: Jesus saith unto her, Woman, what have I to do with thee? mine hour is not yet come.
John|2.kjvWhy: the King James keeps the idiom literally and lets it sound strange
John|2.others: Versions read what have I to do with thee, woman what does this have to do with me, or woman why do you involve me.
John|2.seeing: Ti emoi kai soi, literally what to me and to you, renders Hebrew mah li walak. It appears in the Septuagint and in the mouths of demons at Mark 1:24. The range runs from hostile to merely marking a separation of concerns.
John|2.why: English has no fixed phrase with the same neutral-to-hostile range, so a translator has to pick a tone the Greek does not specify.
John|2.rule: When a Greek sentence is ungrammatical or odd word for word, check whether it is a Hebrew phrase transported whole. The New Testament is full of them.
John|2.choosing: Why do you involve me is what most modern versions settle on. All versions agree the tone is uncertain and none footnotes how wide the range is.

John|2.title: John 2:4b
John|2.summary: Mine hour is not yet come. A word John uses as a countdown to one event.
John|2.plain: **His hour had come.** English uses hour for a decisive moment too, and never means sixty minutes when it does.
John|2.whyThis: Because hour here is not a time of day, it is a fixed reference to the cross, and John repeats it through the whole Gospel until it arrives.
John|2.others: Every version reads hour or time.
John|2.seeing: Hora is an hour, but John uses it as a technical marker. It is not yet come at 2:4, 7:30 and 8:20; it has come at 12:23, 13:1 and 17:1. The pattern is a structural device across the book.
John|2.why: English hour carries the decisive sense, so little is lost in the word. What is lost is that these are the same word used deliberately across twenty chapters.
John|2.rule: When a common word recurs in the same phrasing across a book, track every occurrence before interpreting any one of them.
John|2.choosing: Hour is the majority rendering and no version departs.

John|2.title: John 2:11
John|2.summary: The beginning of miracles. John's word is sign, and he never uses the usual word for miracle.
John|2.plain: **A sign of trouble.** A sign points past itself. A **marvel** stops at itself. Two different jobs and English has both words.
John|2.whyThis: Because English miracle points at the wonder and John's word points at what the act means, which is the difference between a spectacle and an argument.
John|2.others: The King James reads miracles. Modern versions read signs.
John|2.seeing: Semeion means a sign, something pointing beyond itself. The other Gospels use dunamis, act of power, and teras, wonder. John uses semeion throughout and structures the first half of his Gospel around seven of them.
John|2.why: English miracle emphasises the breach of ordinary cause. Sign emphasises significance. The Greek word chosen is the second one and the King James printed the first.
John|2.rule: When one Gospel consistently uses a different word from the other three for the same events, the difference is the writer's argument.
John|2.choosing: Signs is what nearly every modern version prints. The King James miracles is the outlier and is the reason the popular phrase is seven miracles rather than seven signs.

John|2.title: John 2:15
John|2.summary: A scourge of small cords. The noun occurs once in the New Testament and is a Latin word in Greek dress.
John|2.plain: English is full of borrowed words you never notice. **Restaurant**, **algebra**, **ketchup**. A borrowed word is a fingerprint of contact between two cultures.
John|2.whyThis: Because the word is a borrowing from Latin, which tells you something about the world the Gospel was written in that no theological point depends on.
John|2.others: Versions read whip or scourge of cords.
John|2.seeing: Phragellion is the Greek spelling of Latin flagellum. It occurs only here in the New Testament. The related verb appears at Matthew 27:26 and Mark 15:15 of the scourging.
John|2.why: English doesn't lose anything here. The point is what the loan word shows about a Greek text written inside a Roman world.
John|2.rule: Loan words in a text date and place it. They are evidence about the writer's setting rather than about his meaning.
John|2.choosing: Whip is what most modern versions print; the King James reads scourge.

John|2.title: John 2:17
John|2.summary: The zeal of thine house hath eaten me up. The verb is consume, and the tense was changed in the quotation.
John|2.plain: Quote a song lyric back at someone but shift it from **it broke me** to **it will break me**, and you have said something the original did not.
John|2.whyThis: Because John quotes Psalm 69 and alters the tense from past to future, which is a deliberate move and invisible unless you check the psalm.
John|2.others: Every version reads consume or eat up.
John|2.seeing: Katesthio is to eat up, devour, consume. The Septuagint of Psalm 69:9 has the aorist, it consumed me. John has the future, it will consume me, which turns a description of past devotion into a prediction.
John|2.why: English can carry the tense, but a reader has to look up the psalm to see that the tense was changed.
John|2.rule: Line up a New Testament quotation against its Old Testament source instead of assuming they match. The differences are almost always deliberate and almost never flagged.
John|2.choosing: Consume is the majority rendering and no version notes the tense change in the text.

John|2.title: John 2:19
John|2.summary: Destroy this temple. Greek has two words for temple and this is the inner one.
John|2.plain: **The house** and **the grounds**. If someone says tear down the house, nobody thinks he means the estate. One word for both and the sentence gets much harder.
John|2.whyThis: Because the accusation at the trial turns on this saying, and the word Jesus uses is not the word for the temple complex. English prints temple for both and the distinction disappears.
John|2.others: Every version reads temple for both Greek words.
John|2.seeing: Naos is the sanctuary proper, the inner building. Hieron is the whole temple precinct including the courts. Verse 14 has Jesus in the hieron; verse 19 has him saying destroy this naos. John then tells you in verse 21 that he meant his body.
John|2.why: English has one word, so the shift from precinct to sanctuary inside five verses cannot be seen.
John|2.rule: Where Greek has two words for one English word, watch for a passage that uses both. The switch is usually doing the work.
John|2.choosing: Temple is universal for both. Some study Bibles note the distinction; no translation marks it.

John|2.title: John 2:23-25
John|2.summary: Many believed. And Jesus did not believe them. The same verb, twice, deliberately.
John|2.plain: **They trusted him, and he did not trust them.** Say it with one verb and it lands. Say it with trust and entrust and it reads as two unrelated facts.
John|2.whyThis: Because the wordplay is the point of the paragraph and every English version hides it by using two different verbs.
John|2.others: Versions read believed in the first clause and entrust or commit himself in the second.
John|2.seeing: Pisteuo appears in verse 23 of the crowd believing and in verse 24 of Jesus not entrusting himself to them. It is the same verb in both, and John is playing one against the other.
John|2.why: There's no single English verb that works both for believing in someone and for entrusting yourself to them, so every version breaks the pair.
John|2.rule: When a paragraph reads as two disconnected statements, check whether one verb is doing both. John does this constantly.
John|2.choosing: Entrust is the majority rendering for the second occurrence; the King James reads commit himself.

John|3.title: John 3:3
John|3.summary: Born again, or born from above. The Greek word means both and Nicodemus hears only one.
John|3.plain: **Can you run that by me again?** **The order came down from on high.** Two different ideas, and imagine one word covering both. Now watch someone answer the wrong one and build a whole confused reply on it.
John|3.whyThis: Because the whole conversation that follows is Nicodemus getting it wrong, and he gets it wrong because the word has two meanings and he picks the wrong one. The misunderstanding is the point, and it is invisible in English.
John|3.kjv: Except a man be born again, he cannot see the kingdom of God.
John|3.kjvWhy: again is the reading that named an entire movement, and it is half the word
John|3.others: King James, NIV and NASB read again. The NRSV and NET read from above and footnote again. The margin of almost every version carries the other.
John|3.seeing: Anothen means from above and also again, a second time. John uses it in the from above sense at 3:31 and 19:11. Jesus almost certainly means from above. Nicodemus takes it as again and asks about re-entering a womb, which is why the next three verses are about correcting him.
John|3.why: English has no word carrying both a direction and a repetition. Whichever one a translator picks, the misunderstanding in verse 4 stops making sense.
John|3.rule: When a character in a narrative misunderstands a saying, check the word they tripped on. A deliberate double meaning is often the reason the scene exists.
John|3.choosing: Again fits Nicodemus's reply and four hundred years of English usage. From above fits John's own use of the word elsewhere and fits the born of the Spirit line that follows. Most commentators take from above as the meaning and again as the misunderstanding the passage is built on.

John|3.title: John 3:5
John|3.summary: Born of water and of the Spirit. One preposition governs both nouns, or two.
John|3.plain: **Made of wood and nails.** One thing, two materials. **Made of wood and of iron.** Now it sounds like two things. English signals it by repeating the preposition and Greek does not have to.
John|3.whyThis: Because whether water and Spirit are two births or one hangs on how the Greek phrase is constructed, and English cannot show that a single preposition is covering both.
John|3.others: Every version reads born of water and the Spirit. None marks whether one birth is meant or two.
John|3.seeing: Ex hudatos kai pneumatos has one preposition governing both nouns joined by kai. In Greek that construction often marks a single idea rather than a pair, which is the grammatical case for reading it as one birth described two ways.
John|3.why: English repeats or drops the preposition and thereby decides. The Greek construction leaves it undecided and the decision gets made in the printing.
John|3.rule: When two nouns share one preposition in Greek, check whether the writer is describing one thing or two. The construction often signals one.
John|3.choosing: Born of water and the Spirit is the majority rendering across all versions. The interpretation is argued in commentaries and no translation takes a side.

John|3.title: John 3:8
John|3.summary: The wind blows where it wills. Wind and Spirit are the same Greek word, and the sentence needs both at once.
John|3.plain: Suppose your language had one word for **a breeze** and **a person's inner life**. A sentence could slide from one to the other and land as a single thought. Translate it into English and you get two nouns and a jump.
John|3.whyThis: Because the sentence is a pun that only works in Greek, and in English it reads as an odd change of subject. One word does both halves.
John|3.kjv: The wind bloweth where it listeth, and thou hearest the sound thereof... so is every one that is born of the Spirit.
John|3.kjvWhy: the King James prints wind and Spirit in one verse, which shows the seam without explaining it
John|3.others: Every version reads wind in the first half and Spirit in the second, because there is no alternative. A few footnote that the Greek is one word.
John|3.seeing: Pneuma covers wind, breath and spirit. So does Hebrew ruach. Jesus is saying one thing about one word: it goes where it wants, you hear it, you cannot track it, and that is what being born of it is like. In Greek the comparison is a single image. In English it is a simile between two unrelated things.
John|3.why: English split what Greek and Hebrew both kept together, so a pun becomes an analogy and loses most of its force.
John|3.rule: When a verse compares two things that share a word in the original, it is usually not a comparison at all. It is one word doing two jobs, and the translation has manufactured the gap.
John|3.choosing: No translator has an option. The only decision is whether to footnote it, and most do not.

John|3.title: John 3:13
John|3.summary: Who is in heaven. Three words that are in some manuscripts and not others.
John|3.plain: Two copies of one letter, one with a clause the other lacks. Nobody forged anything. Someone either added a line or dropped one, and you have to decide which is more likely.
John|3.whyThis: Because the clause makes a claim about Jesus being in heaven while speaking on earth, and it is absent from the earliest copies. If you want to see why footnotes exist, this is a short clear example.
John|3.others: The King James and NKJV print who is in heaven. Nearly every modern version omits it and footnotes it.
John|3.seeing: Ho on en to ourano appears in the majority of later manuscripts and is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The usual judgment is that it was added by a scribe making an orthodox point explicit.
John|3.why: Not a translation problem. English can print it or not, and the question is which Greek text is being translated.
John|3.rule: When the King James has words a modern version lacks, the difference is usually the Greek text behind them rather than anyone's theology.
John|3.choosing: Modern versions omit it by a large majority; the King James and its descendants keep it.

John|3.title: John 3:15
John|3.summary: Believeth in him. The phrase can attach to believe or to eternal life.
John|3.plain: **He signed the letter in the office.** Did he sign in the office, or was it the letter that was in the office? English has this ambiguity constantly.
John|3.whyThis: Because the prepositional phrase can go with either verb and the two readings say different things: believing in him, or having life in him.
John|3.others: The King James reads believeth in him should not perish. Modern versions vary between in him believing and has eternal life in him.
John|3.seeing: En auto can modify pisteuon, believing in him, or zoen aionion, eternal life in him. John elsewhere uses eis auton for believing into, not en auto, which is the argument for attaching it to the life.
John|3.why: English word order forces the phrase next to one verb or the other, which decides the question in the act of printing.
John|3.rule: When a version rearranges a clause rather than changing its words, a modifying phrase has been reattached. That is a decision, not a style choice.
John|3.choosing: Most versions print may have eternal life in him; the King James attaches the phrase to believing instead.

John|3.title: John 3:16a
John|3.summary: For God so loved the world. So means in this way, not so very much.
John|3.plain: **He so loved the work that he stayed late.** Modern ears hear how much. **Hold the brush so.** That is the older sense, meaning in this manner. English kept the word and quietly dropped one of its two jobs.
John|3.whyThis: Because it is the most quoted verse in the English-speaking world and its second word is misread by nearly everyone who quotes it. Not a rare word, not a disputed text. An adverb.
John|3.kjv: For God so loved the world, that he gave his only begotten Son.
John|3.kjvWhy: so was correct in 1611 and now reads as an intensifier
John|3.others: Every English version reads so. The CSB footnotes in this way. The NET renders it this is the way God loved the world, which is the only major version to force the issue.
John|3.seeing: Houtos is an adverb of manner, not degree. It points forward to the clause that follows: God loved the world in this way, namely that he gave. The verse is not measuring the size of God's love. It is naming the shape of it.
John|3.why: English so does carry both senses, which is why the rendering survives untouched. But usage has shifted so far toward degree that almost no reader hears manner.
John|3.rule: The most dangerous English words are the ones that still technically carry the original range but have drifted in everyday use. Nothing looks wrong, so nobody checks.
John|3.choosing: There is no dispute in the Greek. The dispute is whether a translator should override four centuries of familiarity to rescue an adverb, and only the NET has been willing to.

John|3.title: John 3:16b
John|3.summary: Everlasting life. The Greek adjective is built on the word for age, not the word for endless.
John|3.plain: **Medieval architecture.** That does not mean architecture that lasts a long time. It means architecture belonging to a particular age. Now imagine your only word for that idea had drifted to mean unending, and you had been reading it that way your whole life.
John|3.whyThis: Because the promise at the end of the verse is built on an adjective whose primary sense is genuinely disputed among scholars, and depending on which side is right, what's being offered shifts between a duration and a kind of life.
John|3.kjv: should not perish, but have everlasting life.
John|3.kjvWhy: everlasting states a duration the Greek adjective does not directly claim
John|3.others: King James reads everlasting. Most modern versions read eternal. Neither carries the age sense, and no major version attempts it.
John|3.seeing: Aionios is the adjective from aion, an age or era, and one influential scholarly reading treats its primary force as belonging to the age to come rather than lasting without end, with endlessness following as a consequence of which age you belong to rather than the word's own content. That reading is contested, not settled: standard lexicons such as BDAG also list a distinct sense, without beginning or end, and note that Greek had a separate word for strict endlessness, aidios, which New Testament writers mostly did not reach for. Which sense is primary in a given verse is part of a live debate tied to larger arguments about universalism, annihilationism, and eternal punishment.
John|3.why: English eternal and everlasting are both about duration. There is no English adjective meaning of the coming age, so the temporal reading is the only one on offer.
John|3.rule: Adjectives built on nouns usually carry the noun with them. Find the noun before you accept the adjective.
John|3.choosing: Nothing textual is at stake, but the semantic question underneath is genuinely live, not settled: whether aionios here primarily means belonging to the age to come or primarily means without end is disputed among lexicographers and theologians. English eternal and everlasting both commit to the duration sense regardless of which side is right, so no English version marks that a real dispute exists underneath the word.

John|3.title: John 3:18-19
John|3.summary: Condemned already. The Greek word is judged, and the noun in the next verse is the judgment.
John|3.plain: **Judge** and **judgment** are obviously related in English. **Condemn** and **judgment** are not, and the connection breaks the moment you print the first one.
John|3.whyThis: Because English condemn is a verdict against someone and Greek krino is the whole process of judging, which can go either way. The paragraph uses the verb and then the noun, and English uses two unrelated words.
John|3.others: The King James reads condemned and condemnation. Most modern versions read judged and judgment.
John|3.seeing: Krino is to judge, to decide, to separate. Krisis is the act or result. Verses 17 to 19 use the word family four times, and the paragraph is built on the repetition.
John|3.why: English condemn presumes the outcome; judge does not. Choosing condemn decides the verse before the reader gets there.
John|3.rule: Word families argue by themselves in Greek. When an English version breaks a family into unrelated words, the argument stops being visible.
John|3.choosing: Judged and judgment are the majority modern renderings; the King James reads condemned and condemnation.

John|3.title: John 3:29
John|3.summary: The friend of the bridegroom. A defined role in Jewish weddings, not a figure of speech.
John|3.plain: **Best man.** If a culture has that role, nobody needs it explained. If it does not, the sentence sounds like sentiment.
John|3.whyThis: Because the phrase is a job with duties rather than a metaphor for a close friend, and John the Baptist is describing his own function by naming an office everyone present recognised.
John|3.others: Every version reads friend of the bridegroom.
John|3.seeing: The shoshbin in Jewish practice arranged the wedding, acted for the groom, and stood at the chamber door waiting for the groom's voice. The joy at hearing that voice is the duty completing, not an emotion being described.
John|3.why: English best man exists but carries none of the legal or custodial duties, so the point of the analogy weakens.
John|3.rule: When a figure of speech in the Bible names a social role, look up the role. Many biblical metaphors are institutions to their first hearers.
John|3.choosing: No English version renders it differently; the phrase itself isn't in question, only whether readers know the office standing behind it.

John|3.title: John 3:31-36
John|3.summary: Where does the speech end? Greek manuscripts have no quotation marks.
John|3.plain: Read a transcript with no quotation marks and you have to work out where the speaking stops. Punctuation was invented long after these texts were written.
John|3.whyThis: Because the paragraph is either John the Baptist still speaking or the Gospel writer commenting, and nothing in the Greek settles it. Every English version decides for you with punctuation.
John|3.others: The King James runs the speech on without marking it. Modern versions close the quotation at verse 30, or 31, or 36, and they do not agree.
John|3.seeing: Ancient Greek manuscripts were written without punctuation, without spaces, and without quotation marks. Where a discourse ends is an editorial judgment, and the same problem appears at John 3:21.
John|3.why: English requires quotation marks. There is no way to print the passage without deciding, and the decision changes who is speaking.
John|3.rule: Quotation marks in an English New Testament are a modern editor's judgment, not a feature of the text. Where versions disagree about them, the speaker is genuinely uncertain.
John|3.choosing: Closing at verse 30 is the most common modern choice, but there is no majority reading and the versions split.

John|3.title: John 3:36
John|3.summary: He that believeth not. The Greek verb in the second half is disobey, not disbelieve.
John|3.plain: **He did not agree.** **He did not comply.** Two different failures, and only one of them is about the mind.
John|3.whyThis: Because the verse sets belief against something, and the something is not unbelief. John switches verbs deliberately and almost every English version prints the same idea twice.
John|3.others: The King James reads believeth not. The ESV and NASB read does not obey. The NIV reads rejects.
John|3.seeing: The first clause uses pisteuo, believe. The second uses apeitheo, to refuse to be persuaded, to disobey. The contrast is between trusting and refusing, not between two states of opinion.
John|3.why: English believe has no natural opposite that means refuse to comply, so versions either print does not believe and lose the switch or print does not obey and surprise the reader.
John|3.rule: When a verse sets up a contrast, check whether both halves use the same root. If they do not, the switch is the argument.
John|3.choosing: Most modern English versions print does not obey; the King James reads believeth not.

John|4.title: John 4:6
John|4.summary: The sixth hour. Which clock John is using is an old and unresolved question.
John|4.plain: **Half six.** In Britain that is six thirty. In parts of Europe the same phrase means half past five. Nothing in the words tells you which convention is in force.
John|4.whyThis: Because John gives times of day several times and the hour count may be Jewish, from sunrise, or Roman civil, from midnight, which moves every one of those scenes by six hours.
John|4.others: Versions print the sixth hour or convert it to about noon. Conversions assume the Jewish reckoning.
John|4.seeing: Jewish reckoning counts from sunrise, making the sixth hour about noon. Roman civil reckoning counts from midnight, making it about six in the morning. John 19:14 is the verse that makes the question urgent, because it conflicts with Mark 15:25 on one reckoning and not the other.
John|4.why: English versions that convert to noon have made the decision invisible; those that print the sixth hour leave it visible and unexplained.
John|4.rule: When a version converts an ancient measurement into a modern one, a convention has been assumed. Look for whether the text ever tells you which.
John|4.choosing: Most modern versions print about noon, quietly assuming Jewish reckoning.

John|4.title: John 4:9
John|4.summary: Have no dealings with. A rare verb, and it may mean do not share vessels.
John|4.plain: A single-occurrence word is a word with no witnesses. You guess from the sentence and from whatever else the culture has left behind.
John|4.whyThis: Because the clause explains the whole scene and the verb occurs once in the New Testament, so what exactly the Jews and Samaritans did not do is not certain.
John|4.others: Versions read have no dealings with, do not associate with, or do not share things in common with.
John|4.seeing: Sugchraomai occurs only here in the New Testament. The narrower reading is that Jews would not use vessels in common with Samaritans, which fits the scene exactly, since the dispute is about a drinking vessel.
John|4.why: There's no English verb for ritual non-sharing of utensils, so every rendering generalises to social avoidance, and the point about the cup is lost.
John|4.rule: When a rare word sits in a clause explaining a scene, read it against the scene. The narrative is usually the best evidence available.
John|4.choosing: Do not associate with is the majority modern rendering; the narrower vessel reading appears in footnotes and commentaries.

John|4.title: John 4:10
John|4.summary: Living water. In ordinary speech it means running water from a spring.
John|4.plain: **Running water.** In a house that means plumbing. Say it to someone at a well and it means a spring rather than a cistern. Same words, two worlds.
John|4.whyThis: Because the woman answers as though he means well water and he means something else, and the misunderstanding only works because the phrase has a plain everyday sense.
John|4.seeing: Hudor zon is the standard phrase for fresh flowing water as against still cistern water, and it carries ritual significance in purification law. The woman hears the ordinary sense and Jesus is using it for something else, which is the same technique as anothen in chapter three.
John|4.why: English living water is not an idiom at all, so it reads as poetry from the first word and the double meaning collapses.
John|4.rule: John builds several conversations on a phrase with a plain sense and a second one. Find the plain sense first or the scene stops working.
John|4.choosing: No English version renders it differently; the ambiguity is lost before any translation choice even enters the picture.

John|4.title: John 4:23-24
John|4.summary: True worshippers. The adjective means real as against counterfeit, not sincere.
John|4.plain: **A true friend.** You mean a real one, not a sincere one. English keeps the sense and uses it less often than it used to.
John|4.whyThis: Because English true has drifted toward sincerity of feeling, and the Greek word is about being the genuine article rather than a copy.
John|4.seeing: Alethinos is genuine, real, the thing itself rather than a representation. It is the word behind the true light, the true bread and the true vine in this Gospel, where in each case something is being contrasted with a lesser version.
John|4.why: English true covers both genuine and sincere, and the second sense now dominates, so a claim about authenticity reads as a claim about attitude.
John|4.rule: When John calls something true, he is usually contrasting it with a copy. List the other occurrences and the pattern becomes obvious.
John|4.choosing: True is universal; genuine or real appear in footnotes.

John|4.title: John 4:24
John|4.summary: God is spirit. Same construction as the last clause of John 1:1, and here nobody reads it as a god.
John|4.plain: **Sam is the doctor.** **Sam is a doctor.** **Sam is doctor.** The third one is not English, and it is what Greek does here. It says what God is by nature, not which spirit God is or that God is one of several.
John|4.whyThis: Because it is the same grammatical situation as John 1:1 with the opposite outcome, and reading them together teaches the rule better than either does alone. Here every version does the qualitative thing without arguing about it.
John|4.kjv: God is a Spirit: and they that worship him must worship him in spirit and in truth.
John|4.kjvWhy: the King James reads a Spirit, which is exactly what the Greek does not say
John|4.others: The King James reads a Spirit. Every modern version reads God is spirit, with no article at all, which is the qualitative rendering.
John|4.seeing: Pneuma stands before the verb with no article, the same shape as theos in John 1:1c. Nobody proposes rendering it a god there and a spirit here, yet the King James did exactly that. Modern versions corrected it, which is the strongest available evidence for how the construction works.
John|4.why: English forces an article or a bare noun and the bare noun sounds ungrammatical in most sentences. Here it does not, which is why the fix was possible.
John|4.rule: When you want to test a grammatical claim, find the same construction in a verse where nothing theological is at stake. If translators handle it one way there and another way in the contested verse, the difference is not grammar.
John|4.choosing: No modern version defends a Spirit. The King James rendering is the outlier, and correcting it is the same move that produces God was the Word rather than a god in chapter one.

John|4.title: John 4:26
John|4.summary: I that speak unto thee am he. The Greek is the same two words as John 8:58.
John|4.plain: **I am.** On its own, in English, it sounds unfinished. Your ear wants a completion. That incompleteness is the whole point.
John|4.whyThis: Because the he is not in the Greek. The words are ego eimi, and this is the first place in the Gospel where Jesus says them, to a Samaritan woman rather than to a crowd.
John|4.others: Every version supplies he or the one. None can print the bare phrase without it sounding broken.
John|4.seeing: Ego eimi with no predicate. English requires a completion, so translators supply he. The same two words appear absolutely at John 8:58, 8:24, 8:28, 13:19 and 18:5-6, and at 18:6 the arresting party falls backward.
John|4.why: English cannot leave a sentence hanging on the verb to be. Something has to follow it, and whatever follows is supplied by the translator.
John|4.rule: When a version prints italics or a footnote on a short word like he, the word is not in the original. Supplied words are marked in some Bibles and not in others.
John|4.choosing: I am he is the majority rendering; I am the one appears in some modern versions.

John|4.title: John 4:35
John|4.summary: White already to harvest. The colour word points at ripeness, and the verb is a command to look.
John|4.plain: **Golden.** English picked a different colour for the same idea. Colour words for ripeness are cultural and rarely transfer.
John|4.whyThis: Because white is not an obvious colour for a ripe field to an English reader, and the imperative in the sentence is doing work that the King James preserves and modern versions soften.
John|4.others: The King James reads white already to harvest. Modern versions read ripe for harvest or white for harvest.
John|4.seeing: Leukos is white or bright. Applied to grain it indicates ripeness, since barley and wheat pale as they dry. Theasasthe is an aorist imperative, a command to look now.
John|4.why: English harvest imagery runs on gold rather than white, so the literal colour reads as odd and most versions substitute ripe.
John|4.rule: Colour terms rarely map between languages. When a colour seems wrong, ask what the colour was being used to indicate.
John|4.choosing: Most modern versions print ripe for harvest; white, the more literal option, is the King James choice.

John|5.title: John 5:2
John|5.summary: Bethesda. The manuscripts do not agree on the name of the pool.
John|5.plain: Three old letters give three spellings of the same village. You would not conclude the village is fictional. You would ask which spelling the writer used.
John|5.whyThis: Because the name varies between Bethesda, Bethsaida and Bethzatha across the manuscripts, and one of the variants was confirmed by an archaeological find rather than by a copy.
John|5.others: The King James reads Bethesda. The NRSV reads Beth-zatha. The NIV reads Bethesda and footnotes the others.
John|5.seeing: Bethesda appears in the later majority, Bethzatha in Sinaiticus, Bethsaida in P75 and Vaticanus. The Copper Scroll from Qumran mentions a pool with a name close to Bethesda, which is external evidence of a kind textual criticism rarely gets.
John|5.why: This isn't a translation loss at all. The versions simply follow different Greek texts.
John|5.rule: Place names vary in manuscripts more than almost anything else, because scribes normalise unfamiliar names to familiar ones.
John|5.choosing: Bethesda is the majority rendering in English versions.

John|5.title: John 5:3-4
John|5.summary: The angel troubling the water. A whole verse that is not in the oldest manuscripts.
John|5.plain: Someone writes an explanation in the margin of a book. The next person to copy it cannot tell margin from text and copies both. Nothing dishonest happened and the book now says more than it did.
John|5.whyThis: Because it is the clearest example in John of an explanatory note migrating from a margin into the text, and it is the reason modern Bibles jump from verse 3 to verse 5.
John|5.others: The King James prints the verse. Nearly every modern version omits it and footnotes it, which is why verse 4 appears to be missing.
John|5.seeing: The passage is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus, Vaticanus and others, and the manuscripts that contain it vary among themselves, which is a common signal of a later addition. It reads as an explanation of why the sick were waiting for the water to move.
John|5.why: Not a translation issue. English versions differ because the Greek texts behind them differ.
John|5.rule: When your Bible skips a verse number, that is not censorship. It is the versification of the King James being preserved so references still work.
John|5.choosing: Modern versions omit by a large majority; the King James and its descendants print it.

John|5.title: John 5:18
John|5.summary: Making himself equal with God. The charge is the narrator's report of what they heard.
John|5.plain: **They said he was claiming to be in charge.** That tells you what they heard. It does not by itself tell you what he said.
John|5.whyThis: Because the verse is regularly quoted as a claim Jesus made, and grammatically it is a charge the authorities made, which is a different kind of evidence.
John|5.others: Every version reads making himself equal with God.
John|5.seeing: The clause is part of the reason given for the hostility, reported by the narrator. John does this repeatedly: he states what the opposition concluded, then lets the following discourse address it. Verse 19 begins the answer.
John|5.why: English can carry this accurately. The difficulty is that a reported accusation reads like a narrator's endorsement when quoted on its own.
John|5.rule: When a verse states what people concluded, the sentence is evidence about them. Whether the conclusion is right is answered elsewhere.
John|5.choosing: There is no translation choice to make here, English can only print making himself equal with God either way. What's contested is whether the accusation was fair, not how to render it.

John|5.title: John 5:27
John|5.summary: Because he is the Son of man. No article, and John never does this anywhere else.
John|5.plain: **He is the manager.** **He is manager.** The second one sounds like a job rather than a person, and English feels the difference even though it is one small word.
John|5.whyThis: Because the phrase appears without the definite article only here in the New Testament, which turns a title into a description and links it to Daniel 7 rather than to the usual self-designation.
John|5.others: Every version reads the Son of Man. None marks the missing article.
John|5.seeing: Huios anthropou without the article, against ho huios tou anthropou everywhere else in the Gospels. Daniel 7:13 in Greek is also anarthrous, one like a son of man, which is the argument that John is pointing at that passage specifically.
John|5.why: English requires an article or none, and none sounds ungrammatical with a title, so every version supplies the.
John|5.rule: When an article is missing in Greek where a writer always uses it elsewhere, the omission is deliberate.
John|5.choosing: The Son of Man is universal; the anarthrous form is noted in commentaries and in no translation.

John|5.title: John 5:39
John|5.summary: Search the scriptures. The Greek form is both a command and a statement.
John|5.plain: **You're reading.** **Read!** In English those look different. Imagine one form that could be either, and only the sentence around it deciding.
John|5.whyThis: Because the verse is quoted as an instruction to study the Bible and the form can equally be a description of what they are already doing, which reverses the sentence.
John|5.others: The King James reads search the scriptures as a command. Most modern versions read you search the scriptures as a statement.
John|5.seeing: Eraunate is identical in form as a present indicative and a present imperative. Read as indicative, the sentence is you search the scriptures because you think you have life in them, and they testify of me, and you will not come to me. That reading fits the rebuke that follows.
John|5.why: English has different forms for a command and a statement, so the printing settles it and the reader never sees the choice.
John|5.rule: Some Greek forms are identical across mood. When a version prints a command and another prints a statement, this is usually why.
John|5.choosing: The statement reading, you search the scriptures, is what most modern versions print; the King James reads it as a command instead.

John|6.title: John 6:27
John|6.summary: Him hath God the Father sealed. A commercial and legal word for marking ownership.
John|6.plain: **Stamped and signed.** A stamp says who stands behind this. It does not say the thing is shut.
John|6.whyThis: Because sealed in English sounds like closing something, and the Greek verb is about stamping a mark of ownership or authentication on goods and documents.
John|6.others: Versions read sealed, set his seal on, or placed his seal of approval on.
John|6.seeing: Sphragizo is to affix a seal: to authenticate a document, to mark goods as owned, to certify. Paul uses it of believers being sealed with the Spirit. The sense is certification, not closure.
John|6.why: English seal kept the closure sense and largely lost the authentication one outside legal language.
John|6.rule: When an English word has narrowed to one of two senses, check which sense the ancient world used more. Commercial vocabulary usually survives in papyri.
John|6.choosing: Most modern versions print set his seal on; the King James reads sealed.

John|6.title: John 6:35
John|6.summary: I am the bread of life. The first of the predicate I am sayings.
John|6.plain: **I am the teacher.** **I am.** The first completes itself. The second does not, and that is a different kind of sentence.
John|6.whyThis: Because the same two words that stand alone at 8:58 here take a predicate, and knowing the difference between the two constructions is what keeps the absolute ones from being flattened.
John|6.others: Every version reads I am the bread of life.
John|6.seeing: Ego eimi followed by a predicate: bread, light, door, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. Seven of them in this Gospel. The absolute form with no predicate, as at 8:58, is a separate construction and the reaction to it is different.
John|6.why: English carries both fine. What English cannot do is signal that the two constructions are the same two words doing different jobs.
John|6.rule: Count both sets. The predicate sayings and the absolute sayings are a deliberate pair and only one of them gets people reaching for stones.
John|6.choosing: I am the bread of life is universal.

John|6.title: John 6:44
John|6.summary: Except the Father draw him. The verb is used of hauling a net and drawing a sword.
John|6.plain: **He drew the curtain.** **They dragged him out.** One English family, and the force in it depends entirely on what is being moved.
John|6.whyThis: Because the whole argument about whether the drawing is irresistible turns on a verb that is used elsewhere of dragging people into court and of hauling a full net ashore.
John|6.others: Every version reads draw or drag.
John|6.seeing: Helkuo is used of hauling a net at John 21:6 and 21:11, of drawing a sword at John 18:10, and of dragging people before magistrates at Acts 16:19. John 12:32 uses the same verb of drawing all people.
John|6.why: English draw covers the whole range too, from a gentle pull to a haul, so the range survives and the force is still decided by context rather than by the word.
John|6.rule: Listing every occurrence of a verb is more useful than any lexicon gloss, especially where a doctrine rests on how forceful it is.
John|6.choosing: Draw is the majority rendering; drag appears where the context is clearly violent.

John|6.title: John 6:51-58
John|6.summary: Whoso eateth my flesh. The verb changes at verse 54 to a word for chewing.
John|6.plain: **Eat** and **chew**. If a speaker switched from the first to the second halfway through an argument, you would hear it, and you would know he was pressing.
John|6.whyThis: Because John switches from the ordinary verb for eating to a blunter one in the middle of the discourse, and every English version prints eat for both, which erases the escalation.
John|6.seeing: Verses 50 to 53 use phago, the ordinary verb for eating. From verse 54 onward John switches to trogo, a verb that can carry a more physical, audible sense of eating but that Matthew 24:38 uses for entirely ordinary eating and drinking, so the switch by itself is not proof of a deliberate shift to gnawing. The switch coinciding with the offence in verse 60 is the stronger argument that it is doing rhetorical work.
John|6.why: English has chew, but it is too physical to print in a solemn discourse, so every version smooths it to eat and the escalation vanishes.
John|6.rule: When an audience reacts badly at a specific verse, look at what changed in the verses just before it.
John|6.choosing: Eat is universal in English versions. The verb change is noted in commentaries, and the NET Bible's own translator's notes flag it too, while cautioning that the switch may simply reflect a stylistic preference for one verb over the other rather than a deliberate escalation to gnawing.

John|6.title: John 6:63
John|6.summary: The flesh profiteth nothing. Said immediately after a discourse about eating flesh.
John|6.plain: **He is my own flesh and blood.** **The spirit is willing but the flesh is weak.** One English word, two unrelated ideas, and you sort them instantly by context.
John|6.whyThis: Because the word is sarx, the same noun used throughout the preceding paragraph, and the sentence either contradicts what has just been said or is using the word in its other sense.
John|6.seeing: Sarx covers meat, the physical body, and a whole orientation of life. Verses 51 to 58 use it in the first sense; verse 63 uses it in the last. The apparent contradiction dissolves once the range is in view and does not dissolve any other way.
John|6.why: English flesh has the same range, so the ambiguity is preserved rather than created. What English cannot do is mark which sense is in play.
John|6.rule: When a paragraph seems to contradict itself one verse later, check whether the shared word is being used in two of its senses.

John|6.title: John 6:70
John|6.summary: One of you is a devil. The Greek noun is slanderer, and it has no article here.
John|6.plain: **He is the accountant.** **He is an accountant.** One picks out a person, the other describes a kind. Greek marks that with the article and here there is none.
John|6.whyThis: Because the English word devil names a specific being and the Greek noun is a description, and the missing article is the same grammatical point as John 1:1.
John|6.others: The King James reads a devil. Modern versions read a devil or a slanderer, and some read the devil.
John|6.seeing: Diabolos means slanderer or accuser, and with the article it becomes the standard title for the accuser. Here it is anarthrous, which is why most versions print a devil rather than the devil.
John|6.why: English devil is only ever a title, so using it descriptively reads as an identification the Greek does not make.
John|6.rule: The same article rule that governs John 1:1 governs ordinary nouns everywhere else. Once you have it, it is reusable.
John|6.choosing: A devil is the majority rendering; a slanderer appears in more literal versions.

John|7.title: John 7:8
John|7.summary: I go not up yet unto this feast. Some manuscripts lack the word yet.
John|7.plain: A letter says **I'm not coming** in one copy and **I'm not coming yet** in another. One of those was easier for a copyist to live with.
John|7.whyThis: Because without yet the sentence is a statement he then reverses two verses later, and with it there is no difficulty at all. The manuscripts split on exactly the word that removes the problem.
John|7.others: The King James reads yet. Most modern versions also read yet; some footnote its absence.
John|7.seeing: Oupo, not yet, appears in P66, P75 and the majority. Ouk, not, appears in Sinaiticus and Codex Bezae. The harder reading is the one without yet, since a scribe has an obvious motive to add it and none to remove it.
John|7.why: Not a translation problem. The versions differ because the Greek texts do.
John|7.rule: The harder reading is usually the older one, because scribes smooth difficulties rather than create them. That principle cuts against the comfortable text here.
John|7.choosing: Yet is the majority rendering across English versions.

John|7.title: John 7:37-38
John|7.summary: Out of his belly shall flow rivers. Whose belly depends on where the sentence is punctuated.
John|7.plain: **Let him come to me and drink. He who believes in me, as the scripture said, out of his heart will flow rivers.** Move the stop one clause earlier and the rivers change owner.
John|7.whyThis: Because moving one stop changes whether the water flows from the believer or from Christ, and the Greek gives no punctuation at all.
John|7.others: Most versions punctuate so the believer is the source. A minority, and many commentators, punctuate so that Christ is.
John|7.seeing: The passage has no punctuation in the manuscripts. Read one way, he who believes is the subject of the flowing. Read the other, the believer is the one who comes and drinks and the rivers flow from Christ. Verse 39 explains the saying as about the Spirit, which bears on the choice without settling it.
John|7.why: English requires a stop somewhere. Wherever it goes, the reader inherits a decision made by an editor.
John|7.rule: Where a version's footnote offers an alternative punctuation, the sentence has two grammatically possible subjects and the printed one is a judgment.
John|7.choosing: The believer as source is the majority printed reading; the Christological punctuation appears in footnotes and in a substantial commentary tradition.

John|7.title: John 7:39
John|7.summary: The Holy Ghost was not yet given. The word given is not in the Greek.
John|7.plain: A sentence reads **he was not yet.** Three later copies read **not yet there**, **not yet given** and **not yet come**. The variety of the repairs is evidence of what the original said.
John|7.whyThis: Because the bare Greek says the Spirit was not yet, which is theologically awkward, and the manuscripts show scribes adding words to fix it in several different ways.
John|7.others: The King James supplies given in italics. Modern versions supply given or had not yet been given, usually without marking it.
John|7.seeing: The best manuscripts read oupo gar en pneuma, for the Spirit was not yet. Various manuscripts add given, holy, upon them, or come. When copies disagree about how to fix a difficulty, the unfixed reading is usually the original.
John|7.why: English cannot print the Spirit was not yet without it reading as a denial, so every version supplies something.
John|7.rule: Italics in a King James New Testament mark words the translators added. That convention is a gift and most readers have never been told what it means.
John|7.choosing: Given is the majority supplied word across English versions.

John|7.title: John 7:53-8:11
John|7.summary: The woman taken in adultery. The best manuscripts do not have this passage.
John|7.plain: A story appears in some old copies of a book, in different places, and in none of the oldest. It may still be a true story about the author's subject. Those are two different questions and most arguments collapse them.
John|7.whyThis: Because it is the most famous disputed passage in the New Testament, the evidence against it is strong, and the honest handling of it is a model for every other textual question.
John|7.others: Every modern version prints it, bracketed, with a note that the earliest manuscripts omit it. The King James prints it without comment.
John|7.seeing: The passage is absent from P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. Where it does appear, manuscripts place it after John 7:52, after John 7:36, after John 21:25, and after Luke 21:38, which is a strong sign of a floating tradition. The vocabulary and style differ from the rest of John.
John|7.why: Nothing here is a translation question. It is entirely about which Greek text is being translated and how honestly the uncertainty is printed.
John|7.rule: When a passage moves around between manuscripts, that movement is itself evidence. Stable text stays put.
