John|7.choosing: Every major English version prints it with brackets or a note; none omits it entirely.

John|8.title: John 8:12
John|8.summary: I am the light of the world. Said during a festival lit by enormous lamps.
John|8.plain: **I'm the one who turns the lights on.** Said in an empty room it is a boast. Said during a blackout it is something else.
John|8.whyThis: Because the saying is timed to a ritual, and the setting is what makes it a claim rather than a metaphor. The Greek is ordinary; the calendar is the information.
John|8.others: Every version reads I am the light of the world.
John|8.seeing: Another predicate I am saying. The context is the Feast of Tabernacles, during which great lamps were lit in the court of the women. Speaking these words in that courtyard at that feast is the point.
John|8.why: The words carry over fine. What's lost is the calendar, which no translation can supply.
John|8.rule: When a saying is dated to a festival, look up what happened at that festival. John dates his scenes carefully and rarely explains why.
John|8.choosing: I am the light of the world is universal.

John|8.title: John 8:24, 28
John|8.summary: If ye believe not that I am. Twice in five verses, with nothing after it.
John|8.plain: **Unless you believe that I am.** Your ear waits for the rest. There is no rest, and that is the construction.
John|8.whyThis: Because these are the absolute sayings, not the predicate ones, and every English version has to supply a word that is not there in order to make a sentence.
John|8.others: Versions supply he, or the one I claim to be, or he is, usually without marking it.
John|8.seeing: Ego eimi with no predicate at all, at verses 24 and 28, then again at 58. The Septuagint uses the same two words at Isaiah 43:10 for the divine self-declaration, which is the ground for reading these as more than a claim to identity.
John|8.why: English requires a completion after the verb to be. Any completion is supplied, and the supplied word is the interpretation.
John|8.rule: When a modern version prints words in italics or adds a footnote reading literally I am, the words are an addition and the bare Greek is the thing to notice.
John|8.choosing: I am he is the majority rendering; the one I claim to be is the NIV's expansion.

John|8.title: John 8:32-34
John|8.summary: The truth shall make you free. And the next sentence is about slavery, not about employment.
John|8.plain: **He's free now.** Free from what? The sentence only means something once you know what was holding him.
John|8.whyThis: Because free and slave are the pair the whole paragraph runs on, and English servant in the King James breaks the pair at exactly the verse where it matters.
John|8.others: The King James reads servant of sin. Modern versions read slave of sin, which keeps the pair intact.
John|8.seeing: Eleutheroo, to set free, and doulos, slave, are the two poles of the argument from verse 32 to verse 36. In Greek the reply in verse 33, we were never in bondage, uses the same root, so the whole exchange is one vocabulary.
John|8.why: English servant implies wages and the option of leaving, which removes the force of the contrast with freedom.
John|8.rule: When a paragraph turns on a contrast, check that both halves are rendered from the same word family. Breaking the family breaks the argument.
John|8.choosing: Modern versions overwhelmingly read slave here; the King James reads servant.

John|8.title: John 8:44
John|8.summary: A liar, and the father of it. The pronoun could be of it or of him.
John|8.plain: **He is the father of it.** Father of the lie, or father of the liar? English keeps the ambiguity here too, and versions still choose.
John|8.whyThis: Because the last clause of the verse is grammatically ambiguous in a way that produces two very different sentences, and English has to print one.
John|8.others: The King James reads the father of it. Most modern versions read the father of lies.
John|8.seeing: Autou can be neuter, of it, referring to the lie, or masculine, of him, referring to the liar. The clause reads he is a liar and the father of autou, and both parses are available.
John|8.why: English it and him force the choice, and the neuter and masculine forms are identical in Greek.
John|8.rule: Greek pronouns are often ambiguous between genders in the genitive. When two versions differ by a single pronoun, this is usually why.
John|8.choosing: The father of lies is the modern reading; the King James reads the father of it.

John|8.title: John 8:56
John|8.summary: Rejoiced to see my day. The verb is closer to exulted, and the seeing is aorist.
John|8.plain: **He was thrilled to see it.** **He was thrilled that he would see it.** English marks that with extra words. Greek marks it with the form of the verb.
John|8.whyThis: Because the sentence makes a claim about Abraham seeing something, and the tenses decide whether that is a past event or a hope.
John|8.others: Versions read rejoiced to see, or was glad that he would see.
John|8.seeing: Agalliaomai is to exult, a stronger verb than ordinary joy. The construction, hina with the aorist subjunctive ide, can mean rejoiced in order to see or rejoiced that he would see, and the following clause, he saw it and was glad, uses a plain aorist.
John|8.why: English has to supply a time relation between the rejoicing and the seeing that the Greek leaves for the reader.
John|8.rule: When two verbs sit next to each other and the versions differ about their order in time, look at the form of the second one.
John|8.choosing: Rejoiced to see is the majority rendering; that he would see appears in some modern versions.

John|8.title: John 8:58
John|8.summary: Before Abraham was, I am. The verb is wrong on purpose.
John|8.plain: **Before the war started, I am here.** Your ear rejects that, and rightly. A speaker who says it in front of you is not making a grammar mistake. They are doing something with the mistake.
John|8.whyThis: Because the crowd picks up stones in the next verse, which means they heard something the English barely registers. The offence is in a two-word phrase and a tense that does not agree with the rest of the sentence.
John|8.kjv: Jesus said unto them, Verily, verily, I say unto you, Before Abraham was, I am.
John|8.kjvWhy: the King James keeps the tense clash rather than smoothing it
John|8.others: Nearly every version reads I am. A handful render I have been, which repairs the grammar and removes the reason anyone reached for a stone.
John|8.seeing: Ego eimi is present tense against a past clause, which is ungrammatical in Greek as it is in English. The same two words render the divine name in the Septuagint at Exodus 3:14, and they run through this Gospel as a formula. The crowd's reaction in verse 59 is the commentary.
John|8.why: English can print the clash, but English readers absorb it as odd phrasing rather than as a claim, because English has no formula attached to those two words.
John|8.rule: When a sentence is grammatically broken in the original and the crowd reacts violently, the breakage is the message. Translations that repair the grammar delete the evidence.
John|8.choosing: I have been is smoother and loses the formula. I am is rough and keeps it. The stones in verse 59 are the argument for keeping it.

John|9.title: John 9:7
John|9.summary: Siloam, which is by interpretation, Sent. John stops to translate again.
John|9.plain: A writer who stops to translate a place name is telling you two things: what it means, and that he expects you not to know.
John|9.whyThis: Because John supplies the meaning of the pool's name in the middle of the narrative, and the word he gives it is the word he has used of Jesus throughout the Gospel.
John|9.others: Every version keeps the gloss, since it is in the text.
John|9.seeing: Siloam is from Hebrew shiloach, from the root to send. John glosses it apestalmenos, sent, which is the perfect participle of the verb he uses of Jesus being sent by the Father over forty times in this Gospel.
John|9.why: Nothing is lost. The connection between the gloss and John's vocabulary elsewhere is the part that has to be noticed rather than translated.
John|9.rule: When a writer glosses a name, check whether the gloss uses vocabulary he uses elsewhere. The translation may be doing double duty.
John|9.choosing: The gloss is printed in every version.

John|9.title: John 9:22
John|9.summary: Put out of the synagogue. A compound word that appears nowhere before John.
John|9.plain: A word that appears nowhere earlier can mean the writer coined it, or that the thing it names was new, or simply that nothing else survives. Those are three different conclusions from one fact.
John|9.whyThis: Because the term has been used to argue that this Gospel was written late, after a formal expulsion policy existed, and the whole argument rests on one rare adjective.
John|9.others: Versions read put out of the synagogue, or excommunicated.
John|9.seeing: Aposunagogos occurs three times, all in John, and nowhere else in Greek literature before him. Whether it reflects a formal first-century policy or an informal local exclusion is argued at length, and the dating of the Gospel is often attached to the answer.
John|9.why: No single English word covers it, so every version uses a phrase, and the fact that the Greek is one coined word disappears.
John|9.rule: When a word occurs only in one author, the absence of other witnesses is a fact about what survives as much as about what existed.
John|9.choosing: Put out of the synagogue is the majority rendering.

John|9.title: John 9:38-39
John|9.summary: Lord, I believe. And he worshipped him. Some manuscripts do not have it.
John|9.plain: A story's last line is missing from two old copies. That is uncomfortable, and it is still evidence.
John|9.whyThis: Because the climax of the chapter, the man's confession and worship, is absent from several early witnesses, and this is a variant that cuts against a conclusion most readers would want to keep.
John|9.others: Every English version prints it. A minority footnote its absence.
John|9.seeing: The words are absent from P75, Sinaiticus in its original hand, and a few others, and present in the great majority. Most editors keep them; some argue they were added to round the narrative off.
John|9.why: Not a translation question. The versions almost all follow the longer text.
John|9.rule: Variants that remove something a reader wants are the ones worth knowing about, because nobody advertises them.
John|9.choosing: The longer text is the overwhelming majority reading in English versions.

John|10.title: John 10:11
John|10.summary: The good shepherd. The adjective is not the ordinary word for good.
John|10.plain: **A good man.** **A good knife.** English uses one word and you know which is meant. Greek has two and the speaker has to choose.
John|10.whyThis: Because Greek has two common adjectives for good and John picks the one about being fine, fit for purpose, admirable, rather than the one about moral goodness.
John|10.seeing: Kalos is beautiful, fine, excellent, fit. Agathos is morally good. The shepherd is kalos, the model shepherd, the one who does the job as it should be done, and the definition given in the same verse is that he lays down his life.
John|10.why: English good covers both and nothing is lost in accuracy, but the choice John made is invisible.
John|10.rule: Where a language has two adjectives for one English word, the one not chosen tells you as much as the one chosen.
John|10.choosing: Good shepherd is universal; model shepherd and true shepherd appear in commentaries.

John|10.title: John 10:16
John|10.summary: One fold, and one shepherd. The Greek uses two different nouns and the King James uses one.
John|10.plain: **One pen** and **one herd** are not the same claim. One is about the enclosure. The other is about the animals.
John|10.whyThis: Because the verse in English says one fold where the Greek says one flock, and the difference has been used in ecclesiastical argument for centuries. This is a rare case of a genuine mistranslation with consequences.
John|10.others: The King James reads one fold. Every modern version reads one flock.
John|10.seeing: The first noun in the verse is aule, a fold or enclosure. The second is poimne, a flock. The Greek says other sheep not of this aule, and they shall become one poimne, one shepherd. The King James printed fold for both, following the Vulgate's ovile.
John|10.why: English has both words. The error is not in the language but in the 1611 rendering, which follows the Latin rather than the Greek.
John|10.rule: Where the King James follows the Vulgate against the Greek, a real correction is available and the modern versions have made it.
John|10.choosing: One flock is what modern versions overwhelmingly print, and outside the King James tradition the correction is universal.

John|10.title: John 10:29
John|10.summary: My Father, which gave them me, is greater than all. The manuscripts disagree about what is greater.
John|10.plain: **What my father gave me is greater than anything.** **My father, who gave it to me, is greater than anyone.** One word of difference, two sentences.
John|10.whyThis: Because the variants make the subject either the Father or the gift, and the two readings say different things about what cannot be taken away.
John|10.others: The King James and NIV read my Father is greater than all. The NRSV and NET read what my Father has given me is greater than all.
John|10.seeing: The variants concern the gender and number of the relative pronoun and the adjective. One family gives the Father as the subject of is greater; another gives the flock. Both are well attested and the editors divide.
John|10.why: Not a translation problem. The versions differ because the Greek texts do.
John|10.rule: When versions differ about who the subject of a sentence is, look for a pronoun variant rather than a translation choice.
John|10.choosing: My Father is greater than all is the majority rendering in English versions.

John|11.title: John 11:3, 5, 36
John|11.summary: Both love-words, one chapter, the same relationship. Whatever they are doing, they are not ranking it.
John|11.plain: If someone calls the same person **my mate** in one sentence and **my friend** two sentences later, you do not conclude the friendship got upgraded. Same thing here, except a lot of sermons draw exactly that conclusion.
John|11.whyThis: Because this is the control experiment for the whole agapao-phileo argument. One chapter, one relationship, both verbs. If you learn only one passage on the love words, learn the one that tests the claim rather than the one that launched it.
John|11.kjv: Lord, behold, he whom thou lovest is sick. ... Now Jesus loved Martha, and her sister, and Lazarus. ... Then said the Jews, Behold how he loved him!
John|11.others: No English version distinguishes them, and almost no study Bible notes that both appear here.
John|11.seeing: Verse 3 uses phileo, on the sisters' lips. Verse 5 uses agapao, in the narrator's voice, about the same three people. Verse 36 uses phileo again, on the crowd's lips. One relationship, one chapter, both verbs.
John|11.why: English merges the two, so an English reader cannot see the alternation at all, and therefore cannot see that it does not line up with any hierarchy.
John|11.rule: Before accepting that two words rank each other, find a passage where both are used of the same thing. If the ranking survives that, it is real. Here it does not.
John|11.choosing: There is no dispute in the text. The dispute is in the pulpit, and this chapter is the cleanest evidence against the claim that agapao is the higher love and phileo the lesser one. It is the same evidence that John 21 supplies, in a different book of the same Gospel.

John|11.title: John 11:33
John|11.summary: He groaned in the spirit. The verb is an anger word, not a grief word.
John|11.plain: **He was moved.** **He bristled.** Two very different reactions, and English has both words available.
John|11.whyThis: Because the English suggests deep sadness and the Greek verb is used of snorting, of stern warning, and of indignation. Whatever Jesus was feeling at the tomb, the word is not simply sorrow.
John|11.others: The King James reads groaned in the spirit. Modern versions read deeply moved, or greatly disturbed, and some footnote angry.
John|11.seeing: Embrimaomai is used of a horse snorting and of giving a stern charge. At Mark 1:43 and Matthew 9:30 it carries sternness. Here and at verse 38 it is paired with troubled himself, and translators who print deeply moved are smoothing a word that ordinarily carries indignation.
John|11.why: No English verb for anger also carries the sense of being inwardly shaken, so every rendering picks one and drops the other.
John|11.rule: When a version's footnote offers angry as an alternative to moved, the word ordinarily means the first and the text has been softened.
John|11.choosing: Deeply moved is the modern reading; the King James reads groaned; angry appears in footnotes.

John|11.title: John 11:35
John|11.summary: Jesus wept. A different verb from the weeping of everyone else in the scene.
John|11.plain: **She was wailing.** **He shed tears.** Two different sounds, and English has words for both.
John|11.whyThis: Because the shortest verse in the English Bible uses a verb that occurs only here in the New Testament, and the mourners two verses earlier are described with a different one.
John|11.seeing: Dakruo, to shed tears, occurs only here in the New Testament. The mourners at verse 33 klaio, which is loud lamentation. The contrast between the professional wailing and the quiet tears is in the vocabulary.
John|11.why: English wept covers both, so the contrast is invisible and the verse reads as the same activity as everyone else's.
John|11.rule: When a narrative uses two different verbs for what looks like the same action, the difference is usually the description.

John|11.title: John 11:48
John|11.summary: The Romans shall come and take away both our place and nation.
John|11.plain: **The House voted.** **Downing Street responded.** English uses places for institutions constantly, and only insiders catch every one.
John|11.whyThis: Because place here is almost certainly the temple, and nothing in the English tips off the reader that a common noun is being used as a euphemism.
John|11.others: Every version reads our place, and some footnote temple.
John|11.seeing: Topos, place, is used in Jewish Greek as a way of referring to the temple without naming it, as at Acts 6:13-14 and 21:28. The Sanhedrin is worrying about the sanctuary and the nation, which is exactly what happened in AD 70.
John|11.why: English place is too general, so the specific reference is lost unless a footnote supplies it.
John|11.rule: Common nouns used as institutional euphemisms are invisible to outsiders. When a sentence seems oddly vague, ask what it was polite not to name.
John|11.choosing: Our place is the majority rendering; our temple appears in some modern versions and in footnotes.

John|12.title: John 12:3
John|12.summary: Ointment of spikenard, very costly. The adjective is a word nobody has settled.
John|12.plain: A recipe with one ingredient nobody can identify. You can still cook it. You just cannot say what it was.
John|12.whyThis: Because the description of the perfume contains a word that may mean pure, or genuine, or liquid, or may be a place name, and no one knows.
John|12.others: Versions read pure nard, genuine nard, or expensive perfume made of pure nard.
John|12.seeing: Pistikes qualifies the nard. Proposals include faithful hence genuine, from pistis; liquid, from a different root; a place of origin; and a trade term. All are guesses and the lexicons say so.
John|12.why: English has to print something, and pure is the usual guess with no marker that it is one.
John|12.rule: When a lexicon entry lists four unrelated possibilities, the word is undetermined and your translation has quietly chosen one.
John|12.choosing: Pure nard is the majority modern rendering.

John|12.title: John 12:32
John|12.summary: I will draw all men unto me. The same verb as the drawing in chapter six.
John|12.plain: **He pulled them in.** Said of a fisherman and of a preacher, and the force differs entirely with the object.
John|12.whyThis: Because the two verses use one verb about two different subjects, and reading them together is how you find out how forceful the word is.
John|12.others: Versions read draw all people, or draw everyone. All men in the King James; all people in most modern versions.
John|12.seeing: Helkuo again, as at 6:44. Here the subject is Christ lifted up and the object is all. Whether all means all without exception or all without distinction is the argument, and the verb does not settle it.
John|12.why: English draw carries the same range, so the question is preserved rather than created.
John|12.rule: Read every occurrence of a verb across a book before deciding how strong it is. One verse is not a sample.
John|12.choosing: Draw all people is what most modern versions print; all men is the King James.

John|12.title: John 12:41
John|12.summary: When he saw his glory. Some manuscripts read when, others read because.
John|12.plain: **He said this when he saw it.** **He said this because he saw it.** One conjunction, two different sentences.
John|12.whyThis: Because the verse identifies whose glory Isaiah saw, and a one-word variant changes it from a statement about timing to a statement about cause.
John|12.others: The King James reads when. Most modern versions read because.
John|12.seeing: Hote, when, appears in the later majority; hoti, because, in P66, P75, Sinaiticus and Vaticanus. The two words differ by one letter. Either way the verse says Isaiah saw his glory and spoke of him, which is a striking identification of the figure in Isaiah 6.
John|12.why: Not a translation question. The conjunction printed follows the Greek text chosen.
John|12.rule: Single-letter variants between common conjunctions are among the most frequent in the manuscripts, and they change sentences more than their size suggests.
John|12.choosing: Because is how most modern versions render it; when is the King James.

John|13.title: John 13:1
John|13.summary: He loved them unto the end. To the finish, or to the utmost.
John|13.plain: **She went to the end.** Until it was over, or as far as anyone could go? English has the same double meaning and usually leaves you to work it out from context. Here the context does not settle it.
John|13.whyThis: Because the phrase opens the second half of the Gospel and sets the tone for everything after it, and it can mean a limit of time or a limit of degree. The chapter that follows is built on whichever one you pick.
John|13.kjv: having loved his own which were in the world, he loved them unto the end.
John|13.kjvWhy: unto the end keeps the ambiguity the modern renderings resolve
John|13.others: The King James and ESV read to the end. The NIV reads the full extent of his love. The NASB reads to the end and footnotes perfectly.
John|13.seeing: Eis telos can be temporal, to the last, or intensive, completely, utterly. Telos itself means both a finish and a goal, which is the same range that makes Romans 10:4 an argument.
John|13.why: English end carries both, but the phrase to the end has hardened into the temporal sense, so a reader gets one of the two for free and never sees the other.
John|13.rule: When you meet a word twice in a tool, the second meeting is the test. You already know telos splits between finish and goal. Watch it split again here.
John|13.choosing: Temporal fits the narrative, which is moving toward the cross. Intensive fits the foot-washing that immediately follows, which is an act of love taken to its limit. Both are defensible and the Greek allows either.

John|13.title: John 13:10
John|13.summary: He that is washed needeth not save to wash his feet. Some copies lack the feet.
John|13.plain: A sentence with three extra words in some copies and not others. Which version a scribe was more likely to produce is the whole question.
John|13.whyThis: Because the shorter reading makes a general statement about cleansing and the longer one makes a specific point about the foot-washing, and the manuscripts split.
John|13.others: Most versions print except for his feet. A minority footnote its absence.
John|13.seeing: Ei me tous podas, except the feet, is absent from Sinaiticus, a Vulgate manuscript and some Old Latin witnesses. Its presence makes the sentence about the immediate scene; its absence makes it about bathing in general.
John|13.why: Not a translation question. English follows whichever Greek text is chosen.
John|13.rule: When a short phrase is missing from a few early witnesses, weigh whether a scribe was more likely to add a clarification or to drop one.
John|13.choosing: Except for his feet is the majority reading in English versions.

John|13.title: John 13:34
John|13.summary: A new commandment. The word for new means fresh in kind, not recent in time.
John|13.plain: **A new car.** **A new lease of life.** One means recently made. The other means a fresh kind of the same thing. English uses one word for both.
John|13.whyThis: Because Greek has two adjectives for new and this is the one about quality rather than chronology, which is the difference between a commandment nobody has heard and one that has been renewed.
John|13.seeing: Kainos is new in kind, fresh, of a different quality. Neos is new in time, recent. The commandment to love is not chronologically new, since Leviticus 19:18 has it, and kainos is the adjective that lets it be both old and new, which is exactly the point 1 John 2:7-8 makes.
John|13.why: English new covers both, so the paradox in 1 John reads as a contradiction rather than as a play on two available adjectives.
John|13.rule: A New Testament writer who seems to contradict himself about whether something is new is usually just switching adjectives; check which one he used.

John|14.title: John 14:1-2
John|14.summary: Ye believe in God, believe also in me. Both verbs could be statements or commands.
John|14.plain: **You trust him. Trust me.** **Trust him and trust me.** **You trust him and you trust me.** Same two words each time, arranged by punctuation and mood.
John|14.whyThis: Because the forms are identical either way, and the four possible combinations give four different sentences, one of which is the King James and another is the NIV.
John|14.others: The King James reads ye believe in God, believe also in me. The NIV reads you believe in God; believe also in me. Others read believe in God, believe also in me, as two commands.
John|14.seeing: Pisteuete is identical as an indicative and an imperative. Both verbs in the verse carry the ambiguity, which yields four grammatically available sentences, and translations have printed at least three of them.
John|14.why: English distinguishes a statement from a command by word order and punctuation, so printing the verse settles it.
John|14.rule: Where the same Greek form is both a statement and a command, look for whether the context is reassurance or instruction. Sometimes it is genuinely both.
John|14.choosing: Two imperatives is the most common modern rendering; the King James takes the first as a statement.

John|14.title: John 14:2
John|14.summary: In my Father's house are many mansions. The noun means a place to stay.
John|14.plain: **Lodgings.** **Quarters.** Neither says anything about grandeur. Mansion did not either, in 1611.
John|14.whyThis: Because mansions in modern English means large houses and the Greek noun means a dwelling place or a stopping place on a journey, which is a different picture entirely.
John|14.others: The King James reads mansions. Modern versions read rooms, dwelling places, or abiding places.
John|14.seeing: Mone is from meno, to remain, and means a place of staying. The related verb runs through chapter 15 as abide. The Latin mansiones, from which the King James mansions comes, meant stopping places on a road.
John|14.why: English mansion has grown from a dwelling into a large house, so the verse now promises architecture rather than a place with the Father.
John|14.rule: When a King James word describes something grand, check whether it was grand in 1611. Several of these words have inflated rather than narrowed.
John|14.choosing: Rooms and dwelling places are what most modern versions print; mansions is the King James.

John|14.title: John 14:16
John|14.summary: Comforter, Helper, Advocate, Counselor, Paraclete. Six versions, six words, one Greek noun nobody can carry.
John|14.plain: **Bring me another chair.** Do you mean one more of these chairs, or a different sort of chair entirely? English uses one word for both and lets you work it out. Greek has two, and the speaker has to pick before the sentence leaves his mouth.
John|14.whyThis: Because the noun has no English equivalent at all, and the six versions on your shelf print six different words for it. When translators cannot agree on a single word for a person of the Trinity, that is worth ten minutes of your time. The adjective in front of it is doing quiet work too, and nobody mentions it.
John|14.kjv: And I will pray the Father, and he shall give you another Comforter, that he may abide with you for ever.
John|14.kjvWhy: Comforter meant strengthener in 1611, from Latin fortis, and now means someone who pats your hand
John|14.others: King James reads Comforter. The ESV and NASB read Helper. The NIV reads Advocate. The NRSV reads Advocate. Older Catholic versions keep Paraclete untranslated, which is the honest surrender.
John|14.seeing: Two things at once. Parakletos is built from para, alongside, and kaleo, to call: one called alongside. In ordinary Greek it was close to a legal supporter, someone who stands with you in a proceeding, which is why Advocate keeps turning up. And the adjective is allos, another of the same kind, rather than heteros, another of a different kind. Jesus is not promising a substitute of a different sort. He is promising another like himself.
John|14.why: English has no noun that covers legal advocate, personal encourager and one who is summoned to stand beside you. Every version picks the shade it thinks matters most and loses the other two. And English lost the distinction between the two kinds of another somewhere in its history, so the adjective disappears entirely.
John|14.rule: When translations scatter this widely on one noun, stop looking for the right English word. There is not one. Learn what the Greek noun covers and read all the renderings as partial views of it.
John|14.choosing: Comforter was accurate when comfort meant to strengthen, from the same root as fortify, and it has since drifted to consolation. Helper is broad enough to be safe and vague enough to be weak. Advocate captures the legal sense and drops the personal one. Paraclete admits defeat and makes the reader look it up, which is arguably the most honest of the four.

John|15.title: John 15:2
John|15.summary: Every branch that beareth not fruit he taketh away. The verb also means lifts up.
John|15.plain: **He picked up the coat.** **He picked up the litter.** Same verb, and one means raising something and the other means removing it. Only the object and the situation tell you which.
John|15.whyThis: Because the two readings are pastorally opposite. One has God removing unfruitful branches, the other has Him lifting them off the ground so they can bear. One verb, and the difference is whether the verse is a threat or a rescue.
John|15.kjv: Every branch in me that beareth not fruit he taketh away.
John|15.kjvWhy: taketh away is the reading almost every English Bible carries, and it is one of two
John|15.others: Nearly every version reads takes away or cuts off. A minority of commentators and study notes argue for lifts up. No major version prints it.
John|15.seeing: Airo means to lift, to raise, to carry, and also to take away or remove. It is the verb used for taking up a bed at John 5:8 and for taking away sin at John 1:29. Vinedressers did lift trailing branches off the ground so they could fruit, which is the practical case for the other reading.
John|15.why: No English verb means lift-and-therefore-carry-off. Pick up comes close, and reads too casual for the register.
John|15.rule: When a verb covers both raising and removing, the choice is usually made by what the interpreter already thinks the passage is about. That is worth noticing in yourself before you settle it.
John|15.choosing: Takes away has the weight of usage, the parallel with the burning in verse 6, and nearly every translation. Lifts up has the horticulture and a kinder reading of the chapter. The lexicon permits both and the context leans toward the first.

John|15.title: John 15:5
John|15.summary: Without me ye can do nothing. The preposition is closer to apart from.
John|15.plain: **Without a coat.** **Apart from the tree.** The first is missing something. The second is detached from it.
John|15.whyThis: Because without in English suggests lacking assistance, and the Greek phrase is about separation, which is the image the whole vine passage is built on.
John|15.others: The King James reads without me. Modern versions read apart from me.
John|15.seeing: Choris means separated from, apart from. In a passage about branches being cut off, the spatial sense is doing the work, and without flattens it to lacking.
John|15.why: English without covers both absence and separation and defaults to absence.
John|15.rule: In a passage built on one image, prepositions usually belong to the image. Read them spatially first.
John|15.choosing: Apart from me is how most modern versions read it; without me is the King James.

John|16.title: John 16:8
John|16.summary: Reprove the world of sin. One verb, three objects, and no agreed rendering.
John|16.plain: **He showed them up.** **He talked them round.** Two different operations, and English keeps them apart.
John|16.whyThis: Because the verb can mean convict, convince, expose or reprove, and which one is chosen decides whether the Spirit is persuading the world or prosecuting it.
John|16.others: The King James reads reprove. Modern versions read convict, prove the world to be in the wrong, or convince.
John|16.seeing: Elencho covers exposing a fault, convicting in a legal sense, and convincing someone of the truth. All three senses are attested and the verse gives no decisive context, which is why the versions scatter.
John|16.why: English has separate words for each sense and no word that covers all three, so the translator must choose.
John|16.rule: When four versions give four different verbs, the Greek word covers all four and none of them is wrong.
John|16.choosing: Convict is the modern reading; reprove is the King James; prove the world to be in the wrong is the NIV's expansion.

John|16.title: John 16:13
John|16.summary: He will shew you things to come. The verb is announce, and the phrase need not mean prediction.
John|16.plain: **What's coming** can mean next week or it can mean the thing already on its way down the track.
John|16.whyThis: Because things to come reads as foretelling the future, and the Greek phrase can equally mean the things that are coming, meaning what is about to happen in the events of the passion and after.
John|16.others: Versions read things to come, what is yet to come, or things that are coming.
John|16.seeing: Ta erchomena is a participle, the coming things. Anangello is to announce or report rather than to predict. Together they may point at the events immediately ahead rather than at the future in general.
John|16.why: English things to come defaults to prophecy, so a phrase about imminent events reads as a promise of foresight.
John|16.rule: Participles used as nouns are usually about what is happening rather than about a fixed category. The coming things is a description, not a genre.
John|16.choosing: What is yet to come is what most modern versions print.

John|17.title: John 17:3
John|17.summary: This is life eternal, that they might know thee. Knowing here is relational, not informational.
John|17.plain: **I know him.** **I know about him.** English has the distinction and uses about to mark it. Hebrew and Greek lean on context instead.
John|17.whyThis: Because the verse defines eternal life, and the definition is a verb that in Hebrew usage means acquaintance and relationship rather than possession of facts.
John|17.seeing: Ginosko translates Hebrew yada, which covers experiential acquaintance, including intimacy. The verse defines the life not by duration but by relationship, which is the strongest internal argument for reading aionios as quality rather than length.
John|17.why: English know covers both senses, so nothing is lost in the word. What is lost is the Hebrew background that makes the relational sense the default.
John|17.rule: When a verse defines a term, the definition outranks every lexicon. John 17:3 defines eternal life inside the text.

John|17.title: John 17:5
John|17.summary: The glory which I had with thee before the world was. Glory again, and para with the dative.
John|17.plain: **He had it with him.** Alongside, in company. Not sent from a distance.
John|17.whyThis: Because the preposition places the glory alongside the Father rather than merely coming from him, echoing the relational placement of John 1:1b even though the Greek construction there, pros with the accusative, is not literally the same as this verse's para with the dative.
John|17.others: Every version reads with thee or in your presence.
John|17.seeing: Para with the dative means beside, in the presence of. The same relational placement as pros ton theon at John 1:1, and the pairing of that verse with this one is the frame of the whole Gospel.
John|17.why: English with is flat enough to carry it, but the deliberate echo of the prologue is not visible.
John|17.rule: When a Gospel's last discourse uses the vocabulary of its opening, the echo is structural. Look for the prologue in the prayer.
John|17.choosing: With you is the majority rendering.

John|18.title: John 18:5-6
John|18.summary: I am he. And they went backward and fell to the ground.
John|18.plain: **I am.** Nobody falls over at a name. The narrator reports a reaction that the printed English does not explain.
John|18.whyThis: Because the arresting party falls over at a two-word answer, and the he is supplied by the translator. The reaction is the strongest internal evidence for how these two words were heard.
John|18.others: Every version supplies he. The reaction in verse 6 is printed unexplained.
John|18.seeing: Ego eimi absolute, twice. Verse 6 then reports that they drew back and fell. John does not comment. The pattern of the absolute sayings through the Gospel, and the Septuagint background at Exodus 3:14 and Isaiah 43:10, is the explanation on offer.
John|18.why: English requires a completion after the verb, so the two-word answer becomes a three-word identification and the reaction stops making sense.
John|18.rule: When a narrative reports a reaction that the English does not account for, look at what was actually said in the original.
John|18.choosing: I am he is the majority rendering.

John|18.title: John 18:28
John|18.summary: Lest they should be defiled. A purity concern stated without explanation.
John|18.plain: A writer who explains one custom and not another is telling you which one he expected you to know.
John|18.whyThis: Because the narrator assumes you know why entering a Gentile building would defile a Jew before Passover, and the assumption dates and places the audience.
John|18.others: Every version reads that they might not be defiled.
John|18.seeing: Miaino, to defile. Entering a Gentile dwelling rendered a Jew ritually unclean, which would have barred participation in the Passover. John glosses Aramaic words for his readers and does not gloss this, which is itself information about what he assumed.
John|18.why: The words themselves lose nothing. It's the background no translation supplies.
John|18.rule: Track what a writer explains and what he does not. The unexplained things tell you about his readers.
John|18.choosing: That they might not be defiled is the majority rendering.

John|19.title: John 19:13
John|19.summary: The Pavement, but in the Hebrew, Gabbatha. Another gloss, in the other direction.
John|19.plain: Writing **the Underground, or as Americans say the subway** tells a reader where you think they live.
John|19.whyThis: Because here John gives the Greek name first and then the Semitic one, which is the reverse of his usual order and tells you which name his readers would recognise.
John|19.seeing: Lithostrotos is Greek for a stone pavement. Gabbatha is Aramaic, probably meaning a ridge or height, and it is not a translation of the Greek but a different name for the same place. John calls it Hebrew, which in this period regularly means Aramaic.
John|19.why: Nothing is lost. The reversal of order and the fact that the two names are not equivalents are the details worth noticing.
John|19.rule: When a writer gives two names for one place, check whether the second translates the first or merely renames it. Often it renames.
John|19.choosing: Both names are printed in every version; Aramaic appears in modern footnotes where the text says Hebrew.

John|19.title: John 19:17
John|19.summary: Golgotha, that is to say, a place of a skull. And John says it the other way round.
John|19.plain: Two glosses in one chapter, in opposite orders, is a pattern rather than a habit.
John|19.whyThis: Because the gloss is given in the usual direction here, Semitic first and Greek second, which makes the reversal four verses earlier worth noticing rather than accidental.
John|19.seeing: Golgotha is Aramaic gulgolta, skull. John glosses it kraniou topos, place of a skull. Latin calvaria gives the English Calvary, which enters through the Vulgate and appears in the King James only at Luke 23:33.
John|19.why: Nothing is lost. Calvary being a Latin word rather than a biblical name is the part most readers have never been told.
John|19.rule: When an English Bible has a familiar name that appears only once, check whether it came in through Latin.
John|19.choosing: Golgotha with the gloss is universal; Calvary appears only in the King James at Luke 23:33.

John|19.title: John 19:30
John|19.summary: It is finished. One word, in a tense that means done and still in force.
John|19.plain: **I locked the door.** That tells you about a moment. **The door is locked.** That tells you about now. Imagine one verb form that says both at once, and imagine it being the last thing someone says.
John|19.whyThis: Because the last word Jesus speaks in this Gospel is one Greek word in a tense English does not have, and the tense is the whole content. Finished as an event is not what it says. Finished and still standing is.
John|19.kjv: When Jesus therefore had received the vinegar, he said, It is finished: and he bowed his head, and gave up the ghost.
John|19.kjvWhy: it is finished is the closest English gets, and it is three words for one
John|19.others: Every version reads it is finished or it is completed. None can carry the tense, and none tries.
John|19.seeing: Tetelestai is perfect tense, passive voice, third person singular. The Greek perfect describes a completed action whose result stands in the present. A popular preaching tradition also holds that tetelestai was written across settled commercial accounts of the period, meaning paid in full; that specific claim traces to a misreading of ancient tax receipts, whose actual abbreviation is a different word, tetelonetai, toll or tax paid, and current papyrological work treats paid in full as a popular legend rather than established usage.
John|19.why: There's no single English word for a completed act with a standing result. It is finished is a present statement about a past act, which is nearer than most languages get, and still two ideas stapled together.
John|19.rule: Greek perfect tense is the one aspect English genuinely cannot carry. When a verse feels like it is saying more than the words do, check whether the verb is perfect.
John|19.choosing: The grammar itself is not in question; every version makes the same perfect-tense compromise. The popular commercial paid in full gloss, often used to make that compromise vivid, is itself disputed and probably should not be leaned on.

John|20.title: John 20:17
John|20.summary: Touch me not. The Greek is stop doing what you are already doing.
John|20.plain: **Do not shout.** **Stop shouting.** The first is a rule for the future. The second says you are shouting right now and should quit. English uses different words. Greek uses different tenses of one verb.
John|20.whyThis: Because the traditional rendering makes Jesus refuse to be touched, which contradicts the invitation to Thomas eight verses later. The contradiction is manufactured by an English tense.
John|20.kjv: Jesus saith unto her, Touch me not; for I am not yet ascended to my Father.
John|20.kjvWhy: touch me not created a four-century problem that the Greek does not contain
John|20.others: The King James reads touch me not. Modern versions read do not cling to me, do not hold on to me, or stop clinging to me. The correction is now near-universal.
John|20.seeing: Haptou is a present imperative with a negative. In Greek that construction ordinarily means stop an action in progress rather than forbid one not yet begun. Mary is already holding him. The command is to let go, not to keep away.
John|20.why: English negative commands have no aspect. Do not touch me is the same shape whether the touching has started or not, so a translator must add words like stop or cling to carry it.
John|20.rule: A negated present imperative in Greek usually means stop. A negated aorist subjunctive usually means do not start. That single distinction fixes a surprising number of hard verses.
John|20.choosing: There is no real dispute left. The King James rendering reflects a grammatical understanding that has since been refined, and every modern version has moved.

John|20.title: John 20:28
John|20.summary: My Lord and my God. Both nouns have the article, which is the point.
John|20.plain: **My manager and my friend.** Both definite, both addressed to one person standing there. Nothing hedged.
John|20.whyThis: Because this is the clearest confession in the Gospel and it is grammatically the mirror image of John 1:1: there the predicate lacked the article, here both nouns have it and are addressed directly.
John|20.others: Every version reads my Lord and my God.
John|20.seeing: Ho kurios mou kai ho theos mou. Both nouns articular, both with the possessive, and the sentence is addressed to Jesus, which the narrative states. Read with John 1:1, the Gospel opens and closes on the same claim made in two different constructions.
John|20.why: English carries this accurately. What English cannot show is that the grammar here is the counterpart of the prologue.
John|20.rule: When a book's last confession uses the vocabulary of its first sentence, the pair is the structure of the book.
John|20.choosing: My Lord and my God is universal.

John|21.title: John 21:15-17
John|21.summary: Two different Greek words for love, and the sermon you have heard about them is probably overselling it.
John|21.plain: **He sipped his coffee, then he drank his tea.** Did the writer mean something by sip against drink, or was he just avoiding saying drink twice? Good writers vary words for the sound of it. Before you build anything on a word change, check whether the writer changed other words in the same breath.
John|21.whyThis: Because this is the most-preached Greek word study in the English-speaking church, and it is the one most likely to be wrong. Learning why it fails teaches you the test you will apply to every word study you hear afterward, which is worth more than the passage itself.
John|21.kjv: Simon, son of Jonas, lovest thou me more than these?
John|21.others: No English version distinguishes the two verbs, because English has one word. Study Bibles and pulpits supply the distinction instead.
John|21.seeing: Jesus asks twice using agapao and once using phileo. Peter answers all three times with phileo. The standard sermon builds a hierarchy out of this, with agapao as the higher divine love and phileo as mere friendship.
John|21.why: English has one verb where Greek has several, so the variation vanishes. That is a real loss. The question is whether anything was in it.
John|21.rule: Before building a doctrine on a word change, check whether the writer varies other words in the same passage. John does, four times over in these three verses, and nobody preaches on those.
John|21.choosing: John also swaps two words for sheep, two for know, and two for feed and tend in the same exchange. None of those carry theological weight, which makes it hard to argue that one of the five variations is loaded and the other four are style. The honest verdict is that the distinction is probably stylistic, that the Septuagint and Koine use the two verbs largely interchangeably, and that This record exists to show you what a divergence looks like when it turns out not to matter.

John|21.title: John 21:15-17b
John|21.summary: Feed my lambs, tend my sheep. Four words vary, not two.
John|21.plain: A writer who swaps four pairs of words in three sentences is avoiding repetition. A writer who swaps one is making a point.
John|21.whyThis: Because the famous variation is the two love-words, and John also varies the word for sheep, the word for know, and the word for feed in the same three verses. That is the evidence that the variation is style.
John|21.others: No version distinguishes any of the pairs, because English has one word for each.
John|21.seeing: Three pairs beyond the love verbs: bosko and poimaino for feed and tend, arnia and probata for lambs and sheep, oida and ginosko for know. All four variations run through the same exchange.
John|21.why: English has one word for each pair, so all four variations vanish and only the first is ever preached.
John|21.rule: Before building on one word change, count the others in the same passage. Four is a style. One is an argument.
John|21.choosing: Feed and take care of are the majority renderings; no version marks any of the pairs.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:1a
Genesis|1.summary: In the beginning, or when God began. The first word is shaped like half a phrase.
Genesis|1.plain: **In the beginning.** Beginning of what? English lets you leave that open. Hebrew usually does not, because a word like that normally has to be attached to something, the way **the top of** needs a stair.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the first three words of the Bible can be read as a complete sentence or as the opening half of a longer one, and the difference decides whether verse 1 describes the first act of creation or sets the scene for it.
Genesis|1.kjv: In the beginning God created the heaven and the earth.
Genesis|1.kjvWhy: In the beginning is the reading four centuries of English readers have taken as the whole sentence
Genesis|1.others: The King James, ESV, NIV and NASB read In the beginning. The JPS reads When God began to create. The NRSV footnotes it and the NET discusses it at length.
Genesis|1.seeing: Bereshit is the noun reshit, beginning, with a prefixed preposition and no definite article. In Hebrew that shape usually signals a construct, a noun leaning on the next word, which would give when God began to create rather than in the beginning. The vowel pointing that makes it absolute was added by scribes over a thousand years later.
Genesis|1.why: English prepositions do not lean. In the beginning is grammatically complete the moment you write it, so the question never arises for an English reader.
Genesis|1.rule: Hebrew nouns that lean on the next word are the commonest structural feature English cannot show. When a translation footnote offers you a whole different sentence shape rather than a different word, this is usually why.
Genesis|1.choosing: Absolute gives a first act of creation and a universe with a start. Construct gives a scene-setting clause with the real main verb in verse 3. The consonants permit both, the ancient versions mostly took it as absolute, and the grammar leans construct. This is a live argument, not a settled one.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:1b
Genesis|1.summary: Created. A verb with only one possible subject in the whole Hebrew Bible.
Genesis|1.plain: Imagine an English verb that only ever takes one subject. Nobody else in the language is allowed to do it. You would learn a lot about what the writers thought of that subject just from the grammar, before anyone made an argument.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because this verb is reserved. It never takes a human subject anywhere in the Hebrew Bible, and knowing that is worth more than any argument about what it does or does not say concerning raw material.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads created. No dispute about the rendering, and a long dispute about what the verb implies.
Genesis|1.seeing: Bara occurs around fifty times and God is the subject every single time. Humans never bara anything. The word says nothing on its own about whether material already existed; that argument runs through other verses and through later theology, not through this verb.
Genesis|1.why: English create is used of anyone. A novelist creates a character, a chef creates a dish. The exclusivity is invisible in translation because English has no reserved verb.
Genesis|1.rule: Before deciding what a word means, check who is allowed to do it. Subject restriction is one of the strongest signals a language gives about a word's weight.
Genesis|1.choosing: Nothing is disputed in translation. What is disputed is whether bara implies creation from nothing, and the honest answer is that the verb alone does not settle it.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:1c
Genesis|1.summary: The heaven and the earth. Not two items. One idea named by its opposite ends.
Genesis|1.plain: **They searched high and low.** Nobody thinks two altitudes were searched. **She read it cover to cover.** Naming the two ends is how English says everything in between, and you have never once stopped to notice.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the phrase is not a list of two things. It is a figure of speech naming a totality by its edges, and reading it as an inventory of sky and dirt misses what the sentence is claiming.
Genesis|1.others: All versions read the heavens and the earth. None flags the construction, and none needs to, because English has the same figure.
Genesis|1.seeing: This is a merism: two opposite terms standing for the whole. Hebrew uses it constantly. The phrase does not mean sky plus ground. It means the entire ordered cosmos, and Hebrew had no single word for that.
Genesis|1.why: English does have this figure, which is why nothing is lost. The problem is that English readers treat biblical phrases as technical and stop hearing the figure they use themselves every day.
Genesis|1.rule: A pair of opposites joined by and is usually one idea, not two. Test it by asking whether the writer meant to exclude the middle. If not, you have a merism.
Genesis|1.choosing: Nothing to choose. This record is here because readers argue about what heaven means as though it were a separate item being inventoried, rather than half of a single figure of speech.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:2
Genesis|1.summary: Moved, hovered, or swept. One rare verb and a bird.
Genesis|1.plain: Suppose you found a word that appears three times in every book ever written in English, and only once does the sentence around it make sense. Every dictionary entry for that word is a guess built on that one sentence. You would want to see the guess. That is exactly the situation here.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the Spirit's first appearance in the Bible is described by a verb that occurs three times in the whole Hebrew Bible, and one of those three is doing all the interpretive work. Every other word in the verse is common. This is the clearest case in Scripture of a doctrine-adjacent image resting on a nearly unattested word.
Genesis|1.kjv: And the Spirit of God moved upon the face of the waters.
Genesis|1.others: Modern versions read hovering, or was moving, or sweeping over. The NET reads moving.
Genesis|1.seeing: The verb is rachaph, and it turns up in just three verses of the Hebrew Bible: Genesis 1:2, Deuteronomy 32:11 where an eagle flutters over its young, and Jeremiah 23:9 where a prophet's bones shake. The third one is a different verb stem and BDB lists it as a separate entry, which means the hovering sense may have only two occurrences, and one of those is the verse being explained. Every lexicon entry for this word is reasoning from a single clear context.
Genesis|1.why: With three occurrences there is no statistical base. Translators are reasoning from one clear context to two unclear ones, and reasonable people weight that differently.
Genesis|1.rule: Look up how many times a word occurs before you trust a definition, and then check whether all those occurrences are even the same word. Under about five, a lexicon is making an argument rather than reporting a fact, and you should want to see the argument.
Genesis|1.choosing: Hovering imports the eagle from Deuteronomy 32:11 and reads the opening of Genesis as protective and parental. Moving treats it as motion over water with no bird attached, which is what the King James, Tyndale, the Geneva and the Revised Version all chose. Hovering is a twentieth-century preference, entering the major English versions with the NIV. Neither is unreasonable and the evidence base is two verses.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:5
Genesis|1.summary: The first day. Literally, one day, a cardinal number, while every later day uses an ordinal.
Genesis|1.plain: English happily uses **day one** and **the first day** interchangeably. Hebrew does not default that way: yom echad is built like counting **day: one** the way you might count reps, while yom sheni, the second day, and every day after it, uses a true ordinal, like second, third, fourth. Only day one breaks the ordinal pattern.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the first day of creation is numbered one, a plain cardinal number, while every day after it is numbered with an ordinal, second, third, fourth, a grammatical inconsistency that has been read as everything from a stylistic accident to a deliberate theological statement that there was, as yet, nothing to count the first day against.
Genesis|1.others: Most versions read the first day, smoothing yom echad into the ordinal pattern the rest of the week uses, treating the grammatical oddity as insignificant.
Genesis|1.seeing: Yom echad, day one, uses the cardinal number one rather than the ordinal rishon, first, which Hebrew does have and uses elsewhere. Every subsequent day in the creation week switches to a true ordinal. One classical explanation, offered by the medieval commentator Ramban, is that first only makes sense once a second exists to compare it to, so before any other day existed, only one, a simple count, was possible; other proposed explanations range from stylistic variation to marking this day as categorically different from the rest.
Genesis|1.why: English first day is a normal, expected ordinal with no oddity to notice, so nothing in translation signals that the underlying Hebrew grammar actually breaks its own pattern on exactly this one day, a small irregularity commentators have found worth explaining for centuries.
Genesis|1.rule: When Hebrew breaks its own established grammatical pattern, as the cardinal yom echad does against the following days' ordinals, treat the break as a detail worth investigating rather than noise a fluent translation can safely smooth away.
Genesis|1.choosing: The first day, the standard English rendering, treats the Hebrew oddity as insignificant variation. Reading yom echad more literally as day one, following Ramban's logic that no second day yet existed to make first meaningful, keeps the grammatical irregularity in view as a deliberate feature rather than papering over it.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:6-8
Genesis|1.summary: Let there be a firmament. A word built on the sense of beating something out flat, likely naming a solid dome, not empty space.
Genesis|1.plain: English firmament sounds vaguely solid but vague enough that most readers picture open sky. The Hebrew word's root is tied to beating out metal into a flat sheet, the same kind of work a smith does hammering a bowl from a lump of metal, which points toward a solid structure holding back water, not simply open air.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the word rendered firmament describes something the linguistic and comparative evidence strongly suggests ancient Israelite readers understood as a solid, beaten-out dome separating waters above from waters below, a genuinely different picture of the sky than the airy, empty expanse most modern readers assume the word means.
Genesis|1.others: Older versions read firmament, itself a transliteration of the Latin firmamentum, translating the Greek stereoma, solid structure. Some modern versions read expanse or sky, softening the solidity the underlying words and root more strongly suggest.
Genesis|1.seeing: Raqia comes from a root meaning to spread out or beat out, the same action used of hammering metal into a thin sheet, and functions in Genesis 1 to separate waters above from waters below, holding the upper waters back the way a solid barrier would. Comparative ancient Near Eastern cosmology regularly pictures the sky as a solid, dome-like structure, and the linguistic, comparative, and contextual evidence together lead most specialists to conclude the original audience understood raqia as solid, not merely as empty, open space.
Genesis|1.why: English firmament and expanse both allow a reader to imagine open air, while the Hebrew word's root and its ancient cosmological context point more strongly toward an actual solid structure, a real difference in what ancient readers likely pictured when they heard the word.
Genesis|1.rule: When translating a cosmological term, check both its root meaning and how the surrounding ancient culture pictured the same concept before assuming a modern, scientifically informed picture of the sky was ever in view. Ancient cosmology and modern cosmology are not obligated to agree, and the text was written within the ancient one.
Genesis|1.choosing: Firmament preserves some sense of solidity but reads as archaic and vague to most modern ears. Expanse or sky, now common in modern versions, more comfortably fits a modern cosmological picture but likely understates how solid the original Hebrew word and its ancient context actually suggest.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:14
Genesis|1.summary: Let them be for signs, and for seasons. Moedim, the same word later naming Israel's appointed feasts.
Genesis|1.plain: English seasons suggests spring, summer, fall, winter, a general climate cycle. The Hebrew word instead points toward scheduled appointments, the same word later used for Israel's specific festival calendar, closer to marking out a calendar of appointments than describing weather patterns.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the word translated seasons here is the same word later used throughout the Torah for God's appointed festival times, so the sun and moon are given, from the fourth day of creation itself, the specific job of marking out the very calendar Israel's worship will later run on.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads seasons, a reasonable general translation, but one that does not carry forward the word's more specific, later technical use for Israel's fixed festival dates.
Genesis|1.seeing: Moedim, appointed times, is the same word Leviticus 23 uses repeatedly for the LORD's own appointed feasts, Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles, and the rest. Its use here at creation's fourth day quietly establishes that the sun and moon's created purpose already included marking out the very calendar those later appointed festivals would run on, tying Israel's worship calendar back to the created order itself.
Genesis|1.why: English seasons names a general climate pattern; it does not carry forward the specific, technical sense of scheduled, appointed occasions that moedim has throughout the rest of the Torah, so the link between creation's fourth day and Israel's later festival calendar disappears once the word becomes a generic English noun.
Genesis|1.rule: When a word appears early in a book and recurs later as a technical or ritual term, read the early occurrence in light of the later one. Moedim at creation is not incidental vocabulary; it is the same word the Torah will use for its most structured religious calendar.
Genesis|1.choosing: Seasons is not wrong, but it undersells the specific, later technical sense of moedim as scheduled sacred appointments. Appointed times keeps the link to Leviticus 23's festival calendar visible, a connection worth knowing even though seasons remains a defensible general translation.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:16
Genesis|1.summary: The greater light and the lesser light. Not shemesh, sun, and yareach, moon, the same words as the sun-god and moon-god.
Genesis|1.plain: Imagine a creation account that carefully avoids saying **the sun** and **the moon** by name, calling them only **the big glowing thing** and **the smaller glowing thing**, specifically because those proper names doubled as the names of rival gods everyone around you worshipped. That is exactly what this verse does.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because Genesis pointedly avoids the ordinary Hebrew words for sun and moon here, calling them only the greater light and the lesser light, even though those ordinary words, shemesh and yareach, were also the names of major sun and moon deities worshipped throughout Egypt and Mesopotamia.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads the greater light and the lesser light, correctly, but nothing in the English signals that Hebrew had two perfectly ordinary, available words, shemesh and yareach, for sun and moon that the verse conspicuously does not use.
Genesis|1.seeing: Shemesh, sun, was also the name of Shamash, the Mesopotamian sun-god; yareach, moon, shares its root with Yarikh, the Canaanite moon-god. Genesis 1 calls them simply hama'or hagadol and hama'or hakaton, the greater light and the lesser light, functional, almost deliberately unglamorous descriptions, stripping them of any name that could double as a divine title and reducing them to created objects doing a job, marking appointed times, rather than deities to be worshipped.
Genesis|1.why: English greater light and lesser light already sound intentionally plain, but without knowing that Hebrew had perfectly good, ordinary proper names available and pointedly did not use them, an English reader cannot see that this is a deliberate polemic against the sun and moon worship of Israel's neighbors, not merely a poetic or repetitive style choice.
Genesis|1.rule: When a text conspicuously avoids an obvious, available word, ask what that word would have implied if used. Genesis 1's avoidance of shemesh and yareach here is a calculated theological move, not an accident of vocabulary or a coincidence of style.
Genesis|1.choosing: No translation dispute over greater light and lesser light as accurate renderings. What is worth flagging is that the deliberate avoidance of the ordinary, available words for sun and moon, precisely because those words were also divine names, is a polemical statement entirely dependent on knowing what words were not used.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:21
Genesis|1.summary: God created great whales. The Hebrew word, tannin, elsewhere names the mythological sea-monster Leviathan.
Genesis|1.plain: Imagine a creation story that lists **the dragon** among the ordinary animals made that day, with no more drama than the fish and birds around it, specifically to say that the terrifying sea-monster other nations feared and worshipped is, in this account, just another creature. That is what tannin is doing here.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the sea creatures God creates here are named with the same word, tannin, that elsewhere names the mythological chaos-monster Leviathan and Rahab, so this verse quietly demotes what other ancient Near Eastern religions treated as a rival cosmic power to just another animal God speaks into being on day five.
Genesis|1.others: Most versions read great whales, great sea creatures, or great sea monsters. The Septuagint translates tannin as dragon everywhere else it appears, but shifts to a more generic sea-monster word here, following the calmer context.
Genesis|1.seeing: Tannin, used here of ordinary sea creatures God creates on day five, is the same word applied to Leviathan and Rahab at Isaiah 27:1 and 51:9, mythological chaos-monsters associated in the wider ancient Near East, especially in Ugaritic literature, with primeval cosmic rebellion against a creator god. By calling these creatures tanninim and placing them calmly among the fish and birds God creates by simple speech, Genesis 1 strips any cosmic rivalry from the picture: the sea monster is not a threat God must defeat in combat, as in neighboring creation myths, but an animal God straightforwardly makes.
Genesis|1.why: English great whales or sea creatures sounds entirely zoological, with no hint that the underlying word is the same one used elsewhere for a mythological chaos-monster; the polemical point, that even the most feared cosmic symbol of chaos is just another creature here, depends entirely on recognizing the shared Hebrew word.
Genesis|1.rule: When Genesis 1 names something with vocabulary that elsewhere carries mythological weight, tehom the deep, tannin the sea monster, read the calm, list-like context as doing real theological work: taking a term charged with meaning in the surrounding culture and deliberately defusing it.
Genesis|1.choosing: Great whales domesticates the word for a modern audience unfamiliar with its mythological associations. Great sea monsters or sea dragons keeps the connection to Leviathan and Rahab visible, letting the verse's quiet polemic against neighboring creation myths register the way it likely did for its original audience.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:26a
Genesis|1.summary: Let us make. A plural announcement followed immediately by a singular act.
Genesis|1.plain: **Let's build a shed.** **I built a shed.** The first sentence includes other people. The second says who swung the hammer. Both can be true of the same shed, and nobody thinks the second contradicts the first.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the plural is the single most argued feature of the creation account, and the argument usually happens without anyone naming what kind of plural it is. The verb form is the evidence and almost nobody looks at it.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads let us make. The disagreement is entirely about who us refers to, and no translation can help.
Genesis|1.seeing: Na'aseh is a cohortative, the Hebrew form for let me or let us. Verse 27 then uses a singular verb three times. Whatever the plural is doing, it is not distributing the act of creating, because the next verse assigns that to one actor.
Genesis|1.why: English let us is the same whether it includes an audience or is a royal flourish. Hebrew has a specific form, and the argument is about what that form is doing here.
Genesis|1.rule: When a verse is famous for one grammatical feature, find out what the next verse does with the same subject. Adjacent verses settle more arguments than lexicons do.
Genesis|1.choosing: A plural of majesty has trouble with this verb form. A Trinitarian reading may be true and still does not describe what a first hearer understood. Address to a divine council explains the plural and leaves the singular in verse 27 intact. All three leave something unexplained, and this one leaves the least.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:26b
Genesis|1.summary: In our image, after our likeness. Two nouns, and probably one idea.
Genesis|1.plain: **Safe and sound.** **Null and void.** English pairs words that mean nearly the same thing all the time, and nobody hunts for the difference between null and void. Hebrew does the same, and readers hunt anyway.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because image and likeness get treated as two different things by an entire tradition, and the Hebrew nouns do not support the distinction. Two words, one idea, and a lot of theology built on the gap between them.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads image and likeness. Some older theological systems treat them as separate endowments, one lost at the fall and one retained.
Genesis|1.seeing: Tselem is a physical representation, including a carved idol. Demut is a resemblance. In Genesis 5:3 the two are swapped around with the prepositions reversed, which is what makes a technical distinction hard to sustain. Read together they say one thing: humanity is God's representative image on the ground, the way a king's statue in a province represented the king.
Genesis|1.why: English can print both nouns but cannot signal that the pair is a single idea, so readers naturally assume two.
Genesis|1.rule: When two near-synonyms appear together, check whether the writer ever swaps or reverses them. If he does, the distinction you are looking for is probably not there.
Genesis|1.choosing: There is no translation dispute. There is a long tradition of distinguishing the two, and the internal evidence at Genesis 5:3 is the argument against it.

Genesis|1.title: Genesis 1:28
Genesis|1.summary: Subdue it, and have dominion. Forceful, even military and royal vocabulary, standing beside Genesis 2's gentler verbs for the same job.
Genesis|1.plain: English subdue and have dominion already sound fairly strong, but the underlying Hebrew is stronger still: kabash is the verb for military conquest, putting a defeated enemy under your foot; radah is royal rule language, a king governing subjects. Two chapters later, the same task is described with work and keep, priestly, custodial language entirely different in tone.
Genesis|1.whyThis: Because the verbs telling humanity to subdue the earth and have dominion over it are genuinely forceful, military and royal vocabulary, not gentle stewardship language, and stand in real tension with Genesis 2:15's gentler service-and-guard verbs for the same human task, a tension worth noticing rather than harmonizing away.
Genesis|1.others: Every version reads subdue and have dominion, correctly conveying real force, though without necessarily flagging how sharply that force contrasts with the gentler abad and shamar, work and keep, used for the same basic human task at Genesis 2:15.
Genesis|1.seeing: Kabash elsewhere describes military subjugation, putting a conquered population under your feet; radah names the kind of rule a king exercises over subjects. Applied to humanity's relationship with the earth and its creatures, both verbs are considerably more forceful than the abad, serve, and shamar, guard, used of Adam's task in the garden at 2:15, creating a real tension between two pictures of the same human vocation, conquest and custodianship, that the text does not explicitly resolve.
Genesis|1.why: English subdue and dominion already register as fairly strong, but readers moving between chapters 1 and 2 in translation do not necessarily notice that the vocabulary shifts from military and royal force to priestly service and guarding, a genuine change in tone between two accounts of humanity's purpose that disappears once both are smoothed into ordinary English.
Genesis|1.rule: When two passages describe what looks like the same task using visibly different registers of vocabulary, forceful versus gentle, royal versus priestly, read the contrast as a real feature of the text's fuller picture rather than assuming the two must simply restate one identical idea.
Genesis|1.choosing: Reading kabash and radah at full force keeps humanity's mandate as active, even aggressive, shaping of a wild and unfinished world. Reading Genesis 2:15's abad and shamar as the fuller, correcting picture treats dominion as answerable to a prior, gentler custodial calling. The text offers both pictures without explicitly ranking one over the other.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:2-3
Genesis|2.summary: God rested. The verb means stopped, not recovered.
Genesis|2.plain: **I stopped for lunch.** That says nothing about being tired. **I rested after the race.** That does, because rest in English leans toward recovering strength. The verb behind Sabbath only ever says the first one.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the Sabbath verb first appears here, before it is ever commanded, and the fourth commandment eight hundred years later uses a different Hebrew word for the same seventh day. What God does on that day is not what most readers picture when they hear rested.
Genesis|2.others: Every English version reads rested here, and later at Exodus 20:11 for the same day, using one English word for two different Hebrew verbs.
Genesis|2.seeing: Vayishbot, from shabat, to cease, desist, stop an activity. It is the root behind the noun Sabbath itself, and it says nothing about fatigue or recovery. Exodus 20:11, the fourth commandment, describes the same day with a different verb, vayanach, from nuach, to settle down or rest. Genesis 2 does not use that verb.
Genesis|2.why: English rest almost always implies tiredness relieved. Hebrew shabat is a verb of stopping, applied here to a God the text never says grew tired. One English word covers a distinction the Hebrew draws across two different books of the Torah.
Genesis|2.rule: Track a key verb across its first occurrence and its most famous one. Genesis 2 and Exodus 20 describe the same seventh day with two different Hebrew verbs, and no English Bible has ever needed two different words to say it.
Genesis|2.choosing: No real dispute over the English gloss; rested is the natural word in both places. What matters here is that the vocabulary shift between Genesis 2 and Exodus 20 disappears once both are translated rest, and it is worth knowing before building an argument about divine fatigue on either verse.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:4a
Genesis|2.summary: These are the generations. A recurring formula, not a genealogy header.
Genesis|2.plain: **Chapter two.** A modern book uses headings to mark a new section. Hebrew narrative uses a repeated phrase instead, the same words every time, like a heading a reader learns to recognize on sight, then watches recur through the whole book.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because this is the first of eleven times this exact formula opens a new section of Genesis, and the phrase is not simply a genealogy header. Missing it means missing how the author signals I am starting something new.
Genesis|2.others: Every version reads generations, or account, or history. None can mark that the identical Hebrew phrase recurs ten more times through Genesis as a structural heading.
Genesis|2.seeing: Toledot, from yalad, to bear or beget, most literally means begettings, what was brought forth. The formula 'these are the toledot of X' opens eleven sections of Genesis, each one introducing what came from the person or thing just named. At 2:4 it stands over the heavens and the earth themselves, extending a genealogical formula to cosmology.
