Genesis|2.why: No single English word is both a genealogical term and a verbatim structural heading repeated across a book. Generations captures the family-tree sense and loses the marker function, so an English reader has no way to notice the repetition without being told.
Genesis|2.rule: When an unusual phrase recurs word for word, treat it as a heading, not ordinary prose. Genesis is built out of ten more of these toledot headings, and the book's own structure is invisible without seeing the word.
Genesis|2.choosing: No translation dispute over the gloss. The issue is that any single English rendering, whether generations, account, or history, cannot also function as a recognizable repeated heading the way the one Hebrew word does across all eleven uses.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:4b
Genesis|2.summary: In the day that the LORD God made. An idiom meaning when, not a calendar entry.
Genesis|2.plain: English can use **day** loosely: **in the day of trouble** means whenever trouble comes, not one sunrise. Hebrew does the same thing here, attaching day to an infinitive rather than a date, and the whole clause simply means when.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the same verse that opens with a genealogical heading closes with a phrase, in the day, that many readers take as a strict twenty-four-hour marker, and the construction is not built the way a plain calendar date is built.
Genesis|2.others: Most versions read when or in the day that, both compatible with either a literal day or a summarizing when. Some readers press day here toward a literal twenty-four-hour marker, which the construction does not by itself require.
Genesis|2.seeing: Beyom is yom, day, prefixed with the preposition and followed by an infinitive construct, asot, making. This beyom-plus-infinitive pattern is a standard Hebrew idiom meaning when or at the time that, attested roughly seventy times in the Hebrew Bible, including at Genesis 5:1 itself. It is a different construction from the numbered yom echad, yom sheni pattern used through chapter one for the six creation days.
Genesis|2.why: English when can carry any duration; English day cannot. Beyom's idiomatic when-sense and yom's literal daylight-sense both get carried by the same English gloss, so a reader cannot see from the translation alone that this construction is not making the same kind of chronological claim the numbered days of chapter one make.
Genesis|2.rule: A preposition-plus-infinitive built on yom is a set idiom meaning when, distinct from yom used with a number or the definite article for a specific day. Check which construction is in front of you before treating day as a chronological claim.
Genesis|2.choosing: No serious lexical dispute; grammarians widely recognize beyom plus infinitive as an idiom for when. The disagreement is theological, about how much weight the idiom should be allowed to carry into the six-day debate of chapter one, which this verse does not by itself settle either way.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:6
Genesis|2.summary: A mist went up. A word used only here and once in Job, and nobody is certain what it names.
Genesis|2.plain: Imagine a word that survives in only two sentences of an entire library. Every dictionary entry for it is built from those two sentences alone. Now picture two ancient translations disagreeing about which of two very different pictures, fog or flood, the word was even pointing at.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the verse that explains how the ground got watered before it ever rained rests on a word that occurs in just two verses of the Old Testament, and the ancient translators already disagreed about what it named.
Genesis|2.others: Most English versions read mist or streams. The Septuagint and the Latin Vulgate both read spring or fountain, not mist, showing the fog reading is not the oldest one on record.
Genesis|2.seeing: Ed occurs at Genesis 2:6 and Job 36:27, and nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible. The traditional mist reading leans on the Job passage; an alternative connects the word to Akkadian edu, a flood or high water, which would make the verse describe subterranean water welling up to irrigate the ground rather than fog settling on it.
Genesis|2.why: English mist and spring point to two different weather pictures, and a word attested twice cannot arbitrate between them. Whichever English word a translator picks quietly closes a question the Hebrew itself leaves open.
Genesis|2.rule: A word this rare is a live question, not a settled fact, however confident a single English gloss makes it look. Check how many times a word occurs before resting an argument on its dictionary definition.
Genesis|2.choosing: Mist keeps the older picture of dew or fog settling. Spring or stream follows the Septuagint, the Vulgate, and the proposed Akkadian cognate, and fits a garden being irrigated by water rising from below rather than settling from above. Both are defensible; neither is provable from two data points.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:7a
Genesis|2.summary: Breathed into his nostrils the breath of life. A different word from the one in chapter one.
Genesis|2.plain: English has **breath**, **wind**, **air** and **gasp**, and you would not use them interchangeably. Other languages divide the same territory along different lines, and the lines never match.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the word for what God breathes in is not the ordinary word for breath or spirit, and the difference is worth knowing before you build anything on this verse about the human soul.
Genesis|2.others: All versions read breath. The distinction from the other Hebrew word is invisible in every English Bible.
Genesis|2.seeing: Neshamah, not ruach. Ruach covers wind, breath and spirit and is the word at Genesis 1:2. Neshamah is narrower, the breath of a living creature, and is used of God and of humans and occasionally of animals. The verse is not saying God put His Spirit in Adam; it uses a different noun for that.
Genesis|2.why: English has one word, breath, standing in for both, so the vocabulary change between chapter one and chapter two cannot be seen.
Genesis|2.rule: When two Hebrew words are both rendered by one English word, the change from one to the other is a signal you will never see. Look for it wherever a doctrine is being built on a single verse.
Genesis|2.choosing: No dispute. This is worth flagging because the ruach and neshamah distinction is routinely collapsed in popular teaching about the human constitution.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:7b
Genesis|2.summary: Man became a living soul. The same phrase is used of the animals.
Genesis|2.plain: **She is a living creature.** That is a statement about being alive, not about having an invisible part. Now imagine your translation used a more spiritual-sounding word in one place and a plainer one somewhere else, for the same original phrase.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the phrase is the standard proof text for humans having a soul, and the identical phrase is used of the animals two chapters earlier. Nothing in the verse is doing what most readers think it is doing.
Genesis|2.kjv: and man became a living soul.
Genesis|2.kjvWhy: a living soul is the rendering the whole soul-and-body tradition is built on
Genesis|2.others: The King James reads a living soul here and a living creature at Genesis 1:24 for the same two words. Modern versions read living being or living creature in both places, which is the correction.
Genesis|2.seeing: Nephesh chayyah. The phrase appears at Genesis 1:20, 21, 24 and 30 of sea creatures, birds and land animals. Nephesh is closer to a life, a self, an appetite, even a throat, than to an immaterial soul. The verse says the man became alive, not that he received a soul the animals lack.
Genesis|2.why: English soul carries centuries of Greek and Christian anthropology that Hebrew nephesh does not. There is no neutral English word, and creature sounds dismissive where soul sounds elevated.
Genesis|2.rule: When one Hebrew phrase is rendered two different ways in the same book, look up the other occurrences. Translators sometimes signal a theology by their choice of English word, and the King James does it here.
Genesis|2.choosing: No Hebrew dispute. Modern versions have standardised on living being, and the King James rendering is the one that produced the popular reading.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:15
Genesis|2.summary: To work it and keep it. The same two verbs describe the Levites guarding the tabernacle.
Genesis|2.plain: **He tends the garden.** **He guards the temple.** English keeps those as two different jobs done by two different kinds of people. This verse uses the same two verbs for Adam that a later book uses for priests on duty.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the two verbs describing Adam's job in the garden are the same two verbs used together elsewhere only for the Levites guarding the tabernacle, and that changes what kind of place the garden is being described as.
Genesis|2.others: Every version reads some pair like work and keep, till and keep, or cultivate and guard. None can show that the identical pair recurs elsewhere as a fixed phrase for priestly duty.
Genesis|2.seeing: Abad, to work or serve, and shamar, to keep or guard, appear together describing Adam's task in the garden. The same two verbs appear together describing the Levites' duty toward the tabernacle at Numbers 3:7-8 and 18:5-6, and shamar alone covers guarding it from intruders at Numbers 1:53. The garden is being described in the vocabulary later used for sanctuary service.
Genesis|2.why: English work and keep are ordinary household words. They carry none of the specialized, cultic resonance the same two verbs carry when the same corpus later uses them for tabernacle duty, so the priestly overtone of Adam's job is simply not visible in translation.
Genesis|2.rule: A common-sounding word pair can be a technical phrase elsewhere in the same body of literature. Before assuming ordinary vocabulary, check whether the same combination recurs in a specialized context.
Genesis|2.choosing: There is no dispute about the plain gloss, work and keep. The disagreement is how much weight to put on the Numbers parallel, whether the echo is a deliberate signal that Eden is being described as sanctuary space, or a coincidence of two common verbs appearing together twice.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:16-17
Genesis|2.summary: Thou shalt surely die. Literally dying, you shall die: the verb said twice.
Genesis|2.plain: English intensifies a verb by adding a word: **you will surely die**, **you will certainly die**. Hebrew has another option: say the verb itself twice, once as a bare noun-form and once conjugated. Dying, you shall die is what the sentence actually does.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the death sentence attached to the one prohibition in the garden is not phrased as an ordinary future-tense statement in Hebrew, and English has no grammatical way to reproduce the doubling that makes it emphatic.
Genesis|2.others: Every version adds an adverb, surely or certainly, to carry the emphasis. None can double the verb the way the Hebrew does, because repeating die die in English reads as a mistake, not as emphasis.
Genesis|2.seeing: Mot tamut pairs the infinitive absolute mot, dying, with the finite verb tamut, you will die, from the same root muth. This infinitive-absolute-plus-finite-verb pattern is a standard Biblical Hebrew device for intensifying a verb, common in legal and covenantal pronouncements, especially death sentences. The same verse already uses the same device positively: akol tokel, freely eat, literally eating you shall eat.
Genesis|2.why: English cannot repeat a bare verb form next to its conjugated self and have it read as intensification rather than a typo. The only available tool is an adverb, which reports that emphasis exists without reproducing the grammatical shape that creates it.
Genesis|2.rule: When two words from the same Hebrew root sit next to each other, one uninflected, look for the infinitive absolute construction. It is the language's built-in italics, and English always has to translate it as a separate word rather than a repeated one.
Genesis|2.choosing: No dispute over the sense; every version agrees the warning is emphatic. What is worth noting is the grammatical device itself: an infinitive doubling a finite verb is a genuine feature of Hebrew with no formal English equivalent, not a stylistic flourish a translator chose.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:18
Genesis|2.summary: Help meet. Two English words that were never one word, and a Hebrew phrase that says something else again.
Genesis|2.plain: **That is a meet reward.** Meet used to mean fitting. It died, and people who still heard it in the phrase started running the two words together into helpmeet, then helpmate. A word that never existed got invented by ears rather than pens.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because two words in this phrase carry most of the modern argument about men and women in the church and the home, and one of them is not a word at all but an English misunderstanding. The verse is quoted constantly by people who have never looked at either half.
Genesis|2.kjv: It is not good that the man should be alone; I will make him an help meet for him.
Genesis|2.kjvWhy: help meet is where the English accident begins
Genesis|2.others: Modern versions read a helper suitable for him, or a helper corresponding to him, or a helper as his complement.
Genesis|2.seeing: The Hebrew is ezer kenegdo. Ezer is a helper, and the word is used most often in the Hebrew Bible of God himself helping Israel, which is not the sense of assistant. Kenegdo is built on neged, meaning in front of or opposite, so the phrase is a helper corresponding to him, one who stands facing him.
Genesis|2.why: Two separate problems stack here. English lost the word meet, meaning fitting, so help meet was misheard as helpmeet and then as helpmate, a word that never existed in the text. And English helper carries a junior connotation that the Hebrew ezer does not.
Genesis|2.rule: When a King James phrase has become a single familiar word, check whether it was ever one word. English drift produces some of the most confident misreadings in the Bible, and they are invisible to a reader who only has the English.
Genesis|2.choosing: There is no real translation dispute here. There is an English-language accident, and then a genuine question about the force of ezer, which every modern version handles slightly differently while none of them says assistant.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:21-22
Genesis|2.summary: One of his ribs. The same word names the side chambers of the tabernacle everywhere else.
Genesis|2.plain: **He built a shelf from one board.** **He built an addition onto the side of the house.** One is a single piece; the other is a whole section. The word behind rib usually means the second kind of thing: a side, a flank, a chamber.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the word for what God takes from the man to build the woman is not the ordinary word for a rib, and in thirty-nine of its other forty-one appearances it names something else entirely.
Genesis|2.kjv: And the LORD God caused a deep sleep to fall upon Adam, and he slept: and he took one of his ribs, and closed up the flesh instead thereof... And the rib, which the LORD God had taken from man, made he a woman, and brought her unto the man.
Genesis|2.kjvWhy: rib is the rendering that shaped the entire Adam's-rib tradition
Genesis|2.others: Every major English version reads rib. A minority of scholars and some newer study notes argue for side, but no widely used translation has switched, so rib remains the reading every reader meets.
Genesis|2.seeing: Tsela occurs forty-one times in thirty-two verses. Only these two, Genesis 2:21-22, are ever rendered rib. Everywhere else, the tabernacle's side chambers and boards at Exodus 25:12 and 26:26-27, the temple's side chambers at 1 Kings 6:5, 34, even a hillside at 2 Samuel 16:13, it is side, side chamber, board, or slope. The single-bone reading rests on these two verses alone.
Genesis|2.why: English rib names one specific bone; English side is broad enough to mean a flank, a section, or a chamber. The Hebrew word defaults to the broad sense everywhere except here, and only the traditional reading of this one story keeps the narrow sense attached to it in English.
Genesis|2.rule: When a word is translated one way in exactly two verses and a completely different way everywhere else, check what is driving the outlier. Sometimes it is genuine context; sometimes it is a translation tradition nobody has revisited.
Genesis|2.choosing: Rib keeps four hundred years of English reading and the picture most people carry of the story. Side follows the word's overwhelming usage elsewhere and reads the operation as taking a whole section, not extracting a single bone. The Hebrew consonants support either; the tradition has settled on the rarer sense.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:23
Genesis|2.summary: She shall be called Woman, because she was taken out of Man. A pun that sounds like a derivation.
Genesis|2.plain: English **woman** really is built from **man**; it comes from Old English wifman. An English reader has no reason to doubt Adam's line is doing the same thing. It is doing something else: making a pun, not reporting where the word came from.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because Adam's own line sounds like a real etymology, woman because taken out of man, and centuries of commentators, Jewish and Christian alike, read it as one. Modern linguists trace the two words to different roots.
Genesis|2.others: Every version keeps the wordplay by translating ish as man and ishah as woman, since English happens to have a matching pair. The English pair is a real derivation; the Hebrew pair, read this way, is not.
Genesis|2.seeing: Ish and ishah sound almost identical, and Genesis 2:23 plays on that resemblance. But the words are generally traced to different roots, ish to a root meaning strength, ishah to a separate root associated with frailty or humanity in general, so the verse is a paronomasia, a sound-based pun dressed up as a derivation, not an actual etymology.
Genesis|2.why: English woman genuinely does derive from man, so an English reader assumes the Hebrew must work the same way and has no signal that it does not. The pun survives in translation only because English happens to have its own unrelated derivation that looks like a match.
Genesis|2.rule: A wordplay that sounds like an etymology is not evidence of one. Ancient authors used sound-based puns constantly and did not intend them as historical linguistics, even where, as here, the pun is doing real literary work.
Genesis|2.choosing: No translation avoids the pun; man and woman is the correct rendering and the resemblance is deliberate in the Hebrew. The only correction needed is not to the translation but to what the wordplay is taken to prove about where the Hebrew words themselves come from.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:24
Genesis|2.summary: One flesh. A kinship word, not only a body word.
Genesis|2.plain: **He's my flesh and blood.** English keeps this sense alive for family, but only as a fixed idiom, sitting beside the ordinary meaning of flesh as tissue. Hebrew basar carries the kinship sense as one of its normal, everyday meanings, not as a leftover expression.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the verse everyone quotes about marriage says one flesh, and flesh in Hebrew names kinship and identity as often as it names tissue, so the phrase is making a bigger claim than a merely physical one.
Genesis|2.others: Every version reads one flesh, and the physical union is certainly included. What is harder to see in English is that basar for kinship is ordinary Hebrew usage on its own, not a special sense invented for this verse.
Genesis|2.seeing: Basar, flesh, is used of blood relatives at Genesis 29:14, Judges 9:2, and 2 Samuel 5:1, where 'your bone and your flesh' means your relative, with no reference to sex or the body. One flesh at 2:24 draws on that same kinship vocabulary: the man and woman become each other's next of kin, a new family unit, with the physical union as the sign of that bond rather than its entire content.
Genesis|2.why: English flesh has narrowed mostly to the physical body, with flesh and blood surviving only as a fixed idiom for family. Hebrew basar keeps both senses live at once, so a single English reading tends to collapse the verse into the physical union alone.
Genesis|2.rule: When a body-part or body-substance word appears in a covenant or family context, check whether the same word carries a kinship sense elsewhere before assuming only the physical meaning is in view.
Genesis|2.choosing: One flesh is not in dispute as a translation. The question is emphasis: whether the phrase is chiefly about sexual union, chiefly about kinship status, or, as the parallel usage suggests, both at once by design.

Genesis|2.title: Genesis 2:25-3:1
Genesis|2.summary: Naked, and not ashamed. Then: the serpent was more crafty. Two words that are near-twins in Hebrew.
Genesis|2.plain: Imagine a story ending one scene with **the couple was bare** and opening the next with **the snake was rare**. You would hear the echo instantly. Hebrew does exactly that with naked and crafty, and English naked and crafty do not rhyme at all.
Genesis|2.whyThis: Because the last word of chapter two and the first real word of chapter three are a matched pair in Hebrew sound, and the pun sets up everything that follows about nakedness and cunning, vanishing the moment the chapter break is translated.
Genesis|2.others: Every version reads naked at 2:25 and crafty, subtil, or shrewd at 3:1, two ordinary, unrelated-sounding English words. None can show that the Hebrew words are built from nearly the same consonants.
Genesis|2.seeing: Arummim, naked, at 2:25 and arum, crafty, at 3:1 share three of their root letters and are near-homonyms in Hebrew, even though most lexicons trace them to distinct roots. The narrator sets the pair back to back on purpose: the humans are arummim and unashamed, and the next creature introduced is arum, using almost the same sound to introduce the opposite of innocence.
Genesis|2.why: English naked and crafty share no sound at all, so a reader moving from 2:25 to 3:1 gets no auditory cue that the story is doing wordplay across the chapter break. The literary hinge the Hebrew builds the scene transition on disappears entirely.
Genesis|2.rule: Chapter and verse divisions are medieval additions, not part of the original text. Read straight across a chapter break before assuming the scene has fully changed; sometimes the Hebrew is still finishing a sound, if not a sentence.
Genesis|2.choosing: No real translation dispute; naked and crafty are both correct. What is worth flagging is that the pun connecting them is a genuine literary feature invisible in every English Bible, not a stretch imposed after the fact.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:8
Genesis|3.summary: The cool of the day. The Hebrew word is the same one translated Spirit.
Genesis|3.plain: English keeps **wind**, **breath**, and **spirit** as three separate words. Hebrew has one word for all three, ruach, the same word from Genesis 1:2. This verse uses it, and cool is not one of the things ruach otherwise ever means.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because the phrase everyone knows as the cool of the day uses the same Hebrew word that means Spirit and wind everywhere else in the Bible, and that word never elsewhere describes a pleasant temperature.
Genesis|3.others: Nearly every version reads cool of the day or evening breeze, following a translation tradition going back through the King James. Some recent scholarship instead reads the phrase as describing an approaching storm.
Genesis|3.seeing: The phrase is leruach hayom, literally in the ruach, wind or spirit, of the day. Ruach is the same noun used of the Spirit of God at Genesis 1:2 and of breath and wind throughout the Hebrew Bible; nowhere else does it mean temperature. Some scholars argue the scene depicts God arriving the way He does elsewhere, in a rushing, forceful wind rather than a mild breeze, making this a small theophany rather than a stroll at sunset.
Genesis|3.why: English cool has no connection to wind, breath, or spirit at all; it names a temperature. Ruach never names a temperature in Hebrew, so the traditional English rendering supplies a sense the word does not otherwise carry, hiding the word's ordinary link to Spirit and storm imagery elsewhere in the Bible.
Genesis|3.rule: When a familiar English phrase does not correspond to any of a word's attested senses, be suspicious of the phrase, not the word. Cool of the day is a translation tradition, not a lexical entry for ruach.
Genesis|3.choosing: Cool of the day preserves the long-settled picture of a garden walk at evening. Wind, or an approaching storm, follows the word's ordinary range and the pattern of divine appearances elsewhere in Scripture. Both are argued in current scholarship; the mild-breeze picture is the inherited default rather than the only reading available.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:15a
Genesis|3.summary: He shall bruise thy head. The Hebrew pronoun is unambiguously masculine, singular, he.
Genesis|3.plain: A single letter can flip a pronoun from **he** to **she** in translation, the way a typo can turn **him** into **her** in English. That is what happened to the Latin Bible used across Europe for over a thousand years, in the one verse that names the serpent's ultimate defeat.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because a single pronoun in this verse triggered a consequential translation dispute in church history, after a Latin copying error turned a masculine he into a feminine she, and the mistake shaped centuries of doctrine before it was caught.
Genesis|3.kjv: And I will put enmity between thee and the woman, and between thy seed and her seed; it shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel.
Genesis|3.kjvWhy: the King James, following the Hebrew and Greek rather than the Vulgate, keeps the masculine pronoun where the dominant Latin Bible for over a thousand years read otherwise
Genesis|3.others: Nearly every English version reads he or it, correctly following the Hebrew masculine singular pronoun. Some older Catholic translations made from the Latin Vulgate read she, following a Latin manuscript tradition that used the feminine ipsa instead of the masculine ipse.
Genesis|3.seeing: Zera, seed or offspring, is grammatically singular and collective, and the pronoun attached to it, hu, is third person masculine singular: he, not she, will crush the serpent's head. Jerome's own Hebrew-based commentary on Genesis confirms the masculine reading; the feminine ipsa that later appeared in some Vulgate copies is now widely regarded as a scribal error introduced after Jerome, not his own translation choice. The modern official Catholic Latin text, the Nova Vulgata, corrected the erroneous ipsa to ipsum, neuter, simply restoring ordinary Latin grammatical agreement with the neuter noun semen, seed; it does not print a masculine ipse, since Latin gender concord here tracks the Latin noun, not a claim about the Hebrew pronoun.
Genesis|3.why: English he and she map cleanly onto Hebrew masculine and feminine pronouns, so there is no translation gap here. The gap was a transmission error inside the Latin manuscript tradition, which English versions, working from Hebrew, never inherited.
Genesis|3.rule: A doctrine built on a single translation's pronoun is only as strong as that translation's manuscript history. Where two major textual traditions disagree, trace the disagreement back to its source before assuming either one preserves the original by default.
Genesis|3.choosing: He or it follows the Hebrew directly and is essentially undisputed among Hebraists across confessional lines, including current Catholic scholarship. She survives mainly in older devotional use built on the Vulgate's feminine variant, which the Catholic Church's own modern Latin text no longer prints.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:15b
Genesis|3.summary: It shall bruise thy head, and thou shalt bruise his heel. Same verb, four occurrences total, and bruise may be too gentle for either half.
Genesis|3.plain: **She bruised her knee.** **He crushed the can.** English has to pick one verb and commit to a severity. The Hebrew verse uses one rare verb for both the fatal blow and the survivable one, and no single English word covers that whole range.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because the verb used for both the serpent's blow and the human's blow turns up only four times in the whole Old Testament, and the traditional gentle-sounding bruise has increasingly been judged too soft for what the word may be doing.
Genesis|3.others: The King James and many traditional versions read bruise for both halves. A growing number of modern versions read crush for the head-strike and strike or bite for the heel-strike, no longer using one English verb for both.
Genesis|3.seeing: Shuph occurs only here, twice, and at Job 9:17 and Psalm 139:11, four occurrences in total, possibly spanning two distinct roots tangled together across them. The attested sense ranges from crush or bruise to a more violent strike or snap at. Because the same rare verb covers a lethal head-wound and a non-lethal heel-wound in one verse, translators have increasingly split it into two different English verbs to fit the two different outcomes, something the Hebrew itself does not do.
Genesis|3.why: No single English verb plausibly covers both a fatal blow to the head and a survivable bite to the heel, the way one Hebrew verb apparently does. Any English rendering has to either flatten the difference with one soft word, as the King James does, or introduce an asymmetry between the two lines that the Hebrew's own choice of vocabulary does not make.
Genesis|3.rule: When one rare verb covers actions of very different severity in the same verse, resist the urge to supply two different English verbs to match the outcomes. That interpretive step may be reasonable, but it is commentary, not translation.
Genesis|3.choosing: Bruise keeps a single, symmetrical verb for both halves, closer to what the Hebrew grammar actually presents. Crush and strike, or crush and bite, read theological weight into each half separately, which fits the traditional reading of the verse as the first promise of the serpent's defeat but goes beyond what shuph alone specifies.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:16a
Genesis|3.summary: Sorrow in childbearing, toil in the field. One Hebrew word, two English words.
Genesis|3.plain: If a story gave two characters the same punishment word and your translation rendered it **sorrow** for one and **toil** for the other, you would read two different sentences. The writer wrote one.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because the same Hebrew noun appears in the woman's sentence and in the man's sentence four verses apart, and English uses two different words for it. The parallel is the point and the translation hides it.
Genesis|3.others: The King James reads sorrow in verse 16 and sorrow in verse 17, keeping the link. Several modern versions read pain for the woman and toil or painful labour for the man, breaking it.
Genesis|3.seeing: Itsabon occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible: twice here, at verses 16 and 17, and once at Genesis 5:29. The word is about painful labour in the sense of hard work, not specifically physical pain. Both sentences are about work becoming hard.
Genesis|3.why: No one English word covers both the pain of childbirth and the grind of farming. Any rendering has to pick a shade, and the parallel dissolves.
Genesis|3.rule: When two verses in the same passage sound like different subjects, check whether they share a word. Passages are often built on repetition that translation smooths away.
Genesis|3.choosing: Pain reads naturally for childbirth and badly for agriculture. Toil reads naturally for agriculture and coldly for childbirth. The King James kept one word for both and is more faithful to the structure than most modern versions here.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:16b
Genesis|3.summary: Thy desire shall be to thy husband. Three occurrences in the whole Bible, and they do not agree.
Genesis|3.plain: A word that turns up three times in an entire library is not defined, it is guessed at. If two of those three appearances point one way and the third points another, every dictionary entry for it is an argument wearing a definition's clothes.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because an entire modern argument about marriage rests on a noun that occurs three times in the Hebrew Bible, and the second occurrence is eight verses later with a very different flavour. Three occurrences is not enough evidence for the weight this word is asked to carry.
Genesis|3.kjv: thy desire shall be to thy husband, and he shall rule over thee.
Genesis|3.kjvWhy: desire is the rendering that shaped every English reading of the verse
Genesis|3.others: Nearly all versions read desire. A minority tradition reads desire to control or contrary to, following an argument from the Genesis 4:7 parallel. The ESV moved to contrary to in 2016 and drew heavy criticism.
Genesis|3.seeing: Teshuqah occurs at Genesis 3:16, Genesis 4:7 and Song of Songs 7:10. At 4:7 sin's teshuqah is toward Cain and he must rule over it, using the same two words as here, which is what drives the control reading. At Song 7:10 it is plainly longing.
Genesis|3.why: English desire covers longing, appetite and craving but not a bid for mastery. Whichever sense a translator picks, the other two occurrences start pulling against it.
Genesis|3.rule: Three occurrences is below the floor where a lexicon can report rather than argue. When a contested doctrine rests on a word this rare, that rarity is the first thing to say out loud.
Genesis|3.choosing: Longing fits Song of Songs and the plain sense. Contrary to or a bid to control fits the Genesis 4:7 parallel and the ruling clause that follows. The parallel is genuinely close and the sample is genuinely tiny, which is why this is filed contested rather than decided.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:20
Genesis|3.summary: He called her Eve, because she was the mother of all living. The name means life.
Genesis|3.plain: Imagine naming a child **Hope** the same afternoon a doctor gives you bad news. The name itself is the argument: things are not only what they look like today. Adam names his wife Life immediately after hearing they will die.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because Eve's name is given at the darkest possible moment, immediately after the sentence of death and exile, and the name itself means the opposite, living or life-giver, a detail a transliterated English name erases completely.
Genesis|3.others: Every English version keeps the King James's transliteration Eve, which carries no meaning to an English ear at all. The meaning survives only in the explanation the verse itself gives, never in the name.
Genesis|3.seeing: Chavah, the Hebrew name behind Eve, is built on the same root as chayah, to live, and chay, living or alive, the same root supplying the explanation the verse itself gives, mother of all living. The name is chosen and explained in the same breath, directly after the curses of chapter 3, as if the verse insists on naming the source of ongoing life at the exact moment mortality is announced.
Genesis|3.why: English Eve is a transliterated sound with no built-in meaning, so an English reader needs the verse's own explanation to know the name means anything at all. In Hebrew the name and its sense are nearly the same word, doing in one breath what English needs a whole clause to do.
Genesis|3.rule: Biblical names are rarely just labels; check whether a name is built on a live root before assuming it is only an identifier. Where the text supplies its own explanation for a name, as it does here, that is the author flagging a wordplay you would otherwise miss.
Genesis|3.choosing: No translation dispute; Eve is the standard transliteration and every version explains the meaning in the clause that follows. This is here only because transliteration, unlike translation, necessarily strips the sense out of a name that was doing real work in Hebrew.

Genesis|3.title: Genesis 3:24
Genesis|3.summary: A flaming sword which turned every way. The verb form says the sword turns itself.
Genesis|3.plain: English can say **self-turning** or **a sword that kept turning on its own**, but it takes extra words to say it. Hebrew builds the same reflexive idea, something happening to itself, directly into one verb form, no extra word needed.
Genesis|3.whyThis: Because the sword guarding Eden is not simply on fire, it is described with a Hebrew verb form that means it is turning itself, and English has no single-word way to build that reflexive sense into an adjective.
Genesis|3.others: Every version reads some form of turning, flashing, or whirling. None can mark, without an added phrase, that the Hebrew verb form itself specifies the sword is the one doing the turning, to itself, continuously.
Genesis|3.seeing: Hammithhapeket is a hitpael participle from haphak, to turn or overturn; the hitpael stem regularly marks reflexive or reciprocal action, something happening to or by the subject itself. The sword is not turned by an unnamed hand; the grammar makes it the agent of its own continuous turning, guarding the way to the tree of life on its own.
Genesis|3.why: English marks reflexive action with a separate word, self- or itself, or with a whole clause. Hebrew can fold that same sense into the verb's own form, so a single participle does work that English needs extra vocabulary to do, and translations regularly drop the reflexive nuance rather than add the extra words.
Genesis|3.rule: The hitpael stem is one of the places Hebrew grammar itself carries meaning with no one-word English equivalent. When you meet it, ask what would need to be added in English to say the same thing, and notice that the Hebrew needed nothing added.
Genesis|3.choosing: No real translation dispute over turned every way as a general sense. The finer point, that the grammar specifies self-turning rather than being turned by something else, is a detail every version states, if at all, with an added phrase rather than showing where it lives in the single Hebrew word.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:1
Genesis|4.summary: I have gotten a man from the LORD. Or: a man, the LORD. The little word between them decides which.
Genesis|4.plain: **I baked a cake, the winner.** Read that as an appositive and you just said the cake is the winner. Read the comma as separating two items and you said something else. Hebrew's et normally marks exactly the appositive-style reading, and that is the problem here.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because Eve's first sentence about her firstborn contains a Hebrew word that is usually the marker for a direct object, and if it is doing that job here, Eve is naming her son alongside the LORD rather than crediting the LORD for him.
Genesis|4.others: Every English version reads from the LORD, with the LORD's help, or a similar rendering that treats et as the preposition with. None reads the more literal, and far stranger, a man, namely the LORD.
Genesis|4.seeing: Et is overwhelmingly the marker introducing a definite direct object, not a preposition meaning with. Read that way, qaniti ish et YHWH would mean I have gotten a man, the LORD, an equation most readers find unthinkable in Eve's mouth. Grammarians have proposed et functioning here as with the help of, but no clearly parallel case elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible confirms that use, which is why the question stays open rather than settled by grammar alone.
Genesis|4.why: English with and English the marker of a direct object are different words doing different jobs, so a translator has to choose one before the sentence reaches an English reader. The ambiguity that makes Hebrew scholars argue about this verse cannot survive into English at all; the English sentence necessarily picks a side.
Genesis|4.rule: When a small grammatical word carries the whole weight of a verse's meaning, check whether its unusual reading here is attested anywhere else in the same corpus. An unparalleled use should be held more loosely than a common one, however theologically attractive it looks.
Genesis|4.choosing: With the LORD's help is the reading every version prints, and it fits ordinary Hebrew usage of et poorly but fits the context comfortably. A man, the LORD, keeps the ordinary grammar but produces a claim nothing else in the passage supports. Both options have a real cost.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:7
Genesis|4.summary: Sin lieth at the door. Its desire is to thee, and thou shalt rule over it. The same crouching-word, and the same two words as 3:16.
Genesis|4.plain: **The dog is lying by the door.** Harmless. Now imagine the word for lying also names a predator waiting in ambush at a doorway in a neighboring language and culture. Lieth sounds passive in English; the word behind it does not.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the word for sin lying at the door is the same word Akkadian uses for a demon crouching at a threshold to ambush whoever comes through, and the verse then repeats, almost word for word, the marriage sentence just given to Eve four verses earlier, only now aimed at her son.
Genesis|4.others: Every English version reads lieth, croucheth, or is crouching, all correctly neutral. Almost none of the popular translations use anything that suggests an ambush or a personified threat, though one modern academic version, the New English Bible, does render it demon.
Genesis|4.seeing: Rovets is a participle of the common verb for an animal lying down, but this personified use of sin as the subject crouching at a door closely resembles the Akkadian rabisu, a demon that lurks at thresholds to attack. Whether the Hebrew word is a deliberate echo of that image or simply the ordinary verb applied metaphorically is debated, but the doorway setting matches the Akkadian pattern closely. The same verse then reuses teshuqah, desire, and the verb mashal, rule over, the identical pairing used of the woman and the man at Genesis 3:16, this time offered to Cain as a warning rather than a sentence.
Genesis|4.why: English lieth or crouches names a posture; it carries none of the threshold-demon association some scholars hear behind the Hebrew word, and English has no way to signal that the sentence structure repeats 3:16's marriage language word for word, since a reader would need to notice both verses share teshuqah and mashal in Hebrew to catch it at all.
Genesis|4.rule: A common word placed in an unusual setting, here an animal-word applied to sin at a doorway, can carry connotations from the culture's wider vocabulary that a plain gloss will not show. And when a rare phrase repeats verbatim a few verses apart, as teshuqah plus mashal does here, treat the second occurrence as commentary on the first.
Genesis|4.choosing: Lieth or crouches is the safe, literal rendering every version uses. Whether to import the Akkadian demon imagery is a judgment call resting on comparative Semitic philology rather than the Hebrew word by itself, which is exactly why mainstream translations have stayed with the neutral gloss.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:8
Genesis|4.summary: Cain talked with Abel his brother. The Hebrew text never says what he said; other ancient witnesses supply Let us go into the field.
Genesis|4.plain: **She told him, and he left.** Told him what? A sentence that introduces speech and never quotes it reads as broken in English the same way it does in Hebrew. Most Bibles quietly patch the gap; the King James, following the Hebrew as it stands, does not.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the Masoretic Hebrew text of this verse has Cain start to speak and then never says what he said, a gap that the Samaritan Pentateuch, the Septuagint, the Vulgate and the Syriac all fill with the same missing line.
Genesis|4.kjv: And Cain talked with Abel his brother: and it came to pass, when they were in the field, that Cain rose up against Abel his brother, and slew him.
Genesis|4.kjvWhy: the King James, like the Masoretic Text it translates, prints the grammatical gap without the missing line the other ancient versions supply
Genesis|4.others: Most modern versions insert Let us go out to the field or similar, following the Samaritan Pentateuch, Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac. The King James and other translations that follow the Masoretic Text as it stands print only talked, with no quoted words.
Genesis|4.seeing: The Hebrew verb for said normally introduces a direct quotation, and here none follows, a real grammatical gap. The Samaritan Pentateuch, the only Hebrew witness among the group, along with the Septuagint, Vulgate and Syriac, all supply nechlecha hasadeh, let us go into the field, closing the gap in slightly different wording across the four.
Genesis|4.why: English cannot leave a said with no quotation and read as ordinary narrative; a translator has to either supply words or leave a sentence English readers will find abrupt. The choice between them is a real textual decision quietly made for most readers by whichever committee translated their Bible.
Genesis|4.rule: When a Hebrew sentence has a grammatical gap that multiple independent ancient versions fill the same way, that convergence is real evidence, even though the Masoretic Hebrew itself may still be defended as original. Check whether a smoothed-over English reading is hiding a textual decision.
Genesis|4.choosing: Supplying let us go into the field, as most modern versions do, produces a smoother, more natural narrative and has broad ancient support outside the Masoretic tradition. Leaving the gap, as the King James does, keeps the harder, better-attested Hebrew text and lets the abruptness stand as Cain's own evasive silence.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:10
Genesis|4.summary: Thy brother's blood crieth. The Hebrew word is plural, bloods, and English cannot say that.
Genesis|4.plain: English blood does not pluralize the way apple does; **bloods** is not a normal English word at all. Hebrew can pluralize dam, blood, to intensify or generalize it, and does so here, and every English version has to silently drop the plural to produce a normal sentence.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the Hebrew word for blood is plural here, and English blood has no plural that means the same thing, so a real feature of the sentence's grammar simply disappears in every translation.
Genesis|4.others: Every version reads blood, singular, because bloods is not usable English. The Septuagint and Vulgate also read the singular, so the flattening is not only a modern-English problem.
Genesis|4.seeing: Damim, the plural of dam, blood, appears here instead of the ordinary singular. The plural of this word elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible regularly marks bloodguilt, violence, or blood shed by violence, rather than blood in the ordinary biological sense, so the grammar itself is already doing some of the accusing before the sentence's meaning is even considered.
Genesis|4.why: English blood is a mass noun with no plural that carries meaning the way Hebrew damim does; bloods simply is not English. A translator has no live option but to render the plural as a singular, which quietly erases a grammatical signal Hebrew readers would have registered automatically.
Genesis|4.rule: Some Hebrew nouns carry meaning in their plural form that has no equivalent plural in English. When a translation looks like a straightforward singular noun, check whether the Hebrew behind it might be plural, and if the plural itself might be idiomatic.
Genesis|4.choosing: Translators never had a real choice here; blood is the only workable English rendering. The interesting question, whether the plural points to bloodguilt generally, multiple wounds, or Abel's unborn descendants, as one old Jewish tradition suggested, cannot be settled by grammar alone and is not something any English translation can flag either way.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:12-16
Genesis|4.summary: A fugitive and a vagabond. Cain then dwells in the land of Nod, wandering, the same word as his curse.
Genesis|4.plain: Imagine a court sentencing someone to **a life of drifting**, and the judgment records afterward that he settled in the town of **Driftwood**. English readers would catch that instantly. Hebrew does the same thing here, and English naming conventions hide it completely.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the curse pronounced on Cain and the name of the land he settles in afterward are built from the same small set of Hebrew sounds, a wordplay that ties his sentence to his address and that no English translation can show.
Genesis|4.others: Every version reads fugitive and vagabond for the curse and Nod as a place name later, treating them as unrelated: one a description, the other a proper noun that needs no translation.
Genesis|4.seeing: Na vanad, restless wanderer, uses forms of the roots nua and nud, both meaning to shake, stagger, or wander. Four verses later Cain settles in the land of Nod, built on the same root nud. The place name is not incidental geography; it is the curse turned into an address, Cain settling, ironically, in the land called Wandering.
Genesis|4.why: English transliterates Nod as a bare place name with no built-in meaning, exactly as it does with Eve, so nothing in an English Bible tips a reader off that it repeats the very word used to curse Cain four verses earlier. The pun that closes the episode is invisible without the Hebrew.
Genesis|4.rule: When a narrative names a place immediately after using an unusual word, check whether the name is built on that word. Hebrew narrators regularly turn a scene's vocabulary into its geography, and translation strips the connection out by default.
Genesis|4.choosing: Every version agrees on fugitive and vagabond, and on transliterating Nod as a bare name; nothing there is in dispute. The pun connecting them is simply lost to transliteration, which is how English necessarily treats a proper noun, whatever meaning that noun is carrying in the original.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:23-24
Genesis|4.summary: I have slain a man. Or: I would slay a man. The same Hebrew perfect tense supports both.
Genesis|4.plain: English can say **I killed him**, reporting a fact, or **I would kill him**, threatening a future act, and the two verbs look completely different. Hebrew's perfect tense can sometimes carry either sense from context alone, and this poem is exactly the case where scholars cannot agree which one it is doing.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the Hebrew verb tense in Lamech's boast can be read either as a confession of a killing he has already done or as a hypothetical threat about a killing he has not, and the two readings paint an entirely different portrait of the man.
Genesis|4.others: Most versions read a completed action, I have killed a man, which is the natural sense of the Hebrew perfect tense read straightforwardly and is how nearly every translation renders it.
Genesis|4.seeing: Haragti, I have killed, is a Hebrew perfect, ordinarily a completed action, and that is how almost every translation reads it: Lamech has already killed someone and is boasting that his vengeance will exceed Cain's sevenfold protection. Some scholars instead read the perfect as a so-called conditional or hypothetical use, common in poetry, so that Lamech is warning any future attacker rather than confessing a past murder: I would kill a man who wounded me, and take vengeance seventy-sevenfold.
Genesis|4.why: English tense marks completed and hypothetical action with entirely different verb forms, so a translator must resolve an ambiguity Hebrew poetry can leave open. Whichever choice is made, the English reader receives a confident portrait, either a murderer boasting or a threat issued in advance, that the Hebrew itself does not force.
Genesis|4.rule: Hebrew's verbal system marks aspect, not strictly tense, and poetry in particular can use the same form for a completed act, a general truth, or a hypothetical one. Where the difference matters to how a character is being portrayed, check whether the verse is prose or poetry, since poetic usage is looser.
Genesis|4.choosing: A completed killing reads Lamech as escalating violence into confessed murder, matching the chapter's downward trajectory from Cain. A hypothetical threat reads the poem as a boast about invincibility rather than a confession, closer to a war-song bravado than a murder record. Both readings are argued by serious commentators and the Hebrew perfect alone does not decide between them.

Genesis|4.title: Genesis 4:26
Genesis|4.summary: Then began men to call upon the name of the LORD. Or: then it became common, in a profaning sense, to call on that name.
Genesis|4.plain: English **began** and English **profaned** share no letters and no sound; nobody would confuse them. The Hebrew word behind began shares its root with the word for profane, and which one this verse means is a live question, not a translator's typo.
Genesis|4.whyThis: Because the verb describing humanity's first public worship of the LORD's name is built on a root that, in its other conjugation, means to profane or defile, and which sense is intended here has divided readers since at least the rabbis.
Genesis|4.others: Nearly every English version reads began, a positive account of the first public worship of God. This is the majority reading and the one nearly all translations print.
Genesis|4.seeing: Huchal is a hophal form that most naturally derives from chalal I, to begin, giving began to call. But chalal is also the root behind chalal III, to profane or defile, and at least one ancient Jewish reading, reflected in Rashi's comment, takes the verse in the profaning sense: it became common, in a degraded way, to invoke the LORD's name, fitting the chapter's downward arc from Cain through Lamech.
Genesis|4.why: English has entirely separate words for began and profaned, so a translation must commit to one root or the other. Hebrew's two roots converge in this one conjugated form, huchal, so the ambiguity that troubles Hebrew readers is invisible the moment an English verb is chosen.
Genesis|4.rule: A Hebrew word that could derive from more than one root with unrelated meanings needs its immediate context checked, and the larger unit it sits in, not just the dictionary entry with the highest frequency. A chapter's overall trajectory, here Cain's line sliding toward Lamech's violence, can be genuine evidence for which root fits.
Genesis|4.choosing: Began to call is the reading nearly every translation prints, treating the verse as a bright note of true worship starting early in human history. The profaning reading, held by Rashi and a minority of modern scholars, fits the chapter's decline from Cain to Lamech but requires choosing the rarer sense of a shared root against the grain of most translation tradition.

Genesis|5.title: Genesis 5:5-31
Genesis|5.summary: And he died. The same two words end almost every entry in the genealogy, on purpose.
Genesis|5.plain: Picture a list where every single line ends with the identical short sentence, on purpose, so the repetition itself becomes the message. English style guides tell writers to vary their sentences. Hebrew narrative sometimes wants the opposite, and this chapter is the clearest example of it in Genesis.
Genesis|5.whyThis: Because the same two Hebrew words close eight of the ten entries in this genealogy like a drumbeat, and English translations, forced to vary their sentence rhythm for readability, smooth away the repetition that is the chapter's entire point.
Genesis|5.others: Every version reads and he died at the end of each entry, correctly. No version can show a reader that this is the identical two-word Hebrew phrase, vayamot, closing verse after verse, because English narrative prose naturally varies its wording anyway.
Genesis|5.seeing: Vayamot, and he died, closes the entries for Adam, Seth, Enosh, Kenan, Mahalalel, Jared, Methuselah, and Lamech, eight refrains in one chapter. The formula is not filler; it is the generational answer to Genesis 3's sentence of death, tolling once per name, following directly after chapter 3's mot tamut warning finally coming due.
Genesis|5.why: English narrative avoids exact repetition as a matter of style, so even a translation that renders and he died correctly every time reads as normal, varied prose rather than as a refrain. The liturgical, tolling effect of the same two words returning eight times is a feature of the Hebrew's deliberate sameness, which English convention works against by instinct.
Genesis|5.rule: When a formula repeats with only names and numbers changing around it, read the repetition as the message, not as a scribe's failure of imagination. Genealogies in Hebrew narrative are rarely neutral bookkeeping; the refrain here is doing theological work chapter 2's warning promised.
Genesis|5.choosing: Every version renders and he died the same correct way, every time; that was never in question. What the English can't preserve, once the repetition is smoothed into ordinary narrative prose, is that the refrain itself is the chapter's real argument.

Genesis|5.title: Genesis 5:24
Genesis|5.summary: Enoch walked with God, and he was not, for God took him. The refrain breaks, and the verb for walked is unusual.
Genesis|5.plain: Imagine a list where every entry ends **and then he died**, except one, which instead says **and then he was gone**. The break itself is the announcement, before you even read what filled the gap. Hebrew builds that exact surprise into this one verse.
Genesis|5.whyThis: Because Enoch's entry breaks the death-refrain that closes every other name in the chapter, and the verb describing his relationship with God is a reflexive form used almost nowhere else of a human being, marking his exit as different in Hebrew grammar as well as in plain content.
Genesis|5.others: Every version reads walked with God and God took him, correctly, but the contrast with the surrounding refrain, and he died, and he died, and he died, is a formatting effect a printed English Bible does not reproduce the way a continuous Hebrew reading does.
Genesis|5.seeing: Vayithhalech, walked, is a hitpael, a reflexive or intensive stem, used of Enoch here and later of Noah at 6:9, rare enough as a description of a human relationship with God that its two uses in Genesis are usually read together. Where the chapter's refrain would put vayamot, and he died, This record instead has einenu, he was not, and God took him, laqach, the same verb used of Elijah's departure centuries later.
Genesis|5.why: English walked with God reads as an ordinary idiom for a godly life; it does not carry the reflexive intensity of the Hebrew stem, nor does it signal, without a reader already knowing the pattern, that this is the one entry in ten where the expected refrain is deliberately withheld.
Genesis|5.rule: In a formulaic passage, the exception is where the meaning concentrates. Before treating a broken pattern as incidental, ask what the formula was doing everywhere else and read the break as the chapter's real point.
Genesis|5.choosing: Translators aren't divided on the plain sense here. What is lost is structural: seeing This record against the refrain it breaks, and noticing that the same rare verb form recurs for Noah two chapters later, both of which require reading the Hebrew continuously rather than verse by isolated verse.

Genesis|5.title: Genesis 5:29
Genesis|5.summary: He called his name Noah, saying, this shall comfort us. Comfort is nacham; the name Noah is built on the different word nuach, rest.
Genesis|5.plain: Imagine naming a baby **Grace** and explaining, **because she will bring us gratitude**. Close, related ideas, but not the same word, and a sharp-eared listener would notice the explanation doesn't quite land on the name. Genesis 5:29 does exactly that in Hebrew.
Genesis|5.whyThis: Because the reason given for Noah's name does not actually match the name, a mismatch visible only in Hebrew: the explanation uses the word for comfort, while the name itself is built on the word for rest, and Lamech's line quietly puns on the gap rather than closing it.
Genesis|5.others: Every version reads Noah and comfort without comment, since English has no built-in way to notice that the name and its stated reason come from two different Hebrew roots that merely sound alike.
Genesis|5.seeing: Noach, the name, is generally traced to the root nuach, to rest or settle. Lamech's explanation uses yenachamenu, from nacham, to comfort or console, a related-sounding but distinct root, the same one behind chapter 6's statement that God was grieved, nacham, that He had made man. The name-explanation is a paronomasia, a sound-play, not a strict derivation, the same kind of move Genesis 2:23 makes with ish and ishah.
Genesis|5.why: English comfort and rest share no sound at all, so an English reader has no way to hear that Lamech's explanation is a near-miss pun rather than a precise etymology. The Hebrew wordplay, closely related consonants doing double duty, is simply gone once translated.
Genesis|5.rule: When a biblical name's stated explanation does not use the exact same root as the name, check whether the text is punning on sound rather than reporting derivation. Hebrew narrators do this regularly, and it is not an error to be corrected but a literary device to be noticed.
Genesis|5.choosing: Both comfort and Noah are rendered correctly in every version; neither word is contested. The point is that the verse's own logic, why this name, works by resemblance rather than by strict etymology, which is exactly the kind of connection English translation cannot preserve.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:2
Genesis|6.summary: The sons of God saw the daughters of men. The oldest reading takes sons of God as divine beings, not a human family line.
Genesis|6.plain: English son of can mean a literal child or a member of a category, **son of the soil**, **sons of thunder**. Hebrew bene elohim works the same way, and here the category in view, sons of the divine realm, is a real option English son of does not rule out but does not spell out either.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the identity of the sons of God who take human wives sets up the whole flood narrative, and which reading you take, divine beings or a righteous human bloodline, comes from the same two Hebrew words carrying two very different ranges elsewhere in the Old Testament.
Genesis|6.others: Most modern versions read sons of God without further comment, leaving the identification to footnotes or study notes. The King James likewise reads sons of God, unglossed.
Genesis|6.seeing: Bene elohim and the singular ben elohim identify members of the divine council elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible, at Job 1:6, 2:1, 38:7, and Psalm 89:6, all contexts where no one reads the phrase as human beings. The earliest interpreters, including the Septuagint tradition, 1 Enoch, and Jubilees, took Genesis 6:2 the same way, as heavenly beings intermarrying with humans. The alternative, that sons of God means the righteous line of Seth marrying Cain's corrupted daughters, is a later reading associated with Julius Africanus and Augustine, developed in reaction against the angelic view rather than growing from Hebrew usage of the phrase itself.
Genesis|6.why: English sons of God carries no built-in link to a divine council, an idea unfamiliar to most modern readers, so the phrase reads as loosely poetic rather than as a technical term with a fixed range of reference elsewhere in the Hebrew Bible.
Genesis|6.rule: Before deciding what a phrase means in one passage, survey every other place the same phrase occurs in the same corpus. Bene elohim is not ambiguous where it appears elsewhere; the ambiguity here is imported by later theological discomfort with what those other passages already say.
Genesis|6.choosing: The divine-council reading is both the oldest attested interpretation and the one that matches every other biblical use of the phrase. The Sethite reading, sons of God as godly men, has no other biblical use of the phrase to support it and arose specifically to avoid the angelic implications, which makes it weaker as a reading of the Hebrew even though it became dominant in later Western Christianity.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:3
Genesis|6.summary: My spirit shall not always strive with man. A verb used only this once, and nobody is fully certain what it says God's spirit will stop doing.
Genesis|6.plain: Imagine a verb that shows up exactly once in every book you own. You would have exactly one sentence to reconstruct its meaning from, and reasonable readers could disagree. That is the situation with the verb translated strive here.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the verb describing what God's Spirit will stop doing to humanity shows up exactly once in the Hebrew Old Testament and nowhere else, and translation committees have split between two genuinely different pictures, one of God arguing with people and one of God's presence simply not staying.
Genesis|6.others: Most versions read strive or contend, following one proposed derivation. A minority tradition reads abide or remain, following a different proposed derivation, giving a noticeably different picture of what is ending.
Genesis|6.seeing: Yadon shows up nowhere else in the Hebrew Old Testament outside this one verse. One proposal derives it from din, to judge or contend, giving strive or contend, God arguing with or opposing humanity's corruption. A second proposal derives it from a root meaning to remain or abide, giving my spirit will not remain in man forever, a statement about withdrawal of presence rather than a legal contest. Both derivations require reasoning from other roots rather than from other occurrences of this exact form.
Genesis|6.why: English strive and English abide describe different relationships, contest versus presence, and a translator must choose one before an English reader ever sees the sentence. With only one occurrence to work from, Hebrew itself does not settle which picture is correct, and English cannot show that uncertainty within the text.
Genesis|6.rule: A word attested exactly once anywhere in a corpus is being reconstructed from etymology and context, not read off a body of established usage. Hold single-occurrence definitions more loosely than a lexicon's confident gloss might suggest.
Genesis|6.choosing: Strive or contend fits a chapter about escalating human violence and portrays God as long-suffering rather than instantly punitive. Abide or remain fits a chapter about the Spirit's presence being withdrawn from corrupted humanity, closer to an exhaustion of patience than an argument. Both readings are defended by serious grammarians working from the same single data point.
Genesis|6.w: yadon (roots proposed: din, judge, or dun, remain)

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:4
Genesis|6.summary: There were giants in the earth. The Hebrew word, Nephilim, does not itself mean giant.
Genesis|6.plain: Imagine a translator centuries ago rendering a foreign name as though it were the English word it merely resembles. Readers ever since picture something the original text never specified, size, when the word may instead be naming a group by what happened to them, not by how tall they stood.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the word behind giants is not a Hebrew word for large size at all, and the King James's giants comes from the Septuagint's Greek gigantes, not from a Hebrew word that means that, shaping a thousand years of popular imagination around a translation of a translation.
Genesis|6.kjv: There were giants in the earth in those days; and also after that, when the sons of God came in unto the daughters of men, and they bare children to them, the same became mighty men which were of old, men of renown.
Genesis|6.kjvWhy: giants is the rendering that shaped the entire popular tradition about this verse, though it comes from the Septuagint's Greek rather than from a translation of the Hebrew word itself
Genesis|6.others: The King James, following the Septuagint's gigantes, reads giants, and that rendering has shaped virtually all popular imagination about this verse. Modern versions increasingly leave Nephilim untranslated, since the Hebrew word's own root does not mean large in stature.
Genesis|6.seeing: Nephilim is usually connected to the root naphal, to fall, giving fallen ones, though the derivation is debated and the word is rare, recurring only here and at Numbers 13:33, where the spies again call inhabitants of Canaan Nephilim and compare themselves to grasshoppers beside them, a comparison about being overwhelmed rather than a precise measurement. The Septuagint's gigantes, giants, is itself an interpretive choice, not a translation of a Hebrew word that means large, and the King James inherited that Greek interpretation rather than translating the Hebrew directly.
Genesis|6.why: English giants specifies enormous physical size; Nephilim, whatever its root, does not obviously specify that on its own. The chain from Hebrew Nephilim to Greek gigantes to English giants adds a claim about height that the Hebrew word itself does not make explicit, though the size language later applied to their descendants, the Anakim, at Numbers 13:33 keeps the association alive.
Genesis|6.rule: When a familiar English word traces back through a second ancient language rather than directly to the Hebrew, check what that intermediate translation was doing. Giants is a translation of a translation, and each step can add a claim the earlier text did not make.
Genesis|6.choosing: Giants keeps the King James's inherited Septuagint reading and the popular tradition built on it. Leaving Nephilim untransliterated, as many modern versions now do, admits that the Hebrew word's own meaning, fallen ones or something similar, is not primarily a statement about height, even though later texts associate the same families with great size.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:6
Genesis|6.summary: It repented the LORD. A verb that means comfort, grieve, relent and change course, all at once.
Genesis|6.plain: **He was sorry.** Sorry about what happened, or sorry enough to undo it? English splits those into regret and relent. One Hebrew word covers both, and the sentence has to tell you which, and sometimes it does not.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the verse is the standard proof text on both sides of the argument about whether God changes, and the verb is the only thing in it under dispute. The same verb turns up in 1 Samuel 15 twice in one chapter pointing opposite directions, which means anyone arguing from it in English is arguing from a translator's choice.
Genesis|6.kjv: And it repented the LORD that he had made man on the earth, and it grieved him at his heart.
Genesis|6.kjvWhy: repented is the word that moved out from under the verse
Genesis|6.others: Modern versions read regretted, was sorry, or was grieved. Repented has dropped out because English repentance now means turning from sin, which is not what the verb says.
Genesis|6.seeing: Nacham covers a range that English splits across several words: to be moved to pity, to console oneself, to grieve, and to change a stated course of action. It is used of God relenting from announced judgment and also of human comfort after a death.
Genesis|6.why: No English verb covers grief and reversal in the same breath. Translators have to pick the shade the context supports, and the shade they pick becomes the theology the reader inherits.
Genesis|6.rule: When a modern version has quietly replaced a King James word, the usual reason is that the English word moved, not that the Hebrew is in doubt. Check the old word's older meaning before assuming a translation agenda.
Genesis|6.choosing: Regretted reads the verb as emotion. Relented reads it as a change of course. The verse supplies both in its two halves, and the second half, it grieved him at his heart, is what makes the emotional reading hard to strip out.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:14a
Genesis|6.summary: Pitch it within and without with pitch. The noun for pitch and the verb for cover share the root behind atonement.
Genesis|6.plain: English **tar** and English **atone** share no sound, no spelling, nothing. A reader moving from Noah's ark to the Day of Atonement chapters later would never connect them. In Hebrew, the two ideas are built from the same three letters.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the instruction to cover the ark with pitch uses the exact same root later used for atonement, the covering of sin on the Day of Atonement, so the ark's waterproofing and Israel's central ritual vocabulary are built from one Hebrew root, a connection no English word for tar or pitch can carry.
Genesis|6.others: Every version reads pitch or tar for the verse's substance and its verb, correctly and unremarkably. No version can show that the same consonants return later as the ordinary Hebrew word for atonement.
Genesis|6.seeing: Kopher, pitch, and the verb kaphar, to cover, here describing waterproofing, come from the same root as kippurim, atonement, the word behind Yom Kippur, the Day of Atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat covering the ark of the covenant later in the Torah. The ark of Noah is, in the vocabulary of the sentence describing it, covered the same way sin is later covered.
Genesis|6.why: English has entirely separate words for a waterproofing tar and a ritual atonement, so the shared Hebrew root, and the theological resonance some readers hear in it, one covering that saves from judgment prefiguring another, cannot survive translation into two unrelated English vocabularies.
Genesis|6.rule: When a mundane, technical instruction, here waterproofing a boat, uses a root that recurs in a book's central ritual vocabulary, that repetition is worth flagging even if the immediate context is entirely practical. Hebrew narrative frequently plants vocabulary early that ritual law develops later.
Genesis|6.choosing: Pitch and cover are the plainly correct sense here, and no version disputes it; the verse is giving construction instructions, not making an atonement statement. The connection to kippurim is an observation about shared vocabulary across the Torah, not a claim that Genesis 6 is itself describing a ritual.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:14b
Genesis|6.summary: Gopher wood. A word used exactly once, and no one knows for certain what tree it names.
Genesis|6.plain: Every English Bible just says **gopher wood**, which sounds specific but is really a translator's shrug: this word occurs nowhere else, so rather than guess at a species, translators simply carried the Hebrew sound into English wholesale.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the wood the ark is built from is named by a word that appears exactly one time anywhere in the Hebrew Old Testament, nowhere else in ancient Hebrew literature, and nobody today can say with confidence what kind of tree it names.
Genesis|6.others: Every version reads gopher wood, transliterating rather than translating, because there is no second occurrence anywhere to translate from. Some modern notes suggest cypress or another conifer as a guess, never as a certainty.
Genesis|6.seeing: Gopher occurs only at Genesis 6:14, a true hapax legomenon with no other biblical or extrabiblical Hebrew attestation to compare it against. Every proposal for its botanical identity, cypress being the most common modern guess, is inferred from context, from shipbuilding plausibility, or from similar-sounding words in related languages, not from a second usage that would confirm it.
Genesis|6.why: English gopher wood looks like a specific, confident botanical term, the way oak or cedar would be, but it is a transliteration standing in for total uncertainty. An English reader cannot tell the difference between a well-attested wood name and a total guess dressed in the same grammatical clothing.
Genesis|6.rule: A transliterated word in an English Bible is often a flag, not a translation: it usually means no one has been confident enough to translate it. Treat every untranslated Hebrew term you meet in English as an invitation to ask why it was left that way.
Genesis|6.choosing: No real choice was available to translators; there is nothing to choose between since the word has no second occurrence to weigh against another. Every specific identification, cypress or otherwise, is an educated guess dressed as a footnote, not a finding.

Genesis|6.title: Genesis 6:16
Genesis|6.summary: A window shalt thou make to the ark. The word may mean light or roof rather than an opening you look through.
Genesis|6.plain: Picture the instructions for a boat saying **make light for it** rather than **put in a window**. Both are ways of solving the same problem, letting light in, but they describe two different building choices, and this word could be pointing at either one.
Genesis|6.whyThis: Because the word every English Bible renders window is a rare term whose root more naturally means light or brightness, and a growing number of modern translations have quietly switched from window to roof for the same Hebrew word.
Genesis|6.others: The King James and many traditional versions read window, connecting the word to an idea of daylight or noon. A number of more recent versions, including the RSV, NIV and ESV, instead read roof, translating the same Hebrew word differently.
Genesis|6.seeing: Tsohar is rare, plausibly related to tzohorayim, noon or midday, and to zohar, radiance or brightness, either of which would support the sense of an opening for light rather than a framed window in the modern sense. Ancient Jewish tradition went further still, reading tsohar as a luminous stone providing light inside the ark, an interpretation preserved in targumic and midrashic sources rather than in any mainstream translation.
Genesis|6.why: English window specifies glass or an opening you look through; roof specifies an entirely different structural feature. The Hebrew word's connection to light or brightness supports either English word depending on how a translator imagines the ark's construction, and the choice changes the mental picture an English reader carries of the vessel.
Genesis|6.rule: When a rare architectural or construction term is translated confidently, check whether that confidence is really coming from the word's root or from a translator's best guess about ancient shipbuilding. Window and roof are not close synonyms, yet both are defended translations of the same Hebrew word here.
Genesis|6.choosing: Window preserves the traditional picture and a plausible link to daylight vocabulary. Roof, now used by several major modern versions, reads the same word as naming a covering that admits light rather than a framed opening, and neither can be confirmed against a second occurrence of the word.

Genesis|7.title: Genesis 7:2
Genesis|7.summary: By sevens, seven and seven. The Hebrew just repeats the numeral; English has to add a preposition to get the same sense.
Genesis|7.plain: Hebrew can say a distributive the way a coach says **two, two, two**, walking down a line splitting people into pairs. Just repeat the number. English cannot do this without inserting a word like **by** or **each**, so shivah shivah becomes by sevens, a translation that adds a word the Hebrew never needed.
