Genesis|7.whyThis: Because the instruction to take clean animals by sevens is built by simply saying the number twice in a row, a distributive construction English cannot reproduce without adding a whole extra phrase, and the doubled number sits one verse away from a different instruction, two of every kind, that reads at first glance like a flat contradiction.
Genesis|7.others: Every version reads by sevens or seven pairs, correctly, for clean animals, against two, two of a kind, three verses earlier at 6:19-20 for animals generally. Read carelessly in translation, the two instructions look like a straightforward contradiction; read together, sevens for the animals fit for sacrifice, twos as the baseline for every kind, they resolve as one instruction refining the other rather than clashing with it.
Genesis|7.seeing: Shivah shivah, literally seven seven, is simple reduplication of the numeral used to express a distributive sense, seven of each. Hebrew forms distributives this way elsewhere, repeating a number or a noun rather than adding a preposition, a pattern with no direct grammatical equivalent in English syntax.
Genesis|7.why: English has no bare-repetition distributive; two two on its own does not read as a grammatical construction the way shivah shivah does in Hebrew, so translators must supply by or each, adding a word that has no counterpart in the Hebrew text itself.
Genesis|7.rule: When you meet a doubled Hebrew word functioning as one grammatical unit, check whether it is marking a distributive sense before assuming it is simple emphasis, and read instructions that seem to conflict across nearby verses as a single set of directions before assuming a contradiction.
Genesis|7.choosing: By sevens follows the Hebrew idiom most closely, but the versions do divide: ESV and NIV read seven pairs, KJV and NASB read by sevens, and the Hebrew doubling will carry either. The apparent tension with the two-of-a-kind instruction at 6:19-20 is a matter of reading both verses as one coherent set of instructions, sevens for clean animals headed for sacrifice, twos as the general rule, rather than a genuine grammatical problem.

Genesis|7.title: Genesis 7:6
Genesis|7.summary: The flood of waters. The word mabbul names only this flood, never an ordinary one.
Genesis|7.plain: English flood covers a river overflowing its banks, a flash flood, a monsoon. Hebrew has ordinary words for those too. This story uses a different word altogether, one that only ever means this specific, singular catastrophe, the way English capitalizes the Flood when it means this one and no other.
Genesis|7.whyThis: Because the Hebrew word for the flood in this story is not the ordinary word for a flood or a downpour; it is used nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible except once, poetically, of this same event, marking Noah's flood off from every other flood the Bible ever mentions.
Genesis|7.others: Every version reads flood, using the ordinary English word for rising water. English has no separate vocabulary item reserved the way mabbul is, so this distinction cannot show up in translation at all.
Genesis|7.seeing: Mabbul appears repeatedly through the flood narrative, Genesis 6-9, and then only once more in the entire Hebrew Bible, at Psalm 29:10, in a poetic line that itself looks back to this event. It is not the Hebrew Bible's general word for a flood or an inundation; those exist separately. A proposed Akkadian cognate exists but is itself rare and specialized rather than the ordinary Akkadian word for flooding, suggesting both languages may have reserved a special term for a catastrophe of this scale.
Genesis|7.why: English flood is a common noun covering any rising water, from a local storm to a global catastrophe, so it cannot mark the same distinction Hebrew draws by using an entirely separate, otherwise unused word only for this one event.
Genesis|7.rule: When a narrative's key noun turns up nowhere else in ordinary usage, check whether the language is marking the event as categorically unique rather than simply describing it. A dedicated vocabulary item is itself a claim about how the event should be remembered.
Genesis|7.choosing: Flood is the only English word on offer, so no version disputes it. The point worth carrying is that Hebrew itself treats this flood as belonging to its own linguistic category, a distinction English flattens the moment the word reaches translation.

Genesis|7.title: Genesis 7:11
Genesis|7.summary: The fountains of the great deep, and the windows of heaven. The word for deep is a cousin of the name of a Babylonian sea-goddess.
Genesis|7.plain: Imagine two neighboring languages both having a word that traces back to the same ancient root for the sea, and one of those languages later personifies that word as a goddess while the other keeps it as an ordinary noun for deep water. That is roughly the relationship between Hebrew tehom and Babylonian Tiamat.
Genesis|7.whyThis: Because the sources of the flood, the deep breaking open and the windows of heaven, use the same word for the deep that opens Genesis 1:2, a word that is a genuine linguistic cousin of the name of the Babylonian chaos goddess Tiamat, though what that relationship proves is more contested than it first sounds.
Genesis|7.others: Every version reads the deep or the great deep, an ordinary common noun with no personal or mythological overtone in English at all.
Genesis|7.seeing: Tehom, the deep, at Genesis 1:2 and again here at 7:11, is a recognized linguistic cognate of Akkadian tiamtu, the ocean, personified in Babylonian myth as the goddess Tiamat, whom Marduk defeats in the creation epic Enuma Elish. Older scholarship argued Genesis preserves a demythologized version of that combat story; more recent comparative Semitic work argues both words simply descend independently from a common Proto-Semitic word for the deep, without one being a suppressed retelling of the other. The windows of heaven, arubbot, opening alongside the deep pictures the flood as creation's waters, once held back at Genesis 1, breaking loose again.
Genesis|7.why: English deep is a plain descriptive noun carrying no mythological freight; a reader has no way to hear a cognate relationship to a Babylonian goddess's name sitting behind the ordinary English word, nor to notice that the flood is described as creation's original waters returning.
Genesis|7.rule: A linguistic cognate between a biblical term and a name from a neighboring mythology is real evidence of shared ancient vocabulary, but it is not by itself proof of borrowing a myth. Keep those two claims, shared word history and shared story, separate, and check which one a given scholar is actually arguing.
Genesis|7.choosing: Every version renders it deep without argument. The live scholarly question is how much weight to put on the tehom/Tiamat connection: strong echo of a suppressed combat myth, or simply two related Semitic languages independently using an inherited word for the sea.

Genesis|8.title: Genesis 8:1
Genesis|8.summary: God remembered Noah. Not recalling a forgotten fact, but acting on a standing promise.
Genesis|8.plain: English **I remembered** can describe a passing thought with no consequence. Hebrew zakar, applied to God, is closer to **I acted on what I remembered**; the word itself carries the following action with it, not just the mental event beforehand.
Genesis|8.whyThis: Because God remembering Noah is not a mental event, recalling something that had slipped from view, but the regular Hebrew way of saying God is about to act on a commitment already made, the same verb used at the turning points of Israel's own later story.
Genesis|8.others: Every version reads remembered, which is not wrong but reads in English as a purely internal, mental act, with no built-in expectation that action follows automatically.
Genesis|8.seeing: Zakar describes God taking covenant action at several turning points: remembering Noah here, remembering Abraham at Genesis 19:29, remembering Rachel at 30:22, and remembering His covenant with Israel groaning in Egypt at Exodus 2:24. In each case what follows is not a change in God's knowledge but a visible act, the waters receding, a child conceived, a deliverance beginning.
Genesis|8.why: English remember describes retrieving information from memory and stops there; it does not by itself imply that action necessarily follows. Hebrew zakar, used of God, regularly functions as the hinge word introducing the deliverance itself, a nuance English remembered does not automatically carry.
Genesis|8.rule: When God is the subject of a verb of mental activity in Hebrew, check whether the verb is functioning idiomatically as the introduction to an action rather than describing an inner mental state the way the same English word would for a human subject.
Genesis|8.choosing: Remembered is the standard, reasonable gloss, and no version seriously disputes it. The nuance worth adding is that this remembering is the narrative hinge, not a preface to it, matching the word's use at other major turning points in Israel's story.

Genesis|8.title: Genesis 8:4
Genesis|8.summary: The mountains of Ararat. A region, plural mountains, not a single named peak.
Genesis|8.plain: **The ark landed in the Rockies** names a mountain range. **The ark landed on Pikes Peak** names one mountain. Genesis says the first kind of thing, and centuries of popular tradition, and most maps and paintings, quietly upgraded it to the second.
Genesis|8.whyThis: Because the verse never says Mount Ararat, a single peak, but the mountains of Ararat, a whole highland region corresponding to a historical kingdom, and the popular picture of one specific volcano is a later identification the text itself does not make.
Genesis|8.others: Every version reads the mountains of Ararat, plural, correctly matching the Hebrew. Popular usage, hymns, and most modern maps nonetheless speak of Mount Ararat, a single volcanic peak in eastern Turkey, as though that were what the verse specifies.
Genesis|8.seeing: Ararat corresponds to Urartu, a real historical kingdom attested in Assyrian records, centered on the highlands around Lake Van in what is now eastern Turkey, Armenia, and northwestern Iran, roughly the ninth through sixth centuries BC. The Hebrew names a mountainous region, not a single summit; the specific volcanic peak now called Mount Ararat received that name only later, as a traditional identification laid onto the biblical region rather than a claim the text itself makes.
Genesis|8.why: English the mountains of Ararat is grammatically plain, but centuries of art, hymnody, and geography teaching have collapsed the region into a single named mountain, an identification English readers absorb from culture rather than from the actual wording of the verse, which never narrows the landing site that far.
Genesis|8.rule: Check whether a familiar geographic identification is actually in the text or was supplied later by tradition. A named region in Hebrew narrative is not automatically a named peak, however confidently later maps draw it that way.
Genesis|8.choosing: Every version renders the wording the same way, mountains, plural; that much is settled. The dispute, where there is one, is entirely about a post-biblical identification, whether the traditional Mount Ararat is the right guess for where in the ancient region of Urartu the ark actually came to rest, a question the Hebrew text does not itself try to answer.

Genesis|8.title: Genesis 8:21a
Genesis|8.summary: The LORD smelled a sweet savour. The word for sweet, soothing, shares Noah's own root.
Genesis|8.plain: Imagine a story where a character named Rest finally brings the household peace, and the text uses the word **restful** to describe the moment it happens. English would catch that instantly. Hebrew does exactly this with Noah and the soothing smell of his offering, and translation erases the connection completely.
Genesis|8.whyThis: Because the smell that pleases God after the flood is described with a word built on the same root as Noah's own name, a quiet echo tying the man whose name means rest to the offering that finally settles God's grief, invisible once both words are translated into unrelated English vocabulary.
Genesis|8.others: Every version reads sweet savour, soothing aroma, or pleasing aroma, all correct and all silent about the wordplay, since English sweet, soothing, or pleasing share no sound with Noah at all.
Genesis|8.seeing: Reyach nichoach, a soothing or restful aroma, uses nichoach, built on the same root as nuach, to rest, the root behind Noah's own name at 5:29. The offering that follows the flood is described, in Hebrew sound, as restful, echoing back to the man whose name promised rest in the first place, a connection reinforced by his father's naming explanation four chapters earlier, even though that earlier explanation had actually reached for comfort, nacham, a related but distinct root.
Genesis|8.why: English sweet, soothing, and pleasing all describe the smell accurately but none of them echoes the sound of Noah, so nothing tips an English reader off that the sentence quietly circles back to the promise made at his naming.
Genesis|8.rule: When a name given earlier in a book carries a live root, watch for that root resurfacing later at a significant turn in the story. Hebrew narrative often plants a name's meaning early and lets it echo, sometimes faintly, sometimes precisely, at a later climax.
Genesis|8.choosing: Sweet savour and its equivalents are uncontested renderings across every version. What's worth noting is a sound-echo of Noah's name that no English rendering of nichoach could preserve, since the connection lives entirely in the shared Hebrew root nuach.

Genesis|8.title: Genesis 8:21b
Genesis|8.summary: The imagination of man's heart is evil from his youth. The same diagnosis as before the flood, now given as the reason God will not flood the earth again.
Genesis|8.plain: Imagine a story where the reason given for a punishment is repeated afterward, word for word, as the reason the punishment will not be repeated. That reversal, same diagnosis, opposite response, is exactly what this verse is doing, and it depends on a reader catching the repetition.
Genesis|8.whyThis: Because this verse repeats, almost word for word, the diagnosis of the human heart that opened the flood story two chapters earlier, and the repetition after judgment, rather than a changed verdict, is the real theological weight of the sentence.
Genesis|8.others: Every version reads roughly the imagination, or inclination, of man's heart is evil, matching Genesis 6:5's similar language, but English translation does not flag for a reader that this is a deliberate callback to the flood's original cause.
Genesis|8.seeing: Yetser, the same word used at Genesis 6:5 to explain why the flood came, every yetser of the thoughts of his heart was only evil continually, recurs here after the flood in nearly identical language. What has changed is not the diagnosis but the response: the same human condition that triggered judgment at 6:5 becomes, at 8:21, the stated reason God commits not to judge the earth this way again.
Genesis|8.why: English imagination or inclination renders yetser accurately in both places, but nothing in the English text signals to a reader that this is the identical phrase recurring, so the deliberate structural echo, same cause, opposite outcome, is visible only to someone reading the Hebrew or already told to look for it.
Genesis|8.rule: When a phrase used to explain a judgment recurs later in a very similar form, check whether the narrative is using the repetition to make a point about mercy or continuity rather than simply repeating itself. Genesis 6:5 and 8:21 are exactly this kind of matched pair.
Genesis|8.choosing: Imagination and inclination are both uncontested renderings. The point worth seeing is structural: the flood does not fix the human condition it responds to; the same diagnosis becomes the basis for restraint rather than for further judgment.

Genesis|9.title: Genesis 9:4
Genesis|9.summary: Flesh with the life thereof, which is the blood thereof, shall ye not eat. Life and blood are named with the same word, nephesh.
Genesis|9.plain: English keeps **blood** and **life** as separate ideas connected only by biology class. This verse states outright, in one Hebrew word doing both jobs, that the blood simply is the life, not a symbol of it or a carrier of it, but the thing itself.
Genesis|9.whyThis: Because the reason given for the new prohibition on eating blood is that the blood is the nephesh, the same word translated soul or life earlier in Genesis, so the verse is making a direct claim about where life resides that English blood and English life do not obviously connect.
Genesis|9.others: Every version reads some form of flesh with the life, which is the blood, correctly, though the repetition of nephesh for both life and, by implication, the animal's very self is not obviously visible in English's two separate words, life and blood.
Genesis|9.seeing: Nephesh, the same word behind a living soul at Genesis 2:7 and the living creatures of chapter 1, is used here to identify the blood directly: basar benaphsho damo, flesh with its life, its blood. The equation, blood is nephesh, becomes the basis for Israel's later dietary law and sacrificial system, restated explicitly at Leviticus 17:11, the life of the flesh is in the blood.
Genesis|9.why: English requires two separate words, life and blood, connected by a verb, to say what Hebrew says by using one word, nephesh, for both. The tight equation Hebrew makes directly, blood is nephesh, becomes in English a looser statement about one thing being associated with another.
Genesis|9.rule: When a text says X is Y using the same underlying word for both sides of the sentence, treat the equation as stronger than an English translation using two different vocabulary words will suggest. Nephesh here is not merely near blood; the text names them with one word.
Genesis|9.choosing: Every version agrees on the basic sense, that blood represents or carries life. The stronger reading, that nephesh here identifies rather than merely associates blood with life, is a matter of how tightly the single Hebrew word is allowed to bind the two ideas together.

Genesis|9.title: Genesis 9:6
Genesis|9.summary: Whoso sheddeth man's blood, by man shall his blood be shed. The Hebrew word order is a mirror around the center.
Genesis|9.plain: English can say **the punishment fits the crime**, but that is commentary, a sentence about the sentence. Hebrew builds the fit directly into word order: sheds, blood, man, man, blood, shed, the same words running forward and then backward around a hinge in the middle.
Genesis|9.whyThis: Because the sentence announcing the death penalty for murder is built as a mirror, the same words appearing in reverse order on either side of the verb, so the grammar itself performs the symmetry the sentence describes, crime answered by an equal and opposite consequence.
Genesis|9.others: Every version reads whoever sheds man's blood, by man his blood shall be shed, correctly following the sense, but English sentence order, subject before verb, cannot reproduce a mirror shape the way Hebrew's more flexible word order can.
Genesis|9.seeing: The Hebrew runs shofekh dam ha'adam, ba'adam damo yishafekh: sheds blood-of-man, by-man his-blood shall-be-shed. The verb for shedding opens the first half and closes the second, the noun for blood and the noun for man swap positions around the center, a structure grammarians call a chiasm, an A-B-C-C'-B'-A' pattern that visually and aurally enacts the very reciprocity, blood for blood, that the sentence is announcing.
Genesis|9.why: English word order is comparatively fixed, subject-verb-object, so it cannot rearrange itself into a mirror shape the way Hebrew's freer word order allows here. A translation can state the principle of equal retribution but cannot make the sentence's shape perform it the way the Hebrew does.
Genesis|9.rule: Look for chiastic word order whenever a verse states a principle of exact correspondence, reciprocity, or reversal. Hebrew narrative and law use mirrored word order as a rhetorical device in its own right, not merely as a stylistic accident, and it rarely survives translation intact.
Genesis|9.choosing: The legal content itself isn't contested; every version agrees on the sense. What is lost is entirely formal: the chiastic shape itself, which is not a matter of word choice but of an arrangement English syntax is not free enough to reproduce.

Genesis|9.title: Genesis 9:27
Genesis|9.summary: God shall enlarge Japheth. The verb for enlarge sounds like the name Japheth itself.
Genesis|9.plain: Imagine blessing a son named **Wade** by saying, **may he wade into wide waters**. The blessing works because it echoes the name, not because it is a technical description of what will literally happen. Hebrew does exactly this with Japheth and the verb for enlarge.
Genesis|9.whyThis: Because Noah's blessing on his third son puns on the son's own name, using a verb that sounds like Japheth's name to describe what will happen to him, exactly the kind of naming wordplay Genesis has already used for Cain, Noah, and Eve.
Genesis|9.others: Every version reads may God enlarge Japheth, or a similar rendering, correctly translating the sense but unable to show that enlarge is chosen partly because of how it sounds next to the name it is blessing.
Genesis|9.seeing: Yapht, may he enlarge, and Yephet, Japheth, share the same consonants differently arranged and pointed, a close enough match that most readers take it as deliberate wordplay rather than coincidence, though the connection is not a strict linguistic derivation and a minority of scholars propose other etymologies for the name itself. The verb's root, pathah, to make wide or open, gives the blessing its content, spreading out, territory, breadth, while its sound ties the blessing directly back to the son's own name.
Genesis|9.why: English enlarge and the name Japheth share no sound at all, so an English reader hears a blessing with content but no wordplay, missing the same naming technique Genesis has already used for Cain at 4:1, Noah at 5:29, and the ish/ishah pun at 2:23.
Genesis|9.rule: When a blessing or judgment is pronounced over a named character, check whether the key verb echoes the name itself. Genesis returns to this device repeatedly, and each occurrence rewards the same kind of listening for sound, not just sense.
Genesis|9.choosing: Enlarge is the uncontested sense of the verb in every version. The wordplay connecting it to Japheth's name is widely recognized but, like the Noah/nacham pun three chapters earlier, not a strict etymology, just a close and probably deliberate resemblance the story is using.

Genesis|10.title: Genesis 10:9
Genesis|10.summary: A mighty hunter before the LORD. Renowned in God's sight, or in open defiance of Him.
Genesis|10.plain: English **before** can mean **in front of, watched by**, as in a performance before an audience, or it can mean **in defiance of**, as in standing before a judge and refusing to yield. Hebrew's lifney carries the same double life, and this verse never tells you which one is meant.
Genesis|10.whyThis: Because the little preposition describing Nimrod's hunting, before the LORD, could mean he was renowned in God's sight or that he was defying God to His face, and Jewish interpreters were already reading it the harsher way at least as early as the rabbis, even though the Hebrew wording itself never forces that choice.
Genesis|10.others: Most English versions read before the LORD without further comment, letting the ambiguity stand. The Septuagint's Greek, enantion, is the same neutral before-God's-presence wording used elsewhere for this construction; the harsher, defiant sense comes later, from rabbinic tradition rather than from the earliest translators.
Genesis|10.seeing: Lifney, literally to the face of, ordinarily means in the presence of or in the sight of, but can also carry a confrontational sense, standing in defiance to someone's face. Jewish tradition going back to early rabbinic sources reads Nimrod negatively, a tyrant hunting men rather than game and provoking God openly, while the plain sense of the Hebrew by itself supports the more neutral reading, a renowned figure whose fame was plain for all, including God, to see.
Genesis|10.why: English before does carry both senses too, in front of an audience or in defiance of an authority, but English readers default to the neutral sense here because the surrounding phrase, mighty hunter, sounds like an honorific rather than an accusation, a bias the bare Hebrew preposition does not itself supply.
Genesis|10.rule: A small preposition can carry a genuinely double range, and later interpretive tradition, here the negative reading of Nimrod, can fill a gap the grammar itself leaves open rather than resolving it. Check whether a confident interpretation is coming from the Hebrew word or from a tradition built around it.
Genesis|10.choosing: Before the LORD, read neutrally, portrays a legendary figure whose renown God Himself would notice. The negative rabbinic tradition instead reads Nimrod as an early type of the tyrant who founded Babel two verses later, a reading the immediate context, his kingdom beginning at Babel, genuinely supports even though the preposition alone does not force it.

Genesis|10.title: Genesis 10:25
Genesis|10.summary: In his days was the earth divided. His name, Peleg, means division.
Genesis|10.plain: Imagine a chronicle naming a child **Splitter** the same year a kingdom splits in two, and stating outright that the timing is the point. Genesis does this routinely, and English transliteration, Peleg as a bare name, hides the built-in explanation every time.
Genesis|10.whyThis: Because the name given to mark a moment of global division is built on the exact Hebrew verb for dividing, another instance of Genesis explaining an event by naming a person after it, the same device already used for Cain, Noah, and Japheth.
Genesis|10.others: Every version reads Peleg as a name and divided as a separate statement, correctly, but with no way to show an English reader that the name itself is the Hebrew word for divided.
Genesis|10.seeing: Peleg is built directly on the verb palag, to divide or split, the same root behind the noun for a water channel or stream at Psalm 1:3 and Job 38:25, and behind the request confuse, divide their tongues at Psalm 55:9, itself a probable echo of the Babel story two verses later in Genesis. What exactly divided in Peleg's days, the population by language at Babel, or a more literal geological or geographic division, is debated, but the naming device itself is the same one Genesis has already used three times before this chapter.
Genesis|10.why: English Peleg is a bare proper name carrying no built-in meaning, so the sentence in his days was the earth divided reads as a coincidence of timing rather than as the name itself supplying the explanation, which is how the Hebrew presents it.
Genesis|10.rule: When Genesis names a person immediately before or after describing a major event, assume the name is doing explanatory work until proven otherwise; this book uses that device more often than any other in the Hebrew Bible.
Genesis|10.choosing: Every version simply transliterates Peleg as a name, with no dispute about that. What exactly was divided, languages at Babel or something more literal and geographic, is a separate and genuinely open question the naming pun itself does not settle.

Genesis|11.title: Genesis 11:1
Genesis|11.summary: The whole earth was of one language. Literally, one lip, and one set of words.
Genesis|11.plain: English keeps **lip service** and **read my lips** as fixed idioms, small leftovers of using a body part to mean speech. Hebrew safah, lip, is the ordinary, everyday word for language itself, not a special poetic flourish, and this verse uses it in its most literal sense: one lip for the whole earth.
Genesis|11.whyThis: Because the sentence introducing the Babel story says, word for word, one lip, using the body part for the language it produces, a figure of speech English keeps for a handful of fixed idioms but does not use as its ordinary word for language the way Hebrew does.
Genesis|11.others: Every version reads one language, correctly capturing the sense, but the substitution of the abstract noun language for the concrete body part lip is invisible once translated.
Genesis|11.seeing: Safah, lip, functions as Hebrew's standard word for language or speech throughout the Old Testament, a settled use of the body part for its function, technically called metonymy. This verse pairs it with devarim achadim, one set of words, so the sentence names both the form of speech, one lip, and its content, one shared vocabulary.
Genesis|11.why: English can say language directly without borrowing a body-part word to do it, so the sentence's underlying image, everyone sharing a single lip, disappears the moment lip becomes the abstract noun language in translation.
Genesis|11.rule: When a Hebrew abstraction is built on a concrete body-part word, notice the image before it dissolves into an English abstraction. Hebrew regularly builds its vocabulary for inner or abstract realities out of very physical, embodied words.
Genesis|11.choosing: One language is the only workable English rendering, and no version disputes it. What's worth flagging is the concrete image, a single lip shared by the whole earth, that the abstract translation necessarily leaves behind.

Genesis|11.title: Genesis 11:4
Genesis|11.summary: A tower whose top may reach unto heaven. Standard ancient building-inscription language, not a literal engineering claim.
Genesis|11.plain: When a modern city calls its tallest building a **skyscraper**, nobody thinks it literally scrapes the sky. Ancient Mesopotamian temple towers, ziggurats, were routinely described in royal inscriptions with the same kind of formulaic exaggeration, reaching to heaven, and Genesis is using their own language against them.
Genesis|11.whyThis: Because a tower whose top reaches to heaven is not a boast about engineering height, it is the standard, formulaic way Mesopotamian building inscriptions described their temple towers, and Genesis is quoting a familiar phrase from that world rather than describing an actual attempt to touch the sky.
Genesis|11.others: Every version reads reach unto heaven, or reach into the heavens, as a literal-sounding architectural boast, since English has no equivalent stock phrase from ancient building inscriptions to signal that this was a known formula rather than a fresh claim.
Genesis|11.seeing: Ziggurats, the stepped temple towers of Mesopotamia, were regularly described in their own dedicatory inscriptions with towers whose head reaches to heaven, standard temple-building language expressing the tower's function as a bridge between the human and divine realms, not a literal claim about altitude. Genesis 11:4 borrows this exact convention, and the builders' accompanying goal, let us make us a name, plays against the divine naming and blessing language of the chapters just before it, humanity securing its own reputation rather than receiving one.
Genesis|11.why: English readers, unfamiliar with Mesopotamian building-inscription conventions, hear reach unto heaven as unique hyperbole invented for this story, when it is in fact the text quoting a genre its original audience would have recognized immediately, the exact vocabulary of the civilization Babel is criticizing.
Genesis|11.rule: Before reading a phrase as this story's own invention, check whether it was stock language in the surrounding ancient culture. Genesis frequently borrows the vocabulary of the civilizations it is critiquing and turns that vocabulary against them.
Genesis|11.choosing: Reach unto heaven is the uncontested sense of the Hebrew in every version. What English cannot supply on its own is the recognition that this is a quoted convention from Mesopotamian temple-building inscriptions, which changes the verse from an isolated boast into a pointed piece of cultural mimicry.
Genesis|11.w: verosho vashamayim, its head in the heavens

Genesis|11.title: Genesis 11:9
Genesis|11.summary: Therefore is the name of it called Babel, because the LORD did there confound. A pun that mocks the city's own name for itself.
Genesis|11.plain: Imagine a city calling itself **Gateway**, and a rival nation nicknaming it **Gatecrash**, close enough in sound to land the joke, and different enough in meaning to be an insult. That is exactly the move Genesis makes with Babel and the Hebrew word for confuse.
Genesis|11.whyThis: Because Babel's own name, in the Akkadian of the empire that built it, meant gate of god, and Genesis renames the city with a Hebrew pun that sounds almost identical but means confusion, turning the city's own proud self-description into a joke at its expense.
Genesis|11.others: Every version reads Babel and confounded or confused, correctly translating both, but with no way to show that the connection between them is a pun rather than an actual derivation, since Babel is simply carried over as a name in English.
Genesis|11.seeing: In Akkadian, the city's own language, Babel is bab-ilu, gate of god, the name Babylon proudly gave itself as the meeting place of heaven and earth. Genesis instead connects the name to the unrelated Hebrew root balal, to confuse or mix up, close enough in sound to register as deliberate wordplay, not a genuine etymology. The Hebrew narrator takes Babylon's own grand self-description and replaces it with mockery, using the empire's most famous city as the counter-example to the naming device used positively for Peleg and Noah earlier in the same block of chapters.
Genesis|11.why: English Babel is simply a transliterated proper name carrying no built-in meaning either way, so an English reader cannot hear either the Akkadian gate of god the city claimed for itself or the Hebrew confusion the narrator substitutes for it.
Genesis|11.rule: When Genesis renames a place or a person with a pun rather than an etymology, ask what the original, often foreign, name was claiming, and read the Hebrew pun as a deliberate answer to that claim rather than a neutral linguistic note.
Genesis|11.choosing: Confounded is the settled sense of balal in every version. The polemical edge, that this pun specifically answers and undercuts Babylon's own proud self-naming, is a matter of reading Genesis against its ancient Near Eastern background, not a textual question translation alone can resolve.

Genesis|12.title: Genesis 12:1
Genesis|12.summary: Get thee out. Literally go, for yourself, or go, to yourself: a pronoun added where none was grammatically needed.
Genesis|12.plain: **Go.** That is a complete command. **Go, for yourself.** That is the same command with something added that changes nothing about the instruction and everything about its weight, making the journey personal rather than merely logistical. Hebrew does exactly that here.
Genesis|12.whyThis: Because God's opening command to Abram contains a small extra word that is grammatically unnecessary, go is a complete command on its own, and that extra word is exactly what gives the phrase its force, famous enough to name the entire Torah portion after it.
Genesis|12.others: Most versions read get thee out, go forth, or simply go, all reasonable renderings that lose the grammatical oddity, an unneeded reflexive pronoun, that Hebrew readers immediately notice.
Genesis|12.seeing: Lech lecha pairs the plain imperative lech, go, with lecha, to or for yourself, a dative pronoun that is not required to complete the sentence's grammar. Its presence signals personal investment or benefit, go for your own sake, into your own becoming, rather than a bare travel instruction, and the same construction recurs at Genesis 22:2 when Abraham is told to go to Moriah, framing his story with two commands that are more than they need to be.
Genesis|12.why: English go is already grammatically complete, so an English translator either drops the redundant pronoun entirely, matching ordinary usage, or must add an interpretive phrase like for your own sake to signal what the Hebrew conveys by the pronoun's mere unnecessary presence.
Genesis|12.rule: Watch for grammatically superfluous words in a Hebrew imperative; a pronoun that is not required to complete the sentence is often doing emphatic or reflexive work that a bare English imperative cannot carry without extra vocabulary.
Genesis|12.choosing: Get thee out and go forth both lose the pronoun's redundancy but keep the sense of departure. No translation captures the personal-stakes nuance of lecha without either paraphrasing or adding a phrase the Hebrew itself achieves with one small, technically unnecessary word.

Genesis|12.title: Genesis 12:3
Genesis|12.summary: In thee shall all families of the earth be blessed. Passive, or reflexive: blessed through you, or blessing themselves by your name.
Genesis|12.plain: English **he was blessed** is passive, something done to him. English **he blessed himself** is reflexive, something he does using himself as the reference point, the way people still say **as rich as Rockefeller** without Rockefeller doing anything for them personally. Hebrew's one verb form here could be doing either job.
Genesis|12.whyThis: Because the verb stem describing how the nations will be blessed through Abram can be read as passive, they will be blessed, or reflexive, they will bless themselves by his example, and the same promise later in Genesis switches to the stem that supports the second reading, while Paul builds an argument in Galatians on the first.
Genesis|12.others: Every English version reads a passive sense, shall be blessed, following the Septuagint, Vulgate, and Targums, and this is the reading Paul follows in Galatians 3:8, applying it to the gospel reaching the nations through Christ.
Genesis|12.seeing: The niphal stem of barakh here can carry a passive sense, will be blessed, or, as niphal sometimes does, a reflexive-reciprocal sense, will bless themselves or one another. When the same promise recurs at Genesis 22:18 and 26:4, it switches to the hitpael stem, which leans more clearly reflexive, nations invoking Abraham's name as a byword for blessing, you have done well, like Abraham, rather than nations passively receiving blessing through him.
Genesis|12.why: English must choose one grammatical voice, passive or reflexive, and commit to it in translation, while Hebrew's niphal here sits genuinely between the two senses in a way no single English verb form preserves, so a reader cannot see that the promise's later restatements shift toward the more clearly reflexive stem.
Genesis|12.rule: When a Hebrew verb stem is capable of more than one voice, check whether the same promise or phrase recurs elsewhere in a different stem. A later restatement in a less ambiguous form, as with the hitpael at 22:18 and 26:4, is real evidence for how an earlier ambiguous form might have been heard.
Genesis|12.choosing: The passive reading, blessed through Abraham as an active channel, is the traditional and Pauline reading and fits the covenant's forward momentum toward a Messiah. The reflexive reading, nations blessing themselves by invoking Abraham's name, fits the hitpael restatements later in Genesis and does not require Abraham to be an active agent of anyone else's blessing, only a byword for it.

Genesis|12.title: Genesis 12:6
Genesis|12.summary: The Canaanite was then in the land. The word then implies the writer already knows a time when the Canaanite was not.
Genesis|12.plain: If a modern account said **the mill was then still standing on Main Street**, you would assume the writer already knew it later burned down. The word then does that work quietly, and Genesis uses it exactly the same way about the Canaanites.
Genesis|12.whyThis: Because a small aside noting that the Canaanite was then in the land only makes sense as a comment written after the Canaanites were no longer there, and that one-word clue about the narrator's vantage point has driven a centuries-long argument about who wrote the passage and when.
Genesis|12.others: Every version reads was then in the land, correctly translating az, then, but the English reader does not necessarily catch that the word implies a later vantage point the way careful readers of the Hebrew, ancient and modern alike, have.
Genesis|12.seeing: Az, then, at this point, most naturally implies a contrast with the narrator's own time, when the Canaanite was no longer in the land, a condition that only obtained centuries after the events described, once Israel had taken the territory. The twelfth-century Jewish commentator Ibn Ezra was already flagging this phrase, along with several others, as evidence that at least some material in the Torah could not have been written by Moses in its final form, a genuinely old observation rather than a modern critical invention.
Genesis|12.why: English then carries the same implication English readers would recognize in any other narrative, but Bible readers often do not pause to apply ordinary reading habits to a text they assume was written entirely at the time of the events it describes.
Genesis|12.rule: Read a small time-marking word like then the same way you would read it in any other narrative: as a signal about the writer's vantage point relative to the events, not only about the events themselves. Doing so here raises a genuine, old, and unresolved authorship question rather than settling one.
Genesis|12.choosing: Reading then as an ordinary editorial aside, whether by Moses or a later editorial hand within an otherwise Mosaic Torah, treats the note as a minor updating gloss. Reading it as evidence of substantially later authorship is a larger claim the single word alone cannot carry by itself, though it has carried real interpretive weight since well before modern critical scholarship existed.

Genesis|14.title: Genesis 14:18a
Genesis|14.summary: Melchizedek, priest of the most high God. A title shared with Canaanite religion, which Abraham treats as naming his own God.
Genesis|14.plain: Imagine meeting a priest from another country who blesses you in the name of **the Almighty**, a title your own religion also uses. Do you correct him, or recognize the same God under a shared word? Genesis has Abraham do the second, and the choice carries weight.
Genesis|14.whyThis: Because the title Melchizedek gives his God, El Elyon, Most High God, is also attested as a title of the high god of the Canaanite pantheon, and Abraham's response, treating Melchizedek's El Elyon as identical to his own LORD, is doing real theological work most English readers never notice is happening.
Genesis|14.others: Every version reads most high God without comment, since El Elyon reads in English as a straightforward divine title with no built-in signal that it was also, independently, a title used of a chief Canaanite deity.
Genesis|14.seeing: El and Elyon both function as attested divine titles in the wider Canaanite religious world, El as the head of the pantheon and Elyon as a title meaning highest or most high. Melchizedek, a Canaanite king-priest of Salem, blesses Abram by El Elyon, and two verses later Abram swears an oath by the LORD, El Elyon, explicitly equating his own God's name with Melchizedek's title, treating them as the same God under different peoples' vocabulary rather than correcting or rejecting the foreign priest's language.
Genesis|14.why: English most high God reads as a generic superlative description; it carries no signal that the underlying Hebrew phrase was also a known title in the surrounding Canaanite religious vocabulary, so the theological move Genesis is making, claiming a foreign priest's God-language as legitimately naming Israel's own God, is invisible without that background.
Genesis|14.rule: When a biblical text uses a title also attested in a neighboring culture's religious vocabulary, ask whether the text is borrowing, rejecting, or reclaiming that vocabulary. Genesis 14 reclaims it: Abraham does not treat Melchizedek as a pagan to be corrected but as a genuine priest of the same God under a shared ancient Near Eastern title.
Genesis|14.choosing: Most high God is the uncontested sense of El Elyon in every version. The larger question, how much weight the shared Canaanite background carries for how this scene functions theologically, is a matter of ancient Near Eastern religious history layered on top of an otherwise straightforward translation.

Genesis|14.title: Genesis 14:18b
Genesis|14.summary: Melchizedek, king of Salem. His name means king of righteousness; Salem means peace.
Genesis|14.plain: Imagine a story where a stranger named **Justice** arrives from the city of **Peace**, and later readers treat both names as meaningful rather than coincidental. That is exactly the case Hebrews later makes about Melchizedek, and it only works if you know what his name and city mean in the original language.
Genesis|14.whyThis: Because Melchizedek's own name and the name of his city both mean something in Hebrew, king of righteousness and king of peace, and the epistle to the Hebrews later reads both meanings as deliberate theological signals, a wordplay English transliteration of a proper name cannot carry at all.
Genesis|14.others: Every version reads Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper names, transliterated, since neither carries any built-in meaning once rendered into English letters.
Genesis|14.seeing: Melchizedek is built from melech, king, and tsedek, righteousness, giving king of righteousness, while Salem, shalem, shares its root with shalom, peace, giving king of peace, or king of Salem read doubly. Hebrews 7:2 explicitly draws out both meanings, treating the king-priest's very name and title as prefiguring the righteousness and peace later associated with the Messiah, an argument that depends entirely on the reader knowing what the Hebrew names mean.
Genesis|14.why: English transliterates both Melchizedek and Salem as bare proper nouns, so a reader meeting Hebrews 7's argument about righteousness and peace can't tell where those concepts come from unless someone explains that the names themselves are doing the work.
Genesis|14.rule: When a name is significant enough that a later biblical writer stops to explain its meaning, as Hebrews does here, treat that explanation as confirmation that Hebrew names throughout Scripture are regularly meant to be heard, not simply used as labels.
Genesis|14.choosing: Melchizedek and Salem draw no real disagreement among translators as proper names; there is no live alternative rendering. What matters here is that the meaning behind both names, preserved and explained in Hebrews 7:2, stays otherwise completely inaccessible to a reader working only from the English text of Genesis.

Genesis|15.title: Genesis 15:2
Genesis|15.summary: The steward of my house is this Eliezer of Damascus. A rare word, ben-meshek, that nobody fully agrees on.
Genesis|15.plain: Imagine a legal document naming an heir with a title so unusual that lawyers today still argue whether it means owner, manager, or errand-runner. That is roughly the situation with ben-meshek here, a phrase modern translations gloss confidently while quietly disagreeing about what it actually names.
Genesis|15.whyThis: Because the phrase identifying Abram's household heir is grammatically strange and the word at its center is rare enough that translators cannot agree whether it names an office, a relationship, or even a person's name, and the oddity may itself be a deliberate pun on the city Damascus.
Genesis|15.others: Most versions read steward of my house or heir of my house, smoothing the phrase into a clear English office. A few older or more literal renderings preserve more of the Hebrew's actual strangeness.
Genesis|15.seeing: Ben-meshek is unusual enough that proposals range from son of acquisition, meaning the one who will inherit, to a verb related to running about in service, to reading meshek as a proper name, Masek, making Eliezer the son of a servant woman by that name rather than a household title at all. Many scholars additionally note that ben-meshek was likely chosen partly for its assonance with the following word, Dammesek, Damascus, a wordplay layered on top of an already rare and difficult phrase.
Genesis|15.why: English steward reads as a clear, ordinary job title; the Hebrew phrase behind it is contested enough that no single English word can represent the genuine uncertainty scholars still have about what ben-meshek names.
Genesis|15.rule: When a translation reads smoothly and confidently, check whether the underlying Hebrew is actually that clear. A fluent English rendering can paper over real uncertainty that specialists are still debating.
Genesis|15.choosing: Steward or heir of my house gives English readers a working sense of the passage without pretending to settle a genuinely contested phrase. No consensus exists on ben-meshek's precise force, and every translation is making a judgment call the Hebrew itself does not fully support.

Genesis|15.title: Genesis 15:6a
Genesis|15.summary: He believed in the LORD. The verb is the root behind amen.
Genesis|15.plain: **He trusted the bridge.** **He believed the story.** English believe drifts toward agreeing with a claim. The older sense is closer to leaning your weight on something, and you can still hear it in **the ice held**.
Genesis|15.whyThis: Because Paul builds the argument of Romans 4 and Galatians 3 on this verse, and the Hebrew verb is in a form that says something about duration that neither Greek nor English carries over.
Genesis|15.others: All versions read believed. None can show the root, and none shows the verb form.
Genesis|15.seeing: He'emin is the hiphil of aman, a root meaning to be firm, reliable, to support. The noun from it is emunah, faithfulness, and the word you say at the end of a prayer is the same root. The verb is closer to he found God reliable and rested on Him than to he accepted a proposition.
Genesis|15.why: English believe has moved toward mental assent. There is no English verb meaning to treat as load-bearing, so the root sense has to be explained rather than translated.
Genesis|15.rule: When a verse is the foundation of a doctrine, look up the root of its main verb. Doctrinal vocabulary drifts faster than ordinary vocabulary, because it gets used more.
Genesis|15.choosing: No dispute in the rendering. The dispute, where there is one, is about how much the root sense should shape the doctrine built on the verse.

Genesis|15.title: Genesis 15:6b
Genesis|15.summary: He counted it to him for righteousness. The verb belongs in a ledger.
Genesis|15.plain: **Put it on my account.** That is a statement about a ledger, not about the truth of anything. Whether the entry reflects what is in your pocket is a separate question from whether the entry was made.
Genesis|15.whyThis: Because the second verb in the verse is an accounting term, and knowing that changes what kind of claim is being made. This is the word Paul reaches for when he argues about reckoning in Romans 4, and it is a ledger word in both languages.
Genesis|15.kjv: And he believed in the LORD; and he counted it to him for righteousness.
Genesis|15.kjvWhy: counted keeps the accounting sense that later renderings soften
Genesis|15.others: The King James reads counted. Modern versions read credited, reckoned or counted. Romans 4 uses the Greek equivalent eleven times in one chapter.
Genesis|15.seeing: Chashav means to think, to plan, and also to reckon or impute in the bookkeeping sense. The Septuagint renders it logizomai, which is likewise an accounting verb, and that is the word Paul repeats through Romans 4. Two languages, the same commercial metaphor, deliberately kept.
Genesis|15.why: English credited carries the accounting sense well. Reckoned has drifted toward supposed. Counted sits between them and is what the King James chose.
Genesis|15.rule: When the Septuagint picks a Greek word in the same semantic field as the Hebrew, that is a translator two thousand years ago telling you what he heard. Those choices are evidence.
Genesis|15.choosing: No real dispute about the verb. What the accounting metaphor implies theologically is a separate and much older argument, and the verb does not settle it.

Genesis|15.title: Genesis 15:18
Genesis|15.summary: The LORD made a covenant with Abram. Literally, cut a covenant, and the chapter just showed you the cutting.
Genesis|15.plain: English **cut a deal** is a dead metaphor; nobody pictures an actual knife. Hebrew **cut a covenant** started out exactly that literal, and Genesis 15 is the one chapter where you get to watch the literal cutting happen right before the idiom is used.
Genesis|15.whyThis: Because the ordinary Hebrew way of saying make a covenant is literally cut a covenant, a phrase that only makes full sense once you have watched Abram cut animals in half and walk between the pieces two verses earlier, an idiom whose literal, physical origin English has long since forgotten.
Genesis|15.others: Every version reads made a covenant, using English's own dead metaphor for finalizing an agreement, correctly conveying the sense but losing any connection to actual cutting.
Genesis|15.seeing: Karat berit, cut a covenant, is the standing Hebrew idiom for covenant-making throughout the Old Testament, and this chapter preserves the ritual behind the dead metaphor: animals are cut in half, and a smoking firepot and flaming torch, representing God, pass between the pieces, a self-maledictory oath in which walking between severed halves meant may I become like these animals if I break this covenant.
Genesis|15.why: English cut a deal is used and heard purely figuratively, with no live memory of an actual cutting ceremony behind it. Hebrew karat berit sits closer to its literal origin, and this chapter is the rare place in the Bible where the idiom's backstory is narrated rather than merely assumed.
Genesis|15.rule: When you meet a fossilized idiom, cut a deal, cut a covenant, ask whether the Bible anywhere narrates the literal action the dead metaphor came from. Genesis 15 is exactly that kind of narration, and it is easy to read straight past it if you already think of covenant-making as an abstract legal event.
Genesis|15.choosing: Translators aren't actually divided here; made a covenant is the only workable English rendering. This note is meant to reconnect the abstract English phrase to the concrete ritual Genesis 15 actually describes just before the idiom is used.

Genesis|16.title: Genesis 16:7-13
Genesis|16.summary: The angel of the LORD found Hagar. She then says the LORD spoke to her, and names him accordingly.
Genesis|16.plain: Imagine a story where a messenger delivers a message, and the recipient afterward says **I spoke with the president**, not **with the president's messenger**. English would read that as either a mistake or a deliberate blurring. Hebrew does this here without comment, and the text seems entirely comfortable with it.
Genesis|16.whyThis: Because the figure who speaks to Hagar is called the angel of the LORD in one verse and then, two verses later, is simply the LORD who has spoken to her, and the Hebrew text moves between the two without any sense of contradiction, exactly the pattern that later drives the whole debate over who or what this figure is.
Genesis|16.others: Every version reads angel of the LORD throughout, correctly, but the shift in verse 13, where Hagar's own words treat the speaker as God directly, is easy to read past without noticing the identification the Hebrew is making.
Genesis|16.seeing: Malach YHWH, the angel, or messenger, of the LORD, speaks to Hagar in the first person as God, promising to multiply her seed, language elsewhere reserved for God's own covenant promises. Hagar then names Him El Roi, the God who sees, and the text states plainly that she saw God and lived, treating messenger and message-giver as interchangeable in a way that has driven a long theological debate: whether this figure is simply God appearing in a form Hagar could address, a distinct angelic being who speaks with delegated divine authority, or, in later Christian reading, a pre-incarnate appearance of the Son.
Genesis|16.why: English angel reads as clearly distinct from God, a messenger sent by someone else; it carries none of the fluidity the Hebrew text displays here, where the messenger's identity and the sender's identity blur without the narrative treating that blur as strange.
Genesis|16.rule: When a figure called the angel of the LORD speaks in the first person as God and is addressed as God by the human who meets him, do not resolve the identification too quickly in either direction. The Hebrew text itself holds messenger and sender together without fully separating them.
Genesis|16.choosing: Translators agree without exception that angel of the LORD is the correct rendering throughout. The theological question, whether this is God Himself in a form Hagar could face, a distinct heavenly being acting with full divine authority, or specifically the pre-incarnate Son, cannot be settled by the Hebrew grammar alone and has divided readers since the church fathers.

Genesis|16.title: Genesis 16:12
Genesis|16.summary: He will be a wild man. The Hebrew literally reads a wild-donkey of a man, animal first.
Genesis|16.plain: English **a wild man** puts man first and wild as a description. Hebrew here reverses that: pere adam is closer to **a wild-donkey, a human one**, animal noun first, human noun second, the reverse of the ordinary Hebrew word order where the describing word comes after the noun it describes.
Genesis|16.whyThis: Because the description of Ishmael's future is built around the Hebrew word for a wild donkey, not a generic word for wildness, and the word order even puts the animal first, making the man the modifier rather than the other way around.
Genesis|16.others: Every version reads wild man, wild donkey of a man, or similar, generally preserving the sense but not always flagging the unusual word order that puts the animal image first.
Genesis|16.seeing: Pere, wild donkey, stands before adam, man, reversing the normal Hebrew pattern where a modifying word follows its noun; the expected order would put man first and wild donkey as the descriptor. Instead the wild donkey, an animal proverbial in the ancient Near East for fierce independence, untamed freedom, and life beyond settled territory, is named first, making it the dominant image and man almost an afterthought clarifying which kind of creature is meant.
Genesis|16.why: English word order cannot easily reproduce this reversal without sounding broken; a wild-donkey man puts the animal first the way the Hebrew does but reads as odd English, so translators default to the more natural wild man, losing the emphasis the unusual Hebrew order creates.
Genesis|16.rule: When a Hebrew phrase's word order runs backward from what the grammar normally expects, that reversal is itself doing rhetorical work, foregrounding whichever word was moved to the front. Do not read past unusual word order as a translator's stylistic accident.
Genesis|16.choosing: Wild man keeps a natural English sentence but loses the foregrounded animal image. Wild donkey of a man, closer to the Hebrew word order, keeps the emphasis but reads awkwardly in English, the standard tradeoff between literal word order and natural target-language phrasing.

Genesis|17.title: Genesis 17:1
Genesis|17.summary: I am the Almighty God. El Shaddai, a title whose root meaning is genuinely uncertain.
Genesis|17.plain: Almighty is confident, clear English. Shaddai's own root is not confident or clear at all; serious scholars have proposed it comes from words for a mountain, for a breast, and for violent overpowering, three pictures of God's power that would each shape the sentence differently if any one were certain.
Genesis|17.whyThis: Because the divine title God reveals at the covenant of circumcision, El Shaddai, has an etymology genuinely unknown, with real scholarly candidates ranging from a mountain-god to a nourishing, breast-associated God, to a God of overpowering destruction, three pictures of God that could hardly be more different.
Genesis|17.others: Every version reads Almighty God, a strong, confident English translation supplying a settled sense the Hebrew word's own etymology does not actually have.
Genesis|17.seeing: Shaddai's derivation is disputed among three live proposals: from Akkadian shadu, mountain, giving God of the mountain, ancient imagery of strength and permanence; from Hebrew shad, breast, giving a nourishing, sustaining God, an image some scholars connect to Jacob's later blessing at Genesis 49:25, blessings of the breasts and of the womb; or from the root shadad, to overpower or destroy, giving a God of overwhelming might. A later Jewish tradition reads it instead as a compound, sha, who, plus dai, is sufficient, giving the all-sufficient one, but this is a homiletical reading of the sound rather than a linguistic derivation.
Genesis|17.why: English Almighty commits to one general sense, overwhelming power, that happens to fit the shadad proposal reasonably well but flattens the genuinely live possibility that the name instead pictures God as a mountain or as a nurturing, breast-like source of sustenance, pictures Almighty does not evoke at all.
Genesis|17.rule: When a divine name's etymology is genuinely disputed among proposals that shape entirely different pictures of God, translating it with one confident English word settles a question scholarship has not settled. Hold the translation more loosely than its confident sound suggests.
Genesis|17.choosing: Almighty is the traditional and functional English rendering, generically capturing power without committing to any one etymology. Each specific proposal, mountain, breast, or overpowering, produces a genuinely different mental picture of what this particular covenant scene is emphasizing about God's character.

Genesis|17.title: Genesis 17:5-15
Genesis|17.summary: Abram becomes Abraham; Sarai becomes Sarah. Both gain the same Hebrew letter, heh, also found in God's own name.
Genesis|17.plain: Imagine two people both receiving a new middle initial on the same day, and that initial turning out to be the same letter that starts the name of the one who renamed them. English spelling, Abram to Abraham, Sarai to Sarah, shows a name simply got longer; it cannot show that the added letter is the same letter both times, or that it echoes God's own name.
Genesis|17.whyThis: Because both Abram and Sarai receive the same added letter in their new names, and that one letter is also half of God's own four-letter name, a detail no transliteration into English letters can show since Abraham and Sarah simply look like longer versions of the old names, not names carrying a piece of God's own name inside them.
Genesis|17.others: Every version reads Abraham and Sarah as the new names, correctly, but English spelling conventions cannot mark that both changes add the identical Hebrew letter, since the added sound lands differently in each English name.
Genesis|17.seeing: Abram, exalted father, gains a heh to become Abraham, popularly associated in the text itself with father of a multitude; Sarai becomes Sarah, both changes inserting the same Hebrew letter heh. That letter is also the second and fourth letter of the divine name YHWH, and a long-standing Jewish reading takes the shared letter as God placing a piece of His own name into both Abraham's and Sarah's identities at the same covenant moment.
Genesis|17.why: English name changes are visible as added syllables, Abram to Abraham, Sarai to Sarah, but the specific added consonant, and its identity in both cases, and its resonance with the divine name, are facts about the Hebrew letters themselves that no English respelling can carry over.
Genesis|17.rule: When two characters receive parallel name changes in the same passage, check what letter or sound was actually added or changed in Hebrew, not just how the English transliteration looks. Two unrelated-looking English changes can be the identical Hebrew move performed twice.
Genesis|17.choosing: Abraham and Sarah as the new names draw no disagreement among translators. The connection to the divine name and the shared letter is an observation about Hebrew orthography that English spelling simply has no mechanism to preserve, however the names are transliterated.
Genesis|17.w: heh (in Abraham and Sarah) cf. YHWH

Genesis|17.title: Genesis 17:17
Genesis|17.summary: Abraham fell upon his face, and laughed. The verb tsachak becomes his son's name, Yitzchak, Isaac, he laughs.
Genesis|17.plain: Imagine naming a baby **Chuckles** because both parents laughed, separately, at the news he was coming, and the joke gets repeated every time someone says his name for the rest of the story. Genesis does exactly this, in Hebrew sound, and English Isaac carries none of the joke.
Genesis|17.whyThis: Because Abraham's laughter at the promise of a son is the first appearance of a pun that repeats twice more across the next four chapters, laughter becoming the very name of the child it is aimed at, a running joke Genesis keeps returning to that a bare English name, Isaac, cannot signal even once.
Genesis|17.others: Every version reads laughed here, correctly, and later reads Isaac as a bare proper name at his birth, with no way for an English reader to hear that the name is the same word as the laughter that preceded it, twice.
Genesis|17.seeing: Tsachak, laughed, here at Abraham's reaction, becomes the root of Yitzchak, Isaac, he laughs or he will laugh, the name eventually given to the promised son. The same pun recurs when Sarah laughs at the promise in Genesis 18:12, and again when Sarah declares after his birth, at 21:6, God hath made me to laugh, so that all that hear will laugh with me, using the same root a third time. The child's very name is the family's skepticism, turned by the end of the story into shared joy, permanently recorded in one repeated Hebrew sound.
Genesis|17.why: English Isaac is a bare transliterated name carrying no meaning at all to an English ear, so the running pun, laughter at disbelief becoming laughter at fulfillment, three separate times across three chapters, is entirely invisible unless a reader is told the name means laughs.
Genesis|17.rule: When a child's name is given following a strong emotional reaction, check whether the name and the reaction share a root. Genesis does this repeatedly, and the pun is often built to recur more than once, turning a single naming moment into a thread running through several later chapters.
Genesis|17.choosing: Laughed and the transliterated name Isaac are both settled; nothing here divides translators. What's worth flagging is that the pun tying them together, and its later repetitions at 18:12 and 21:6, depends entirely on hearing tsachak inside Yitzchak, something no English rendering of either word can supply on its own.

Genesis|18.title: Genesis 18:1-2
Genesis|18.summary: The LORD appeared unto him. He lifted up his eyes, and lo, three men stood by him.
Genesis|18.plain: Imagine a story that opens **the president visited the office**, and the next sentence says **three people walked in and sat down**, with no further comment distinguishing which one was the president. English narrative would flag that explicitly. This chapter does not, and the ambiguity is the point.
Genesis|18.whyThis: Because the chapter opens by flatly stating the LORD appeared to Abraham, and the very next clause describes three ordinary men walking up, with no seam or explanation connecting the two, making this the most direct statement in the Old Testament that God can simply be one of the figures standing in front of you.
Genesis|18.others: Every version reads the LORD appeared and then three men, correctly, but English readers often smooth the transition into an assumption, three angels, or three men who turn out to represent God, without registering how directly the Hebrew text itself equates the first sentence's subject, the LORD, with one of the figures who then eats a meal.
Genesis|18.seeing: The chapter's subject through the meal and the questions about Sarah's laughter remains the LORD in the singular, even while two of the three figures leave for Sodom and are called angels there, while the LORD continues speaking with Abraham alone. The text does not explain the mechanics; it simply narrates a scene in which God, in some form Abraham can host at his table, is present alongside two other beings later identified as angels.
Genesis|18.why: English readers, trained by later theology to expect God's appearances to be marked as visibly supernatural, glide past how ordinary and physical this scene is in the Hebrew: sitting, eating, conversing, with no special visual marker distinguishing the LORD from the other two until the narrative itself tells you two of them go on to Sodom.
Genesis|18.rule: When a Hebrew narrative names God as the subject and then describes ordinary human action, do not assume later theological categories, angel, theophany, appearance, were doing organizing work for the original audience the way they do for later readers. Let the plain narrative sequence stand before importing the categories used to explain it.
Genesis|18.choosing: The wording itself draws no disagreement among translators. The theological question, whether this scene depicts God directly in human form, an angel acting with full divine authority and identified as the LORD by convention, or some combination, is a live one this text raises but does not itself resolve any more than Genesis 16 or Genesis 32 do.

Genesis|18.title: Genesis 18:19
Genesis|18.summary: I know him, that he will command his children. Know here names a relationship, not a fact.
Genesis|18.plain: English **I know that fact** and **I know my spouse** both use the same verb, but everyone hears the difference from context. Hebrew yada spans that same range but leans harder toward the relational end, used of covenant partners choosing and being chosen, not only of holding information.
Genesis|18.whyThis: Because God says I know Abraham using the same Hebrew verb used elsewhere of covenant relationship and even of sexual intimacy, a verb that names an entire category of relational, chosen closeness that English know, a verb mostly about facts and information, does not cover.
Genesis|18.others: Every version reads know or have chosen, both reasonable, since English know already covers relational closeness in some contexts, though not as centrally as Hebrew yada does.
Genesis|18.seeing: Yada covers factual knowledge but also intimate, covenantal, and elective relationship: it is the verb used of a husband knowing his wife at Genesis 4:1, of covenant partners recognizing mutual obligation in ancient treaty language, and here of God's chosen, purposeful relationship with Abraham, entered into precisely so that Abraham will direct his household toward righteousness and justice.
Genesis|18.why: English know defaults to information first and relationship only by context or added words, spouse, friend, personally. Hebrew yada carries the relational, chosen sense as one of its ordinary meanings, so a bare English I know understates the covenant weight the Hebrew verb is carrying here.
Genesis|18.rule: When God or a covenant partner is the subject of know in the Hebrew Bible, weight the relational and elective sense at least as heavily as the informational one. The word is regularly doing covenant work, not simply reporting mental content.
Genesis|18.choosing: Know or have chosen both work as English glosses; neither alone captures the full range, factual awareness, intimate relationship, and covenant recognition, that yada carries as a single word here.

Genesis|19.title: Genesis 19:24
Genesis|19.summary: The LORD rained brimstone and fire from the LORD out of heaven. The LORD is named twice in one sentence.
Genesis|19.plain: English would normally say **he sent fire from himself**, not **he sent fire from him**, repeating the name rather than using a pronoun. Hebrew does exactly the version that repeats the name, and readers ancient and modern have asked why.
Genesis|19.whyThis: Because the sentence naming who rained fire on Sodom mentions the LORD twice, once as the one who rains it and once as the source it rains from, a repetition ancient rabbis themselves flagged as suspicious enough to argue about, since a single, simpler wording was available and not used.
Genesis|19.others: Every version preserves both occurrences of the LORD, correctly following the Hebrew text, but English punctuation and flow make the repetition read as simply emphatic rather than as a genuinely debated grammatical oddity.
Genesis|19.seeing: The verse could have read from Him, using a pronoun, but instead repeats the divine name, the LORD... from the LORD. The Babylonian Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin 38b, records a debate in which a heretic cites exactly this repetition as evidence for two powers in heaven, two divine figures, one on earth doing the raining and one in heaven as the source, and a rabbinic answer defends the repetition as simply a feature of Hebrew style, comparing it to Lamech's poetic repetition at Genesis 4:23.
Genesis|19.why: English narrative avoids this kind of repeated proper noun within one sentence as poor style, replacing the second occurrence with a pronoun by reflex, which quietly resolves an ambiguity the Hebrew leaves standing and that ancient readers found worth debating.
Genesis|19.rule: When a Hebrew sentence repeats a divine name where a pronoun would have been simpler and more natural, do not assume the repetition is stylistically neutral. Ancient readers, not only modern critical scholars, noticed and argued about exactly this kind of doubling.
Genesis|19.choosing: Reading the repetition as ordinary Hebrew style, echoing the rabbis' own answer at Sanhedrin 38b, keeps the verse safely monotheistic and uncomplicated. Reading it as a genuine trace of two divine figures is a minority position with ancient roots in Second Temple and early rabbinic-era debate, not a modern invention, though it remains a minority reading.

Genesis|19.title: Genesis 19:26
Genesis|19.summary: His wife looked back from behind him. The verb is a deliberate, longing gaze, not a startled glance.
Genesis|19.plain: English **she looked back** covers everything from a half-second reflex glance to a long, wistful stare. Hebrew nabat leans hard toward the second: an intent, lingering look, closer to gazing after something you want than to a quick backward check.
Genesis|19.whyThis: Because the verb for Lot's wife looking back is not the word for a quick, involuntary glance; it is the verb Hebrew uses for a deliberate, lingering gaze, so her punishment answers a real choice to look longingly, not an understandable reflex.
Genesis|19.others: Every version reads looked back, an accurate but broad English verb that does not distinguish a reflex from a deliberate gaze the way the underlying Hebrew word does.
Genesis|19.seeing: Nabat means to look intently, to regard with attention, sometimes with implied longing or favor, distinct from more neutral seeing-verbs elsewhere in the same episode, including the different verb the text uses when the two visiting men look down toward Sodom at 18:16, and again when Abraham himself looks toward Sodom the next morning at 19:28. The choice of nabat for Lot's wife signals a fixed, desiring look back at the life and city she was leaving, not a startled reflex any fleeing person might have had.
Genesis|19.why: English looked back is neutral about intent; it fits both an accidental glance and a deliberate lingering gaze equally well, so the verse's implicit moral distinction, that this was chosen longing rather than reflex, requires knowing which Hebrew verb is actually being used.
Genesis|19.rule: When a narrative's moral weight depends on whether an action was deliberate or reflexive, check the specific verb Hebrew chose rather than assuming a general seeing-verb was neutral. Hebrew has multiple words for looking, and the choice among them often carries the judgment English has to state separately, if at all.
Genesis|19.choosing: Looked back as the basic sense is not in dispute among translators. The nuance, that nabat specifically implies a lingering, desiring look rather than a glance, is a matter of vocabulary precision that most English translations do not have the means to flag without an added phrase.

Genesis|19.title: Genesis 19:37
Genesis|19.summary: She called his name Moab. The name echoes me'av, from a father, memorializing how he was conceived.
Genesis|19.plain: Imagine a family naming a child born under scandalous circumstances something that sounds, to everyone who ever hears it, like a quiet confession of exactly what happened. That is what Moab does in Hebrew, a permanent, audible reminder built into a nation's own name.
Genesis|19.whyThis: Because the name given to Lot's firstborn son by his own daughter sounds like the Hebrew phrase for from a father, a pun that permanently records the shameful circumstances of his conception in the very name later nations, Israel's neighbors and frequent enemies, carried forever.
Genesis|19.others: Every version reads Moab as a bare proper name, transliterated, with no built-in meaning visible to an English reader at all.
Genesis|19.seeing: Moab, mo'av, closely resembles me'av, from a father, a near-pun rather than a formally marked possessive construction, unlike his half-brother's name, Ben-ammi, son of my people, given to the second daughter's son in the very next verse, which does mark the relationship explicitly. Both names function as the daughters' own memorial of the incestuous circumstances of their sons' births, embedded permanently in the names of the nations, Moab and Ammon, that descend from them.
Genesis|19.why: English Moab is simply a place-name and a people-name with no internal meaning an English reader can access, so the built-in, self-incriminating pun Genesis records is invisible unless a reader is told what the Hebrew consonants echo.
Genesis|19.rule: When Genesis names a nation's ancestor at a morally loaded moment in the narrative, check whether the name itself is doing commentary. The naming device Genesis has already used for Cain, Noah, Peleg, and Japheth continues here, aimed at explaining two neighboring nations' origins rather than a single Israelite ancestor.
Genesis|19.choosing: Moab as a transliterated proper name is not contested. The pun is a matter of Hebrew sound that no English rendering of the name itself can carry, unlike Ben-ammi the following verse, whose meaning, son of my people, is stated as an explicit possessive rather than merely echoed.

Genesis|20.title: Genesis 20:7
Genesis|20.summary: He is a prophet, and he shall pray for thee. The word's first use in the Bible names an intercessor, not a predictor.
Genesis|20.plain: Modern English **prophet** usually means someone who predicts the future. The very first time the Bible uses the word for a person, at this verse, the job described is prayer on someone else's behalf, not prediction, a baseline sense English usage has since narrowed away from.
