Genesis|37.choosing: Grave keeps the reference concrete and avoids importing later theology, but undersells sheol's broader, shared-underworld sense. Hell imports specific, later doctrinal content the Hebrew word does not clearly carry on its own. Leaving sheol untranslated, increasingly common in modern versions, is the most honest option, though it asks more of the reader.

Genesis|38.title: Genesis 38:14
Genesis|38.summary: She sat in an open place. The Hebrew could be a place name, Enaim, or literally the opening of the eyes.
Genesis|38.plain: English **open place** reads as a simple description of visibility. The underlying Hebrear could instead be naming an actual town, or could be building a scene where a woman positions herself to be seen at exactly the place named eyes, a difference between plain geography and deliberate staging.
Genesis|38.whyThis: Because the place where Tamar waits for Judah is described by a phrase that could be either a proper place name or a literal idiom meaning the opening of the eyes, and which reading is correct changes whether the scene has a specific, mappable location or a more pointed, almost symbolic staging.
Genesis|38.others: The King James reads in an open place, treating the phrase as a description. Other versions, ancient and modern, read it as the place name Enaim, following Joshua 15:34's mention of a town by that name in the same region.
Genesis|38.seeing: Petach eynayim, most literally opening of the eyes, or the entrance to Eynayim, sits at a genuine crossroads of interpretation: eynayim, eyes, is also plausibly the name of a real town (Joshua 15:34 names Eynayim in the same district), so the phrase could simply mean at the entrance to Eynayim, a geographic marker, or it could be functioning idiomatically, describing a conspicuous, visible spot where Tamar deliberately positions herself to be noticed, playing on the literal sense of eyes even if the place also had that name.
Genesis|38.why: English open place picks the idiomatic, staging-focused reading and loses any sense that a real place name might be doing double duty; a straightforward place-name translation, Enaim, loses the wordplay on eyes and visibility that a scene built around deception and seeing so pointedly seems to want.
Genesis|38.rule: When a place name in Hebrew is also a meaningful common word, consider that the narrator may be using it for both functions at once, real geography and pointed wordplay, rather than choosing between them.
Genesis|38.choosing: Reading it as a real place name, Enaim, keeps the scene concretely located. Reading it idiomatically, the opening of the eyes, or a visible crossroads, keeps the wordplay alive in a story centrally about who sees and who is deceived. Both readings may be simultaneously true, which no single English rendering can hold at once.

Genesis|39.title: Genesis 39:2
Genesis|39.summary: The LORD was with Joseph. A recurring formula that replaces direct divine speech for the rest of the book.
Genesis|39.plain: Compare a story where a character regularly hears a voice from the sky to one where the narrator simply keeps saying, quietly, things kept working out because of him. Genesis switches from the first kind of story to the second exactly when Joseph's story begins, and the switch is easy to read past if you are not watching for it.
Genesis|39.whyThis: Because the Joseph story never once has God speak directly the way He does constantly to Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob, and instead repeats one quiet formula, the LORD was with him, a structural shift in how divine presence is narrated that a reader moving straight from Jacob's chapters into Joseph's can easily fail to notice.
Genesis|39.others: Every version reads the LORD was with him or similar at each recurrence, translating the phrase accurately, but nothing marks for an English reader that this repeated formula is functioning as a deliberate substitute for the direct divine dialogue that filled every earlier patriarchal narrative.
Genesis|39.seeing: Hayah YHWH ito, the LORD was with him, recurs across the Joseph narrative, at 39:2, 39:3, and again at 39:21, 23, doing the narrative work that direct divine speech, I am the LORD, fear not, I will bless thee, did constantly for Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob. God's presence in Joseph's story is asserted by the narrator rather than staged in direct dialogue; Joseph himself never has a recorded conversation with God the way his ancestors repeatedly did.
Genesis|39.why: English translates each recurrence of the formula accurately and locally, but a reader moving chapter by chapter experiences the shift as smooth continuation rather than as the deliberate structural change it is: a book that has been built on direct divine speech suddenly narrates providence instead of staging it.
Genesis|39.rule: Track how a book represents divine presence, direct speech versus narratorial assertion, as its own literary feature, not merely as background theology. A shift in that pattern, as happens at the start of the Joseph story, is a compositional choice worth noticing on its own terms.
Genesis|39.choosing: The LORD was with him is translated accurately every time it recurs. What's worth flagging is the larger structural pattern the repeated phrase belongs to, a genuine shift in how this book narrates God's involvement, invisible if each occurrence is read only as a local statement about Joseph's luck.

Genesis|40.title: Genesis 40:13-19
Genesis|40.summary: Pharaoh shall lift up thine head. For the butler, restored to office. For the baker, the same phrase, with one word added, means beheaded.
Genesis|40.plain: Imagine telling two coworkers on the same day, **you're getting a promotion** and **you're getting let go**, using the exact same sentence structure for both, except one has a single extra word that flips the entire meaning. That is precisely what Joseph's Hebrew does here, and it is chilling specifically because both men hear almost the same words.
Genesis|40.whyThis: Because Joseph gives both prisoners their interpretation using the same Hebrew idiom, lift up thy head, and the identical phrase means restoration for one man and beheading for the other, a single grim pun holding both fates in one sentence structure.
Genesis|40.others: Every version reads lift up thine head for the butler and either the same phrase or lift up thy head from off thee for the baker, correctly conveying restoration and execution respectively, though not every translation preserves how close the two phrasings actually sit to each other in Hebrew.
Genesis|40.seeing: Yissa Pharaoh et rosh'cha, Pharaoh will lift up your head, is used of the butler's restoration to office at 40:13. The identical core phrase returns at 40:19 for the baker, with one addition, me'aleicha, from off you, turning restore your position into remove your head, the same idiom completing itself in two opposite directions depending on a single added phrase.
Genesis|40.why: English restoration language, promoted, and execution language, beheaded, share no vocabulary at all, so the Hebrew's grim wordplay, one shared idiom branching into life and death, is completely invisible once each fate gets its own separate English phrase.
Genesis|40.rule: When a narrator delivers parallel news to two characters using visibly similar phrasing, check how closely the underlying words actually match. Shared vocabulary delivering opposite outcomes is a real literary technique, not a translation coincidence, and it is often lost the moment each outcome gets its own natural-sounding English sentence.
Genesis|40.choosing: Both outcomes are stated plainly by the narrative regardless of phrasing, so no version gets this wrong. What's worth noticing is the wordplay connecting them: the same lift up your head idiom branching into opposite fates, a genuine literary effect that separate, natural-sounding English sentences for each man cannot reproduce.

Genesis|41.title: Genesis 41:45
Genesis|41.summary: Pharaoh called Joseph's name Zaphnath-paaneah. An Egyptian name whose meaning remains genuinely disputed.
Genesis|41.plain: Imagine being given a foreign title at a new job, one your own language cannot quite parse, and centuries later linguists are still debating what your new employers actually meant by it. That is Joseph's situation with this Egyptian name, preserved in Hebrew letters that do not map cleanly back onto Egyptian.
Genesis|41.whyThis: Because Pharaoh renames Joseph with an Egyptian name whose meaning specialists still cannot agree on after centuries of study, ranging from the god speaks and he lives to revealer of secrets to sustainer of the land, each proposal casting Joseph's new Egyptian identity in a slightly different light.
Genesis|41.others: Every version simply transliterates Zaphnath-paaneah, since there is no settled English translation to offer, a rare case where translators default to preserving the sound rather than committing to a contested meaning.
Genesis|41.seeing: Ancient Jewish tradition, reflected in the Targums and in Josephus, read the name as revealer of secrets or finder of mysteries, fitting Joseph's role as dream interpreter. Modern Egyptological proposals instead connect the second element to Egyptian ankh, life, favoring readings like the god speaks and he lives or one who sustains life, fitting his administrative role feeding Egypt during famine. No consensus exists, and the name's precise Egyptian derivation remains an open linguistic question.
Genesis|41.why: English transliteration preserves the name's sound but supplies no meaning at all, so nothing in the English text signals that ancient and modern interpreters have offered genuinely different pictures of what Pharaoh was naming Joseph, interpreter of dreams or sustainer of life, unless both proposals are spelled out separately.
Genesis|41.rule: When a foreign name is transliterated rather than translated, that is often the clearest possible signal that its meaning is unsettled. Check what proposals exist rather than assuming transliteration means no meaning was ever intended.
Genesis|41.choosing: No single translation is offered by any version, appropriately, given the genuine uncertainty. The competing proposals, revealer of secrets versus sustainer of life, cast Joseph's new identity in different lights, interpreter or administrator, neither confirmable from the Hebrew spelling alone.

Genesis|41.title: Genesis 41:51-52
Genesis|41.summary: Manasseh, for God hath made me forget; Ephraim, for God hath caused me to be fruitful. Two more names built from the naming sentence itself.
Genesis|41.plain: By now the pattern should look familiar: Reuben, Simeon, Levi, Judah, Dan, Naphtali, Gad, Asher, Issachar, Zebulun, Joseph, and now Manasseh and Ephraim, thirteen names in a row each built as a pun on the parent's own explanatory sentence. English transliteration keeps none of the wordplay, in Canaan or, as here, in Egypt.
Genesis|41.whyThis: Because Joseph names his two Egyptian-born sons with Hebrew puns on his own experience, forgetting his suffering and being made fruitful in it, continuing the family's long-running habit of building children's names directly out of a parent's own words, now transplanted into a foreign land and a foreign language.
Genesis|41.others: Every version reads Manasseh and Ephraim as bare transliterated names, with Joseph's explanatory statements translated separately and accurately, but without connecting either name back to its own root the way the Hebrew explicitly does.
Genesis|41.seeing: Menashsheh echoes nashah, to forget, from Joseph's own words, God hath made me forget all my toil, and all my father's house. Ephraim echoes parah, to be fruitful, from for God hath caused me to be fruitful in the land of my affliction. Both names complete the pattern established across every one of Jacob's own sons' births, now applied one generation later, to children born not in Canaan but in Egypt, under Joseph's Egyptian name and Egyptian wife.
Genesis|41.why: English Manasseh and Ephraim are bare proper nouns; the sentences explaining them read as separate commentary rather than as the linguistic source the names were extracted from, so the pattern completing itself one generation later, in a foreign land, is invisible without the Hebrew roots.
Genesis|41.rule: Continue tracking the birth-naming-pun device established across Genesis 29-30 all the way through the Joseph narrative. The device does not stop with Jacob's own sons; it continues into the next generation, even after the family relocates to Egypt.
Genesis|41.choosing: Neither name nor its accompanying explanation is in dispute in any version. This record rounds out the pattern already established for the rest of the twelve tribes' names, showing it persists one generation further, into Joseph's own Egyptian-born sons.

Genesis|42.title: Genesis 42:23
Genesis|42.summary: He spake unto them by an interpreter. The same root, melitz, later names a mediator or advocate in Job.
Genesis|42.plain: English keeps **interpreter** and **advocate** as unrelated professions, one translates languages, the other argues a case. Hebrew melitz can name either role, an intermediary standing between two parties who cannot otherwise communicate, whether the gap is language or guilt.
Genesis|42.whyThis: Because the word naming the interpreter standing between Joseph and his brothers is the same root later used of a heavenly mediator pleading a sufferer's case in the book of Job, so an ordinary logistical detail, a translator was present, shares vocabulary with one of the Old Testament's few pictures of intercession before God.
Genesis|42.others: Every version reads interpreter here, correctly, with no reason for an English reader to connect the word to anything beyond ordinary translation between Hebrew and Egyptian speakers.
Genesis|42.seeing: Melitz names the professional interpreter mediating between Joseph, speaking Egyptian, and his brothers, speaking Hebrew, unaware Joseph understands them. The same root reappears at Job 33:23, where a heavenly melitz, one of a thousand, pleads a sufferer's case and finds a ransom for him, a figurative use scholars regularly read as intercessor or advocate, and again at Isaiah 43:27, of a divinely commissioned spokesman.
Genesis|42.why: Hebrew melitz spans both a language-translator and a legal-or-spiritual advocate; no single English word does, so the incidental detail in Joseph's story and the loaded theological image in Job read as completely unconnected once each gets its own natural English word.
Genesis|42.rule: A word doing mundane, logistical work in one passage can be the same root doing theological heavy lifting elsewhere. Track a root's range across the whole Hebrew Bible before assuming its use in a narrative aside is unrelated to its use in a more weighted passage.
Genesis|42.choosing: Interpreter is the right sense here, and no version renders it otherwise. Worth flagging is the shared root with Job's mediator figure, a connection of vocabulary, not necessarily of theological intent, that Genesis 42:23 on its own gives no indication of anticipating.

Genesis|44.title: Genesis 44:30
Genesis|44.summary: His life is bound up in the lad's life. Nephesh, the same word as living soul, used twice, bound together.
Genesis|44.plain: English keeps **life** fairly abstract, a general condition rather than a tangible thing you could tie to something. Hebrew nephesh is closer to a person's whole self or throat, concrete enough that describing two nephashot as bound, keshurah, together pictures an actual physical or emotional cord, not merely a sentiment.
Genesis|44.whyThis: Because Judah's plea for Benjamin uses nephesh twice in one clause, his life is bound up in the lad's life, the same word already carrying breath, self, and life throughout Genesis, now doing the work of describing one person's whole identity as literally tied to another's survival.
Genesis|44.others: Every version reads his life is bound up in the lad's life, correctly, but the repetition of the same underlying Hebrew word, nephesh, for both father and son is smoothed into a single English word, life, used generically rather than as the loaded term it is throughout the rest of Genesis.
Genesis|44.seeing: Nafsho keshurah b'nafsho, his nephesh is bound in his nephesh, repeats the word already met as the breath of life at 2:7 and living soul throughout chapter 1, now applied twice in one clause to describe Jacob's and Benjamin's selves as tied together, not merely emotionally attached in the abstract sense English life suggests, but bound, a term elsewhere used of physical tying and knotting.
Genesis|44.why: English life is a broad, somewhat abstract noun; nephesh carries a more concrete, almost tangible sense of self or living being throughout Genesis, so describing two nephashot as tied or bound together lands with more physical force in Hebrew than his life is bound up in his life does in ordinary English.
Genesis|44.rule: When nephesh recurs at an emotionally weighted moment late in a book, read it against its earlier, more concrete uses, breath, living soul, throat, appetite, rather than assuming it has quietly become the abstract English word life. The word's physical undertone rarely disappears.
Genesis|44.choosing: Every version lands on the same basic sense, deep attachment. What's easy to lose is nephesh's more concrete, physical undertone, given how loaded the word has already become across chapters 1, 2, and 9 of the same book.

Genesis|45.title: Genesis 45:8
Genesis|45.summary: He hath made me a father to Pharaoh. An Egyptian administrative title, not a family claim.
Genesis|45.plain: English father names a family role. A modern equivalent to this ancient title might be something like chief advisor, or elder statesman, an honorific for a senior official's wisdom and standing, not a literal parental claim, the way a company might informally call a longtime advisor its godfather without meaning it genealogically.
Genesis|45.whyThis: Because Joseph describes his own rank as father to Pharaoh, a title that sounds like a family relationship in English but was a documented Egyptian administrative title for a high official or vizier, a detail archaeology confirms independently of the biblical text.
Genesis|45.others: Every version reads father to Pharaoh, accurately translating the Hebrew, but without noting that the phrase names a known ancient Egyptian court title rather than describing an actual family relationship.
Genesis|45.seeing: Egyptian inscriptions independently attest father of the god, it-netjer, as a title held by senior advisors and officials serving a pharaoh, unrelated to blood kinship and instead marking someone as a trusted source of wisdom and counsel, paired here with lord of all his household and ruler over all the land of Egypt, both concrete administrative claims matching the historically attested role of a vizier.
Genesis|45.why: English father, standing alone, suggests literal parentage or, at best, a vague honorific; it does not carry the specific, documented administrative weight the Egyptian title held, so a reader unfamiliar with Egyptian court titulature can miss that Joseph is describing a specific, historically real office rather than a sentimental relationship.
Genesis|45.rule: When a biblical figure describes a foreign court position using a kinship word, father, brother, son, check whether the surrounding culture used that vocabulary as an administrative title before reading it as a literal family claim.
Genesis|45.choosing: Father to Pharaoh is an accurate rendering of the Hebrew, and no version disputes that. What it needs is the extrabiblical Egyptian background confirming this was a real administrative title, which strengthens rather than merely illustrates the account's claim that Joseph held genuine high office.

Genesis|45.title: Genesis 45:26
Genesis|45.summary: Jacob's heart fainted. A rare verb some read as his heart simply stopped, not merely swooned.
Genesis|45.plain: English fainted suggests a brief swoon, someone who recovers in a moment. If the stronger reading of the rare Hebrew verb is right, the sentence is closer to his heart stopped, a far more severe, almost fatal reaction to shocking news, before Jacob's spirit revives in the very next verse.
Genesis|45.whyThis: Because the verb describing Jacob's reaction to the news that Joseph is alive is a rare word some scholars read as far stronger than the mild fainted most versions print, closer to his heart simply stopped, a genuinely different picture of the moment's shock.
Genesis|45.others: Most versions read fainted, was stunned, or did not believe them, softer options for a word whose exact force is genuinely unclear given how rarely it occurs.
Genesis|45.seeing: Vayafag, from the rare root pug, appears seldom enough in the Hebrew Bible that its precise force is debated; at Lamentations 2:18 the same root clearly means cease or stop, which has led some readers, including the medieval commentator Ibn Ezra, to render this verse in stronger terms than a simple faint, and Robert Alter's translation renders it 'his heart went numb' rather than the milder, more traditional fainted.
Genesis|45.why: English fainted names a brief, recoverable swoon; if pug's stronger sense of ceasing or stopping is correct here, the verse is describing something closer to a genuine, momentary cardiac event, a considerably more severe reaction that softer English translations do not convey.
Genesis|45.rule: When a rare verb's few other occurrences point toward a stronger sense than the traditional English gloss suggests, weigh the stronger reading seriously rather than defaulting to whichever translation sounds most familiar. Familiarity is not evidence.
Genesis|45.choosing: Fainted or was stunned keeps the traditional, milder reading and fits smoothly with Jacob's quick recovery the following verse. His heart stopped, following the word's clearer sense at Lamentations 2:18, reads the shock as considerably more severe, a nearly fatal jolt rather than a brief swoon.

Genesis|47.title: Genesis 47:26
Genesis|47.summary: Joseph made it a law over the land of Egypt unto this day. A phrase marking the narrator's own, later vantage point.
Genesis|47.plain: Any time a story says **the custom continues to this day**, you know the narrator is speaking from a point well after the events described, looking back. Genesis uses this exact device repeatedly, and each occurrence is a small, explicit admission of how much later the writing itself sits.
Genesis|47.whyThis: Because this verse closes Joseph's land law with unto this day, a small formula that recurs across Genesis at moments when the narrator is explicitly comparing the story's own time to the reader's later present, adding one more data point to the same authorship question already raised at 12:6 and 36:31.
Genesis|47.others: Every version reads unto this day, correctly, without flagging that the phrase recurs as a set formula across the book, each time doing the same kind of retrospective work.
Genesis|47.seeing: Ad hayom hazeh, unto this day, recurs at several points across Genesis: over the Moabites and Ammonites' origin at 19:38, over the well-name dispute at 26:33, over the prohibition on eating the hip sinew after Jacob's wrestling match at 32:32, and here over Joseph's land law. Each occurrence marks a custom, name, or law that the narrator says persisted into his own, later time, the same kind of vantage-point marker already flagged at Genesis 12:6 and 36:31.
Genesis|47.why: English unto this day reads as simple continuity language, still true, without necessarily prompting a reader to ask precisely whose today is meant, though the phrase only makes sense from a vantage point later than the events it is attached to, exactly like an ordinary historical document's own dateline.
Genesis|47.rule: Track a small recurring formula across an entire book rather than treating each occurrence as a standalone detail. Ad hayom hazeh recurring at several separate, unconnected points across Genesis strengthens, rather than merely repeats, the authorship question each individual occurrence raises on its own.
Genesis|47.choosing: Reading each occurrence as a minor, later editorial gloss within an otherwise earlier Mosaic Torah keeps the formula's implications small and local. Reading the pattern cumulatively, alongside 12:6 and 36:31, strengthens the case that at least some material in Genesis reached its final written form from a vantage point considerably later than the events it narrates.

Genesis|47.title: Genesis 47:29
Genesis|47.summary: Put, I pray thee, thy hand under my thigh. An oath sworn on the organ of generation, not literally the thigh.
Genesis|47.plain: English keeps a handful of body-part euphemisms too, **swear on your life**, **cross your heart**, phrases everyone understands are not literally about hearts or lives being physically handled. Thigh functions the same way here, a polite substitution for the procreative organs, tying an oath about burial and lineage to the part of the body most associated with generations yet to come.
Genesis|47.whyThis: Because the oath gesture Jacob demands of Joseph, a hand placed under his thigh, is a euphemism most premodern and modern interpreters agree refers to the genitals, tying the promise directly to lineage and covenant rather than to a body part chosen at random.
Genesis|47.others: Every version reads thigh, correctly translating the Hebrew word, though few flag for a modern reader that the gesture is a recognized euphemism rather than an arbitrary physical formality.
Genesis|47.seeing: Yarech, thigh, functions here, as it does at Genesis 24:2 for Abraham's servant, as a euphemistic reference to the genitals, the seat of generative power and lineage; Rashi and the wider Jewish exegetical tradition read the gesture as touching the sign of circumcision itself, binding the oath to the covenant marked in the flesh. The gesture appears only in these two oath scenes in Genesis, both involving a solemn promise about descendants and inheritance.
Genesis|47.why: English thigh names an ordinary body part with no euphemistic weight at all, so a modern reader has no built-in signal that the gesture is a delicate substitution for something more intimate, tying the promise to lineage and covenant rather than to an arbitrary physical ritual.
Genesis|47.rule: When an oath gesture in Hebrew narrative involves an unusual body part, check whether ancient interpreters read it euphemistically before assuming the literal reading is complete. Genesis uses this exact gesture only twice, both times for solemn promises about descendants.
Genesis|47.choosing: Thigh is the literal word, and every version renders it that way without dispute. The euphemistic reading, genitals as the seat of lineage, tied to the covenant sign of circumcision, is the dominant traditional interpretation and fits both scenes' shared focus on descendants and inheritance far better than a literal, arbitrary reading of the gesture would.

Genesis|48.title: Genesis 48:16
Genesis|48.summary: The Angel which redeemed me from all evil. The first use of go'el, redeemer, in the Bible, applied to an angel.
Genesis|48.plain: English redeemer sounds like a purely spiritual title. In Hebrew law, go'el names something concrete and legal: the nearest relative obligated to buy back a family member's lost land, freedom, or life, the way a modern next of kin might be legally bound to step in. Jacob is applying that specific, legal family role to the angel who has watched over him.
Genesis|48.whyThis: Because this is the first time in the Bible the word redeemer, go'el, is applied to anyone, and Jacob applies it not to God directly but to the angel who has been with him, a legal-kinship term for the nearest relative obligated to rescue a family member, now used of a heavenly figure.
Genesis|48.others: Every version reads redeemed or delivered, correctly conveying rescue, but without necessarily flagging that go'el is a specific legal-kinship term, not a general word for saving someone.
Genesis|48.seeing: Go'el names the kinsman-redeemer throughout the Hebrew Bible, the nearest relative legally obligated to redeem land, avenge blood, or rescue a family member from servitude, most fully developed later in Ruth and in Levitical law. This is the word's first appearance in the Bible, and Jacob applies it not to God under His ordinary names but to the angel who has accompanied him, treating that figure as functioning in the specific legal role of nearest kinsman-protector.
Genesis|48.why: English redeemed carries broad, largely religious connotations by now; it does not automatically evoke the specific legal picture of a family member obligated by kinship law to rescue you, so the precision of Jacob's word choice, applying a technical family-law term to an angel, is easy to miss.
Genesis|48.rule: When a word's first biblical occurrence is doing specific legal or social work later developed at length elsewhere, as go'el is here, read that first occurrence in light of its fuller later development rather than assuming it is simply a poetic synonym for saved or helped.
Genesis|48.choosing: Redeemed is the agreed sense in every version. The larger question, whether this angel is a created being functioning in a kinsman-redeemer role or something more, is a live theological debate the word's first, loaded appearance here helps generate rather than settle.

Genesis|48.title: Genesis 48:22
Genesis|48.summary: I have given to thee one portion above thy brethren. Literally, one shechem, the same word as the city Shechem.
Genesis|48.plain: Imagine an inheritance clause that says **I leave you one extra Boston**, using a place name as a unit of measurement. That is roughly what Jacob's Hebrew does here, naming an amount of land with the same word as a specific city his sons had once conquered by the sword.
Genesis|48.whyThis: Because the extra portion Jacob gives Joseph is called one shechem, the same word as the city of Shechem where Jacob's sons had earlier taken bloody vengeance, so an ordinary word for a portion or ridge of land doubles as a pointed reference back to a specific, violent chapter of the family's own history.
Genesis|48.others: Every version reads one portion, or a similar generic English phrase, correctly conveying the sense of an extra share but with no way to preserve the pun on the place name Shechem.
Genesis|48.seeing: Shechem ordinarily means shoulder or a ridge of high ground, and functions here as a play on words with the city of Shechem, the site of Simeon and Levi's violent reprisal after Dinah's assault at Genesis 34. Jacob's phrase, one shechem, can be read as simply one portion or, more pointedly, as a wry reference to the very city his sons had taken by force, now formally assigned to Joseph's line.
Genesis|48.why: English portion is a generic word with no double meaning at all, so the pun connecting Joseph's extra inheritance to the specific, bloody history of Shechem in chapter 34 disappears completely once shechem is translated as a plain, place-name-free noun.
Genesis|48.rule: When an inheritance or blessing names a quantity using a word that also happens to be a place name from earlier in the same book, consider that the connection may be deliberate rather than coincidental, especially where the place carries real narrative weight, as Shechem does here.
Genesis|48.choosing: Portion is the agreed general sense in every version. The pun connecting it to the city of Shechem is, by the Anchor Bible's own description, an obscure allusion, acknowledged but not fully explained by any major commentary, which is itself part of why it is worth flagging rather than resolving.

Genesis|49.title: Genesis 49:6
Genesis|49.summary: They digged down a wall. Or: they hamstrung oxen. The consonants are the same; only the vowels, added centuries later, decide.
Genesis|49.plain: Imagine a sentence in a language written without vowels, where the same three letters could spell either **wall** or **ox** depending on how you say it aloud. That is exactly the situation here: shr can be read shor, ox, or shur, wall, and the Hebrew text as originally written does not settle which.
Genesis|49.whyThis: Because Jacob's condemnation of Simeon and Levi's violence hinges on a word that could mean either ox or wall depending only on which vowels are supplied, since the consonants alone do not decide it, and the King James chose differently than the Masoretic tradition it otherwise follows.
Genesis|49.kjv: O my soul, come not thou into their secret; unto their assembly, mine honour, be not thou united: for in their anger they slew a man, and in their selfwill they digged down a wall.
Genesis|49.kjvWhy: digged down a wall is the reading the King James chose against the Masoretic vowel pointing, following the Vulgate and the Targums instead
Genesis|49.others: The King James reads wall, following the Vulgate's murum and the Targums. Most modern versions read oxen, following the Masoretic Text's own vowel pointing and the Septuagint's tauron, bull.
Genesis|49.seeing: The consonantal text שור can be vocalized shor, ox, matching the Masoretic tradition's own pointing and the Septuagint's Greek, or shur, wall, matching the Vulgate and the Aramaic Targums. Since vowel points were added to the Hebrew text centuries after the consonants were fixed, this is a case where two ancient, respected translation traditions genuinely disagree on which vowels the unpointed consonants originally carried.
Genesis|49.why: English wall and English ox are entirely different images, one a act of vandalism against property, the other a crippling act of violence against animals, so the translation a reader receives depends entirely on a vowel-pointing decision made centuries after the consonants themselves were fixed, a decision no English reader can see happening.
Genesis|49.rule: Remember that the earliest Hebrew text was consonants only; vowel points were a later addition, authoritative but not infallible. Where ancient versions split over the same consonants, as they do here, the ambiguity is genuine and older than any existing manuscript with vowels.
Genesis|49.choosing: Wall follows the Vulgate and Targums and reads Simeon and Levi's violence as including property destruction. Oxen follows the Masoretic Text's own pointing and the Septuagint, reading the violence as extending to hamstringing livestock, itself a serious act of economic sabotage in the ancient world. Both are defensible from the same unpointed consonants.

Genesis|49.title: Genesis 49:10
Genesis|49.summary: Until Shiloh come. A word read as a place, a title, or a messianic figure, and translators still disagree.
Genesis|49.plain: Picture a single word in a will that could mean **until the town**, **until it is rightfully his**, or **until the promised heir**, three entirely different legal outcomes hanging on one ambiguous term. Shiloh in this verse creates exactly that kind of interpretive fork.
Genesis|49.whyThis: Because the word marking when the sceptre will finally leave Judah's line, Shiloh, is one of the hardest words in the whole Hebrew Bible to pin down, read as a place name, a title meaning he to whom it belongs, or a messianic designation, three genuinely different prophecies packed into one obscure word.
Genesis|49.others: Some versions transliterate Shiloh as a place name. Others read until he comes to whom it belongs or until tribute comes to him, treating the Hebrew as a title or a corrupted phrase rather than a proper noun. The Septuagint avoids the term Shiloh altogether, translating around it.
Genesis|49.seeing: The Masoretic vowel pointing supports reading Shiloh as a proper name, but an alternative reading divides the same or very similar consonants into shelloh, that which belongs to him, or ad ki yavo shiloh could reflect a slightly different original phrase now obscured by scribal transmission. Jewish and Christian interpreters alike have long read the verse messianically, a ruler to whom ultimate authority belongs, while others read Shiloh as the town in Ephraim later associated with the tabernacle, an intelligible but contextually awkward reading given the verse is about Judah's own line.
Genesis|49.why: English translations must commit to treating Shiloh as either a proper name or a spelled-out title, decisions that produce visibly different English sentences, so a reader of any single translation has no way to see how contested the underlying Hebrew word actually is.
Genesis|49.rule: When a single word anchors a famous prophetic verse and ancient translations, the Septuagint included, visibly struggle with or avoid it, treat that struggle as evidence of real difficulty in the source text, not merely as translators failing to agree on an otherwise clear word.
Genesis|49.choosing: Shiloh as a place name is grammatically straightforward but sits awkwardly in a blessing focused on Judah's own future rule. He to whom it belongs, reading the same consonants as a title, fits the immediate context of ongoing rule and has driven the dominant messianic reading in both Jewish and Christian tradition, though it requires reparsing the consonants against the Masoretic vowel points.

Genesis|50.title: Genesis 50:20
Genesis|50.summary: Ye thought evil against me; but God meant it unto good. The same verb, chashav, reckon, used of Abraham's faith at 15:6.
Genesis|50.plain: English think and mean are ordinary, general verbs. Hebrew chashav is closer to an accountant's word, to reckon or calculate a value, and the same word used of God crediting Abraham's faith as righteousness earlier in Genesis is used twice in this one sentence, once for the brothers' malicious calculation, once for God's redemptive one.
Genesis|50.whyThis: Because Joseph's famous line to his brothers uses the same accounting verb, chashav, already met at Genesis 15:6 for God reckoning Abraham's faith as righteousness, so the whole Joseph story closes with the identical ledger-word that opened the covenant's central statement about faith, now applied to good and evil rather than to belief.
Genesis|50.others: Every version reads meant or intended, both reasonable general translations that lose the more technical, ledger-like flavor chashav carries, and its earlier, weightier use at 15:6.
Genesis|50.seeing: Chashavtem alai ra'ah, chashvah l'tovah, you reckoned against me evil, He reckoned it for good, repeats the same root twice with opposite objects in one verse, the very verb rendered counted at Genesis 15:6, where the LORD counted Abraham's faith as righteousness. The whole Joseph narrative, and in a sense the whole patriarchal history Genesis has been tracking, closes on the same accounting vocabulary it used to describe the foundational moment of Abraham's faith.
Genesis|50.why: English think and mean are colorless, general-purpose verbs; they do not preserve the specific, weighted accounting sense that ties Joseph's closing statement back to Abraham's reckoned faith fourteen chapters and several generations earlier in the same book.
Genesis|50.rule: When a book's final major statement repeats a rare or theologically loaded verb from earlier in the same book, read the recurrence as a deliberate bookend, not a coincidence of common vocabulary. Chashav's return here closes a loop opened at 15:6.
Genesis|50.choosing: Meant or intended captures the sentence's plain sense, and every version agrees on that much. What matters is the specific word choice, chashav, which ties Joseph's closing theological statement about providence directly back to Abraham's reckoned faith, a connection no English synonym preserves.

Genesis|50.title: Genesis 50:26
Genesis|50.summary: He was put in a coffin in Egypt. The Hebrew word, aron, is the same word later used for the Ark of the Covenant.
Genesis|50.plain: English keeps coffin and ark as entirely separate words, one for the dead, one for the sacred. Hebrew aron names both a burial box and the gold-covered chest holding the covenant tablets, the very same noun doing both jobs, so Genesis closes with a word it will not fully cash in until Exodus and beyond.
Genesis|50.whyThis: Because the very last word of Genesis, coffin, is the same Hebrew word later used for the Ark of the Covenant, so the book ends with Joseph sealed in the same kind of box that will eventually carry Israel's most sacred object, a wordplay that closes the book on an image it will not explain for many chapters yet.
Genesis|50.others: Every version reads coffin, correctly, since English has no reason to use the same word it will later use for the Ark of the Covenant, severing a connection the Hebrew text itself preserves by repeating the identical noun.
Genesis|50.seeing: Aron names Joseph's coffin here, the very first occurrence of the word anywhere in the Bible, and the same word later names the Ark of the Covenant carrying the tablets of the law through the wilderness. Jewish tradition already noticed the parallel: two arons traveled with Israel through the wilderness, one holding the bones of the dead Joseph, the other holding the covenant of the living God, Joseph's own bones eventually carried out of Egypt at the Exodus and buried in the promised land.
Genesis|50.why: English coffin and ark share no sound or spelling at all, so the deliberate closing image, Genesis ending on the same word its sequel will use for its most sacred object, is entirely invisible without knowing the underlying Hebrew noun is identical in both cases.
Genesis|50.rule: Pay attention to a book's very last word as carefully as its first. Genesis opens with bereshit, a word already carrying interpretive weight, and closes with aron, a word that will not detonate its full significance until much later in the story, a deliberate structural echo across the whole Torah.
Genesis|50.choosing: Coffin is the correct sense here, and no version renders it otherwise. What matters is the word's later, much weightier reuse for the Ark of the Covenant, a connection built entirely into the Hebrew vocabulary, invisible the moment English gives the two objects two different names.

Psalm|1.title: Psalm 1:1
Psalm|1.summary: Blessed is the man. The Hebrew is a plural exclamation, not a description.
Psalm|1.plain: **Lucky him!** is not the same sentence as **He is lucky.** The first is something you shout. The second is something you assess. English can do both and the difference is in the punctuation more than the words.
Psalm|1.whyThis: Because the first word of the Psalter is not an adjective describing a man, and reading it as one turns an exclamation into a character assessment. Every Beatitude in the New Testament inherits the same problem.
Psalm|1.others: All versions read blessed or happy. None renders it as an exclamation, because English has no comfortable way to shout a noun.
Psalm|1.seeing: Ashrei is a plural noun in the construct, closer to O the happinesses of the man who. It is not the same word as barak, which is the verb for blessing someone. The psalm opens with a cry, not a definition, and the Septuagint's makarios carries that into the Beatitudes.
Psalm|1.why: English blessed is a participle and behaves like an adjective. There is no English noun you can put at the front of a sentence to mean how fortunate is the one who.
Psalm|1.rule: When a verse opens with a single word that feels like a verdict, check whether the original is a noun. Hebrew exclamations often arrive as nouns and English converts them to adjectives without asking.
Psalm|1.choosing: Every version agrees on blessed; nothing here is a rendering dispute. What needs correcting is the mental picture: readers routinely take blessed as a state conferred rather than a condition observed, and the grammar points the other way.

Psalm|1.title: Psalm 1:2
Psalm|1.summary: In his law doth he meditate day and night. The verb, hagah, means mutter or growl, not silent reflection.
Psalm|1.plain: English meditate suggests sitting quietly with your eyes closed, thinking. Hagah pictures something noisier: lips moving, words repeated under your breath, closer to how you might quietly recite a phone number to remember it, or the low, steady growl of an animal that will not let go of what it has caught.
Psalm|1.whyThis: Because the verb translated meditate names an audible, physical activity, closer to muttering or growling, the same word used of a lion growling over its prey, not the silent, internal mental picture most English readers attach to meditation.
Psalm|1.others: Every version reads meditate, a reasonable English word but one that has drifted toward silence and stillness in modern usage, away from the vocal, physical picture the Hebrew verb actually paints.
Psalm|1.seeing: Hagah is used elsewhere of a lion growling low over its kill at Isaiah 31:4 and of a dove's mournful cooing at Isaiah 38:14, an onomatopoeic word for a low, continuous vocal sound. Applied to studying the law day and night, it pictures someone murmuring the text aloud, repeating it under their breath, physically working it over with their mouth, not sitting in silent contemplation.
Psalm|1.why: English meditate has shifted toward quiet, internal mental stillness, especially through modern popular usage, so a reader pictures something close to the opposite of what hagah actually describes: an active, murmuring, half-vocal engagement with the words themselves.
Psalm|1.rule: When a spiritual practice-word in the Bible sounds like a modern wellness term, meditate, contemplate, check whether the underlying Hebrew or Greek word describes something more physical, vocal, or active than the modern English term now suggests.
Psalm|1.choosing: Meditate keeps the traditional, respected English rendering but invites a picture closer to modern mindfulness than the Hebrew supports. Mutter or murmur is more accurate to hagah's sound-based sense but strips away the devotional dignity English readers expect the verse to carry.

Psalm|2.title: Psalm 2:7
Psalm|2.summary: This day have I begotten thee. A coronation formula marking a specific day, not a timeless statement.
Psalm|2.plain: English today names a specific date, not eternity, and Hebrew hayom, this day, works exactly the same way everywhere else it appears in the Bible. Read plainly, in its own ancient political context, the verse is closer to a king's formal adoption ceremony, this day you become my son and heir, than to a claim about existing outside of time.
Psalm|2.whyThis: Because this day have I begotten thee uses a specific, present-tense time marker, hayom, this day, that in its many hundreds of other occurrences in the Hebrew Bible never points to a timeless, eternal moment, fitting an ancient Near Eastern coronation formula of covenant adoption rather than a statement about eternal generation.
Psalm|2.others: Every version reads this day have I begotten thee, correctly, though later Christian doctrinal debate about eternal generation has sometimes led readers to treat hayom as figurative or timeless rather than as the ordinary temporal marker it is everywhere else.
Psalm|2.seeing: Hayom, this day, occurs 458 times in the Hebrew Bible and elsewhere always marks a specific point in time, never an eternal or timeless one. In its ancient Near Eastern context, the verse reflects a royal coronation or covenant-adoption formula, a great king declaring a vassal king his son at the moment of covenant, political and legal adoption language rather than a claim about biological or metaphysical origin.
Psalm|2.why: English this day is unambiguous about marking a specific moment; the theological weight later Christian tradition placed on this verse, arguing for the Son's eternal generation, sits in some tension with hayom's ordinary, everywhere-else meaning, a tension worth naming rather than smoothing over.
Psalm|2.rule: Before reading later doctrinal categories back into an Old Testament phrase, check how the same small, ordinary words, today, this day, function everywhere else in the same corpus. A time marker that always marks time elsewhere is unlikely to suddenly mean timeless here.
Psalm|2.choosing: Reading the verse in its ancient Near Eastern coronation-formula context treats it as adoption language for a specific king on a specific day, the reading Acts 13:33 explicitly applies to Jesus's resurrection as a new, specific moment. Reading it as pointing toward eternal generation, the position the Council of Nicaea later affirmed doctrinally, requires treating hayom less literally than its 457 other occurrences suggest.

Psalm|2.title: Psalm 2:12
Psalm|2.summary: Kiss the Son. Or: kiss purely, do homage in purity. The word bar is Aramaic for son, but also Hebrew for grain, clean, or pure.
Psalm|2.plain: Imagine a poem written in English that suddenly drops in a French word for exactly one line, close enough in spelling to an ordinary English word that readers argue for centuries about which one was meant. That is the situation with bar here: an Aramaic loanword for son, or a Hebrew word for purity, spelled almost the same way.
Psalm|2.whyThis: Because the word rendered Son here is bar, the ordinary Aramaic word for son, not the Hebrew ben used everywhere else in this very psalm, an unusual language switch inside one poem that some scholars read instead as an entirely different Hebrew word meaning purity.
Psalm|2.kjv: Kiss the Son, lest he be angry, and ye perish from the way, when his wrath is kindled but a little. Blessed are all they that put their trust in him.
Psalm|2.kjvWhy: kiss the Son is the rendering that shaped the whole messianic tradition around this verse, resting on reading bar as the Aramaic word for son inside an otherwise Hebrew poem
Psalm|2.others: The King James reads kiss the Son, capitalizing it as a messianic title. Some Jewish translations and a number of scholarly treatments read kiss purely, or do homage in purity, treating bar as the Hebrew word for pure or clean rather than as an Aramaic loanword.
Psalm|2.seeing: Bar, in Aramaic, is the ordinary word for son, used throughout Aramaic portions of Daniel and Ezra; the same consonants in Hebrew mean grain, or, adjectivally, pure or clean. The rest of the psalm, including verse 7's begotten language, uses the ordinary Hebrew ben for son, making bar's sudden appearance here either a deliberate, striking Aramaism, possibly chosen for its impact on Gentile kings who would have understood Aramaic, or simply the ordinary Hebrew word for purity, unrelated to sonship at all.
Psalm|2.why: English Son capitalizes and commits to the Aramaic-loanword reading; English purity commits to the alternative Hebrew reading entirely. A translator must choose one, permanently closing off the other possibility that the bare Hebrew consonants themselves leave genuinely open.
Psalm|2.rule: When a single word could belong to two different languages sharing a script, check whether the surrounding text is otherwise consistent in its language choices. An isolated switch, as bar would be here, is unusual enough to weigh both directions seriously rather than defaulting to whichever reading a translation tradition has already settled on.
Psalm|2.choosing: Kiss the Son fits the psalm's messianic trajectory and its influential place in later messianic reading, but requires accepting an isolated Aramaic loanword in an otherwise Hebrew composition. Kiss purely or do homage in purity keeps the whole psalm in consistent Hebrew vocabulary but loses the direct filial title some later interpreters, and much later devotional tradition, have built upon this verse.

Psalm|4.title: Psalm 4:2
Psalm|4.summary: Selah. A notation appearing seventy-one times in the Psalms whose exact meaning nobody today can confirm.
Psalm|4.plain: Imagine a symbol printed seventy times across a hymnal that every choir director interprets slightly differently, some reading it as a rest, some as a key change, some as a cue to raise their voices, because nobody alive actually knows what the symbol's original composer meant by it. That is Selah's situation today.
Psalm|4.whyThis: Because Selah appears seventy-one times across the Psalms and its precise meaning is genuinely unknown, a musical or liturgical notation every reader has silently skipped past for centuries without anyone being fully sure what it originally instructed the reader, singer, or musician to do.
Psalm|4.others: Every version simply transliterates Selah rather than translating it, since there is no settled English equivalent, a rare case where a whole word is left untouched precisely because its meaning cannot be pinned down.
Psalm|4.seeing: Selah occurs seventy-one times in the Psalms and three more in Habakkuk, almost always in poems marked for a choirmaster or musical performance, strongly suggesting some kind of musical or liturgical function: a pause, a musical interlude, a signal to raise the volume or change key, a cue for the singers or a physical gesture like prostration. No single explanation commands scholarly consensus, and the word's precise etymology remains debated.
Psalm|4.why: English readers meet Selah as an untranslated word sitting inconspicuously at the end of a verse, easy to skip entirely, with no built-in signal of how significant, or how genuinely mysterious, that one word actually is to specialists who have studied it for centuries without settling its meaning.
Psalm|4.rule: A transliterated word that recurs dozens of times across a book, rather than being translated even loosely, is often a strong signal of real uncertainty, not merely a technical term everyone already understands. Selah is one of the clearest examples of this pattern anywhere in the Bible.
Psalm|4.choosing: No English translation is offered by any major version, appropriately, given the genuine uncertainty. Whether Selah functioned as a pause, an instrumental interlude, a dynamic marking, or a congregational cue remains an open question that seventy-one occurrences have not resolved.

Psalm|7.title: Psalm 7:1
Psalm|7.summary: A Shiggaion of David. A label used only twice in the whole Bible, with no confirmed meaning.
Psalm|7.plain: Imagine a musical score marked with a term you find in only one other piece of sheet music ever written, no dictionary, no manual, nothing to compare it against except that one other piece. That is Shiggaion's situation: two data points, and centuries of guessing between them.
Psalm|7.whyThis: Because the musical or literary label in this psalm's own heading, Shiggaion, occurs only twice in the entire Bible, here and in Habakkuk 3:1, leaving its precise meaning, a wild, impassioned song, a wandering melody, or something else entirely, a matter of educated guesswork rather than settled fact.
Psalm|7.others: Every version simply transliterates Shiggaion, since there is no settled English equivalent, treating it the way Selah is treated, as a technical term left in its original form rather than translated.
Psalm|7.seeing: Shiggaion appears in the heading of this psalm and, in its plural form shigionoth, in the heading of Habakkuk 3, a prayer explicitly set to music. Proposed derivations connect it to a root meaning to wander or reel, suggesting a wild, emotionally intense, perhaps irregular musical or poetic form, a dithyramb or rhapsody in the loose sense of impassioned, less formally structured song, though no occurrence outside these two headings exists to confirm the guess.
Psalm|7.why: English readers meet Shiggaion as an untranslated label at the top of a psalm, easy to skip past as mere technical scaffolding, with no way to sense how genuinely uncertain its meaning is, resting on only two attestations in the whole Bible.
Psalm|7.rule: A technical heading transliterated rather than translated, especially one this rare, is worth pausing on rather than skimming past. The translator's silence is itself information about how much, or how little, is actually known.
Psalm|7.choosing: No translation is offered by any major version. The proposed sense, an intense, perhaps musically irregular or emotionally wild composition, is a reasonable guess from the proposed root and from the psalm's own agitated content, but remains unconfirmed by any third occurrence.

Psalm|8.title: Psalm 8:5
Psalm|8.summary: A little lower than the angels. The Hebrew says elohim.
Psalm|8.plain: Suppose a sentence said someone was ranked just below **the management**, and a later translation rendered it just below **the supervisors**. Narrower, tidier, and it quietly decides a question the original left open.
Psalm|8.whyThis: Because the verse says humans were made a little lower than something, and the something is elohim. If you have worked any of the council passages, you already know that word does not automatically mean angels, and here the New Testament quotes the Greek rather than the Hebrew.
Psalm|8.kjv: For thou hast made him a little lower than the angels, and hast crowned him with glory and honour.
Psalm|8.kjvWhy: the angels is the Septuagint's word, printed as if it were the Hebrew
Psalm|8.others: The King James and NIV read the angels. The ESV and NASB read the heavenly beings or God, with footnotes. The NET reads the heavenly beings. The split runs straight down the middle of the modern versions.
Psalm|8.seeing: The Hebrew is elohim, the same word used of God, of the divine council, and of a dead prophet at 1 Samuel 28:13. The Septuagint rendered it angelous, angels, and Hebrews 2:7 quotes that Greek. So the New Testament is not translating the Hebrew here; it is quoting a translation.
Psalm|8.why: A rank is something English is forced to pick. Elohim marks which realm a being belongs to rather than where it stands in a hierarchy, and no English noun does that.
Psalm|8.rule: When the New Testament quotes an Old Testament verse and the wording does not match your Old Testament, check the Septuagint before assuming anyone made a mistake. Very often the quotation is accurate to a different text.
Psalm|8.choosing: God fits the Hebrew word and makes a strong claim about human status. Angels fits the Septuagint, the letter to the Hebrews, and a long tradition. Heavenly beings splits the difference and is the most common modern compromise. All three are defensible and the Hebrew alone does not settle it.

Psalm|14.title: Psalm 14:1
Psalm|14.summary: The fool hath said in his heart, There is no God. Nabal names moral corruption, not stupidity.
Psalm|14.plain: English fool can mean someone unintelligent or someone acting rashly, but rarely names deliberate moral corruption on its own. Hebrew nabal leans hard toward the second sense: not someone who reasoned badly, but someone whose whole conduct, not merely their opinions, is godless and reckless.
Psalm|14.whyThis: Because the word translated fool names moral corruption and godless conduct, not low intelligence, so the verse is not describing an intellectual position, atheism reasoned to, but a moral posture, a refusal of God that reshapes how a person actually lives.
Psalm|14.others: Every version reads fool, a reasonable general term, though English fool more readily suggests low intelligence than the specifically moral corruption nabal carries in Hebrew.
Psalm|14.seeing: Nabal describes moral disgrace and godless behavior throughout the Hebrew Bible, most vividly embodied in the character actually named Nabal at 1 Samuel 25, whose wife explicitly says his name means what he is, folly is with him. The verse is not describing careful philosophical atheism; it is describing someone whose denial of God flows from, and licenses, a corrupted way of living, closer to godless or morally reckless than to unintelligent.
Psalm|14.why: English fool primarily suggests poor judgment or low intelligence to a modern reader; it does not automatically carry the moral, almost ethical-character weight nabal has throughout the Hebrew Bible, so the verse can be misread as a comment on intellectual sophistication rather than on moral corruption.
Psalm|14.rule: A Hebrew word for foolishness in a moral or theological context is worth sorting by family: does it belong with nabal, moral corruption, or with a word for simple lack of understanding? The two are not the same category in Hebrew the way English fool tends to flatten them.
Psalm|14.choosing: Fool is the traditional and workable English rendering. Godless or morally corrupt more precisely conveys nabal's actual charge, that the denial in view is a matter of character and conduct, not primarily of intellectual argument.

Psalm|16.title: Psalm 16:10
Psalm|16.summary: Neither wilt thou suffer thine Holy One to see corruption. Shachat most literally means pit, the grave, with decay only as an extension.
Psalm|16.plain: English corruption names a process, decaying, rotting. Hebrew shachat more literally names a place, the pit or grave itself. Saying someone will not see the pit is a slightly different claim from saying they will not experience decay, though the two ideas sit close enough together that the shift from one sense to the other carries real theological weight.
Psalm|16.whyThis: Because the Hebrew word behind corruption most literally means pit, the grave itself, and only carries the extended sense of bodily decay by association, a real translation choice Acts 2 leans on heavily when applying this verse to the resurrection.
Psalm|16.others: Most versions read corruption or decay, following the extended, figurative sense the Septuagint's Greek diaphthora already carries and that Peter's speech in Acts 2:27 explicitly builds its resurrection argument on.
Psalm|16.seeing: Shachat's root sense is pit, the grave as a physical location; its extended, figurative sense as corruption or decay is a natural association, since a body left in a pit decays, but it is genuinely a step beyond the word's most literal meaning. The Septuagint translates it with Greek diaphthora, decay or corruption, and Peter's sermon in Acts 2:27, 31 builds directly on that Greek sense to argue Jesus's body did not decay in the tomb, an argument that depends on reading shachat through its Greek translation's extended sense rather than its bare Hebrew literal one.
Psalm|16.why: English corruption commits to the figurative, decay-focused sense; a more literal English rendering, the pit or the grave, would describe David's hope in terms of place rather than process, a real difference in emphasis that the New Testament's own use of this verse leans into rather than flattens.
Psalm|16.rule: A New Testament argument that depends on one specific sense of an Old Testament word is worth checking twice: is that sense the word's most literal one, or an extension the Greek translation makes more explicit than the Hebrew does on its own? Both can be legitimate, but they are not identical claims.
Psalm|16.choosing: Corruption or decay follows the Septuagint and the New Testament's own argument, reading the verse as a resurrection promise about the body not decaying. The pit or the grave keeps closer to shachat's most literal Hebrew sense, a hope about not remaining in the place of the dead, which decay is naturally associated with but is not, strictly, the same claim.

Psalm|17.title: Psalm 17:8
Psalm|17.summary: Keep me as the apple of the eye. Literally, the little man, or the daughter of the eye: the pupil.
Psalm|17.plain: Look closely into someone's eye and you will see a tiny reflection of yourself in the dark center. Hebrew names that reflection ishon, a little man, and calls the pupil itself bat ayin, daughter of the eye. English apple has nothing to do with either image; it entered the phrase only because Old English speakers happened to also call the pupil an apple, for its round shape.
Psalm|17.whyThis: Because apple of the eye is not what the Hebrew says at all; the phrase literally names the pupil, called the little man of the daughter of the eye, a vivid image of the tiny reflected figure you see when you look closely into someone's eye, an image English apple replaced centuries ago and everyone has used ever since without knowing why.
Psalm|17.others: Every version reads apple of the eye, correctly preserving the sense, precious and closely guarded, but the actual images behind the Hebrew words, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, are entirely absent from apple, which has no connection to eyes in ordinary English at all.
Psalm|17.seeing: Ishon, commonly translated pupil here, more literally means little man, describing the miniature reflected image visible in someone's eye when you look closely into it; bat ayin, daughter of the eye, is a separate Hebrew idiom for the same part of the eye. English apple entered this specific phrase from Old English, itself a separate, unrelated tradition of calling the pupil an apple for its round shape, coincidentally landing near enough in sense to survive translation even though it shares no image with the Hebrew at all.
Psalm|17.why: English apple of the eye is now a fixed idiom meaning precious and beloved, entirely detached from any eye-related image for most speakers; it happens to preserve roughly the right sentiment while completely replacing the Hebrew's actual pictures, a tiny reflected person, a daughter, with a fruit that has nothing to do with either.
Psalm|17.rule: A translated idiom that still works can hide the fact that its underlying image has been entirely swapped out. Check what the original words are actually picturing, not just whether the resulting English phrase still makes emotional sense.
Psalm|17.choosing: No translation dispute over the sentiment, precious and closely guarded. The entry exists because apple of the eye survives as a working English idiom purely by coincidence of separate traditions, not because it translates the Hebrew's actual images of a little reflected man or a daughter of the eye.

Psalm|19.title: Psalm 19:1
Psalm|19.summary: The heavens declare the glory of God. The Hebrew noun means weight before it means brightness.
Psalm|19.plain: **His word carries weight.** **That was a weighty decision.** English already uses heaviness for importance, and nobody thinks about scales. Now imagine that were your only word for importance, and it never lost the physical sense.
Psalm|19.whyThis: Because glory is the single most-used and least-examined word in Christian vocabulary, and the Hebrew behind it is concrete. Learning what it weighs changes every verse it appears in.
Psalm|19.others: Every version reads glory. None can carry the root, and the English word has drifted toward radiance and applause.
Psalm|19.seeing: Kavod is from a root meaning heavy. The same root gives the verb in honour thy father, which is closer to treat as weighty than to feel warmly toward. Kavod is substance, the reason something registers, and in the Septuagint it becomes doxa, which then carries the Hebrew sense into the New Testament.
Psalm|19.why: English glory came in through Latin gloria, which was about renown and splendour. The heaviness never made the trip, so the English word and the Hebrew word overlap without matching.
Psalm|19.rule: Abstract theological nouns almost always come from concrete roots. Find the concrete sense and the abstract one stops floating.
Psalm|19.choosing: Nothing is disputed. No English word means weight and importance and radiance at once, so glory is the least bad option and has been for a thousand years.

Psalm|19.title: Psalm 19:4
Psalm|19.summary: Their line is gone out through all the earth. Paul quotes it in Romans 10:18 as their voice, or sound.
Psalm|19.plain: English line and voice are entirely different words describing entirely different things, a measuring cord versus a sound. The Hebrew word here, qav, line, and the Greek word Paul quotes, phthongos, sound, look close enough in Hebrew consonants, qavam versus qolam, that the difference could be an old textual variant rather than a loose paraphrase.
Psalm|19.whyThis: Because the Hebrew word here, line, and the Greek word Paul quotes in Romans 10:18, sound or voice, are different enough that scholars have long suspected either a genuine textual variant or a deliberate reinterpretation, with Paul's whole argument in Romans depending on the version he quotes.
Psalm|19.others: The Hebrew Masoretic Text reads their line, kav, has gone out. The Septuagint, and Paul quoting it at Romans 10:18, reads their voice or sound has gone out, following Greek phthongos.
Psalm|19.seeing: Qav, line or measuring cord, and qol, voice or sound, are close enough in Hebrew spelling, qavam versus qolam, that some scholars propose the Septuagint's translators worked from a manuscript that actually read qolam, voice, rather than qavam, line, a genuine textual variant rather than a free translation choice. Others read it as an interpretive extension, since a cord can also mean a musical string, and a string produces a sound.
Psalm|19.why: English readers of Romans 10:18 meet voice or sound with no indication that the Old Testament passage being quoted, in most English Bibles' Old Testament translation, actually says line, a visibly different word, leaving the connection between the two texts looking looser than it may actually be.
Psalm|19.rule: A New Testament quotation that uses a noticeably different word than your English Old Testament translation is worth checking against the Septuagint. It may reflect a genuine textual variant in the underlying Hebrew consonants rather than loose paraphrase.
Psalm|19.choosing: Line, following the Masoretic Text, pictures a measuring cord stretched across creation, marking out its extent. Voice or sound, following the Septuagint and Paul's quotation, pictures creation's silent testimony as itself a kind of speech, the reading Paul's argument in Romans 10 needs to make its point about creation preaching to all nations.

Psalm|22.title: Psalm 22:1
Psalm|22.summary: My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? The Gospels' version mixes Hebrew Eli with an Aramaic verb, not the Psalm's own Hebrew azavtani.
Psalm|22.plain: Imagine quoting a well-known English psalm but swapping in a word from a different, related dialect partway through, the kind of thing a bilingual speaker does without necessarily noticing. That is roughly what happens between the Hebrew Psalm and the Gospels' Greek transliteration of what Jesus said.
Psalm|22.whyThis: Because when Jesus quotes this verse from the cross, the Gospels record a mix of Hebrew and Aramaic, not the pure Hebrew of the Psalm itself, a small but real linguistic detail about which language, or blend of languages, Jesus was actually praying in at that moment.
Psalm|22.others: Every version of the Gospels reads my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me, translating the transliterated cry accurately, but without flagging that the underlying words Matthew and Mark preserve are not simply the Hebrew of Psalm 22:1 itself.
Psalm|22.seeing: Psalm 22:1's Hebrew reads Eli, Eli, lamah azavtani, using the Hebrew verb azav, forsake. The Gospels transliterate Jesus's cry as Eli or Eloi, lama sabachthani, using sabachthani, built on the Aramaic verb shevaq, not the Hebrew azav, while Eli or Eloi themselves could belong to either language. The mix suggests Jesus was praying the psalm through the Aramaic he ordinarily spoke, likely drawing on an Aramaic Targum tradition of the psalm rather than reciting the Hebrew text word for word.
Psalm|22.why: English translations of both the Psalm and the Gospel accounts read forsaken in both places, so the fact that two different verbs, from two different though related languages, lie behind that one English word in each source is invisible without comparing the underlying transliterations directly.
Psalm|22.rule: If a quotation is given in transliterated form rather than translated, check the actual sounds preserved rather than assuming they simply reproduce the Hebrew original. Bilingual or Aramaic-influenced quotation was ordinary in first-century Judea.
Psalm|22.choosing: Both the Psalm and the Gospels translate as forsaken without controversy. What gets smoothed away once both texts land in the same English phrase is a small, human detail: the exact words Jesus is recorded saying blend Hebrew and Aramaic.
Psalm|22.w: Eli Eli lamah azavtani (Hebrew) / shevaqtani (Aramaic, behind sabachthani)

Psalm|22.title: Psalm 22:16
Psalm|22.summary: They pierced my hands and my feet, or like a lion. One letter, and it is the wrong length in some copies.
Psalm|22.plain: Imagine two letters in your alphabet that differ only by how far the stroke comes down. A tired copyist in poor light makes one slightly short, and four hundred years later two communities are arguing about what the sentence says. Nobody had to be dishonest for that to happen.
Psalm|22.whyThis: Because this is the most argued single word between Jewish and Christian readers of the Psalms, the evidence is genuinely split, and both sides routinely overstate what they have. If you learn one textual problem in the Old Testament, learn this one.
Psalm|22.kjv: For dogs have compassed me: the assembly of the wicked have inclosed me: they pierced my hands and my feet.
Psalm|22.kjvWhy: pierced is the reading the King James took from the versions rather than from the Masoretic Hebrew
Psalm|22.others: Almost every Christian English version reads pierced. Jewish publications read like a lion. The NIV footnotes both. The King James reads pierced without a note.
Psalm|22.seeing: The Masoretic Text reads ka'ari, like a lion, which leaves the line with no verb. The Septuagint, the Peshitta, and Jerome's earlier Gallican Psalter (the version behind the standard Vulgate text) all read a verb meaning dug or pierced. A fragment from Nahal Hever, 5/6HevPs, dated to roughly the middle of the first century, has the word ending in a vav rather than a yod, which makes it a third-person plural verb.
Psalm|22.why: The difference is a vav against a yod, two letters distinguished mainly by length. This is not a translation problem at all. It is a copying problem, and English can only report the outcome.
Psalm|22.rule: When two communities read the same verse in opposite directions, find out whether the disagreement is about meaning or about letters. Here it is letters, which makes it checkable rather than merely arguable.
Psalm|22.choosing: The case for pierced: three ancient versions, the Nahal Hever fragment, the minority Masoretic notes, and the fact that the Masoretic reading leaves the clause without a verb. The case against: Nahal Hever is not Qumran and is later than the Qumran material, the fragment is faded and has been read both ways, the Targum supports the lion reading, and Aquila, Symmachus, and Jerome's later translation direct from the Hebrew (his Psalterium iuxta Hebraeos, a different edition from the Gallican Psalter cited above) all render the hands and feet as bound rather than pierced. Anyone who tells you this is closed has not read the other side.

Psalm|23.title: Psalm 23:4
Psalm|23.summary: The valley of the shadow of death. Possibly not shadow plus death at all, but one word meaning deepest darkness.
Psalm|23.plain: English shadow of death is a vivid compound, two ideas fused into one image. Some scholars argue the underlying Hebrew was never really shadow plus death at all, but a single intensive word built the way English forms darkness from dark, later reread by tradition as though it contained the separate word for death.
Psalm|23.whyThis: Because the famous phrase valley of the shadow of death may not contain the word death at all, some scholars arguing the Hebrew is really one intensive word for the deepest possible darkness, later re-pointed by tradition to look like a compound of shadow and death.
Psalm|23.others: Every version reads shadow of death or, in some more recent translations, deep darkness or deepest darkness, reflecting this exact disagreement about the word's actual construction.
Psalm|23.seeing: Tsalmavet looks like a compound of tsel, shadow, and mavet, death, but some scholars argue it derives instead from a root meaning simply intense darkness, with the ending later re-pointed by the Masoretic vocalizers to resemble mavet, death, once that reading had become traditional. An Akkadian cognate meaning darkness supports the intensive-darkness reading, while the traditional compound reading, shadow of death, has by far the longer devotional history and remains linguistically defensible either way.
Psalm|23.why: English shadow of death carries centuries of funeral and mortality associations built on the compound reading; deep darkness or deepest darkness conveys a more general, if still ominous, sense of danger and gloom without necessarily invoking death specifically, a real difference in what the verse is picturing.
Psalm|23.rule: When a compound-looking Hebrew word could also be analyzed as a single intensive form, check whether the compound reading might be a later, traditional reinterpretation of an originally simpler word. Both readings can be linguistically defensible at once, as they are here.
Psalm|23.choosing: Shadow of death keeps the traditional, deeply loved reading and its long devotional history, the one nearly every reader already carries. Deepest darkness follows the intensive-noun analysis and a plausible Akkadian cognate, and either way the psalm is naming the darkest, most dangerous place a shepherd would need to walk a flock through.
Psalm|23.w: tsalmavet (tsel, shadow + mavet, death, or one intensive noun)

Psalm|23.title: Psalm 23:6a
Psalm|23.summary: I will dwell in the house of the LORD. The consonants also allow I will return.
Psalm|23.plain: Write **RD** and let a reader supply the vowels. Read, red, ride, rode, rude. Hebrew was written without vowels for centuries, and the marks that fix them were added long after the words were.
Psalm|23.whyThis: Because the last line of the most memorised psalm in the language may say something other than what everyone recites, and the difference is one vowel that was not written down for a thousand years.
Psalm|23.others: Every English version reads dwell. The footnotes in the NET and a handful of academic translations note the alternative.
Psalm|23.seeing: The Masoretic pointing, weshavti, actually parses most straightforwardly as a form of shuv, to return, giving I will return to the house of the LORD. The traditional dwell reading instead takes the word as built from yashav, to dwell or sit, the reading nearly every version and most of Jewish and Christian interpretive tradition has long assumed, even though the pointed form's more natural derivation is from shuv; Hebrew grammarians continue to debate how to explain the mismatch. The vowel points were added by the Masoretes between roughly the seventh and tenth centuries.
Psalm|23.why: English has to print one word. There is no way to render a sentence that is undecided between dwelling and returning without a footnote.
Psalm|23.rule: Hebrew vowel points are a later layer. When a translation footnote offers a completely different verb rather than a different shade, the consonants are usually the reason.
Psalm|23.choosing: Dwell has the ancient versions, the Septuagint included, and nearly universal traditional usage behind it, even though the pointed Hebrew form more naturally parses as shuv, return. Return follows the pointed consonants' more straightforward grammatical derivation and fits a psalm about being led back, but stays the minority reading precisely because dwell is so deeply established.
