Dwell remains the better-supported reading on tradition and versional evidence; the grammar of the pointing itself is the part that actually favors return.

Psalm|23.title: Psalm 23:6b
Psalm|23.summary: Goodness and mercy shall follow me. Mercy is chesed, and mercy is the weakest word for it.
Psalm|23.plain: **She stood by him.** That is not kindness, and it is not duty either. It is both at once, and English needs a phrase because it has no noun for it. Some languages have the noun.
Psalm|23.whyThis: Because mercy in that famous line is chesed, the single most important word in the Hebrew Bible for how God relates to people, and mercy is the shade of it that carries least.
Psalm|23.kjv: Surely goodness and mercy shall follow me all the days of my life.
Psalm|23.kjvWhy: mercy is the rendering that put the gentlest possible word in the most memorised line
Psalm|23.others: The King James reads mercy. Modern versions read steadfast love, unfailing love, faithful love, loyal love or covenant loyalty. No two agree, which tells you the word has no English equivalent.
Psalm|23.seeing: Chesed is loyalty inside a committed relationship: what you owe and also what you freely give, with no line between them. It is the word in Exodus 34:6 where God describes himself, and the Greek behind John's grace and truth. Mercy suggests leniency toward someone in trouble, which is only a corner of it.
Psalm|23.why: English split obligation from affection. Duty is cold, love is warm, and chesed is both in one noun, so every English rendering has to pick a side or use two words.
Psalm|23.rule: When you see five different English renderings of one word across five Bibles, stop looking for the right one. The spread is the information.
Psalm|23.choosing: Mercy is memorable and narrow. Steadfast love is accurate and clumsy. Covenant loyalty is precise and reads like a legal term. The line is quoted at funerals, which is why nobody has been willing to change it.

Psalm|27.title: Psalm 27:13
Psalm|27.summary: I had fainted, unless I had believed. The Hebrew leaves the unless-clause without its other half.
Psalm|27.plain: English can do this too: **if you hadn't come when you did...** and just stop there, trusting the listener to feel what would have happened rather than saying it. Hebrew does exactly that here, an unfinished sentence used on purpose, not a translation gap.
Psalm|27.whyThis: Because the Hebrew sentence literally begins unless I had believed, and then simply never finishes, an intentionally broken construction the Masoretes themselves flagged as unusual, leaving the reader to feel the collapse the speaker cannot bring himself to name.
Psalm|27.others: Most versions supply the missing clause in some form, I had fainted, or I would have despaired, to make the sentence read smoothly in English, since English style expects a conditional clause to be completed.
Psalm|27.seeing: Lule, unless, opens the clause and then the sentence simply stops, aposiopesis, a deliberate breaking-off used elsewhere in both Hebrew and Greek rhetoric for emotional effect, the speaker unable or unwilling to name the catastrophe that would otherwise have followed. The word lule itself is among a small set of words the Masoretes marked with unusual pointing, flagging it as textually noteworthy even within the Hebrew tradition's own transmission.
Psalm|27.why: English readers meeting a smoothed-out I had fainted unless I had believed do not experience the sentence as broken at all, so the rhetorical effect of the original, a speaker who cannot finish naming his own despair, is supplied by the translator rather than felt as the text's own deliberate collapse.
Psalm|27.rule: When a Hebrew conditional clause seems to be missing its other half, do not assume a copying error before considering aposiopesis, a deliberate broken-off sentence used for genuine emotional weight. Some of Scripture's most intense moments are marked by grammar failing on purpose.
Psalm|27.choosing: Filling in the missing clause, as every English translation does, produces smooth, readable English at the cost of the original's raw, unfinished quality. Leaving the sentence broken, unless I had believed..., closer to the Hebrew's actual shape, better preserves the emotional collapse the verse is enacting rather than merely describing.

Psalm|29.title: Psalm 29:1
Psalm|29.summary: Ascribe unto the LORD, O ye mighty. Literally, sons of the elim, gods, the divine council again.
Psalm|29.plain: English mighty ones reads as a vague compliment, powerful people or important figures. Bene elim is the same technical phrase already met describing heavenly beings surrounding God's throne, an audience of gods, not an audience of impressive humans, being summoned to worship.
Psalm|29.whyThis: Because the psalm opens by addressing sons of the mighty, bene elim, the same divine-council phrase already met at Genesis 6:2 and recurring at Psalm 89:6, calling heavenly beings, not human worshippers, to ascribe glory to the LORD.
Psalm|29.others: Most versions read O ye mighty, sons of the mighty, or heavenly beings, a range reflecting real disagreement about how directly to render bene elim's divine-council background into English.
Psalm|29.seeing: Bene elim, sons of the elim, gods, occurs only here and at Psalm 89:6, and closely parallels the Canaanite divine-council phrase sons of El attested in Ugaritic mythological texts, where it names the assembly of lesser gods surrounding the high god El. The psalm opens by summoning this same heavenly assembly, not human worshippers, to acknowledge the LORD's glory, the same divine-council imagery already met at Genesis 6:2 and Psalm 82:1.
Psalm|29.why: English mighty ones or you heavenly beings both lose the specific technical weight bene elim carries as a recognized ancient Near Eastern divine-council term, so a reader cannot easily connect this opening line to the same council imagery running through Genesis 6, Psalm 82, and Psalm 89.
Psalm|29.rule: Track bene elohim, bene elim, and edat el, each a variant of the same divine-council phrase, across their several occurrences rather than treating each one as an isolated poetic flourish. The psalms and Genesis are drawing on one shared, coherent picture of a heavenly assembly.
Psalm|29.choosing: Mighty ones or heavenly beings both work as general English glosses. Sons of the gods, or sons of the elim, kept closer to the Hebrew, more directly connects this opening summons to the same council-of-gods imagery already established at Genesis 6:2, Psalm 82:1, and Psalm 89:6.

Psalm|32.title: Psalm 32:1
Psalm|32.summary: Blessed is he whose sin is covered. Kasah, cover, a near relative of kaphar, the atonement verb.
Psalm|32.plain: English forgiven describes a legal or relational state, a debt cancelled. Hebrew covered pictures something more concrete: sin as a thing hidden from view, the way pitch covered the ark's seams against the flood. The two Hebrew cover-words, kasah and kaphar, are separate roots but sit in the same conceptual family running through Israel's sacrificial vocabulary.
Psalm|32.whyThis: Because whose sin is covered uses kasah, cover or conceal, a close relative of kaphar, the atonement verb already met at Genesis 6:14 for pitching Noah's ark, so forgiveness here is pictured with the same family of covering-language that runs through the Torah's whole sacrificial system.
Psalm|32.others: Every version reads covered, correctly, but without necessarily connecting the image to the broader covering-vocabulary, kaphar, atonement, kapporet, the mercy seat, that structures Israel's entire sacrificial system.
Psalm|32.seeing: Kesui, covered, here comes from kasah, a distinct root from kaphar, to cover or atone, the verb already met describing Noah pitching the ark at Genesis 6:14 and standing behind kippurim, atonement, and kapporet, the mercy seat. The two roots are not identical, but they occupy the same semantic neighborhood, covering as the central image for how sin is dealt with, whether by a flood-proof coat of pitch or by sacrificial atonement.
Psalm|32.why: English forgiven and covered read as roughly synonymous religious vocabulary; the specific, concrete image of covering, and its resonance with the unrelated-but-neighboring root kaphar running through the sacrificial system, is invisible without tracking the Hebrew vocabulary of covering across these related but distinct words.
Psalm|32.rule: When a psalm uses covering language for sin or forgiveness, listen for an echo of the sacrificial system's own covering vocabulary, kaphar, kapporet, even where the specific root used, as here, is a different, related word rather than the identical one.
Psalm|32.choosing: Covered is the uncontested sense of kasah here. What's worth seeing is how this verse's covering image sits inside the larger family of Hebrew covering-vocabulary for sin and atonement, connecting an ordinary psalm of confession to the sacrificial system's central metaphor.

Psalm|34.title: Psalm 34:20
Psalm|34.summary: He keepeth all his bones: not one of them is broken. Quoted at John 19:36, itself echoing the Passover lamb's own unbroken bones.
Psalm|34.plain: English readers meeting John 19:36's claim, a bone of him shall not be broken, may not immediately connect it backward to this psalm, or further back still to the instructions for the Passover lamb, three texts chained together by one repeated detail most translations do not flag as connected.
Psalm|34.whyThis: Because this verse's promise that not one of the righteous sufferer's bones will be broken is quoted directly in John 19:36 about the crucifixion, itself deliberately echoing the Passover lamb regulation that none of its bones be broken, tying three separate texts into one chain of promise and fulfillment.
Psalm|34.others: Every version reads not one of them is broken here and a bone of him shall not be broken at John 19:36, both accurate translations, but with no built-in cross-reference showing the deliberate three-way echo running from Exodus through this psalm to the Gospel.
Psalm|34.seeing: The promise that the righteous sufferer's bones will be kept unbroken here is picked up explicitly at John 19:36, applied to the soldiers' decision not to break Jesus's legs, itself already echoing Exodus 12:46's regulation that none of the Passover lamb's bones be broken. John's Gospel draws all three together, casting Jesus's death in the vocabulary both of this psalm's righteous sufferer and of the Passover lamb whose blood marked Israel's houses for deliverance.
Psalm|34.why: English readers of John 19:36 alone may recognize the quotation as scriptural without necessarily tracing it back through this specific psalm to the even older Passover regulation, a three-text chain that requires deliberately cross-referencing rather than reading any one passage in isolation.
Psalm|34.rule: When the New Testament explicitly quotes an Old Testament verse using fulfilled language, check whether that Old Testament verse is itself already echoing something still earlier in the Hebrew Bible. Fulfillment quotations are sometimes the last link in a chain, not the first.
Psalm|34.choosing: The wording of both passages translates without dispute. What's easy to miss is the full three-part chain, Passover lamb, righteous sufferer, crucified Jesus, that a reader encountering only one of the three texts at a time would likely never notice.

Psalm|37.title: Psalm 37:11
Psalm|37.summary: The meek shall inherit the earth. Anav ranges from humble in spirit to poor and afflicted in circumstance.
Psalm|37.plain: English meek names a personality trait, gentle, unassuming. Hebrew anav can mean that, but just as often names an economic and social condition, the poor, the oppressed, people ground down by circumstance rather than people who have simply cultivated humility. The verse could be promising a virtue's reward or the poor's vindication, or both at once.
Psalm|37.whyThis: Because the word translated meek, anav, spans humble in disposition and poor or afflicted in social and economic circumstance, and which sense dominates changes whether the promise is chiefly about a virtue or chiefly about a reversal of fortune for the oppressed.
Psalm|37.others: Most English versions read meek or humble, emphasizing character. Some scholars and a minority of translations lean toward poor or oppressed, emphasizing social and economic reversal, closer to the concerns voiced throughout the rest of Psalm 37 about the wicked prospering at others' expense.
Psalm|37.seeing: Anav describes both a virtue, humility or gentleness, and a social condition, poverty or affliction, throughout the Hebrew Bible, including of Moses at Numbers 12:3. The Septuagint's Greek praeis, gentle, behind Matthew 5:5's meek, leans toward the virtue sense, but the wider context of Psalm 37, contrasting the wicked's temporary prosperity with the eventual vindication of those they oppress, fits the social-economic sense just as naturally, perhaps more so.
Psalm|37.why: English meek carries almost entirely personality-trait connotations today, gentle, unassertive, so a modern reader easily misses that the same Hebrew word could equally, or primarily, be naming the economically and socially oppressed, whose inheritance of the land is a reversal of fortune, not merely a reward for good temperament.
Psalm|37.rule: If a Hebrew word spans both a character trait and a social-economic condition, check the surrounding context for which sense is doing the heavier lifting, rather than defaulting to whichever sense your own culture's translation tradition has favored.
Psalm|37.choosing: Meek or humble, following the Septuagint's praeis and most English tradition, reads the promise as a reward for personal virtue. Poor or oppressed, following anav's equally attested social sense and Psalm 37's larger theme of reversal for the oppressed, reads the same promise as vindication for those ground down by the wicked the psalm spends most of its length condemning.

Psalm|39.title: Psalm 39:6
Psalm|39.summary: Every man walketh in a vain shew. Betselem, in an image, the identical word as image of God at Genesis 1:27.
Psalm|39.plain: Imagine a poem describing people as merely walking shadows, using the very word your culture reserves for the divine spark supposedly placed in every human being. That collision, exalted origin and shadowy transience sharing one word, is exactly what this verse may be doing in Hebrew.
Psalm|39.whyThis: Because every man walketh in a vain shew uses the exact same Hebrew word, tselem, image, already met describing humanity made in God's own image at Genesis 1:26-27, so the psalm may be making a pointed, bitter echo: the same word naming our exalted origin now naming our shadowy, insubstantial transience.
Psalm|39.others: Most versions read vain shew, phantom, or shadow, all reasonable renderings of tselem's more common sense of image or likeness applied here to something insubstantial, but none can show the reader that this is the identical word from Genesis 1's creation account.
Psalm|39.seeing: Tselem is the same word rendered image at Genesis 1:26-27, humanity made betselem elohim, in the image of God. Here the psalmist says every man walks betselem, in an image, or, read more literally, as a mere image or shadow of himself, insubstantial and passing. Whether the psalmist intends a deliberate echo of Genesis or is simply using tselem's separate, attested sense of shadow or phantom is debated, but the shared vocabulary invites the connection: the very word for humanity's God-given dignity also names our fleeting insubstantiality.
Psalm|39.why: English vain shew or phantom reads as ordinary, unremarkable vocabulary for transience; it carries no built-in echo of a creation account written many psalms earlier in the same collection, so the potential irony, exalted image-bearers reduced to mere images of themselves, is invisible without knowing both passages use the identical Hebrew word.
Psalm|39.rule: When a psalm uses vocabulary shared with Genesis's foundational statements about humanity, check whether the poet is drawing a deliberate, even ironic, contrast rather than simply reusing common religious language. Shared roots across very different genres are often doing real interpretive work.
Psalm|39.choosing: Reading tselem here as unrelated to Genesis 1 treats it as simply the ordinary word for a fleeting shadow or phantom. Reading it as a deliberate echo turns the verse into a pointed reflection on human transience measured against human dignity, using the very word that named that dignity in the first place.

Psalm|40.title: Psalm 40:6
Psalm|40.summary: Mine ears hast thou opened. Hebrews 10:5 quotes it as a body hast thou prepared me, following the Greek, not the Hebrew.
Psalm|40.plain: English ears and English body describe entirely different things. The Hebrew verse pictures God carving or digging open a servant's ears, attentive obedience pictured physically. The Greek Septuagint, which Hebrews quotes directly, instead reads a body prepared, generalizing from the specific body part, ears, to the whole body, a deliberate interpretive move, not an error.
Psalm|40.whyThis: Because the Hebrew says mine ears hast thou dug open, a vivid image of attentive obedience, while Hebrews 10:5 quotes this verse as a body hast thou prepared me, following the Septuagint's Greek rather than the Hebrew, a real and consequential difference the author of Hebrews builds a whole argument about the incarnation on.
Psalm|40.others: Old Testament translations of the Psalm read ears, following the Hebrew. New Testament translations of Hebrews 10:5 read a body, following the Greek Septuagint that Hebrews itself quotes.
Psalm|40.seeing: Oznayim karita li, ears you have dug for me, is a vivid Hebrew idiom for being made attentive and obedient, evoking either a servant's pierced ear marking permanent service or simply the carving-open of hearing itself. The Septuagint's Greek translators rendered this soma de katertiso moi, a body you have prepared for me, generalizing from the specific detail, ears, to the whole body the ears belong to, and Hebrews 10:5 quotes that Greek version directly, building an argument about Christ's incarnate body on a translation choice the Hebrew text does not itself make.
Psalm|40.why: English readers moving between the Old Testament Psalm and the New Testament's quotation of it encounter two different images, ears and body, with no built-in explanation that the difference traces back to a translation decision made centuries earlier by the Septuagint's Greek translators, one that the author of Hebrews inherited and built theology upon.
Psalm|40.rule: When the New Testament quotes the Old Testament and the wording differs noticeably from your Old Testament translation, check whether the quotation follows the Septuagint's Greek rather than the Hebrew original. This is common, and it is not evidence of error, but it is a real translation layer worth seeing.
Psalm|40.choosing: Ears, following the Hebrew, keeps the psalm's own vivid image of attentive, obedient hearing. A body, following the Septuagint and Hebrews's quotation of it, generalizes that image into the whole incarnate body, the reading the book of Hebrews needs for its argument about Christ's bodily self-offering.
Psalm|40.w: oznayim karita li (Hebrew) / soma de katertiso moi (LXX, behind Hebrews 10:5)

Psalm|41.title: Psalm 41:9
Psalm|41.summary: Mine own familiar friend hath lifted up his heel against me. Akev, heel, the same root as Jacob's name, applied by Jesus to Judas's betrayal.
Psalm|41.plain: English lifted up his heel reads as an odd, archaic idiom for betrayal, with no built-in connection to anything else in the Bible. In Hebrew, the heel-word carries a long history: it is Jacob's own name, tied since Genesis to grasping, supplanting, and betrayal, and this psalm's use of it for betrayal by a trusted friend is precisely the verse Jesus applies to Judas.
Psalm|41.whyThis: Because the phrase lifted up his heel against me uses akev, heel, the same root behind Jacob's own name and his lifelong association with heel-grabbing and betrayal, and Jesus applies this exact verse to Judas, a betrayer, at the last meal they share together.
Psalm|41.others: Every version reads lifted up his heel against me or a similar phrase, correctly, and John 13:18's Gospel citation of this verse for Judas is well known, but neither translation shows an English reader that heel here is the same word running through Jacob's whole story.
Psalm|41.seeing: Akev, heel, is the same root behind Ya'akov, Jacob, first explained at Genesis 25:26 as grasping his brother's heel at birth, and reinterpreted by Esau at Genesis 27:36 as supplanted, deceived, a betrayal sense the root carries elsewhere too. Jesus quotes this exact verse, he that eateth bread with me hath lifted up his heel against me, at John 13:18, applying it directly to Judas's betrayal at a shared meal, drawing on the same heel-vocabulary that has carried treachery and supplanting since Jacob's own birth.
Psalm|41.why: English lifted up his heel is an isolated, archaic-sounding idiom for betrayal with no visible connection to anything else in the Bible; the Hebrew reader, by contrast, hears the same root that has already carried deception and supplanting since Genesis, so Jesus's quotation of this verse for Judas draws on a much older web of association an English reader cannot access.
Psalm|41.rule: If a quotation applies an Old Testament verse to a specific act of betrayal, check whether the underlying Hebrew vocabulary already carries that association elsewhere in the Bible. The heel-root's long history with deception, running from Jacob through this psalm to Judas, is exactly this kind of accumulated resonance.
Psalm|41.choosing: Lifted up his heel is the uncontested sense here; no rendering is in dispute. What's worth tracing is this verse's vocabulary back through the same root's long biblical history with deception and betrayal, a thread running from Jacob's birth through this psalm to Jesus's own application of the verse to Judas.

Psalm|42.title: Psalm 42:1
Psalm|42.summary: As the hart panteth after the water brooks. Arag, a rare verb for an audible cry of longing, not quiet heavy breathing.
Psalm|42.plain: English pants describes a physical action, hard breathing, mostly silent. Hebrew arag pictures something noisier and more desperate, closer to a lost animal crying out, bleating for its mother or its herd, unable to find its way. The soul is not merely tired and breathing hard; it is crying aloud in desperation.
Psalm|42.whyThis: Because the verb for panteth occurs only three times in the whole Hebrew Bible and describes an audible, almost bleating cry of desperate longing, closer to a lost lamb crying for its mother than to the quiet physical image of heavy breathing English panteth suggests.
Psalm|42.others: Every version reads panteth, an accurate but physically narrower English verb than the Hebrew's onomatopoeic, sound-based image of a distressed animal's cry.
Psalm|42.seeing: Arag occurs only here, twice in this psalm, and once more at Joel 1:20, always describing the desperate, audible longing of an animal, close to a bleating or braying cry rather than simple physical panting. The image is not a deer breathing hard after running; it is a deer crying out, its very life depending on finding water, a cry the psalmist applies directly to his own soul's desperation for God.
Psalm|42.why: English panteth suggests only physical exertion, quiet and mostly involuntary; it misses the vocal, almost anguished cry the rare Hebrew verb actually pictures, an animal crying out because it knows it will perish without what it seeks.
Psalm|42.rule: When a translated verb for physical action sounds ordinary in English, check whether the Hebrew original is describing something more vocal or desperate. A rare, nearly onomatopoeic verb like arag often carries far more emotional weight than its common English gloss suggests.
Psalm|42.choosing: Panteth is the traditional, poetic English rendering and captures physical desperation well. Cries out, or a more vivid rendering closer to bleats, better conveys arag's audible, almost anguished sense, an animal, or a soul, crying aloud rather than merely breathing hard.

Psalm|45.title: Psalm 45:6
Psalm|45.summary: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever. The king addressed directly as elohim, quoted of the Son at Hebrews 1:8.
Psalm|45.plain: English can say **your throne, God**, addressing someone as God directly, or **God is your throne**, making God the foundation rather than the one addressed. The Hebrew grammar here genuinely supports reading it the first way, and whether a human king is really being called God, even in an exalted, honorific sense, is exactly what makes the verse so debated.
Psalm|45.whyThis: Because this royal wedding psalm appears to address the human king directly as elohim, God, a startling title for a mortal ruler, and Hebrews 1:8 quotes exactly this reading and applies it to the Son, making the verse's grammar a genuinely load-bearing question for New Testament Christology.
Psalm|45.kjv: Thy throne, O God, is for ever and ever: the sceptre of thy kingdom is a right sceptre.
Psalm|45.kjvWhy: thy throne, O God is for ever and ever preserves the direct address to the king as elohim, the reading Hebrews 1:8 builds on
Psalm|45.others: Most versions read thy throne, O God, following the vocative reading and the Septuagint's own rendering, which Hebrews 1:8 quotes directly. A minority reading takes it as God is your throne, avoiding a direct divine address to the human king.
Psalm|45.seeing: Elohim occurs four times in this psalm, at verses 2, 6, and twice in 7, with the surrounding occurrences clearly referring to God; the vocative reading, thy throne, O God, treats verse 6 as continuing that pattern, an extraordinarily exalted address to the Davidic king as God's own representative, perhaps even more than merely representative. The Septuagint reads it the same vocative way, and Hebrews 1:8 quotes that Greek text directly, applying the address to the Son as part of its argument for his superiority over the angels.
Psalm|45.why: English must choose a subject and an address; thy throne, O God directly calls the addressee God, while God is your throne makes God a foundation rather than a title, two genuinely different claims that the Hebrew grammar, ambiguous enough to be argued for centuries, does not force in only one direction.
Psalm|45.rule: When a psalm's grammar allows a human figure to be addressed with divine vocabulary, take the ambiguity seriously rather than resolving it by assuming discomfort with the direct reading. Ancient Israelite royal ideology could apply exalted, even startling language to its kings as God's representatives.
Psalm|45.choosing: Thy throne, O God follows the Septuagint, matches the surrounding elohim occurrences in the same psalm, and is the reading Hebrews 1:8 explicitly builds on. God is your throne avoids directly calling a human king God but requires reading the Hebrew syntax somewhat less naturally against its immediate context.

Psalm|46.title: Psalm 46:10
Psalm|46.summary: Be still, and know that I am God. Harpu is a military command: cease fire, stand down, not sit quietly.
Psalm|46.plain: English be still now overwhelmingly suggests quiet, calm, meditative stillness, the kind of stillness you seek in a busy day. The Hebrew verb behind it is a battlefield command, closer to stand down or drop your weapons, addressed to warring nations being told the fighting is over because this King has already won.
Psalm|46.whyThis: Because be still translates a military command meaning cease fighting, drop your weapons, stand down, not an invitation to quiet, meditative stillness, and the verse's popular use today, embroidered on pillows and read over yoga mats, means almost the opposite of what the Hebrew verb actually commands.
Psalm|46.others: Every version reads be still, correctly capturing the verb's basic sense of ceasing an activity, but English still now carries almost entirely calm, contemplative connotations the Hebrew military command did not originally have.
Psalm|46.seeing: Harpu, from raphah, to slacken, let drop, or cease, functions elsewhere as a command to lower one's hands or stand down from conflict. In its context here, surrounded by verses about nations raging, kingdoms being moved, and wars being made to cease to the end of the earth, the command reads as a ceasefire order to combatants who have lost, not an invitation to a quiet devotional moment, recognize that this God has already won and stop fighting Him.
Psalm|46.why: English be still has drifted almost entirely toward contemplative, meditative stillness in contemporary popular usage, precisely the association a phrase like this needs today, while the Hebrew military command it translates is addressed to defeated combatants being ordered to stand down, a considerably more confrontational and specific scene.
Psalm|46.rule: When a devotional phrase has become detached from its original context through repeated popular quotation, go back and read the surrounding verses. Be still and know that I am God sits inside a psalm about warfare and national upheaval, not a quiet room.
Psalm|46.choosing: Be still preserves the beloved, contemplative popular reading many readers already carry. Stand down, or cease fighting, closer to the Hebrew military command and its surrounding context of nations raging and wars ceasing, recovers the verse's original, more confrontational scene: a ceasefire ordered by the victor, not a suggestion to relax.

Psalm|47.title: Psalm 47:7
Psalm|47.summary: Sing praises with understanding. Maskil, a term of uncertain meaning, also a mysterious label heading thirteen other psalms.
Psalm|47.plain: Imagine a musical score marked **con espressione** in a language you do not fully speak: you know it means something like play this thoughtfully, but the precise technical instruction is lost. Maskil sits in exactly that gap, translated here as an ordinary phrase but elsewhere standing alone as an unexplained genre label.
Psalm|47.whyThis: Because sing praises with understanding translates maskil, a word of genuinely uncertain meaning that also appears as a mysterious genre label in thirteen other psalm titles, functioning something like Selah, a technical term everyone reads past without knowing exactly what it instructs.
Psalm|47.others: Here, most versions read with understanding or wisely, treating maskil as an ordinary adverbial phrase. In the thirteen psalm titles where it appears alone, Psalms 32, 42, 44, 45, 52, 53, 54, 55, 74, 78, 88, 89, and 142, most versions simply transliterate it as Maskil, a proper label rather than a translated word.
Psalm|47.seeing: Maskil comes from sakal, to be wise, prudent, or to have insight, the same root behind the wisdom vocabulary used throughout Proverbs. As a standalone heading over thirteen psalms, its precise genre meaning, contemplative poem, skillful composition, or didactic instruction-psalm, is genuinely debated, since the label itself is never defined and the psalms it heads do not share an obvious common form.
Psalm|47.why: English readers meeting maskil translated as with understanding in running text, as here, have no way to connect it to the same word standing untranslated as a technical heading over a baker's dozen of other psalms, a term functioning much like Selah: recognized as significant, but not confidently defined.
Psalm|47.rule: When a Hebrew root shows up both inside a verse's ordinary vocabulary and as an untranslated technical heading elsewhere in the same book, connect the two rather than treating them as unrelated. The heading use is often the more mysterious, and the ordinary use can be a clue to what the label might mean.
Psalm|47.choosing: With understanding or wisely works well as ordinary English inside this verse. As a genre heading elsewhere, Maskil is usually left untranslated, honestly reflecting that no one is fully certain what technical instruction or genre classification the word was originally meant to convey.

Psalm|48.title: Psalm 48:2
Psalm|48.summary: Mount Zion, on the sides of the north. Yarkete tsaphon, likely naming Mount Zaphon, the Canaanite storm-god Baal's own mythological mountain.
Psalm|48.plain: Imagine a hymn claiming your own local hill is really Mount Olympus, the true home of the gods, aimed directly at a rival religion's most sacred site. That is roughly the claim this verse may be making, borrowing the name of Baal's own mountain and applying it to Zion instead.
Psalm|48.whyThis: Because sides of the north translates yarkete tsaphon, a phrase that in the wider ancient Near East named Mount Zaphon, the specific mountain where Canaanite mythology placed the storm-god Baal's throne, so the psalm may be making a direct, pointed claim: Zion, not Zaphon, is the true mountain of the gods.
Psalm|48.others: Every version reads sides of the north, the far north, or recesses of the north, a geographically vague-sounding English phrase that gives no indication the underlying words are very likely naming a specific, religiously loaded mountain in Canaanite mythology.
Psalm|48.seeing: Tsaphon, north, is also the proper name of Mount Zaphon, modern Jebel Aqraa on the Syrian coast, the Canaanite storm-god Baal's mythological dwelling and the meeting place of the gods in Ugaritic texts. Applying yarkete tsaphon, the recesses of Zaphon, to Mount Zion is very likely a deliberate polemical claim, asserting that Zion, not Baal's mountain, is the true cosmic mountain and true seat of divine assembly, the same move already seen in Psalm 29's likely adaptation of Baal-hymn material.
Psalm|48.why: English sides of the north reads as a plain, if slightly odd, compass direction; it gives no hint that the underlying Hebrew is very likely naming a specific rival deity's mythological mountain, turning an apparently geographic description into a pointed theological claim.
Psalm|48.rule: When Genesis or the Psalms use vocabulary that doubles as a proper name from neighboring mythology, tsaphon here, tehom at Genesis 1:2, tannin at Genesis 1:21, read the passage as likely making a deliberate comparative or polemical claim rather than simply describing geography or nature.
Psalm|48.choosing: Sides of the north, read as plain geography, misses the likely mythological reference entirely. Reading tsaphon as naming Mount Zaphon directly casts the verse as a pointed claim that Zion has displaced Baal's own mountain as the true dwelling place of God, a reading well supported by the wider comparative evidence and by Psalm 29's similar move.

Psalm|51.title: Psalm 51:5
Psalm|51.summary: Behold, I was shapen in iniquity; and in sin did my mother conceive me. A statement about the depth of David's guilt, later read as a doctrine of universal inherited sin.
Psalm|51.plain: Saying **I've been like this my whole life** can be an ordinary way of confessing how deep-rooted your own fault is, without making a claim about every other person who has ever been born. Whether David's statement here works the same way, or is meant to describe something true of all humanity, is exactly what later theology had to decide.
Psalm|51.whyThis: Because David traces his sinfulness all the way back to his conception, a statement later Christian tradition, beginning with Augustine, built into the doctrine of original sin, though the Hebrew itself is making a more limited claim about the depth of David's own guilt, not necessarily a formal statement about universal inherited human depravity.
Psalm|51.others: Every version reads shapen or brought forth in iniquity, correctly, and in sin did my mother conceive me, tracing sinfulness back to conception, though the theological weight placed on that tracing varies enormously between traditions.
Psalm|51.seeing: Chollalti, shapen or brought forth, uses a verb for the pains and process of birth, tracing David's sinfulness rhetorically back to the very beginning of his existence, a hyperbolic intensification of his guilt in a psalm of extreme penitence rather than, on its own, a formal doctrinal statement about the inherited sinfulness of every human being. Augustine's later use of this verse as a foundational proof-text for original sin reads a universal, systematic claim into language that in its immediate context is emphasizing the depth and totality of one particular man's guilt.
Psalm|51.why: English shapen in iniquity and conceived in sin, read through centuries of the doctrine of original sin, now carry theological freight for many readers that the Hebrew poetry's own immediate purpose, David's personal, hyperbolic confession of total guilt, may not itself have been making as a systematic claim about human nature in general.
Psalm|51.rule: When a devotional or poetic statement becomes a doctrinal proof-text centuries later, check what work the language was doing in its own immediate context before assuming the later doctrine is simply reading the text straight. Intensifying personal confession and systematic theological claim are not automatically the same thing.
Psalm|51.choosing: Reading the verse as a personal, hyperbolic confession keeps it inside David's own psalm of extreme penitence, emphasizing the totality of his guilt rather than making a claim about anyone else. Reading it as a foundational statement about universal inherited sinfulness, the reading Augustine established and much later theology followed, extends the verse considerably beyond what its immediate poetic context by itself requires.

Psalm|51.title: Psalm 51:10a
Psalm|51.summary: Create in me a clean heart. The verb is the one only God is ever allowed to do.
Psalm|51.plain: If a language had one verb reserved for a single person, and a petitioner used it about himself, you would notice. In English the same request reads as a polite way of saying please change me.
Psalm|51.whyThis: Because the verb in this line is the reserved creation verb from Genesis 1:1, and David uses it of a heart. That is a deliberate echo and it is completely invisible in English, where create is an ordinary word.
Psalm|51.others: All versions read create. The reservation of the verb cannot be shown and is not footnoted anywhere.
Psalm|51.seeing: Bara, the verb of Genesis 1:1, used around fifty times and never with a human subject. David is not asking for improvement. He is asking for the creation verb to be used on him, which is a request for something that does not yet exist rather than repair of something damaged. Lev here is the seat of thought and will, the same word as the Shema.
Psalm|51.why: English create is used of anyone and anything. There is no way to signal that a verb is restricted, so the echo of the first sentence of the Bible simply does not survive.
Psalm|51.rule: When a psalm uses an unusual verb, check where else that verb appears. Hebrew poets quote Genesis constantly and almost never announce it.
Psalm|51.choosing: Nothing to choose. Create is correct and carries none of the weight.

Psalm|51.title: Psalm 51:10b
Psalm|51.summary: Renew a right spirit within me. The same noun runs through the next two verses meaning different things.
Psalm|51.plain: A paragraph that uses one word three times is building something. A translation that renders it three different ways leaves you reading three sentences that happen to be next to each other.
Psalm|51.whyThis: Because the second half of the line asks for a right spirit, and the next two verses use the same noun twice more in two different senses. Three occurrences of one word in three verses, rendered three ways.
Psalm|51.others: Versions read a right spirit, a steadfast spirit, a loyal spirit. Verse 11 reads thy holy Spirit and verse 12 reads a free or willing spirit. Same noun each time.
Psalm|51.seeing: Ruach appears at verses 10, 11 and 12: a steadfast ruach in the man, God's holy ruach not taken away, and a willing ruach to uphold him. The psalm is asking for an exchange of inner dispositions and grounding it in God's own. In Hebrew that is one word repeating. In English it is a human attitude, then the third person of the Trinity, then a human attitude again.
Psalm|51.why: English spirit covers the human inner life and the divine person, but readers switch registers between the two and the repetition reads as coincidence rather than structure.
Psalm|51.rule: Count the repetitions before you interpret the passage. Hebrew poetry argues by repeating a word, and English translation argues by varying it.
Psalm|51.choosing: No dispute. Every version renders all three accurately and none of them can show that they are one word.

Psalm|60.title: Psalm 60:8
Psalm|60.summary: Over Edom will I cast out my shoe. A legal gesture claiming ownership, the same custom used to finalize a transaction at Ruth 4:7.
Psalm|60.plain: Imagine a culture where signing a deed involved physically removing your shoe and handing it to the other party, a small ritual gesture that meant something specific and binding. Casting a shoe over a territory in this psalm performs the same kind of formal claim, not a random insult but a recognized legal act.
Psalm|60.whyThis: Because casting a shoe over Edom is a specific ancient legal gesture claiming ownership, the same gesture used to finalize a property transfer at Ruth 4:7, so the psalm is not describing a casual insult but performing a formal, recognizable claim of possession over conquered territory.
Psalm|60.others: Every version reads cast out my shoe or throw my sandal, accurately translating the gesture but without necessarily explaining that it names a specific, recognized ancient legal custom rather than a colorful metaphor invented for this poem alone.
Psalm|60.seeing: Casting or removing a shoe functioned as a formal gesture of transferring or claiming property rights, most explicitly explained at Ruth 4:7-8, where a shoe is removed to finalize a land transaction between kinsmen. Applying the same gesture to Edom in this military psalm claims the territory the way a shoe-casting would finalize any other property claim, a specific legal idiom repurposed for national conquest.
Psalm|60.why: English cast out my shoe reads as an odd, perhaps contemptuous gesture with no built-in explanation, so a reader has no way to connect it to the specific, documented legal custom Ruth 4:7 explains in detail, a connection that turns a strange image into a recognizable formal claim.
Psalm|60.rule: When an unusual physical gesture appears in poetry, check whether a narrative passage elsewhere explains the same gesture in a legal or social context. Ruth 4:7's explicit explanation of shoe-removal is exactly the kind of key that unlocks this psalm's otherwise puzzling image.
Psalm|60.choosing: Cast out my shoe is not seriously disputed as the literal rendering. What the translation leaves out is the legal background, explained directly at Ruth 4:7, that turns what looks like an arbitrary insult into a specific, formal claim of ownership over Edom.

Psalm|68.title: Psalm 68:4
Psalm|68.summary: Extol him that rideth upon the heavens. The title matches rider of the clouds, Baal's own standing epithet in Ugaritic.
Psalm|68.plain: Imagine a hymn calling your God by the exact title a rival religion uses for its own storm-god, on purpose, to claim that title belongs to the true God instead. That is what this verse very likely does, taking rider of the clouds straight from Canaanite mythology and redirecting it.
Psalm|68.whyThis: Because extol him that rideth upon the heavens closely echoes rider of the clouds, a standing title for the Canaanite storm-god Baal in Ugaritic mythology, applying his signature epithet directly to the LORD, the same polemical move already met at Psalm 29 and Psalm 48.
Psalm|68.others: Every version reads rideth upon the heavens or rides through the deserts, both reasonable translations of an ambiguous Hebrew word, but neither flags that the underlying phrase closely matches a specific, attested divine title from the surrounding culture.
Psalm|68.seeing: Rokev ba'aravot, rider on the clouds or plains, closely parallels rkb 'rpt, rider of the clouds, a fixed epithet for Baal repeated throughout Ugaritic mythological texts. Applying the identical image directly to the LORD is very likely a deliberate theological claim, that Israel's God, not Baal, is the true rider of the storm clouds, joining Psalm 29's storm-theophany language and Psalm 48's likely claim on Mount Zaphon as a third instance of this same polemical pattern in the Psalter.
Psalm|68.why: English readers meeting rideth upon the heavens hear generic, majestic imagery with no signal that the phrase is likely quoting, and redirecting, a specific rival deity's own standing title, a claim that only registers once the Ugaritic parallel is known.
Psalm|68.rule: When the Psalter applies storm or sky imagery to the LORD using phrasing that closely parallels an attested Canaanite divine epithet, read it as part of a consistent, deliberate pattern of theological reclamation running through multiple psalms, not as an isolated poetic coincidence.
Psalm|68.choosing: Reading the phrase as generic praise imagery misses the likely polemical point. Reading it as a direct appropriation of Baal's own title, alongside Psalm 29 and Psalm 48's similar moves, casts this verse as part of a sustained pattern across the Psalter, actively contesting Canaanite religious claims rather than merely borrowing poetic flourish.

Psalm|68.title: Psalm 68:18
Psalm|68.summary: Thou hast received gifts for men. Ephesians 4:8 quotes it as gave gifts to men, matching the Aramaic Targum's own reading, not the Hebrew or Greek Old Testament.
Psalm|68.plain: English received and gave describe opposite transactions, one direction of gift-giving versus the other. The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read received; Paul's letter reads gave. Rather than a simple error, this exact reversal already exists in the Aramaic Targum, a translation tradition Paul may well have known and be deliberately following.
Psalm|68.whyThis: Because the Hebrew says the victor received gifts from conquered men, while Ephesians 4:8 quotes this verse as gave gifts to men, an opposite direction the Aramaic Targum tradition already reads the same way, meaning Paul is very likely following a known interpretive tradition rather than simply misquoting.
Psalm|68.others: Old Testament translations of the Psalm read received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint. Ephesians 4:8 reads gave gifts, matching neither the Hebrew nor the Greek Old Testament but matching the Aramaic Targum's rendering of the same verse.
Psalm|68.seeing: The Hebrew and the Septuagint's Greek both read the victor receiving tribute-gifts from conquered peoples after ascending in triumph. The Aramaic Targum on this psalm instead reads gave gifts to the sons of men, and Ephesians 4:8 follows that same direction, either drawing directly on the Targum tradition or on a similar interpretive current, applying the psalm to Christ distributing spiritual gifts to the church after his ascension rather than receiving tribute as a conquering king.
Psalm|68.why: English readers of Ephesians 4:8 encountering a New Testament quotation reversed from their Old Testament translation may assume an error or a loose paraphrase, when in fact an entire, attested Jewish translation tradition, the Targum, already reads the verse the same reversed way Paul does.
Psalm|68.rule: A New Testament quotation that appears to reverse or significantly alter its Old Testament source is worth checking against the Aramaic Targum tradition before you call it careless or wrong. Targums frequently interpret rather than merely translate, and New Testament writers sometimes follow that interpretive tradition directly.
Psalm|68.choosing: Received gifts, following the Hebrew and Septuagint, reads the psalm as describing a conquering king collecting tribute. Gave gifts, following the Targum and Ephesians 4:8, reads the same ascension imagery as a generous king distributing gifts to his people, the reading Paul needs for his argument about spiritual gifts given to the church.

Psalm|72.title: Psalm 72:17
Psalm|72.summary: His name shall be continued as long as the sun. Yinnon, a word used only here, read by Jewish tradition as one of the Messiah's own names.
Psalm|72.plain: Imagine a phrase, his name shall endure, where one Hebrew word for endure occurs nowhere else in the whole Bible, rare enough that later readers began treating it not as an ordinary verb but as a proper name in its own right, Yinnon, a title for a future king to come. English continued keeps the ordinary verb sense and loses the name entirely.
Psalm|72.whyThis: Because before the sun his name shall be continued contains a word, yinnon, that occurs only this once in the entire Hebrew Bible, and Jewish tradition took it as an actual name of the Messiah rather than simply a verb meaning endure, a reading no English translation preserves.
Psalm|72.others: Every version reads shall be continued, endure, or flourish, treating yinnon as an ordinary Hebrew verb, correctly by the plain grammar, though without capturing the tradition that reads it as a proper name.
Psalm|72.seeing: Yinnon, related to a root meaning to sprout, flourish, or continue, is a hapax, its only appearance anywhere in the Hebrew Bible. The Babylonian Talmud, tractate Sanhedrin 98b, records the tradition that Yinnon is one of the Messiah's names, reading the phrase not as his name shall endure but as before the sun, his name is Yinnon, treating the rare word as a title rather than a verb, and connecting it to the wider cluster of sprouting and branch vocabulary associated with messianic expectation.
Psalm|72.why: English continued or endure smooths yinnon into an ordinary predicate, erasing the possibility, taken seriously in the Talmud, that the word functions as an actual name being assigned to a future king, a reading no single-word English translation of a verb can preserve.
Psalm|72.rule: When a word is a hapax legomenon and later interpretive tradition treats it as a proper name rather than an ordinary word, take that tradition seriously as evidence of how ancient readers themselves heard the rare word, not merely as a curiosity.
Psalm|72.choosing: Reading yinnon as an ordinary verb, shall be continued or shall endure, matches standard grammatical analysis and is what every translation prints. Reading it as the proper name Yinnon, following the Talmudic tradition, treats this hapax legomenon as a genuine messianic title embedded in an otherwise royal psalm.

Psalm|72.title: Psalm 72:20
Psalm|72.summary: The prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended. Yet David's name appears on psalms well after this point.
Psalm|72.plain: Imagine a book with a note halfway through saying the author's contributions end here, and then the same author's chapters keep appearing for the rest of the book. That contradiction is a visible seam, evidence the book was assembled out of smaller pieces at different times, exactly what this verse shows about how the Psalter itself was put together.
Psalm|72.whyThis: Because this closing line explicitly states the prayers of David are ended, yet psalms attributed to David appear repeatedly after this point across the rest of the Psalter, showing this verse is a leftover editorial marker from an earlier stage of compiling the book, not a claim true of the finished collection as it now stands.
Psalm|72.others: Every version reads the prayers of David the son of Jesse are ended, accurately translating a straightforward Hebrew sentence, but without necessarily flagging how strange the claim is once a reader notices David's name reattached to psalms later in the book, including 86, 101, 103, and many more.
Psalm|72.seeing: This colophon almost certainly closes an earlier, smaller collection of Davidic psalms compiled before the Psalter reached its final, five-book form, a collection later scribes and editors incorporated into the larger work without removing this now-outdated closing note. Scholars debate whether it originally marked the end of a scroll or a specific anthology, but either way it is a visible fossil of the book's own layered compilation history, left standing even after later editors kept adding more Davidic psalms beyond it.
Psalm|72.why: English readers meeting the prayers of David are ended at Psalm 72 have no reason to notice the claim is factually overtaken by dozens of later psalms in the same book still attributed to David, so the verse's real function, as a preserved trace of an earlier editorial stage, is invisible without checking the rest of the Psalter's attributions.
Psalm|72.rule: When an editorial statement inside a biblical book is contradicted by material appearing later in the same book, read the contradiction as evidence of the book's compilation history rather than assuming either the statement or the later material must be in error. Both can be original to their own stage of the text's growth.
Psalm|72.choosing: Reading the colophon as simply describing Book II, Psalms 42-72, as a self-contained Davidic collection treats it as accurate for its original, smaller context. Reading it as a claim about David's total contribution to the finished Psalter runs immediately into the dozens of Davidic psalms that follow, showing the verse was never updated to match the book's later growth.

Psalm|74.title: Psalm 74:14
Psalm|74.summary: Thou brakest the heads of leviathan in pieces. The multi-headed sea-dragon of the same chaos-combat imagery already met in Genesis.
Psalm|74.plain: English sea monster sounds like generic mythology, a fantasy creature. In the wider ancient Near East, defeating a multi-headed sea dragon was the specific, well-known story of how a storm-god established order over chaos at the world's beginning, and this psalm applies that same combat imagery directly to the LORD's own creative victory.
Psalm|74.whyThis: Because breaking the heads of leviathan echoes a specific ancient Near Eastern combat myth, the storm-god defeating a multi-headed sea dragon, already met as the tannin of Genesis 1:21 and the tehom of Genesis 1:2 and 7:11, applied here directly to God defeating chaos at creation.
Psalm|74.others: Every version reads leviathan, correctly, but without connecting it to the same combat-with-chaos imagery already surfacing at Genesis 1:2's tehom, Genesis 1:21's taninim, and now here, named directly as a multi-headed creature being crushed in battle.
Psalm|74.seeing: Leviathan here, with its plural heads explicitly broken, matches the Canaanite mythological pattern of the storm-god defeating a multi-headed sea serpent, called Lotan in Ugaritic texts, cognate to Hebrew Leviathan. The psalm applies this widely attested ancient combat myth directly to the LORD, casting creation itself as a decisive victory over chaos, the same underlying imagery already met calmly defused at Genesis 1:21's taninim and now presented here in full battle terms.
Psalm|74.why: English leviathan reads as an obscure creature name with no built-in mythological context; the specific, attested ancient Near Eastern combat-with-chaos pattern it draws on, and the way this psalm intensifies that imagery into open battle language compared to Genesis 1's calmer listing, is invisible without the comparative background.
Psalm|74.rule: Track chaos-monster vocabulary, tehom, tannin, leviathan, rahab, across its several occurrences and note how differently each context handles it, calmly defused as in Genesis 1, or in full mythological combat as here. The same underlying imagery can be deployed very differently depending on a passage's purpose.
Psalm|74.choosing: Leviathan as the name is not in question. What matters here is connecting this verse's battle imagery to the same ancient Near Eastern combat-myth pattern already met in a calmer form at Genesis 1:21, showing how differently biblical texts can handle the identical inherited imagery.

Psalm|82.title: Psalm 82:1
Psalm|82.summary: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods. One Hebrew word, both times.
Psalm|82.plain: **Animal** covers a whale and a mouse. It tells you what kind of thing something is, not how big or important. Now imagine your only word for **person** worked that way too, so a king and a newborn got the same label and rank had to come from somewhere else in the sentence.
Psalm|82.whyThis: Because the verse uses elohim twice in one sentence for two different referents, which is the clearest possible demonstration that the word is a category and not a rank. Every argument about this psalm runs through that one fact.
Psalm|82.kjv: God standeth in the congregation of the mighty; he judgeth among the gods.
Psalm|82.kjvWhy: the King James prints God once and gods once for the same Hebrew word, which shows the problem on the page
Psalm|82.others: All versions print God for the first and gods or divine beings for the second. The NET reads the great assembly and the divine assembly. Nobody renders both the same way, because the sentence would stop making sense.
Psalm|82.seeing: Elohim appears twice here for two different referents, and it is plural in form both times. The word marks which realm a being belongs to, not where it stands in a hierarchy, which is why the same word covers Yahweh, the beings He judges, and a dead prophet at 1 Samuel 28:13.
Psalm|82.why: English has God with a capital and god with a small one, and the distinction is one of identity. Hebrew has one word making a distinction of realm. The capital letter is a translator's decision that Hebrew never had to make, because Hebrew had no capitals.
Psalm|82.rule: When one word is rendered two different ways in a single sentence, the translator has made an interpretive decision you cannot see. That is the place to stop and look.
Psalm|82.choosing: There is no way to print both as gods without sounding polytheistic, and no way to print both as God without nonsense. Every version takes the same route. The interpretive question of who the second group is belongs to the Divine Council Index, not here.

Psalm|84.title: Psalm 84:10
Psalm|84.summary: I had rather be a doorkeeper in the house of my God. Histopheph, a verb used only here, meaning to sit at the threshold.
Psalm|84.plain: English doorkeeper names a job, someone who controls who comes and goes. The rarer Hebrew verb behind it more literally pictures simply sitting on the threshold itself, not necessarily working there, just being allowed to occupy that lowest, humblest spot at the edge of the sanctuary rather than dwelling comfortably inside wickedness.
Psalm|84.whyThis: Because I had rather be a doorkeeper translates a verb that is a hapax legomenon, found nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, more literally meaning to sit at the threshold, a humbler and more specific image than the King James's doorkeeper, and fittingly written by a family whose actual job was guarding the temple's entrances.
Psalm|84.others: Every version reads doorkeeper, stand at the threshold, or a similar phrase, generally capturing the sense of humble proximity, though the King James's doorkeeper implies an active job the rare verb does not specifically require.
Psalm|84.seeing: Histopheph, from a root connected to saph, threshold, occurs nowhere else in the Hebrew Bible, making its precise nuance a matter of informed inference rather than confirmed usage. Its likely sense is simply to sit or linger at the threshold, a posture of humble access rather than active employment as a gatekeeper, fittingly written in a psalm attributed to the sons of Korah, whose own hereditary role was guarding the tabernacle's entrances.
Psalm|84.why: English doorkeeper suggests active employment, a job with responsibilities; the rarer Hebrew verb's likely sense, simply sitting at the threshold, pictures something more passive and humble, being allowed to remain at the edge rather than performing a role, a real difference in what the psalmist is actually preferring.
Psalm|84.rule: When a hapax legomenon is translated with a confident-sounding English job title, check whether the Hebrew root actually specifies an occupation or simply a posture or location. Doorkeeper implies more active duty than sit at the threshold does.
Psalm|84.choosing: Doorkeeper is the traditional, vivid English rendering, fitting the Korahite family's actual temple role. Sit at the threshold, closer to the verb's probable root sense, emphasizes humble proximity over active employment, a subtly different, more passive picture of what the psalmist says he would prefer.

Psalm|88.title: Psalm 88:5
Psalm|88.summary: Free among the dead, like the slain that lie in the grave. Chophshi ordinarily means released or liberated, an odd, bitter word choice for death.
Psalm|88.plain: English free among the dead sounds almost like a comfort, freedom from earthly troubles. The Hebrew word's ordinary sense, released or liberated, applied to the dead, has struck many readers as bitterly ironic rather than comforting, and scholars disagree sharply about what specific, grim idea the psalmist actually means by it.
Psalm|88.whyThis: Because free among the dead uses a word, chophshi, that ordinarily means released or liberated, a strange, even bitter description of death that scholars read in several different, unresolved ways, none of them simply meaning free in any positive sense.
Psalm|88.others: The King James reads free among the dead, following chophshi's ordinary sense. Some modern versions read forsaken, abandoned, or cast off, reading the word's application to death as inherently bitter rather than literally about freedom.
Psalm|88.seeing: Chophshi ordinarily describes a freed slave or someone released from obligation, a positive term everywhere else it occurs. Applied to the dead here, proposals range from freed from God's obligations and no longer able to serve or praise Him, to stripped, like a corpse looted on a battlefield, to a reading connecting the word to a term for a leper's isolated house, marking the psalmist, or the dead generally, as ritually cut off. No single proposal has won full scholarly consensus.
Psalm|88.why: English free carries entirely positive connotations; if the Hebrew word is being used ironically or in some specialized, grim sense scholars still debate, the plain English rendering can accidentally make the verse sound comforting when it may be doing the opposite, describing utter abandonment.
Psalm|88.rule: When an ordinarily positive word is applied to a grim or negative subject, resist smoothing the translation into straightforward positive English. The friction between the word's normal sense and its dark context is very likely the point, not an accident to resolve.
Psalm|88.choosing: Free among the dead keeps chophshi's ordinary sense and lets the reader feel the strangeness of applying freedom-language to death. Forsaken, abandoned, or stripped resolve the friction into more straightforwardly negative English, at the cost of losing the word's genuinely ironic, unsettling original ambiguity.

Psalm|89.title: Psalm 89:10
Psalm|89.summary: Thou hast broken Rahab in pieces. A different word entirely from Rahab the woman of Jericho.
Psalm|89.plain: Imagine two English words, spelled and pronounced identically, that happen to come from completely different roots with completely different meanings, the way bank the riverbank and bank the money-building share nothing but sound. Rahab the mythological sea monster and Rahab the woman of Jericho are exactly this kind of coincidence, invisible once both are simply transliterated the same way.
Psalm|89.whyThis: Because Rahab here is spelled with entirely different Hebrew consonants from Rahab the woman of Jericho, two completely unrelated words that happen to sound identical once transliterated into English, a false connection English spelling makes nearly impossible to avoid.
Psalm|89.others: Every version transliterates both as Rahab, correctly reflecting how each name sounds, but with no way to show an English reader that the underlying Hebrew spellings and roots are entirely unrelated.
Psalm|89.seeing: The mythological Rahab here is spelled with a heh, from a root meaning storm, arrogance, or, poetically, a primeval chaos-monster, used elsewhere as a symbolic name for Egypt at Isaiah 51:9-10. Rahab of Jericho is spelled with a chet, from a root meaning wide or broad, an entirely separate word. English transliteration erases the difference, producing one identical-looking name for two unconnected Hebrew words.
Psalm|89.why: English readers meeting Rahab in this psalm and Rahab in Joshua have every reason to assume the same figure or at least a related word is meant in both places, when in fact the Hebrew spellings share no root at all, only an accident of how both happen to sound once flattened into English letters.
Psalm|89.rule: Never assume two identically transliterated biblical names are linguistically related. Hebrew has more consonant distinctions than English transliteration preserves, and coincidental sound-alikes across unrelated roots are common enough to always check rather than assume.
Psalm|89.choosing: Rahab as the name is not disputed in either passage. What needs correcting is the natural but mistaken assumption that this psalm's chaos-monster Rahab and Joshua's Rahab of Jericho are in any way the same word or share any linguistic history.
Psalm|89.w: Rahab (chaos-monster, heh) / Rachav (Rahab of Jericho, chet)

Psalm|90.title: Psalm 90:2
Psalm|90.summary: From everlasting to everlasting, thou art God. Olam names indefinite, out-of-sight time rather than philosophical eternity.
Psalm|90.plain: English everlasting and eternity name an abstract philosophical category, time without beginning or end, argued about by theologians and philosophers. Hebrew olam is more concrete: time so far back, or so far forward, that it disappears from view, hidden beyond what anyone can trace, a spatial metaphor for duration rather than a formal metaphysical claim.
Psalm|90.whyThis: Because olam, translated everlasting, is built on a root meaning hidden or concealed, and names indefinite, out-of-sight duration in both directions of time, closer to time out of mind than to the fully abstract philosophical concept of eternity English everlasting now carries.
Psalm|90.others: Every version reads everlasting or eternity, correctly conveying the sense of vast duration, though importing centuries of philosophical precision the Hebrew word's own root, hiddenness, does not specifically supply.
Psalm|90.seeing: Olam derives from a root associated with concealment or the vanishing point, the place where something passes out of sight, and by extension names time so extended it cannot be traced to its origin or end, whether looking backward or forward. Me'olam ad olam, from olam to olam, expresses the same idea by doubling the word in both directions rather than by asserting a formal doctrine of timelessness.
Psalm|90.why: English everlasting and eternity carry the weight of later philosophical and theological precision about timelessness; Hebrew olam's own etymology points instead toward duration too vast or too hidden to trace, a related but not identical idea, closer to beyond memory or beyond sight than to a formal metaphysical claim about existing outside time altogether.
Psalm|90.rule: When translating time-vocabulary from Hebrew, check whether the English word imports later philosophical categories, timelessness, eternity as a formal metaphysical state, that the Hebrew root itself, often built on very concrete physical images, does not specifically require.
Psalm|90.choosing: Everlasting or eternity are the natural, traditional English renderings and are not wrong, since the psalm is certainly making a claim about God's duration exceeding any human measure. What is worth keeping in view is that olam's own root sense, hidden or vanishing from sight, pictures indefinite, untraceable duration rather than formally asserting timelessness as a philosophical category.

Psalm|91.title: Psalm 91:6
Psalm|91.summary: The destruction that wasteth at noonday. Some ancient versions personify qeteb as a demon; the Hebrew itself, and the King James, keep it impersonal.
Psalm|91.plain: English destruction names an impersonal force, something that happens rather than someone who acts. Ancient translators working from the same Hebrew word sometimes heard something more personal in it, a noonday demon, an actual malevolent figure, rather than a mere abstract calamity.
Psalm|91.whyThis: Because the destruction that wasteth at noonday translates qeteb, a rare word some ancient translators read as an actual demon, while the King James, following the Hebrew more literally, keeps it as an impersonal force, a real translation-history divergence over whether this danger has a face.
Psalm|91.others: The King James reads destruction, following the Hebrew closely and leaving qeteb impersonal. The Latin Vulgate reads daemonium meridianum, the noonday demon, a personification carried into later Catholic translation tradition and still remembered in the modern idiom the noonday demon for creeping despair.
Psalm|91.seeing: Qeteb, from a root associated with cutting off, names ruin or destruction, appearing also at Deuteronomy 32:24 among a list of divine judgments. The Hebrew word itself does not require a personal, demonic reading, but the Greek Septuagint and especially Jerome's Latin Vulgate render it as an actual noonday demon, a personification that later Jewish and early Christian tradition developed further into full-blown spiritual warfare imagery, including a Hebrew exorcism version of this psalm among the Dead Sea Scrolls (11Q11, the Apocryphal Psalms scroll) used against demons, and, separately, an Aramaic Targum tradition that also personifies the danger.
Psalm|91.why: English destruction reads as a plain, impersonal abstraction; the Latin daemonium meridianum, noonday demon, which shaped a long devotional and artistic tradition, personifies the same word into an actual malevolent being, a real difference in how frightening and how agentive the danger described is.
Psalm|91.rule: When an ancient translation, especially the Vulgate, personifies an abstract Hebrew noun into a named demon or spirit, treat that as a documented interpretive tradition worth knowing, even where it goes beyond what the Hebrew word itself strictly requires.
Psalm|91.choosing: Destruction, following the Hebrew and the King James, keeps the danger impersonal, an abstract calamity rather than an agent. The noonday demon, following the Vulgate's personification, casts the same danger as an actual malevolent spiritual being, the reading behind the phrase's continuing life in the idiom noonday demon for creeping spiritual despair.

Psalm|93.title: Psalm 93:1
Psalm|93.summary: The LORD reigneth. Malakh could mean has become king, marking a specific moment, or reigns, describing an ongoing state.
Psalm|93.plain: English reigns describes an ongoing condition, no particular starting point implied. English has become king marks a specific event, a coronation. The single Hebrew verb malakh, in this unusual position after its subject, has been read both ways by serious scholars, and the choice changes whether this psalm is commemorating an event or simply declaring a permanent truth.
Psalm|93.whyThis: Because the LORD reigneth translates a verb form that could mean God has just now become king, a specific coronation moment, or has always reigned, an ongoing state, and which reading is correct shapes whether this and the surrounding enthronement psalms describe a fresh event or a timeless truth.
Psalm|93.others: Most versions read the LORD reigneth or the LORD is king, favoring the ongoing-state sense, though many scholarly treatments of this and the other enthronement psalms, 47, 96-99, favor has become king, treating them as ritually commemorating a specific moment of divine coronation.
Psalm|93.seeing: Malakh, in the unusual construction of a finite verb following its subject YHWH, fronting the subject ahead of the verb rather than Hebrew's more expected verb-first word order, has been read by many scholars as ingressive, marking entry into a new state, the LORD has just become king, fitting a proposed annual enthronement festival reenacting God's kingship. Others read it as simply durative, the LORD reigns, an ongoing, already-established truth restated rather than newly announced.
Psalm|93.why: A specific verb tense and aspect, has become or reigns, is a choice English is forced to make, committing the translation to one reading of an event that Hebrew's own grammar leaves genuinely more open. It's a real interpretive decision every English translation makes without flagging it as one.
Psalm|93.rule: When a psalm's central verb sits in an unusual grammatical position, check whether that position is a recognized marker of ingressive aspect, entering a new state, rather than assuming an ordinary durative sense by default. Word order in Hebrew poetry can carry real grammatical weight.
Psalm|93.choosing: The LORD reigns, the durative reading, fits a straightforward declaration of God's permanent kingship. The LORD has become king, the ingressive reading, fits a proposed liturgical reenactment of a specific coronation moment, tying this psalm to a cluster of similar enthronement psalms that may have functioned together in a now-lost festival setting.

Psalm|95.title: Psalm 95:8
Psalm|95.summary: As at Meribah, and as in the day of Massah. Both place names and, simultaneously, the ordinary words for strife and testing.
Psalm|95.plain: Imagine a warning that says **don't act like you did at Grudge City**, where Grudge City is both a real, mappable town and, transparently, a description of what happened there. Meribah, strife, and Massah, testing, work exactly that way, and English place names like Meribah carry none of that built-in description.
Psalm|95.whyThis: Because Meribah and Massah are both real place names and, at the same time, ordinary Hebrew words meaning strife and testing, so the warning harden not your heart as at Meribah is simultaneously a historical reference and a description, a double function English proper nouns cannot perform.
Psalm|95.others: Every version reads Meribah and Massah as bare transliterated place names, correctly identifying the location from Exodus 17, but without conveying that both names are, simultaneously, the ordinary Hebrew words for the very behavior being condemned.
Psalm|95.seeing: Meribah, from the root riv, to strive or contend, and Massah, from nasah, to test, both name the specific location at Exodus 17:7 where Israel quarreled with Moses and tested the LORD over water, and both function as plain common nouns describing exactly that behavior. The Septuagint and Targum translations sometimes render them as common nouns, strife and testing, rather than transliterated place names, making the double function explicit in a way the Hebrew leaves the reader to notice on their own.
Psalm|95.why: English Meribah and Massah are bare geographic labels with no built-in meaning, so the warning's rhetorical force, do not repeat the very thing this place is named for, is completely inaccessible unless a reader is told what the two names actually mean.
Psalm|95.rule: When a warning or exhortation invokes a place name from Israel's history, check whether the name itself is also a common noun describing the event that happened there. Hebrew place names frequently double as built-in commentary the way Meribah and Massah do here.
Psalm|95.choosing: Meribah and Massah, transliterated as bare place names, is the standard and necessary translation, since English has no way to render a word as both proper noun and common noun simultaneously. What matters is recovering the double meaning that the bare transliteration necessarily discards.

Psalm|100.title: Psalm 100:3
Psalm|100.summary: It is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves. Or: and his we are. One preserved letter apart, and Jewish scribal tradition marks both readings.
Psalm|100.plain: Imagine a manuscript where the copied text says one thing, but a note in the margin says the correct reading is something else, and later editions have to choose which one to print as the main text. That is exactly the situation here: the Masoretes wrote lo, not, but flagged in the margin that lo, to him, might be intended instead.
Psalm|100.whyThis: Because the Hebrew text as written says and not we ourselves, while an ancient scribal marginal note flags a different reading, and his we are, a single-letter difference the Masoretes themselves preserved as an open question rather than silently correcting.
Psalm|100.kjv: Know ye that the LORD he is God: it is he that hath made us, and not we ourselves; we are his people, and the sheep of his pasture.
Psalm|100.kjvWhy: and not we ourselves is the reading the King James took from the written consonants, against the scribal note suggesting a different reading
Psalm|100.others: Some modern versions follow the marginal note, reading and his we are, others follow the written text, and not we ourselves; the Septuagint and the King James both follow the written text, while the Aramaic Targum and Jerome's separate translation follow the marginal reading.
Psalm|100.seeing: The written consonantal text, the ketiv, reads lo with an alef, not, giving he made us, and not we ourselves. A Masoretic marginal note, the qere, suggests lo with a vav instead, to him, giving and his we are, we belong to him. The two readings differ by a single consonant and produce genuinely different theological emphases, human dependence on God for existence itself, or human belonging to God as covenant possession.
Psalm|100.why: English translations must print one reading or the other as the main text, so a reader of any single version cannot tell that the Hebrew textual tradition itself preserves both options side by side, neither one silently erased in favor of the other.
Psalm|100.rule: When a Masoretic marginal note, qere, differs from the written consonantal text, ketiv, do not assume the marginal note simply corrects an error. Both readings were deliberately preserved together, and translators genuinely disagree on which to follow as the primary text.
Psalm|100.choosing: And not we ourselves, following the written consonants and the Septuagint, emphasizes total dependence on God as creator. And his we are, following the marginal note and the Targum, emphasizes covenant belonging. The Masoretic tradition itself declines to resolve which was originally intended, preserving both.
Psalm|100.w: velo anachnu (ketiv, not) / velo anachnu (qere, to him) / (le + 3ms suffix, no independent Strong's number)

Psalm|103.title: Psalm 103:12
Psalm|103.summary: As far as the east is from the west. A deliberately chosen pair of directions with no meeting point, unlike north and south.
Psalm|103.plain: Travel far enough north and you reach a point where north stops meaning anything, the pole; the same happens going south. Travel east, though, and you are still traveling east forever; there is no eastern pole where the direction runs out. The psalm's choice of east and west, not north and south, pictures a separation with literally no endpoint.
