Psalm|103.whyThis: Because the psalm specifically picks east and west rather than north and south to describe how far God removes our sins, and that choice is not arbitrary: north and south have fixed endpoints, the poles, where the directions meet, while east and west never converge anywhere on earth.
Psalm|103.others: Every version reads east and west, accurately translating the specific pair of directions the Hebrew names, though without necessarily prompting a reader to notice why this particular pair, rather than north and south, was chosen.
Psalm|103.seeing: Mizrach, east, and ma'arav, west, name directions that never converge anywhere on the earth's surface, unlike north and south, which meet at the poles. The poetic choice is precise: describing the removal of sin as far as the east is from the west pictures a genuinely infinite, ever-increasing distance, not simply a very large but ultimately bounded one, the way north and south, converging at fixed points, would have implied.
Psalm|103.why: English readers hear east and west as simply one reasonable pair of opposite directions among several, north and south being equally obvious alternatives, with no built-in signal that the poet specifically avoided the pair that has actual meeting points on a globe.
Psalm|103.rule: When Hebrew poetry chooses one pair of opposites over an equally available alternative, ask whether the specific pair chosen carries a meaning the alternative would not. Here, the choice of east/west over north/south is doing real conceptual work: describing infinite rather than merely large distance.
Psalm|103.choosing: East and west as the rendering is not in dispute. What is worth making explicit is the deliberate reasoning behind the choice, a pairing of directions with no geometric meeting point, that most readers absorb as simply poetic without registering as a precise, considered image.

Psalm|104.title: Psalm 104:4
Psalm|104.summary: Who maketh his angels spirits. Ruach, the same word for wind, breath, and spirit, used twice in one sentence about natural forces.
Psalm|104.plain: English angels and English winds name completely different kinds of things, spiritual beings versus weather. The Hebrew word ruach spans both, and this verse's other use of ruach in the same breath, describing actual wind, tilts the more natural reading toward God making the winds themselves his messengers, not creating angelic beings out of wind.
Psalm|104.whyThis: Because who maketh his angels spirits uses ruach, the same word meaning wind, breath, or spirit already met throughout Genesis, and in this verse's own immediate context the word more naturally means wind, making natural forces God's servants, a different claim than making heavenly beings out of wind.
Psalm|104.others: Every version reads angels spirits, following the Septuagint's angelous, angels, and pneumata, spirits or winds, the reading Hebrews 1:7 explicitly builds on. Some modern versions instead read he makes the winds his messengers, treating the verse as being about natural forces, not angelic beings.
Psalm|104.seeing: Ruach occurs twice in this two-verse Hebrew sentence, and the first occurrence, describing God walking on the wings of the ruach, clearly means wind, making it more natural to read the second occurrence the same way rather than switching senses mid-sentence, giving he makes the winds his messengers, natural forces personified as servants, a common ancient Near Eastern image for divine sovereignty over nature. The Septuagint instead reads both occurrences as angels and spirits, the reading Hebrews 1:7 explicitly quotes to argue that angels are servants subordinate to the Son.
Psalm|104.why: English must choose either angels/spirits, following the Septuagint's interpretive translation, or winds/messengers, following the more natural Hebrew reading in context, and Hebrews 1:7's well-known quotation locks many readers into the angelic sense without their ever seeing the more natural, nature-focused alternative reading.
Psalm|104.rule: When ruach appears twice in close proximity, check whether both occurrences plausibly share the same sense, wind, breath, or spirit, before assuming a shift in meaning mid-passage. The most natural reading often keeps the sense consistent within one sentence.
Psalm|104.choosing: Angels spirits, following the Septuagint and Hebrews 1:7, reads the verse as being about heavenly beings and grounds an argument about angelic subordination to Christ. Winds his messengers, following the more natural sense of ruach's first occurrence in the same sentence, reads the verse as praising God's sovereignty over natural forces, a psalm about creation rather than angelology.

Psalm|105.title: Psalm 105:18
Psalm|105.summary: The iron entered into his soul. The Hebrew more literally reads his soul came into iron, a difficult phrase ancient translators handled differently.
Psalm|105.plain: English the iron entered into his soul is now a familiar idiom for deep inner anguish, but it is also a slightly unusual translation choice: the Hebrew word order more literally has his soul entering iron, not the other way around, a small but real difference ancient translators noticed and handled in at least three different ways.
Psalm|105.whyThis: Because the Hebrew literally reads his soul came into iron, an unusual, difficult phrase ancient translators rendered in several different directions before it settled into the now-famous English idiom the iron entered into his soul, a phrase whose familiar English meaning may go beyond what the difficult Hebrew actually specifies.
Psalm|105.others: Most versions read some form of describing Joseph's affliction in prison, his feet hurt with fetters, his neck or person constrained by iron, with varying degrees of literalness about the famous his soul entered iron phrase.
Psalm|105.seeing: The Hebrew reads nephesh, soul, life, or person, as entering into iron, backward from the more intuitive image of iron entering a person. The Syriac keeps this direction, his soul went into iron; the Aramaic Targum reverses it, the chain of iron went into his soul; the widely beloved English phrase, the iron entered into his soul, popularized through the Book of Common Prayer, follows the Targum's reversed direction rather than the more literal Hebrew word order.
Psalm|105.why: English readers who know the phrase the iron entered into his soul as a beautiful, familiar idiom for suffering may not realize the phrase's exact grammatical direction was already being debated and reversed by ancient translators, since the literal Hebrew has the person entering the iron, not the iron entering the person.
Psalm|105.rule: When a beloved, idiomatic English Bible phrase sounds too poetically perfect to be a plain translation, check its actual grammatical direction against the Hebrew. Some of the most famous English biblical phrases, like this one, already represent an ancient interpretive choice rather than a purely literal rendering.
Psalm|105.choosing: His soul entered into iron, closer to the literal Hebrew word order, pictures Joseph's whole self being absorbed into confinement. The iron entered into his soul, the beloved reversed idiom following the Targum, pictures suffering piercing inward instead, the version that became proverbial in English despite reversing the Hebrew's own direction.
Psalm|105.w: barzel ba'ah naphsho (his soul came into iron)

Psalm|110.title: Psalm 110:1
Psalm|110.summary: The LORD said unto my Lord. Two different Hebrew words, and English uses one.
Psalm|110.plain: Imagine a sentence where two people are both called **sir**, and your only clue to which is which is how the printer set the type. That is what an English Bible is doing here, and almost nobody has been told the convention.
Psalm|110.whyThis: Because it is the Old Testament verse the New Testament quotes more than any other, the whole argument turns on two words that English prints identically, and the King James actually shows you the difference if you know to look at the capitals.
Psalm|110.kjv: The LORD said unto my Lord, Sit thou at my right hand, until I make thine enemies thy footstool.
Psalm|110.kjvWhy: the small capitals and the lower case are doing the work that two Hebrew words do
Psalm|110.others: Every version distinguishes them by capitalisation: LORD in small capitals for the first, Lord for the second. No version uses two different words, and the convention is explained in a preface most readers skip.
Psalm|110.seeing: The first word is the divine name, printed LORD in small capitals wherever it occurs. The second is adoni, my lord, an ordinary term used of human superiors. So the line is the divine name speaking to someone the psalmist calls my lord. Jesus builds an argument on exactly this at Matthew 22:41-46, and it only works if the two are different.
Psalm|110.why: English has one word for both and has solved it with typography rather than vocabulary. That works in print and fails completely when read aloud, which is how most people meet the verse.
Psalm|110.rule: Small capitals in an English Old Testament are not emphasis. They mark the divine name. Once you know that, a large number of verses become visible that were not before.
Psalm|110.choosing: Nothing is disputed in translation. The convention is universal and the failure is that it is never taught, so a verse the New Testament quotes constantly reads as a repetition in English.

Psalm|116.title: Psalm 116:15
Psalm|116.summary: Precious in the sight of the LORD is the death of his saints. Or: grievous, costly, in the LORD's sight.
Psalm|116.plain: English precious and English grievous describe nearly opposite reactions, treasuring something versus being pained by it. Yaqar's ordinary Hebrew sense leans toward precious or valuable, but a minority reading, built on the word's sense in the closely related language Aramaic, argues for grievous instead, a real difference in what the verse claims God feels about a believer's death.
Psalm|116.whyThis: Because yaqar usually means precious or valuable, but a minority scholarly reading, defended etymologically through Aramaic, argues it means grievous or costly here instead, producing a nearly opposite theological claim about how God regards the death of the faithful.
Psalm|116.others: Every major version reads precious, following yaqar's dominant Hebrew sense. A minority of scholars, most notably John Emerton, argue for grievous or costly, based on the word's attested Aramaic and later Rabbinic Hebrew sense.
Psalm|116.seeing: Yaqar's ordinary Hebrew range covers precious, valuable, weighty, or honored, and this is how the word functions in its other eight occurrences across the Psalms. The grievous reading depends on importing a sense well-attested in Aramaic and Rabbinic Hebrew but, by Emerton's own admission, not clearly attested in Hebrew itself at this early period, making the grievous reading linguistically possible but resting on evidence from a related, later-developing language rather than from Hebrew usage contemporary with the psalm.
Psalm|116.why: English precious and grievous land in almost opposite emotional registers, and a reader meeting only the traditional precious rendering would never guess that a real, if minority, scholarly case exists for reading the verse as saying God finds the death of His faithful costly or painful rather than something to be treasured.
Psalm|116.rule: When a minority reading depends on evidence from a related language rather than the text's own contemporary vocabulary, weigh it seriously but note the evidentiary gap. Grievous for yaqar is a real proposal, but it leans on Aramaic usage not securely attested in Hebrew at this period.
Psalm|116.choosing: Precious, the traditional and dominant reading, treats the verse as comfort: God treasures the death of His faithful ones rather than treating it lightly. Grievous, the minority reading, treats the verse as lament: death, even of the faithful, costs God something, a reading some find pastorally and theologically more satisfying but resting on thinner direct Hebrew evidence.

Psalm|118.title: Psalm 118:22
Psalm|118.summary: The head stone of the corner. Either the foundation stone set first, or the capstone set last at the very top.
Psalm|118.plain: English cornerstone today usually suggests a foundation, the first stone laid, everything built outward from it. But rosh, head, can just as naturally suggest the topmost position, a capstone or keystone placed last to complete an arch or wall. The Hebrew phrase does not clearly specify which end of the building process is meant.
Psalm|118.whyThis: Because head of the corner could mean either the foundational cornerstone set first, the base everything else rests on, or the capstone or keystone set last at the very top, two structurally opposite positions in a building that carry very different implications for what kind of rejection-then-honor this verse is describing.
Psalm|118.others: Most versions read cornerstone, assuming the foundational sense. Some scholars argue for capstone or keystone instead, the crowning stone rather than the base, and note that the Greek phrase quoted in the New Testament, kephale gonias, head of the corner, preserves the same ambiguity rather than resolving it.
Psalm|118.seeing: Rosh pinnah, head of the corner, could describe either the first stone set at a building's foundation, establishing the entire structure's alignment, or the final stone set at the top of an arch or wall, completing rather than beginning the construction. Both are attested architectural uses of similar terminology, and scholars including R.T. France and Ulrich Luz have argued that Matthew's own quotation of this verse deliberately keeps both images alive rather than committing to one.
Psalm|118.why: English cornerstone has settled almost entirely into the foundational sense in modern usage, a building's first and most important stone; readers rarely consider that the Hebrew, and the Greek that quotes it in the New Testament, may instead or additionally be picturing a capstone crowning a structure already built, a different and arguably more dramatic image of exaltation after rejection.
Psalm|118.rule: When an architectural metaphor is quoted repeatedly across Scripture, check whether the underlying term specifies which part of the building process is meant before assuming the modern default sense. Ancient building vocabulary did not always map onto modern architectural categories the way translation can imply.
Psalm|118.choosing: Cornerstone, the foundational reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the very basis the whole structure depends on from the ground up. Capstone or keystone, the completion reading, pictures the rejected stone becoming the final, crowning piece that finishes and holds together a structure already otherwise built, arguably a more dramatic reversal from rejection to climactic honor.

Psalm|118.title: Psalm 118:25
Psalm|118.summary: Save now, I beseech thee, O LORD. Hoshia na, the Hebrew behind Hosanna, is a plea for rescue, not originally a shout of praise.
Psalm|118.plain: English Hosanna today functions almost entirely as an exclamation of praise, sung joyfully with no sense of urgency or need. Its Hebrew source, hoshia na, save now, please, is a direct, urgent request, closer to help! or save us, please! than to hooray, a request that only gradually softened into a celebratory shout over the centuries.
Psalm|118.whyThis: Because Hosanna is not originally a shout of praise at all; it transliterates the Hebrew hoshia na, save now, please save, a direct, urgent request for rescue that only later drifted, well after the New Testament era, into a general exclamation of celebration and praise.
Psalm|118.others: Every version of Psalm 118:25 reads save now or save, I pray, correctly preserving the plea. The transliterated Hosanna, carried untranslated into the Gospels at Jesus's triumphal entry, has since taken on an almost entirely different function as an exclamation of praise rather than a request.
Psalm|118.seeing: Hoshia na combines the imperative save with na, a particle of entreaty, please, we beg you, forming a direct, urgent petition for rescue in its original psalm context, thanking God for past deliverance while pleading for continued help. By the time the crowds shout Hosanna at Jesus's entry into Jerusalem, the word may already be functioning more as an acclamation than a literal plea, and it has continued drifting toward pure celebratory praise in most religious usage ever since.
Psalm|118.why: English speakers using or hearing Hosanna today, especially in Christian worship, generally experience it as a shout of triumphant praise with no sense of urgent request, the opposite of hoshia na's original, plain meaning as a plea for God to save, now, please.
Psalm|118.rule: When a Hebrew or Aramaic word survives in English purely as a transliterated exclamation, check its original grammatical function, imperative, plea, statement, before assuming its current devotional use matches what the word was actually doing in its source context.
Psalm|118.choosing: Hosanna as a shout of praise reflects how the word has functioned in worship for most of Christian history. Save now, please save, recovering the word's original urgent, petitionary sense, changes the emotional register of the triumphal entry scene considerably: a crowd crying out for rescue, not simply cheering.

Psalm|121.title: Psalm 121:1
Psalm|121.summary: I will lift up mine eyes unto the hills, from whence cometh my help. Or: unto the hills, where does my help come from?
Psalm|121.plain: English needs a question mark to signal a question; Hebrew, written originally without any punctuation at all, relies on word order and interrogative particles that can be genuinely ambiguous. Read one way, the hills themselves are the source of help; read the other way, the hills are only where the question is asked, and the real answer follows in the next verse: the LORD.
Psalm|121.whyThis: Because ancient Hebrew had no punctuation, the opening line could be read either as a statement, my help comes from the hills, or as a question, from where does my help come, and the two readings produce nearly opposite theological claims about where help actually originates.
Psalm|121.others: Older versions read the line as a statement, help comes from the hills, treating the hills favorably. Most modern versions instead punctuate it as a question, where does my help come from, deliberately setting up verse 2's answer, my help cometh from the LORD, as a correction or clarification.
Psalm|121.seeing: Me'ayin, from where, functions grammatically as an interrogative in Hebrew, supporting the question reading, though older translation tradition read the sentence as a simple declarative statement instead. Read as a question, the psalm sets up a deliberate contrast: looking toward the hills, which in the ancient Near East were often associated with pagan high places and local shrines, only to answer that true help comes not from the hills themselves but from the LORD who made them.
Psalm|121.why: English readers of the older, statement-based translation hear the hills themselves credited as a source of help; readers of the modern question-based translation instead hear the psalm posing a question it deliberately answers in the very next line, a considerably different rhetorical structure with real theological stakes about where help actually originates.
Psalm|121.rule: When Hebrew poetry lacks the punctuation cues English relies on, check whether an interrogative particle like me'ayin is present and whether reading the line as a question versus a statement changes the passage's theological logic. The difference is not merely stylistic.
Psalm|121.choosing: Reading the opening line as a statement credits the hills themselves as a source of help, an older but now less favored translation tradition. Reading it as a question, now the dominant modern approach, sets up a pointed contrast with verse 2's answer, redirecting help away from the hills and toward the LORD who made them.
Psalm|121.w: me'ayin yavo ezri (from where does my help come)

Psalm|127.title: Psalm 127:2
Psalm|127.summary: So he giveth his beloved sleep. Or: he gives to his beloved even in their sleep, provision without anxious toil.
Psalm|127.plain: English he gives his beloved sleep sounds like a straightforward gift, rest itself as the present. A different, equally defensible reading treats sleep as describing when the gift happens rather than what the gift is: God provides everything his beloved need even while, effortlessly, they are asleep, a claim about provision without striving rather than a claim about the gift of rest specifically.
Psalm|127.whyThis: Because the famous phrase he giveth his beloved sleep is, by the commentators' own admission, genuinely obscure in Hebrew, and could just as plausibly mean God provides for his beloved even while they sleep, a considerably different claim about effortless provision versus the simple gift of rest itself.
Psalm|127.others: The King James and many traditional versions read he giveth his beloved sleep, treating rest as the gift itself. Other versions and commentators read he provides for his beloved even in their sleep, or a similar phrase, treating sleep as the circumstance during which provision happens rather than the provision itself.
Psalm|127.seeing: The Hebrew construction genuinely supports both readings, and the ambiguity is old enough that the Septuagint and Latin Vulgate already handle it with some interpretive looseness rather than settling it definitively. The verse's larger point, contrasted with rising early and staying up late in anxious toil, works either way: whether the gift is sleep itself or effortless provision that continues even during sleep, both readings emphasize God's care operating apart from human striving.
Psalm|127.why: English he giveth his beloved sleep commits to one specific gift, rest; the alternative reading commits instead to a broader claim about provision happening automatically, without effort, even during sleep, a difference in emphasis between what is given and how effortlessly it arrives.
Psalm|127.rule: When a beloved, quotable English phrase turns out to rest on a genuinely ambiguous Hebrew construction, hold the familiar wording a little more loosely. Sometimes the memorable translation has settled one of two equally live readings simply by being first, or by being more quotable.
Psalm|127.choosing: He giveth his beloved sleep is the more famous, more quotable English rendering, treating rest as the specific gift described. He provides for his beloved even while they sleep broadens the claim to effortless provision generally, a reading some scholars find better fits the psalm's contrast with anxious toil in the surrounding verses.

Psalm|139.title: Psalm 139:16
Psalm|139.summary: Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect. Golmi, an unformed, still-shapeless mass, the word later Judaism borrowed to name the golem.
Psalm|139.plain: English substance is a broad, generic word for material or stuff. The Hebrew golmi is far more specific and vivid: something rolled up, folded, or wadded together, still without shape, like an embryo or a formless lump of clay, an image later Jewish folklore turned into a proper name, the golem, an artificial being shaped from clay before receiving breath or speech.
Psalm|139.whyThis: Because golmi, translated my substance, yet being unperfect, is a rare Hebrew word for a rolled-up, still-shapeless mass, the very word later Jewish tradition borrowed wholesale to name the golem, an animated figure made of unformed clay, a link English substance entirely hides.
Psalm|139.kjv: Thine eyes did see my substance, yet being unperfect; and in thy book all my members were written, which in continuance were fashioned, when as yet there was none of them.
Psalm|139.kjvWhy: unperfect is the King James's attempt at a rare Hebrew word for an unformed, still-shapeless mass, the same word later Jewish folklore borrowed to name an animated being made of shapeless clay
Psalm|139.others: The King James reads my substance, yet being unperfect, while modern versions typically read my unformed substance or my unformed body, both attempts at the same rare, vivid word for shapeless, still-forming matter.
Psalm|139.seeing: Golem, from the root galam, to wrap or fold up, is a hapax legomenon with no other biblical occurrence, making its precise sense harder to fix from context alone, though cognate evidence and later usage both point toward an unformed, rolled-together mass, fitting the verse's larger picture of God observing and recording a body before it has taken shape in the womb. Later Rabbinic and medieval Jewish tradition took this same rare word and used it to name an artificially animated being formed from clay, the golem of folklore, borrowing directly from this psalm's picture of unformed material awaiting its final shape.
Psalm|139.why: English substance gives no hint that the underlying Hebrew word is rare enough to appear only this once in the entire Bible, or that it is the very word later Jewish folklore would adopt to name an animated clay figure, a etymological thread entirely invisible in translation.
Psalm|139.rule: A Hebrew word that occurs only once in the entire Bible has no other biblical context to check it against, so its precise sense often has to be reconstructed from its root and from how later tradition used the same word.
Psalm|139.choosing: My substance, yet being unperfect, and my unformed substance both attempt to render a word with no other biblical occurrence to compare it against. What is worth surfacing is the word's vivid, concrete root sense, a rolled-up, shapeless mass, and its unexpected afterlife as the name for the golem of later Jewish legend.

Psalm|141.title: Psalm 141:5
Psalm|141.summary: Let the righteous smite me; it shall be a kindness... for yet my prayer also shall be in their calamities. A notoriously difficult Hebrew text; ancient and modern versions diverge sharply.
Psalm|141.plain: Most difficult verses in the Bible are difficult because a word is rare or a construction is ambiguous. This verse is difficult on a larger scale: the Hebrew sentence structure itself seems disrupted, producing a cluster of renderings, about oil, about the wicked, about prayer amid calamity, that do not simply vary in nuance but sometimes struggle to agree on the verse's basic subject.
Psalm|141.whyThis: Because the Hebrew of let the righteous smite me... but let not my head be void of it is widely regarded by scholars as among the most textually difficult passages in the entire Psalter, with ancient versions and modern translations diverging so sharply that some renderings barely resemble one another.
Psalm|141.others: The King James reads let not my head refuse the oil of the righteous's rebuke as a kindness, continuing with a difficult clause about prayer during the wicked's calamities. Other versions rearrange the clauses substantially, and some modern scholarly translations mark the Hebrew here as simply uncertain rather than offering a confident rendering.
Psalm|141.seeing: Hebrew scholars and commentators, including the editors of the Biblia Hebraica Stuttgartensia's critical apparatus, flag this verse's text as corrupt or seriously disturbed, likely the result of a scribal error at some point in the transmission process that later copyists could not fully repair. The Septuagint's Greek rendering diverges enough from the Masoretic Hebrew to confirm that the difficulty is ancient, not a modern translation problem, and it does not by itself resolve what the original Hebrew said.
Psalm|141.why: English readers meeting any single confident-sounding translation of this verse would never guess that the underlying Hebrew is treated by specialists as one of the more textually uncertain verses in the Psalms, closer to an educated reconstruction than to a settled rendering.
Psalm|141.rule: When a verse's ancient versions diverge unusually sharply from one another and from the Masoretic Hebrew, and a critical apparatus flags the text itself as uncertain, treat any single confident English rendering with real caution. Not every translation difficulty is resolvable by better Hebrew knowledge alone; sometimes the transmitted text itself is the problem.
Psalm|141.choosing: No single rendering can claim confident priority here; the King James, and the many modern versions that diverge from it and from each other, are all working with a Hebrew text that specialists themselves regard as disturbed. The point here is to flag the difficulty rather than to adjudicate between renderings that the evidence does not clearly decide.
Psalm|141.w: rosh'i (my head), verse marked as textually uncertain in the critical apparatus

Psalm|145.title: Psalm 145:13
Psalm|145.summary: The LORD is faithful in all his words, and holy in all his works. Missing between this and the previous verse: an entire nun line, preserved outside the Masoretic Text.
Psalm|145.plain: An acrostic poem uses each letter of the alphabet in order to begin a new line, aleph, bet, gimel, and so on. Psalm 145 does this for twenty-one of Hebrew's twenty-two letters, but the line that should begin with nun, the fourteenth letter, is simply absent from the standard Hebrew text used for most translations, an acrostic with a missing rung.
Psalm|145.whyThis: Because Psalm 145 is an acrostic with one line per letter of the Hebrew alphabet, but the Masoretic Text is missing an entire line for the letter nun, a gap that the Dead Sea Scrolls, the Septuagint, and the Syriac all independently fill with a preserved verse the Hebrew tradition somehow lost.
Psalm|145.others: Older versions, including the King James, translate straight through the Masoretic Text's gap without any indication a line is missing, since the manuscripts underlying them did not preserve the nun line. Many modern versions now include a bracketed or footnoted nun line, following its recovery from a Dead Sea Scroll and its independent presence in the Septuagint and Syriac, typically rendered along the lines of the LORD is faithful in all his words, and gracious in all his deeds.
Psalm|145.seeing: A Psalms scroll from Qumran Cave 11 preserves the missing nun line, and the Septuagint and Syriac translations, working from Hebrew manuscripts earlier or different from the later Masoretic tradition, both independently attest to a nun verse in roughly the same position, strong evidence the line was genuinely part of the psalm's original acrostic structure and dropped out of the specific manuscript line the Masoretic Text descends from, likely through a simple scribal skip between two similar-looking lines.
Psalm|145.why: English readers of translations based solely on the Masoretic Text encounter what looks like a complete acrostic psalm, with no hint that one letter's line is missing, and that other ancient witnesses, independently of each other, preserve the very line the Hebrew tradition lost.
Psalm|145.rule: When a Hebrew acrostic poem is missing a letter's line in the Masoretic Text, check the Dead Sea Scrolls and other ancient versions before assuming the poem was always incomplete. An acrostic's own structure can help detect and even help recover a loss that occurred somewhere in the copying process.
Psalm|145.choosing: Reading straight through the gap, as the King James and older versions do, preserves the Masoretic Text exactly as received but obscures that a line is missing at all. Including the recovered nun line, as many modern versions now do, restores the psalm's full twenty-two-letter acrostic structure using evidence outside the Masoretic tradition.
Psalm|145.w: (nun), the fourteenth Hebrew letter, its acrostic line absent from the Masoretic Text

Psalm|150.title: Psalm 150:4
Psalm|150.summary: Praise him with stringed instruments and organs. Ugav, an ancient reed or wind instrument, not the keyboard instrument organ now names.
Psalm|150.plain: When the King James translators wrote organ, English organ could still refer more loosely to a wind instrument generally; it had not yet narrowed almost entirely to the large keyboard-and-pipes instrument found in churches and concert halls today. Ugav, the Hebrew word being translated, is some kind of ancient reed pipe or simple wind instrument, sharing essentially nothing with a modern pipe organ beyond both moving air to make sound.
Psalm|150.whyThis: Because organs, in the King James's praise him with stringed instruments and organs, translates ugav, an ancient reed or wind instrument with no keyboard, no pipes in the modern sense, and no resemblance to the large keyboard instrument organ names today, a case of the English word's own meaning drifting far past the Hebrew it once fairly translated.
Psalm|150.others: The King James reads organs, a translation that was defensible in its own era's broader sense of the English word. Modern versions typically read pipe, pipes, or flute, moving away from organ precisely because the English word has since drifted toward a specific large keyboard instrument the Hebrew ugav could never have meant.
Psalm|150.seeing: Ugav appears only a handful of times in the Hebrew Bible, always paired with kinnor, harp or lyre, as a summary pair for stringed and wind instruments generally, and comparative and etymological evidence points to some kind of simple reed pipe or flute rather than any complex mechanism. The English word organ has undergone its own centuries-long semantic narrowing, from a general term for a tool or instrument, still visible in phrases like organ of speech, toward its now-dominant sense, a large keyboard wind instrument, leaving the King James's organs increasingly misleading to modern ears even though it was a reasonable translation choice in the 1600s.
Psalm|150.why: English organ today calls to mind a specific large keyboard instrument with pipes, an image with no connection to ugav's simple reed-pipe or flute-like character, so a modern reader hears something closer to a cathedral organ than to the humble wind instrument the Hebrew actually names.
Psalm|150.rule: When an old English translation's word has since narrowed or shifted in its everyday meaning, check whether the translation was accurate for its own time even though it now misleads. Organ for ugav is a textbook case of translation drift caused entirely by the target language changing, not by any error in the original choice.
Psalm|150.choosing: Organs, the King James's reading, reflects a now-outdated broader sense of the English word and was a fair choice in its own time. Pipe, pipes, or flute, the modern rendering, better conveys ugav's simple reed-instrument character to a reader for whom organ now means something else entirely.
